parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each part: (i) cornea (ii) retina (iii) optic nerve.
parts.answer: (i) refracts / bends light (ii) contains light receptors that change light into impulses (iii) carries impulses to the brain

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why no image is seen if light falls on the blind spot.
parts.answer: There are no light receptors there (it is where the optic nerve leaves the eye).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which part of the eye controls how much light enters it?
A cornea
B iris
C lens
D retina
parts.answer: B iris
parts.working: The iris contains circular and radial muscles that change the size of the pupil, so it controls the light entering. The lens (C) focuses light but does not control the amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these structures in the order in which light passes through or reaches them: lens, retina, cornea, pupil.
parts.answer: cornea → pupil → lens → retina

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the eye an image is formed.
parts.answer: on the retina

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the structure that carries impulses from the eye to the brain.
parts.answer: optic nerve

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the part of the eye that matches each description:
(i) the transparent front layer that refracts light
(ii) the hole through which light enters the inner eye
(iii) the structure that changes shape to focus light
(iv) the fibres that attach the lens to the ciliary muscle
(v) the area of the retina where there are no light-sensitive cells
parts.answer: (i) cornea (ii) pupil (iii) lens (iv) suspensory ligaments (v) blind spot

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student looks up from her book to watch a bird far away. What happens in her eyes?
A ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes fatter
B ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments become tight, lens becomes thinner
C ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments slacken, lens becomes thinner
D ciliary muscles contract, suspensory ligaments become tight, lens becomes fatter
parts.answer: B ciliary muscles relax, suspensory ligaments become tight, lens becomes thinner
parts.working: For a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thinner, so light is refracted less. A is the change for a near object.

practice.stem: Ali walks out of a dark cinema into bright midday sunshine in Islamabad. His pupils quickly become smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the iris that make the pupil smaller.
parts.answer: The circular muscles contract; the radial muscles relax.
parts.working: B1 circular contract; B1 radial relax

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this response is useful.
parts.answer: Less light enters, protecting the retina from damage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of response this is and give one feature of it.
parts.answer: A reflex action; it is automatic / involuntary / rapid / does not need conscious thought.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term sense organ.
parts.answer: A group of receptor cells that respond to a specific stimulus (e.g. light, sound, touch, temperature, chemicals).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete: Stimulus | sense organ
light | ?
sound | ?
chemicals in food | ?
temperature change | ?
parts.answer: eye; ear; tongue (and nose); skin
parts.working: B2 all four; B1 two or three

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the eye sends information to the brain.
parts.answer: Light receptors in the retina are stimulated and produce electrical impulses; impulses travel along the optic nerve (sensory neurones) to the brain.
parts.working: B1 receptors in retina stimulated / impulses; B1 along optic nerve

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cricket fielder in Rawalpindi watches the ball leave the bat 60 m away and then watches it until it is close enough to catch. Copy and complete the table to show the state of each structure.
structure | ball far away | ball close
ciliary muscle | ? | ?
suspensory ligaments | ? | ?
lens | ? | ?
parts.answer: far: ciliary muscle relaxed, suspensory ligaments tight (taut), lens thin/less convex; close: ciliary muscle contracted, suspensory ligaments slack, lens thick/more convex

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lens must be more convex to focus light from the ball when it is close.
parts.answer: Light rays from a near object are diverging more when they reach the eye; a fatter lens bends (refracts) them more so they still focus on the retina.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rays from near object diverge more; more refraction needed to focus on retina.

practice.stem:
A student measured the pupil diameter of a volunteer in light of different intensities.
light intensity / lux | 10 | 100 | 500 | 1000 | 5000
pupil diameter / mm | 7.0 | 5.6 | 4.2 | 3.5 | 2.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between light intensity and pupil diameter.
parts.answer: As light intensity increases, pupil diameter decreases; the decrease is fastest at low light intensities and then levels off (e.g. 7.0 mm at 10 lux to 2.8 mm at 5000 lux).
parts.working: B1 inverse relationship; B1 detail with figures or levelling off.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in pupil diameter between 10 lux and 5000 lux.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pupil becomes smaller in bright light.
parts.answer: To reduce the amount of light entering the eye; too much light would damage the light-sensitive cells of the retina.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before examining the retina, an eye doctor puts drops into a patient's eyes. The drops relax the circular muscles of the iris. State and explain the effect on the pupil.
parts.answer: The pupil dilates (widens): the circular muscles are relaxed so they cannot constrict the pupil, and the radial muscles pull it wider open.
parts.working: 1 mark dilates; 1 mark explanation linked to muscles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this makes it easier for the doctor to see the retina.
parts.answer: A wider pupil lets the doctor see more of the retina / lets more light in to see the retina.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The patient is advised to wear sunglasses and not to drive for a few hours. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The pupil cannot become smaller, so too much light enters in bright conditions; this causes glare/dazzle and could damage the retina, and vision may be unclear for driving.
parts.working: 1 mark each: pupil reflex cannot reduce light; glare / risk to retina / poor vision when driving.

practice.stem: A pharmacist looks at a distant shelf and then reads the small print on a medicine label held 25 cm from her eyes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in the eye that allow the label to be seen clearly.
parts.answer: Ciliary muscles contract; suspensory ligaments slacken / become loose; lens becomes thicker / more convex (and refracts light more).

parts.label: b
parts.text: As people age, the lens becomes less elastic. Suggest why older people often find it difficult to read small print but can still see distant objects clearly.
parts.answer: The lens cannot become fat / round enough on its own when the ligaments slacken; so light from near objects is not focused on the retina, whereas the thin lens shape for distant vision is still achieved.
parts.working: B1 lens cannot become thicker / more convex; B1 near image not focused on retina

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A person walks from a sunny street into a dim room. Which changes happen in the iris?
A circular muscles contract, radial muscles relax, pupil becomes smaller
B circular muscles relax, radial muscles contract, pupil becomes larger
C circular muscles relax, radial muscles relax, pupil becomes larger
D circular muscles contract, radial muscles contract, pupil becomes smaller
parts.answer: B circular muscles relax, radial muscles contract, pupil becomes larger
parts.working: In dim light the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax, which widens (dilates) the pupil to let in more light. A is the response to bright light; the two muscle sets are antagonistic, so they never both contract or both relax (C, D).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pupil reflex is a reflex action. Identify the receptor, the coordinator and the effector in this reflex.
parts.answer: receptor: light-sensitive cells of the retina; coordinator: brain (central nervous system); effector: muscles of the iris

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is an advantage that this response is a reflex rather than a voluntary action.
parts.answer: It is automatic and fast, so the retina is protected from sudden bright light before damage is done, without needing to think about it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rapid/automatic; protects retina from damage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: After a head injury, a doctor shines a torch into each eye of an unconscious patient. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To check that the nerve pathway through the brain is working: if the pupils do not constrict, the brain (or nerves) may be damaged.
parts.working: B1 tests whether the brain/reflex pathway is working.

practice.stem:
The near point is the closest distance at which a person can focus on an object. The table (figures for this question) shows mean near points for people of different ages.
age / years | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
near point / cm | 7 | 10 | 14 | 22 | 40 | 100

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the near point changes with age.
parts.answer: The near point increases with age; slowly at first (7 cm at 10 years to 14 cm at 30) and then much faster after 40 (100 cm at 60).
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 rate increases with age, with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times further away the near point is at 50 years than at 20 years.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain, in terms of the lens and ciliary muscle, why the near point moves further away with age.
parts.answer: The lens becomes less elastic/stiffer; when the ciliary muscle contracts and the suspensory ligaments slacken, the lens cannot become as round/convex; so light from close objects cannot be refracted enough to focus on the retina.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether people aged 40–50 years have a greater near point than people aged 15–20 years. You may use a metre rule and a card with small printed text. Include the variables you would control, how you would take readings and how you would present and use the results.
parts.answer: A clear plan: compare two age groups; hold card at arm's length and move it slowly towards one eye (other eye covered) until print blurs; measure distance from eye to card; repeat three times per person and find the mean; use at least 10 people per group; control: same card/text size, same light level, same eye, no glasses (or all with usual glasses); compare group means in a table/bar chart; conclusion if mean is larger for older group.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: independent variable two age groups; dependent near point measured with rule from eye to card; method of moving card until text blurs; one eye covered / same eye; same text size; same light intensity; glasses rule stated; repeats and mean per person; sample size ≥ 10 per group; results table/bar chart and compare means; safety/ethics (consent).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens in the skin of a person who is too hot?
A arterioles near the skin surface constrict
B sweat production decreases
C arterioles near the skin surface dilate
D skin muscles shiver
parts.answer: C arterioles near the skin surface dilate
parts.working: Vasodilation of arterioles supplying skin capillaries sends more blood near the surface, so more heat is lost by radiation. A (vasoconstriction) happens when the body is too cold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the normal core body temperature of a human (the set point).
parts.answer: About 37 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term homeostasis.
parts.answer: Maintaining a constant internal environment; within set limits.
parts.working: B1 constant internal environment / conditions; B1 within narrow limits / around a set point

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the body that monitors blood temperature.
parts.answer: The brain (hypothalamus).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure in the skin produces sweat?
A arteriole
B hair erector muscle
C fatty tissue
D sweat gland
parts.answer: D sweat gland
parts.working: Sweat glands secrete sweat onto the skin surface. Arterioles (A) change blood flow, not sweat production.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the structure in the skin or body that carries out each function:
(i) reduces heat loss by insulating the body
(ii) contracts to make a hair stand upright
(iii) contracts rapidly to make heat when a person shivers
parts.answer: (i) fatty tissue (layer of fat) (ii) hair erector muscle (iii) skeletal muscles

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table using 'increases', 'decreases', 'contract' or 'relax' and similar words.
response | when too hot | when too cold
sweat production | ? | ?
arterioles supplying skin capillaries | ? | ?
shivering | ? | ?
hair erector muscles | ? | ?
parts.answer: sweat: increases / decreases; arterioles: dilate (widen) / constrict (narrow); shivering: none / starts (muscles contract rapidly); hair erector muscles: relax (hairs lie flat) / contract (hairs stand up)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the part of the brain that detects a change in blood temperature.
parts.answer: hypothalamus

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how sweating helps to cool the body.
parts.answer: Water in sweat evaporates from the skin surface; evaporation uses heat energy from the skin, cooling it.
parts.working: B1 evaporation of sweat; B1 takes heat (energy) from the body / skin

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sweating cools the body less effectively on a hot, humid day in Lahore during the monsoon.
parts.answer: Air already has a high water vapour content, so sweat evaporates more slowly; less heat is removed.
parts.working: B1 less evaporation; B1 less heat lost

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person sweating heavily for a long time should drink water with a little salt.
parts.answer: Sweat contains water and salts, which must be replaced.

practice.stem:
A cricketer's core temperature was measured every 10 minutes during a 30-minute run and the rest afterwards.
time / min | 0 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
temperature / °C | 37.0 | 37.2 | 37.6 | 38.1 | 37.9 | 37.4 | 37.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum rise in core temperature above the starting value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two changes in the skin that would have brought the temperature back down after 30 minutes.
parts.answer: Vasodilation of arterioles near skin surface (skin looks flushed); increased sweating.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the temperature rose during running.
parts.answer: Muscles respired more to release energy for contraction; respiration releases heat (as a by-product).
parts.working: B1 more respiration in muscles; B1 releases heat

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which response happens in the skin of a person who is too cold?
A sweat production increases and arterioles dilate
B arterioles supplying the skin capillaries constrict and hair erector muscles contract
C shivering stops and hair erector muscles relax
D arterioles dilate and sweat glands release more sweat
parts.answer: B arterioles supplying the skin capillaries constrict and hair erector muscles contract
parts.working: In the cold, the arterioles constrict so less warm blood reaches the skin surface, and the hair erector muscles contract to trap a layer of air; both reduce heat loss. A and D are responses to heat. C is wrong because shivering starts in the cold, it does not stop.

practice.stem: A volunteer sat in a cold room at 8 °C for 30 minutes. Her skin temperature fell from 33.0 °C to 25.5 °C. Her core temperature fell from 37.0 °C to 36.8 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fall in skin temperature and the fall in core temperature over the 30 minutes.
parts.answer: skin: 7.5 °C; core: 0.2 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the skin temperature fell much more than the core temperature.
parts.answer: Arterioles supplying the skin capillaries constrict (vasoconstriction); less warm blood flows near the surface so the skin cools; heat is kept in the core, so core temperature stays near 37 °C / set point.
parts.working: 1 mark each: vasoconstriction; less blood to skin surface so skin cools / less heat lost; core kept near set point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: On a winter morning in Quetta, a boy's fingers look pale. Explain why.
parts.answer: Cold is detected; arterioles supplying the skin capillaries constrict (vasoconstriction); less blood flows through the skin capillaries, so the skin looks pale.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this response helps to keep his core temperature constant.
parts.answer: Less warm blood near the surface means less heat is lost by radiation to the air, so heat is conserved in the core.

practice.stem:
A student filled two identical flasks with 200 cm³ of water at 80 °C. Flask A was left uncovered; flask B was wrapped in a 2 cm layer of cotton wool.
time / min | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10
temperature A / °C | 80 | 74 | 69 | 65 | 61 | 58
temperature B / °C | 80 | 78 | 76 | 74 | 73 | 72

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the fall in temperature in each flask over 10 minutes and the mean rate of cooling of flask A in °C per minute.
parts.answer: A: 22 °C; B: 8 °C; rate for A 2.2 °C per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from these results.
parts.answer: The wrapped flask (B) lost heat more slowly, so a layer of insulation reduces heat loss.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this experiment models the role of fatty tissue in the skin.
parts.answer: The cotton wool acts like the fat layer: both are insulators that reduce heat loss from the body.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same in both flasks.
parts.answer: volume of water; starting temperature; size/type of flask; room temperature

practice.stem: A mountaineer on K2 is exposed to very cold wind and her core temperature begins to fall below the set point.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain two ways in which the climber's body responds to reduce heat loss and increase heat production.
parts.answer: Vasoconstriction: arterioles to skin capillaries narrow, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost by radiation. Shivering: rapid muscle contractions increase respiration, releasing heat. (Also: less sweating; hairs raised trap insulating air.)
parts.working: For each of two responses: B1 response, B1 explanation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these responses are an example of negative feedback.
parts.answer: A fall in temperature below the set point is detected; responses act to bring the temperature back up towards the set point (reverse the change).
parts.working: B1 change from set point detected; B1 response reverses the change / returns to set point

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaporating 1 g of sweat removes about 2.4 kJ of heat from the skin. A labourer building a road in Multan loses 1500 g of sweat in one hour, but only 60 % of it evaporates; the rest drips off. Calculate the heat removed by evaporation in that hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sweat that drips off the body does not help to cool it.
parts.answer: Cooling happens when sweat evaporates, because heat energy from the skin is used to turn the water into vapour; sweat that drips off has not evaporated, so it takes little heat from the skin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the labourer should drink more water than he normally does.
parts.answer: To replace the large volume of water lost in sweat / prevent dehydration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two cubes are used as models of a baby and an adult. Cube P has sides of 2 cm and cube Q has sides of 6 cm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube.
parts.answer: P: SA 24 cm², volume 8 cm³, ratio 3 : 1; Q: SA 216 cm², volume 216 cm³, ratio 1 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a newborn baby loses heat faster than an adult.
parts.answer: The baby has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so it has more surface for heat to be lost from per unit of body volume that produces heat.
parts.working: 1 mark each: larger SA:V; more surface for heat loss relative to heat-producing volume.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Premature babies have very little fat under their skin. Suggest why they are kept in warm incubators.
parts.answer: Little fatty tissue means poor insulation; together with their high SA:V they cannot keep their core at 37 °C, so the incubator keeps them warm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation, using two thermometers, cotton cloth and a fan, to show that evaporation of water from a surface causes cooling, as sweating does. Include how you would make the test fair, what you would measure and how you would show the result.
parts.answer: Two identical thermometers, one bulb wrapped in dry cloth, the other in cloth soaked in water at room temperature; place both in the same air flow from the fan; record temperatures every minute for 10 minutes; repeat three times; control: same cloth, same water temperature, same distance from fan, same room temperature; plot temperature against time; wet bulb should fall lower, showing evaporation cools.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: wet and dry thermometer comparison; water at room temperature; same cloth/amount; same air flow/distance from fan; starting temperature recorded; readings at regular intervals; repeats/mean; table and line graph; expected result explained; extension (e.g. with and without fan to show effect of moving air).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which neurone carries impulses from the central nervous system to an effector?
A sensory neurone
B relay neurone
C motor neurone
D receptor cell
parts.answer: C motor neurone
parts.working: Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands). Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put the parts of the reflex arc in the correct order: motor neurone, receptor, effector, relay neurone, sensory neurone.
parts.answer: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one pair out of place

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the receptor and the effector when a hand is pulled away from a hot pan.
parts.answer: Receptor: (heat / pain) receptors in the skin. Effector: muscle in the arm (biceps).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where relay neurones are found.
parts.answer: In the central nervous system / spinal cord.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structures make up the peripheral nervous system?
A the brain only
B the spinal cord only
C the brain and spinal cord
D the nerves
parts.answer: D the nerves
parts.working: The peripheral nervous system is the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. C is the central nervous system.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A dust particle flies towards Sana's eye and she blinks. For this response, state:
(i) the stimulus
(ii) the receptor
(iii) the coordinator
(iv) the effector
(v) the response
parts.answer: (i) the approaching dust / object touching or near the eye (ii) receptors in the eye/eyelid (light or touch receptors) (iii) brain / central nervous system (iv) eyelid muscles (v) the eyelid closes (blink)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features of the way the nervous system sends messages, compared with hormones.
parts.answer: electrical impulses; very fast; short-lived effect; travel along neurones to a precise target

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a neurone and a nerve.
parts.answer: A neurone is a single nerve cell; a nerve is a bundle of many neurones.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the two types of effector.
parts.answer: muscles and glands

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two parts of the central nervous system.
parts.answer: Brain and spinal cord

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two differences between a voluntary action and a reflex action.
parts.answer: Voluntary: needs conscious thought / slower / involves the brain making a decision / can be learned. Reflex: automatic, fast, does not need conscious thought, same response every time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a reflex action and explain how it helps to protect the body.
parts.answer: Blinking when something approaches the eye — prevents damage to the eye (or withdrawing hand from a sharp pin — prevents injury).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where are the synapses in a simple reflex arc that includes a relay neurone?
A in the receptor and in the effector
B in the spinal cord, between the sensory and relay neurones and between the relay and motor neurones
C in the brain only, between sensory and motor neurones
D along the axon of the sensory neurone
parts.answer: B in the spinal cord, between the sensory and relay neurones and between the relay and motor neurones
parts.working: The relay neurone lies in the spinal cord, so the junctions between sensory→relay and relay→motor neurones are there. A spinal reflex does not need the brain (C).

practice.stem:
A student tested her reaction time on a computer. She pressed a key as soon as she saw a light, and then (in another test) as soon as she heard a sound.
trial | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
light / ms | 245 | 260 | 238 | 252 | 250
sound / ms | 190 | 205 | 198 | 186 | 201

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean reaction time to each stimulus.
parts.answer: light 249 ms; sound 196 ms

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much faster the mean response to sound was than to light.
parts.answer: 53 ms

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why pressing the key is a voluntary action and not a reflex.
parts.answer: The student decides to respond / it is under conscious control; the impulse passes through the brain (cerebrum) where a decision is made, so it is slower than a reflex.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor taps just below a patient's kneecap and the lower leg kicks forwards. Describe the pathway of the impulse from the receptor to the effector.
parts.answer: Stretch receptor in the thigh muscle/tendon is stimulated; impulse passes along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord; crosses a synapse to a motor neurone (directly or via a relay neurone); motor neurone carries impulse to the thigh muscle (effector), which contracts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three in sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The patient cannot stop his leg moving even when he tries. Explain why.
parts.answer: It is a reflex: the impulse goes through the spinal cord and does not need the brain to decide; the response happens before the brain can act.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When a nurse gives an injection, a pain reflex would normally pull the arm away. Many patients keep their arm still. Explain how the brain makes this possible.
parts.answer: The brain knows the injection is coming; it sends impulses down the spinal cord to the motor neurones (by relay neurones); these impulses stop/override the reflex so the arm muscles do not contract.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of reflex actions that are not normally controlled by the brain.
parts.answer: They are very fast / automatic, so they protect the body from harm.

practice.stem: Student A holds a 30 cm ruler at its top end. Student B places finger and thumb level with the 0 cm mark without touching it. A drops the ruler without warning and B catches it. The distance fallen is read where B catches it. Five trials gave: 16 cm, 14 cm, 13 cm, 11 cm, 10 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean distance the ruler fell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the trend in the results and suggest a reason for it.
parts.answer: The distance (reaction time) decreased with each trial; the student learned / anticipated the drop (practice effect).
parts.working: B1 decreasing trend; B1 learning / practice / anticipation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why catching the ruler is not a reflex action.
parts.answer: It involves a decision by the brain / conscious thought; the response can be changed or improved by learning.
parts.working: B1 brain / conscious decision; B1 learned / not automatic

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to improve this investigation.
parts.answer: Have practice trials first / use the same hand and starting position / do more repeats and find a mean / use different students.

practice.stem: A boy walking barefoot in a field steps on a sharp acacia thorn and quickly lifts his foot.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway of the nerve impulse from the moment the foot touches the thorn to the leg moving.
parts.answer: Pain receptor in the skin of the foot stimulated; impulse along sensory neurone to spinal cord; passes across synapse to relay neurone in spinal cord; then to motor neurone; to leg muscles (effector), which contract and lift the foot.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: receptor in skin; sensory neurone; spinal cord / relay neurone; synapse(s); motor neurone; muscle contracts

parts.label: b
parts.text: The boy feels the pain slightly after his foot moves. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The reflex arc passes through the spinal cord and does not need the brain; impulses to the brain travel further / through more synapses, so awareness comes later.
parts.working: B1 reflex via spinal cord, not brain; B1 impulse to brain takes longer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Patient X has a damaged sensory neurone in one finger. Patient Y has a damaged motor neurone to the same arm muscle. Each touches a hot object with that finger. Predict, with reasons, whether each person (i) pulls the hand away and (ii) feels the heat.
parts.answer: X: does not pull hand away and does not feel the heat, because no impulse reaches the spinal cord or brain. Y: feels the heat because the sensory pathway to the brain works, but cannot pull the hand away because no impulse reaches the muscle.
parts.working: 1 mark each for X withdrawal, X feeling, Y feeling, Y withdrawal – each with a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person with damage to the spinal cord in the lower back may lose feeling and movement in the legs but not in the arms.
parts.answer: Nerves from the legs join the spinal cord below the damage; impulses cannot pass up to the brain or down to the leg muscles; nerves from the arms join above the damage, so they still work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a withdrawal reflex, the impulse travels 1.0 m along a sensory neurone and 1.0 m along a motor neurone at 80 m/s. Each of the two synapses delays the impulse by 0.5 ms. Calculate the total time from stimulus to the impulse reaching the muscle. Give your answer in ms.
parts.answer: 26 ms
parts.working: M1 2.0 ÷ 80 = 0.025 s = 25 ms along neurones; M1 synapse delay 2 × 0.5 = 1 ms; A1 26 ms.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A voluntary response to the same stimulus takes about 250 ms. Suggest why it takes so much longer.
parts.answer: The impulse must travel further, to the brain, and pass across many more synapses; time is needed for the brain to process the information and decide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation, using the ruler-drop test, to find out whether people catch a ruler faster with their dominant hand than with their other hand. Include the variables to control, how you would collect reliable results and how you would process them.
parts.answer: Partner drops a 30 cm ruler without warning, catcher's thumb and finger level with 0 cm; record distance fallen for each hand; 10 drops per hand, alternate the hand to avoid practice effect, discard practice drops; control same ruler, same starting position, same person dropping, same arm rest on table, no distractions; use 10+ people; calculate mean distance for each hand (convert to time with a conversion table if given); compare means; shorter distance = faster reaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: IV hand used; DV distance fallen/time; starting position fixed; no warning given; same dropper/ruler; forearm resting on bench; repeats and mean; order alternated/practice effect controlled; several volunteers; table and bar chart; conclusion criterion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms (i) phototropism (ii) gravitropism.
parts.answer: (i) a response in which part of a plant grows towards or away from the direction of light (ii) a response in which part of a plant grows towards or away from gravity

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether each response is positive or negative: (i) a shoot growing towards light (ii) a root growing downwards (iii) a shoot growing upwards in the dark.
parts.answer: (i) positive phototropism (ii) positive gravitropism (iii) negative gravitropism

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A root grows downwards towards the pull of gravity. What is this response called?
A negative gravitropism
B negative phototropism
C positive gravitropism
D positive phototropism
parts.answer: C positive gravitropism
parts.working: Growth towards the stimulus is positive, and the stimulus is gravity, so it is positive gravitropism. A describes a shoot growing upwards, away from gravity.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sentences using words from this list: auxin, tip, elongation, shaded, diffuses, division.
Plant shoots make a hormone called ___ in their ___. It ___ down the shoot and collects on the ___ side when light comes from one side. It stimulates cell ___, so this side grows longer.
parts.answer: auxin; tip; diffuses; shaded; elongation
parts.working: All five correct 3 marks; 3–4 correct 2 marks; 1–2 correct 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Each statement contains one mistake. Rewrite each statement correctly.
(i) A root grows downwards because it shows negative gravitropism.
(ii) A shoot bends towards light because it shows negative phototropism.
(iii) Phototropism is a response to gravity.
parts.answer: (i) A root shows positive gravitropism (it grows towards the pull of gravity). (ii) A shoot shows positive phototropism (it grows towards light). (iii) Phototropism is a response to light.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct correction (the correct type or the correct stimulus must be named).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a shoot that grows towards light helps a young plant to survive.
parts.answer: It reaches the light so its leaves can photosynthesise and make food for growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reaches the light; leaves can photosynthesise and make food.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shoot is lit from one side only. Which statement explains why it bends towards the light?
A light destroys auxin on the lit side, so the lit side grows faster
B auxin collects on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation there
C auxin collects on the lit side and stimulates cell division there
D auxin collects on the shaded side and stops cells growing there
parts.answer: B auxin collects on the shaded side and stimulates cell elongation there
parts.working: Auxin made in the shoot tip moves to the shaded side, where it causes cells to elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light. A is a common misconception: light does not destroy auxin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the advantage to a seedling of its shoot growing upwards and its root growing downwards.
parts.answer: Shoot grows up towards light for photosynthesis; root grows down into soil for water / mineral ions and anchorage.
parts.working: B1 shoot – light / photosynthesis; B1 root – water / anchorage

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bean seedling is laid on its side in the dark. Describe and explain how the shoot responds, in terms of auxin.
parts.answer: Auxin collects on the lower side of the shoot; stimulates cell elongation on the lower side; so the shoot curves upwards (negative gravitropism).
parts.working: B1 auxin to lower side; B1 more elongation on lower side; B1 shoot bends upwards

practice.stem:
Cress seedlings were lit from one side. The angle of curvature of the shoots was measured.
time / h | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8
mean angle / ° | 0 | 8 | 20 | 34 | 41

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of curvature over the 8 hours, in degrees per hour.
parts.answer: 5.125 ° per hour (accept 5.1)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the 2-hour period in which the curvature increased most.
parts.answer: 4 to 6 hours (14°)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the seedlings bent towards the light.
parts.answer: Auxin made in the tip moves to the shaded side; it stimulates cell elongation there; the shaded side grows faster/longer, so the shoot curves towards the light.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student keeps a pot plant on a windowsill in her flat in Karachi. After two weeks the stem has bent towards the window. Explain this response.
parts.answer: Light comes from one side; auxin collects on the shaded side (away from the window); cells there elongate more, so the stem bends towards the light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Her mother turns the pot half a turn every day. Suggest why the plant then grows straight.
parts.answer: Each side is shaded in turn, so auxin and cell elongation are spread evenly over time; no side grows faster overall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an experiment, auxin was collected from each side of shoot tips lit from one side. The lit side gave 27 units and the shaded side gave 63 units. Calculate the percentage of the total auxin that was on the shaded side.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this uneven distribution causes a shoot to bend.
parts.answer: More auxin on the shaded side causes more cell elongation there, so the shaded side grows longer and the shoot curves towards the light.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The total amount of auxin was about the same as in tips kept in the dark. State what this suggests about the effect of light on auxin.
parts.answer: Light does not destroy auxin; it causes auxin to move to the shaded side.

practice.stem:
Three maize seedlings were placed in a box with light coming from one side only.
Seedling X: untreated — after 2 days it had bent towards the light.
Seedling Y: tip cut off — no bending and very little growth.
Seedling Z: tip covered with an aluminium foil cap — grew straight up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling X.
parts.answer: Auxin is made in the tip; it moved to the shaded side; caused greater cell elongation on the shaded side, so the shoot bent towards the light.
parts.working: B1 auxin from tip; B1 moves to shaded side; B1 cells on shaded side elongate more

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling Y.
parts.answer: The tip, which makes auxin (and detects light), was removed, so no auxin and no bending / growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling Z.
parts.answer: The foil cap stopped light reaching the tip; so auxin was not redistributed and the shoot grew straight up (evenly).
parts.working: B1 tip cannot detect light; B1 auxin evenly distributed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how a synthetic auxin weedkiller kills broad-leaved weeds such as thistles in a wheat field.
parts.answer: It causes rapid, uncontrolled growth / elongation of the weeds; they cannot sustain this (use up food reserves), so they die.
parts.working: B1 rapid / uncontrolled growth; B1 plant dies / exhausts reserves

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the weedkiller does not kill the wheat.
parts.answer: Wheat (narrow-leaved) absorbs less / is less sensitive to the weedkiller.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one advantage of using a selective weedkiller rather than pulling out weeds by hand.
parts.answer: Quicker / cheaper for large areas / less labour.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shoot is placed horizontally on a clinostat that turns slowly, in the dark. Which result after three days is expected, and why?
A the shoot bends upwards because auxin collects on the lower side
B the shoot grows straight because gravity acts on all sides equally and auxin is evenly spread
C the shoot bends downwards because auxin is destroyed on the upper side
D the shoot stops growing because auxin needs light
parts.answer: B the shoot grows straight because gravity acts on all sides equally and auxin is evenly spread
parts.working: Rotation means no side stays lowest for long, so auxin is not concentrated on one side and the shoot grows straight. A is what happens on a still (non-rotating) shoot.

practice.stem:
Oat seedlings were kept in the dark. Shoot tips were cut off some seedlings and stood on a small agar block for 3 hours, then removed.
P: tip removed, nothing added — no bending, little growth.
Q: tip removed, the agar block that had held tips placed on the LEFT side of the cut surface — shoot bent to the RIGHT.
R: tip removed, a plain agar block (never touched by tips) placed on the left side — no bending.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the result for seedling Q.
parts.answer: Auxin from the tips diffused into the agar block and then into the left side of the shoot; cells on the left elongated more, so the shoot bent to the right.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why seedlings P and R did not bend.
parts.answer: P: the tip, the source of auxin, was removed, so no auxin and little growth; R: plain agar contains no auxin, so neither side grows more.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of seedling R.
parts.answer: A control: to show that the bending was caused by auxin and not by the agar block itself.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the experiment was carried out in the dark.
parts.answer: So that light from one side does not affect the distribution of auxin / cause bending.

practice.stem:
A synthetic auxin weedkiller was sprayed on plots of wheat with broad-leaved weeds. (Figures for this question.)
concentration / mg per dm³ | 0 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 80
wheat growth / % of normal | 100 | 100 | 97 | 92 | 60
weeds surviving / % | 100 | 70 | 35 | 8 | 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to choose the lowest concentration that kills at least 90 % of the weeds while keeping wheat growth at 90 % or more of normal. Show how you decided.
parts.answer: 40 mg/dm³ (weeds 8 % surviving, wheat 92 %)
parts.working: M1 compares both rows; A1 40 mg/dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a concentration of 80 mg/dm³ would not be used, even though it kills more weeds.
parts.answer: It reduces wheat growth to 60 % of normal, so the crop yield falls; only 6 % more weeds are killed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how a synthetic auxin can kill broad-leaved weeds.
parts.answer: It causes very fast, uncontrolled growth/cell elongation; the plant cannot support this and uses up its food reserves, so it dies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether it is the tip of a shoot that detects light. You are given germinating maize seedlings, small caps made of aluminium foil, a lamp, and boxes with a hole in one side.
parts.answer: Groups of at least 10 seedlings: (1) untreated; (2) tip covered with foil cap; (3) foil collar around the shoot below the tip (tip uncovered); place each group in a box with light entering from one side only through the hole; same lamp distance, same temperature, same age/height of seedlings, same watering; after 1–2 days measure the angle of bending with a protractor; record in a table and find mean angle; if tip-covered seedlings do not bend but collared seedlings do, the tip detects light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: untreated control; tip covered; region below tip covered (control for foil); light from one side; controlled variables (×2 max); sample size/repeats; measurement of curvature with protractor; time stated; table/means; conclusion criterion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
When insulin is secreted, in which organ is most of the extra glucose converted to glycogen?
A kidney
B liver
C pancreas
D stomach
parts.answer: B liver
parts.working: Insulin causes the liver (and muscles) to take up glucose and store it as glycogen. The pancreas (C) secretes insulin but does not store the glycogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sequence of events after a meal of rice by filling each gap.
blood glucose rises → detected by the ___ → which secretes the hormone ___ into the blood → the ___ converts glucose into ___ → blood glucose falls
parts.answer: pancreas; insulin; liver; glycogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: A condition in which the pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin, so blood glucose cannot be controlled.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two signs or symptoms of untreated type 1 diabetes.
parts.answer: high blood glucose; glucose in urine; extreme thirst; frequent urination; tiredness; weight loss

parts.label: c
parts.text: Apart from insulin injections, state two ways in which a person with type 1 diabetes manages the condition.
parts.answer: regularly measures blood glucose; controls the diet (amount and timing of carbohydrate); regular exercise / adjusts food with exercise

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement describes the pancreas, the liver or both.
(i) secretes insulin and glucagon
(ii) stores glycogen
(iii) detects changes in blood glucose concentration
(iv) converts glycogen to glucose when glucagon arrives
parts.answer: (i) pancreas (ii) liver (accept liver, also muscles) (iii) pancreas (iv) liver

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Blood glucose concentration rises after a meal. Which response occurs?
A the pancreas releases glucagon and the liver converts glycogen to glucose
B the pancreas releases insulin and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
C the liver releases insulin and the pancreas stores glycogen
D the adrenal glands release insulin and muscles release glucose
parts.answer: B the pancreas releases insulin and the liver converts glucose to glycogen
parts.working: Insulin from the pancreas makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen. A is the response to low blood glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the hormone that is released when blood glucose falls too low, and the organ that secretes it.
parts.answer: Glucagon; pancreas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how this hormone raises blood glucose.
parts.answer: It causes the liver to break down glycogen to glucose, which is released into the blood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how type 1 diabetes is treated, and state one sign of the condition.
parts.answer: Treated by insulin injections (plus controlled diet / exercise and monitoring blood glucose). Sign: high blood glucose / glucose in urine / thirst / tiredness / weight loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is important to keep blood glucose concentration within narrow limits. Refer to what happens when it is too low and when it is too high.
parts.answer: Too low: cells, especially brain cells, do not get enough glucose for respiration, so they lack energy (person may become confused/faint). Too high: water leaves body cells by osmosis because the blood has a lower water potential; glucose is lost in urine; cells/organs can be damaged.
parts.working: 2 marks for 'too low' points and 2 marks for 'too high' points.

practice.stem:
A student ate a plate of rice after an overnight fast. His blood glucose and insulin levels were measured. (Figures for this question.)
time / min | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120 | 150
blood glucose / mmol per dm³ | 5.0 | 8.2 | 7.0 | 5.8 | 5.0 | 4.8
insulin / arbitrary units | 10 | 45 | 60 | 35 | 15 | 10

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time at which (i) blood glucose was highest and (ii) insulin was highest.
parts.answer: (i) 30 min (ii) 60 min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the insulin level was at 60 minutes than at 0 minutes.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the link between the two sets of results.
parts.answer: The rise in glucose is detected by the pancreas, which secretes more insulin; insulin causes the liver/cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen, so glucose falls; as glucose falls, less insulin is secreted (negative feedback), and insulin peaks after glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During a long football match a player's muscles use a lot of glucose. Name the hormone secreted by the pancreas in response and describe how it keeps blood glucose up.
parts.answer: glucagon; it travels in the blood to the liver; the liver converts glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood
parts.working: 1 mark glucagon; 2 marks for the liver/glycogen → glucose points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one other hormone that raises blood glucose during exciting moments of the match.
parts.answer: adrenaline

parts.label: a
parts.text: An adult has 5.0 dm³ of blood. Before breakfast the glucose concentration is 0.9 g per dm³. Calculate the total mass of glucose in the blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One hour after breakfast the concentration is 1.4 g per dm³. Calculate the extra mass of glucose in the blood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The breakfast contained about 60 g of carbohydrate. Suggest why the extra glucose in the blood is much less than 60 g.
parts.answer: Digestion and absorption take time, so not all is absorbed at once; insulin causes glucose to be removed from the blood and stored as glycogen/used in respiration as it is absorbed.

practice.stem:
A healthy student drank a glucose solution after fasting. Her blood glucose concentration was measured.
time / min | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120
blood glucose / mg per 100 cm³ | 90 | 150 | 135 | 105 | 92

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in blood glucose from 0 to 30 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the concentration returned to normal by 120 minutes.
parts.answer: The rise was detected by the pancreas; it secreted insulin into the blood; insulin caused the liver / muscles to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen (and cells to respire more glucose).
parts.working: B1 pancreas detects / secretes insulin; B1 insulin travels in blood to liver; B1 glucose → glycogen

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the results would differ for a person with type 1 diabetes, and explain why.
parts.answer: Glucose would rise higher and stay high for longer; because the pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin.
parts.working: B1 higher / does not return to normal; B1 no / little insulin

practice.stem:
Two people, A and B, each ate the same sugary breakfast cereal after an overnight fast. (Figures for this question.)
time / min | 0 | 30 | 60 | 90 | 120 | 150
A / mmol per dm³ | 4.8 | 7.6 | 6.4 | 5.2 | 4.9 | 4.8
B / mmol per dm³ | 7.5 | 12.0 | 15.2 | 14.1 | 12.6 | 11.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose appears in the urine when blood glucose is above 10 mmol per dm³. State how many of B's readings were above this value.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference between A and B at 120 minutes.
parts.answer: 7.7 mmol per dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify which person has type 1 diabetes. Give three pieces of evidence from the data.
parts.answer: B: starting (fasting) glucose is higher (7.5 v 4.8); rises much higher (peak 15.2 v 7.6); peak is later (60 v 30 min); still high at 150 min (11.4, above starting value), while A returns to normal by 120 min.
parts.working: 1 mark for B with at least one reason; 1 mark each for further evidence, max 3.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why B's blood glucose stays high.
parts.answer: B's pancreas makes little or no insulin; so the liver does not convert glucose to glycogen / cells do not take up glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Control of blood glucose is an example of negative feedback. Explain what this means, using the events after blood glucose has risen.
parts.answer: A rise above the set point is detected by the pancreas; insulin is secreted and causes glucose to be removed; as glucose returns to the set point, the stimulus is reduced, so less insulin is secreted; the response reverses the change.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three points, must include the response reducing/switching off once normal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what would happen to blood glucose if the pancreas kept secreting insulin even after the concentration had returned to normal.
parts.answer: Glucose would keep being removed so the concentration would fall too low (hypoglycaemia); brain cells would lack glucose and the person could faint.

practice.stem: A woman ate dinner at 9 p.m. and nothing else until breakfast at 7 a.m. Her liver contained about 100 g of glycogen at 9 p.m. and 40 g at 7 a.m. (Figures for this question.)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in liver glycogen overnight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean mass of glycogen used per hour.
parts.answer: 6 g per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how her blood glucose concentration was kept constant while she slept and ate nothing.
parts.answer: Blood glucose begins to fall as cells use it in respiration; the pancreas detects this and secretes glucagon; glucagon causes the liver to break down glycogen to glucose, which enters the blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ayesha has type 1 diabetes and plays in a school football match in Peshawar. Her doctor advises her to eat a small carbohydrate snack before the match and to inject slightly less insulin than usual. Explain both pieces of advice.
parts.answer: During exercise muscles use more glucose in respiration, so blood glucose falls; the snack adds glucose to the blood; insulin lowers blood glucose further, so a smaller dose reduces the risk of glucose falling too low (hypoglycaemia).

parts.label: b
parts.text: She also carries glucose tablets. Suggest when she would use them and why they work quickly.
parts.answer: If she feels faint/shaky (signs of low blood glucose); glucose needs no digestion and is absorbed into the blood quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a synapse?
A a bundle of neurones
B a junction between two neurones
C the cell body of a relay neurone
D a receptor in the skin
parts.answer: B a junction between two neurones
parts.working: A synapse is the junction (with a small gap) between two neurones. A bundle of neurones is a nerve (A).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The statements describe how an impulse crosses a synapse. Put them in the correct order, starting with P.
P an impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone
Q the neurotransmitter binds to receptor proteins on the next neurone
R vesicles release neurotransmitter into the gap
S an impulse is started in the next neurone
T the neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap
parts.answer: P, R, T, Q, S
parts.working: 3 marks all correct; 2 marks one pair swapped; 1 mark R before T before Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name:
(i) the type of chemical that carries the signal across a synapse
(ii) the structures in which this chemical is stored
(iii) the structures it binds to on the next neurone
parts.answer: (i) neurotransmitter (ii) vesicles (iii) receptors / receptor proteins

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether the signal crossing the gap is electrical or chemical.
parts.answer: chemical

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement about synapses is true or false.
(i) Impulses can cross a synapse in both directions.
(ii) The neurotransmitter crosses the gap by diffusion.
(iii) There are synapses in the spinal cord.
(iv) Neurones touch each other at a synapse.
parts.answer: (i) false (ii) true (iii) true (iv) false

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an impulse passes across a synapse.
parts.answer: Impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone; vesicles release neurotransmitter into the gap; neurotransmitter diffuses across the gap; binds to receptor proteins on the next neurone; which starts an impulse in it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the five points

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the process by which the neurotransmitter crosses the gap.
parts.answer: Diffusion

parts.label: a
parts.text: A reflex arc contains a sensory neurone, a relay neurone and a motor neurone. State how many synapses between neurones the impulse crosses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each synapse delays the impulse by 0.6 ms. The whole reflex takes 25 ms. Calculate the total synaptic delay and the percentage of the reflex time it makes up.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a reflex arc has fewer synapses than the pathway for a voluntary action.
parts.answer: Fewer synapses means less delay, so the reflex is faster (the pathway does not go through the brain's many neurones).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Drug Q has a shape very like a neurotransmitter and also starts impulses when it binds. Suggest the effect of drug Q at a synapse.
parts.answer: It binds to the receptors on the next neurone and starts impulses even when no neurotransmitter has been released, so more impulses are sent / the pathway is over-stimulated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nicotine acts in a similar way at some synapses. Suggest why people who smoke feel its effects within seconds.
parts.answer: Nicotine is absorbed quickly across the alveoli into the blood and carried to the brain, where it binds to receptors at synapses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a synapse in words. Include the part of each neurone involved.
parts.answer: the end of the first (presynaptic) neurone contains vesicles of neurotransmitter; a narrow gap separates it from the next neurone; the membrane of the next (postsynaptic) neurone has receptor proteins

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a neurotransmitter binds only to its own receptors.
parts.answer: The receptor is a protein with a specific shape; only a molecule with a complementary shape (the neurotransmitter) fits it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the way a signal travels along a neurone with the way it crosses a synapse.
parts.answer: Along the neurone it is an electrical impulse; across the synapse it is chemical (neurotransmitter); crossing the synapse is slower (diffusion) than travel along the neurone; along a neurone it can be long distance, the gap is tiny.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three valid comparisons (both sides needed).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why can nerve impulses cross a synapse in one direction only?
A the synaptic gap is wider at one end
B neurotransmitter is released only from the first neurone and receptors are only on the second neurone
C the second neurone has no cell membrane
D impulses travel by electricity across the gap
parts.answer: B neurotransmitter is released only from the first neurone and receptors are only on the second neurone
parts.working: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only in the neurone before the gap, and receptor proteins are only on the neurone after it. D is wrong: the signal crosses the gap as a chemical, not electrically.

practice.stem: A medicine, drug D, has a molecular shape very similar to a neurotransmitter but does not start impulses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how drug D affects transmission across a synapse.
parts.answer: It has a similar shape to the neurotransmitter, so it binds to the receptors; this blocks the neurotransmitter, so fewer impulses are started in the next neurone.
parts.working: B1 binds to / blocks receptors; B1 fewer / no impulses in next neurone

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a drug that blocks the receptors at synapses between motor neurones and muscles could cause paralysis.
parts.answer: Impulses cannot pass from motor neurones to muscles; so muscles do not contract.
parts.working: B1 no impulse transmitted to muscle; B1 muscles do not contract

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one role of synapses in the nervous system.
parts.answer: Ensure impulses travel in one direction / allow impulses to be passed between neurones / allow connections with many neurones.

practice.stem: A researcher stimulated a neurone 50 times per second and recorded impulses in the neurone on the other side of a synapse. Without toxin there were 50 impulses per second; with the toxin there were 12 per second.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A toxin from a bacterium stops many vesicles releasing their contents. Calculate the percentage decrease in impulses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stopping vesicles releasing their contents reduces the impulses in the second neurone.
parts.answer: Less neurotransmitter is released into the gap; fewer neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across and bind to receptors; fewer impulses are started in the second neurone.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a person poisoned with this toxin may have difficulty breathing.
parts.answer: Impulses do not reach the breathing muscles (diaphragm/intercostal muscles), so they do not contract properly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The gap at a synapse is about 20 nm wide. 1 mm = 1 000 000 nm. Calculate how many gaps of this width would fit side by side in 1 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this information to explain why a chemical signal can cross a synapse quickly even though it moves by diffusion.
parts.answer: The distance is extremely short, so diffusion across it takes very little time; the neurotransmitter is released in high concentration, giving a steep gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why impulses can travel only one way across a synapse.
parts.answer: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only on one side (the first neurone); receptors are only on the other side (the next neurone).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some organophosphate pesticides sprayed on cotton crops stop the enzyme that normally breaks down neurotransmitter in the synaptic gap. Suggest and explain the effect of these pesticides at synapses to muscles.
parts.answer: Neurotransmitter is not broken down and stays bound to / keeps reaching the receptors; impulses keep being started in the next cell; muscles keep contracting / twitch uncontrollably.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two precautions a farm worker should take when spraying these pesticides.
parts.answer: wear gloves, mask and protective clothing; do not spray in wind / stand upwind; wash hands before eating

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pain is felt when impulses travel from pain receptors through synapses to the brain. Suggest two different ways in which a painkilling drug could act at a synapse to reduce the feeling of pain.
parts.answer: block/bind to the receptors so the neurotransmitter cannot bind; reduce the release of neurotransmitter from vesicles; (accept: cause neurotransmitter to be removed/broken down faster)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Such drugs often make people feel sleepy. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The drug is carried in the blood to all parts of the brain; it also affects synapses in other pathways (those that keep us alert), reducing their activity.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gland secretes adrenaline?
A pancreas
B adrenal gland
C testis
D ovary
parts.answer: B adrenal gland
parts.working: Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands (above the kidneys). The pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State where in the body each gland is found:
(i) adrenal glands
(ii) pancreas
(iii) testes
parts.answer: (i) on top of the kidneys (ii) in the abdomen, below/behind the stomach, next to the small intestine (iii) in the scrotum

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the hormone made by the ovaries that controls female secondary sexual characteristics.
parts.answer: oestrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the part of the blood that carries hormones.
parts.answer: plasma

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hormones reach every part of the body but affect only certain organs. State the name given to these organs.
parts.answer: target organs

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which hormonal responses differ from nervous responses.
parts.answer: slower; longer lasting; carried by blood not neurones; can affect several organs at once

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each hormone to its main effect.
hormones: adrenaline, glucagon, insulin, testosterone
effects: (i) lowers blood glucose (ii) raises blood glucose by causing glycogen breakdown in the liver (iii) increases heart rate in fear (iv) causes the voice to deepen at puberty
parts.answer: (i) insulin (ii) glucagon (iii) adrenaline (iv) testosterone

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which hormones and nerve impulses are similar.
parts.answer: both coordinate/send messages between parts of the body; both bring about responses in effectors/target organs; both help maintain homeostasis

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gland that secretes a hormone in response to fear.
parts.answer: adrenal gland

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of the term hormone.
parts.answer: A chemical substance produced by a gland; carried by the blood; which alters the activity of one or more specific target organs.
parts.working: B1 chemical made by gland; B1 transported in blood (to target organs)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table.
hormone | gland
insulin | ?
testosterone | ?
oestrogen | ?
parts.answer: pancreas; testes; ovaries

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two differences between nervous control and hormonal control.
parts.answer: Nervous: electrical impulses, along neurones, very fast, short-lasting. Hormonal: chemical, in blood, slower, longer-lasting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid differences

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which effect does adrenaline have on the body?
A pupils become smaller
B breathing rate increases
C heart rate decreases
D blood glucose concentration falls
parts.answer: B breathing rate increases
parts.working: Adrenaline prepares the body for action: breathing rate and heart rate increase, pupils widen and blood glucose rises. A, C and D are the opposite effects.

practice.stem: A student's heart rate was 72 beats per minute while she watched the calm start of a film. During a frightening scene it rose to 108 beats per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in heart rate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the hormone responsible for this change and the gland that secretes it.
parts.answer: adrenaline; adrenal gland

parts.label: c
parts.text: The heart rate took about 10 minutes to return to 72 beats per minute after the scene. Suggest why it did not fall immediately.
parts.answer: Adrenaline remains in the blood for some time until it is broken down/removed, so its effect lasts longer than a nerve impulse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Adrenaline causes the liver to release glucose into the blood. Explain how this helps a person who is running from danger.
parts.answer: More glucose is carried to the muscles; it is used in respiration; more energy is released for muscle contraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other effect of adrenaline that helps the muscles to receive more oxygen.
parts.answer: increased heart rate (more blood pumped) or increased breathing rate

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes into a duct leading to the small intestine, and hormones directly into the blood. Name one enzyme and one hormone made by the pancreas.
parts.answer: enzyme: amylase / lipase / protease (trypsin); hormone: insulin / glucagon

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the hormones are released into the blood rather than into a duct.
parts.answer: The blood carries the hormones round the whole body; so they reach target organs such as the liver that are far from the pancreas.

practice.stem: A goalkeeper in a hockey match in Karachi feels nervous as a penalty shoot-out begins, and his adrenal glands secrete adrenaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three effects of adrenaline on the body.
parts.answer: Increases heart rate; increases breathing rate; dilates pupils; increases blood glucose concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how two of these effects help the goalkeeper's muscles during the shoot-out.
parts.answer: Faster heart rate delivers more oxygen and glucose to muscles; more glucose in blood is available; so more aerobic respiration releases more energy for muscle contraction.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen / glucose delivered; B1 more respiration; B1 more energy for contraction

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows typical times for two responses.
response | time to begin / s | time effect lasts / s
pulling hand from a hot pan | 0.02 | 0.5
heart rate rise caused by adrenaline | 10 | 300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times longer a hormonal response takes to begin than a reflex response.
parts.answer: 500 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times longer the hormonal effect lasts.
parts.answer: 600 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the differences in speed and duration in terms of how each message travels and is removed.
parts.answer: Nerve impulses are electrical and travel very fast along neurones directly to the effector; hormones travel more slowly in the blood plasma; nerve effects stop as soon as impulses stop; hormones stay in the blood until broken down/removed (by the liver), so the effect lasts longer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two secondary sexual characteristics in boys caused by testosterone and two in girls caused by oestrogen.
parts.answer: boys: growth of facial/body hair; voice deepens; muscles develop; penis/testes enlarge; girls: breasts develop; hips widen; growth of pubic/underarm hair; menstrual cycle starts
parts.working: 1 mark each, two from each list.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why these characteristics develop only at puberty, even though the testes and ovaries are present from birth.
parts.answer: The testes/ovaries only begin to secrete large amounts of these hormones at puberty; the changes are caused by the hormones reaching their target organs in the blood.

practice.stem:
A tourist in Hunza made a bungee jump. The concentration of adrenaline in her blood was measured. (Figures for this question.)
time | 5 min before | at jump | 10 min after | 30 min after
adrenaline / nmol per dm³ | 0.4 | 4.0 | 1.2 | 0.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the concentration of adrenaline changes during the period shown.
parts.answer: Rises sharply from 0.4 to a peak of 4.0 at the jump; then falls, quickly at first (1.2 after 10 min) then slowly, to 0.5 by 30 min – near the starting value.
parts.working: 1 mark rise to peak; 1 mark fall with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times the concentration increased from before the jump to the jump, and the percentage fall in the 10 minutes after the jump.
parts.answer: 10 times; 70 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the high concentration of adrenaline prepares the body for action during the jump.
parts.answer: Increases heart rate and breathing rate so more oxygen reaches muscles; raises blood glucose for respiration; widens pupils so more light enters; more energy released in muscles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three effects linked to their benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Both glucagon and adrenaline cause the liver to release glucose. Explain the different situations in which each hormone is secreted.
parts.answer: Glucagon is secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose falls below the set point (homeostasis, e.g. between meals); adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands in fear, stress or excitement, even when blood glucose is normal; adrenaline prepares the body in advance for sudden activity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage for blood glucose to rise before a sprint begins, not after.
parts.answer: Muscles need extra glucose for respiration as soon as the activity starts; waiting for glucose to fall first would leave the muscles short of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an endocrine gland.
parts.answer: A gland that secretes hormones directly into the blood (it has no duct).
parts.working: 1 mark secretes hormones; 1 mark into the blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two hormones made by the pancreas that control blood glucose.
parts.answer: insulin and glucagon

parts.label: a
parts.text:
From this list choose the hormones that answer each question: adrenaline, glucagon, insulin, oestrogen, testosterone.
(i) Which two are made by the gonads (testes or ovaries)?
(ii) Which three can change blood glucose concentration?
parts.answer: (i) oestrogen and testosterone (ii) adrenaline, glucagon, insulin

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Each statement contains one mistake. Rewrite each correctly.
(i) Hormones are carried by neurones.
(ii) Adrenaline is made in the pancreas.
(iii) Insulin raises blood glucose.
parts.answer: (i) Hormones are carried by the blood (plasma). (ii) Adrenaline is made in the adrenal glands. (iii) Insulin lowers blood glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage.
A hormone is a ___ substance produced by a ___ and carried by the ___. It alters the activity of one or more specific ___ organs.
parts.answer: chemical; gland; blood; target

parts.label: a
parts.text: Both the nervous system and hormones coordinate the body. State what carries the message in each.
parts.answer: nervous system: electrical impulses along neurones; hormones: chemicals carried in the blood

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which system can affect many organs in different parts of the body at the same time, and why.
parts.answer: hormones, because the blood carries them to all parts of the body

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before giving a speech at a school assembly, Hamza notices his heart pounding and his breathing getting faster. During the speech he touches a very hot microphone stand and instantly pulls his hand away. For each response, state whether it is mainly nervous or hormonal and give one reason.
parts.answer: pounding heart/fast breathing: hormonal (adrenaline) – slower to start, lasts for minutes, affects several organs; pulling hand away: nervous (reflex) – very fast, short-lived, one effector
parts.working: 1 mark for each type, 1 mark for each reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Auxin is a plant hormone. State one way in which auxin is similar to animal hormones.
parts.answer: it is a chemical made in one part and acts in another / transported away from where it is made / affects growth or activity of target cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which auxin is different from adrenaline.
parts.answer: auxin moves by diffusion through cells, not in blood; it is made in shoot tips, not a gland; it controls growth (cell elongation), which is slow, whereas adrenaline has fast effects

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows the mean testosterone concentration in the blood of boys of different ages.
age / years | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18
testosterone / nmol per dm³ | 0.3 | 1.5 | 8.0 | 15.0 | 20.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in testosterone concentration with age.
parts.answer: Very low at 10 years (0.3); rises slowly to 12 then rapidly between 12 and 16 (1.5 to 15.0); continues to rise more slowly to 20.0 at 18.
parts.working: 1 mark overall increase; 1 mark fastest rise 12–16 with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the concentration is at 16 years than at 10 years.
parts.answer: 50 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two changes in the boys' bodies that would happen during the period of fastest rise.
parts.answer: voice deepens; facial and body hair grows; muscles develop; growth spurt; testes produce sperm

parts.label: a
parts.text: An insulin pen cartridge contains 3 cm³ of insulin at 100 units per cm³. A patient injects 12 units before breakfast, 10 units before lunch and 14 units before dinner. Calculate how many complete days one cartridge lasts.
parts.answer: 8 days
parts.working: M1 300 units ÷ 36 units per day = 8.3; A1 8 complete days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient checks her blood glucose before deciding the dose for each meal.
parts.answer: The dose must match the glucose level and the carbohydrate she will eat; too much insulin would make blood glucose fall dangerously low.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why insulin is injected and not taken as a tablet.
parts.answer: Insulin is a protein; it would be digested by protease enzymes in the stomach/small intestine before it could be absorbed.

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows the oestrogen concentration in a woman's blood during one 28-day menstrual cycle.
day | 1 | 5 | 9 | 12 | 14 | 21 | 28
oestrogen / arbitrary units | 40 | 60 | 120 | 300 | 180 | 150 | 50

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the day on which oestrogen concentration is highest.
parts.answer: day 12

parts.label: b
parts.text: Oestrogen is made in the ovaries. Describe one effect of the rising oestrogen between day 5 and day 12 on the uterus.
parts.answer: It causes the lining of the uterus to thicken / rebuild (become rich in blood vessels) after menstruation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the event that happens at about day 14.
parts.answer: ovulation (release of an egg)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the way in which the body responds to (i) touching a hot iron and (ii) a rise in blood glucose after a meal. Refer to the type of signal, how it travels, speed and duration.
parts.answer: (i) Nervous: electrical impulses; along neurones; very fast; short-lived response (muscle contracts). (ii) Hormonal: chemical (insulin); carried in the blood plasma; slower; longer-lasting; can affect several target organs (liver, muscles).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six comparison points, at least one from each response: electrical vs chemical; neurones vs blood; fast vs slow; short vs long-lasting; specific effector vs target organs; reflex via spinal cord vs pancreas detects change

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the control of blood glucose is an example of homeostasis.
parts.answer: It keeps the internal environment (blood glucose) constant within narrow limits; by negative feedback that reverses changes from the set point.
parts.working: B1 constant internal conditions; B1 negative feedback / returns to normal

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student takes an early lunch of rice and dal at 12:00, sleeps from 14:00 to 15:00 and runs a 400 m race at 17:00. Describe and explain the roles of insulin, glucagon and adrenaline in controlling her blood glucose during the day.
parts.answer: After lunch: glucose absorbed, blood glucose rises; pancreas secretes insulin; liver/muscles convert glucose to glycogen; glucose falls back to set point. During the nap/long gap: glucose used in respiration falls below set point; pancreas secretes glucagon; liver breaks down glycogen to glucose. Before/during race: excitement – adrenal glands secrete adrenaline; liver releases glucose; extra glucose for muscle respiration; negative feedback keeps glucose near set point.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six points, at least one point for each hormone for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rare tumour of the adrenal gland releases large amounts of adrenaline at random times. Suggest three symptoms the patient might notice, and explain each.
