parts.answer: Use the enzyme for a reaction, then after the reaction add fresh substrate to the same enzyme and measure the rate; compare the rate with a fresh enzyme sample. If the enzyme is not used up, the second reaction proceeds at a similar rate, showing the enzyme still works.
parts.working: Any four: repeat with fresh substrate using the same enzyme; measure the rate of the second reaction; compare with the first or a fresh enzyme; a similar rate shows that the enzyme is not used up.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student boils a lipase solution, then uses it to digest fat. Explain why the rate of digestion is slower than with an unboiled lipase solution.
parts.answer: Boiling denatures the enzyme: the heat changes the shape of the active site, so the fat no longer fits and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form each second, so the rate is slower or stops.
parts.working: 1 mark: boiling denatures the enzyme; 1 mark: the active site shape changes so the substrate does not fit; 1 mark: fewer enzyme-substrate complexes so slower rate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An enzyme from the human small intestine was tested at different temperatures. Above 45 °C its activity fell quickly. What is the best explanation?
A The substrate molecules move too slowly.
B The enzyme is denatured and its active site changes shape.
C The enzyme molecules are used up in the reaction.
D The products break down into the substrate.
parts.answer: B The enzyme is denatured and its active site changes shape.
parts.working: High temperature breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the substrate no longer fits. A is wrong: molecules move faster, not slower, when heated.

practice.stem:
The activity of an enzyme from human cells and the same type of enzyme from bacteria living in a hot spring were measured.
Temperature / °C: 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 | 80
Human enzyme activity / units: 20 | 45 | 80 | 40 | 5 | 0 | 0
Bacterial enzyme activity / units: 5 | 10 | 20 | 35 | 60 | 90 | 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for each enzyme.
parts.answer: human enzyme 40 °C; bacterial enzyme 70 °C

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the human enzyme has no activity at 70 °C.
parts.answer: It is denatured; its active site has changed shape so the substrate cannot fit.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the bacterial enzyme is useful in an industrial process carried out at high temperature.
parts.answer: It works fastest at high temperature and is not denatured there.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
At what temperature do the enzymes in the human body work best?
A 0 °C
B 37 °C
C 60 °C
D 80 °C
parts.answer: B 37 °C
parts.working: Human enzymes have their optimum close to body temperature, about 37 °C. At 0 °C reactions are very slow, and at 60 °C and 80 °C most human enzymes are denatured.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens to the kinetic energy of enzyme and substrate molecules as the temperature increases, and what this does to the collisions between them.
parts.answer: The molecules move faster and have more kinetic energy, so they collide more frequently and more of the collisions have enough energy to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
parts.working: 1 mark: molecules have more kinetic energy and move faster; 1 mark: more frequent and more successful collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of the temperature at which an enzyme works fastest, and state what happens to the enzyme above this temperature.
parts.answer: Optimum temperature; above it the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured, which is permanent.
parts.working: 1 mark: optimum temperature; 1 mark: enzyme denatures (active site changes shape).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain how the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction changes as temperature rises from 10 °C to 70 °C, for an enzyme with an optimum of 40 °C.
parts.answer: Rate rises from 10 °C to 40 °C because molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, forming more enzyme–substrate complexes; maximum at the optimum (40 °C); above 40 °C rate falls quickly as the enzyme is denatured, active site changes shape, substrate no longer fits; at about 70 °C there is no activity.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 5: rate increases to 40 °C; more kinetic energy; more collisions / more enzyme–substrate complexes; fastest at optimum; rate falls above optimum; denaturation; active site shape changed / substrate cannot fit; no activity at high temperature / irreversible.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which graph shape best describes the activity of a human enzyme as temperature rises from 0 °C to 60 °C?
A a straight line falling steadily
B a curve rising to a peak near 37 °C, then falling sharply
C a flat line at the same rate at every temperature
D a curve rising steadily with no peak
parts.answer: B a curve rising to a peak near 37 °C, then falling sharply
parts.working: Activity increases with temperature up to the optimum, around 37 °C, and then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures. A, C and D do not show the rise to an optimum followed by a sharp fall.

practice.stem:
A student added amylase to starch solution at five temperatures and recorded the time (s) for the blue-black colour with iodine to disappear.
Temperature (°C) | Time (s)
20 | 200
30 | 125
40 | 80
50 | 60
60 | 150

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of reaction, 1000 ÷ time, at 50 °C and at 60 °C. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the optimum temperature shown by the data.
parts.working: The shortest time (highest rate) is at 50 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the change in rate between 50 °C and 60 °C.
parts.answer: The enzyme is denatured at 60 °C because its active site changes shape; fewer successful collisions occur, so the rate falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzyme denatured or active site changed; 1 mark: fewer successful enzyme-substrate collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction increases as the temperature rises from 10 °C to 35 °C.
parts.answer: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so enzyme and substrate collide more often; a greater proportion of the collisions have enough energy to form the enzyme-substrate complex, so more successful collisions occur per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: more kinetic energy; 1 mark: more frequent collisions; 1 mark: more successful collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two variables that must be controlled in an investigation of the effect of temperature on an enzyme-controlled reaction.
parts.answer: Enzyme concentration (or volume); substrate concentration (or volume); pH; time or measurement method (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct control variables.

practice.stem:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on an enzyme. The enzyme and substrate solutions were placed separately in water baths for 5 minutes, then mixed, and the time for a colour change was recorded.
Temperature / °C: 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60
Time / s: 400 | 190 | 95 | 60 | 85 | 300

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate, 1000 ÷ time, at each temperature to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: B2 all six correct; B1 four or five correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster the reaction was at 30 °C than at 10 °C. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 4.2 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the temperature range in which the optimum lies and describe how to find it more precisely.
parts.answer: Between 30 °C and 50 °C (near 40 °C); repeat at 1–2 °C intervals between 30 °C and 50 °C (e.g. 32, 34 … 48 °C).
parts.working: B1 30–50 °C; B1 smaller intervals in that range.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the solutions were left in the water bath for 5 minutes before they were mixed.
parts.answer: So that both the enzyme and the substrate reach the required temperature before the reaction starts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe an investigation to find the optimum temperature of catalase from liver. Include the equipment, the variables, how the rate is measured, and one way to make the results reliable.
parts.answer: Use liver extract and hydrogen peroxide in separate water baths at set temperatures (e.g. 10 °C steps) and allow each to reach the temperature before mixing. Measure the rate by the volume of oxygen produced per minute. Keep the enzyme and substrate volumes the same and repeat each temperature, then calculate averages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: water baths at set temperatures; pre-warm before mixing; independent variable temperature and dependent variable oxygen volume or rate; control variables (volumes, concentration); repeat and average.

practice.stem: A reaction produces product at a rate of 0.45 cm³ per minute at 30 °C and 0.72 cm³ per minute at 40 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate between 30 °C and 40 °C.
parts.working: (0.72 − 0.45) ÷ 0.45 × 100 = 60 %. 1 mark for method, 1 mark for answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether a 10 °C rise always gives the same percentage increase in rate.
parts.answer: No. The rise is not constant; it slows as the optimum is approached, then the rate falls when the enzyme denatures.
parts.working: 1 mark: not the same at every step; 1 mark: rate increase slows near the optimum and then the enzyme denatures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an enzyme can be frozen for storage without losing much activity, but is destroyed when heated to 80 °C.
parts.answer: Freezing slows the molecules but does not change the shape of the active site, so the enzyme keeps its activity when thawed. Heating to 80 °C breaks the bonds that hold the enzyme's three-dimensional shape, so the active site changes permanently and the enzyme is denatured.
parts.working: 1 mark: freezing does not break bonds or denature; 1 mark: heating breaks bonds holding the shape; 1 mark: active site changes permanently (denatured).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cold-water fish has an enzyme with an optimum temperature of 20 °C, and a human enzyme has an optimum of 37 °C. Explain how the optimum temperature of each enzyme relates to the environment of its organism.
parts.answer: Each enzyme's optimum matches the normal temperature of its organism: the fish enzyme works best in cold water near 20 °C, and the human enzyme at body temperature, 37 °C. The different optima come from differences in enzyme structure (amino acid sequence) that suit each organism.
parts.working: 1 mark: fish enzyme suits cold water; 1 mark: human enzyme suits body temperature; 1 mark: enzyme structure differs between organisms.

practice.stem:
The activity of an enzyme was measured at different pH values.
pH: 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 | 11
Activity / units: 4 | 18 | 42 | 60 | 35 | 10 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum pH for this enzyme.
parts.answer: pH 8

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of pH on the activity of this enzyme.
parts.answer: Activity rises from pH 5 to a maximum at pH 8 and then falls sharply to zero at pH 11.
parts.working: B1 increase up to pH 8; B1 decrease above pH 8 with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which part of the human gut this enzyme might work in. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Small intestine (duodenum), because conditions there are slightly alkaline.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What happens to an enzyme's active site when the pH moves far from its optimum?
A it becomes larger and works faster
B its shape changes so the substrate no longer fits
C the substrate changes shape instead
D the enzyme becomes more soluble and works faster
parts.answer: B its shape changes so the substrate no longer fits
parts.working: Extreme pH changes the bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. A and D claim faster action, and C describes the wrong molecule.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum pH for: (i) salivary amylase; (ii) pepsin.
parts.answer: (i) about pH 7; (ii) about pH 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the acid found in the stomach, and the cells in the stomach lining that produce it.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid; parietal (acid-secreting) cells of the stomach lining.
parts.working: 1 mark for hydrochloric acid; 1 mark for parietal cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one variable that must be kept constant when testing the effect of pH on an enzyme, and explain why.
parts.answer: Temperature (or enzyme and substrate concentration); so that pH is the only variable changing and the test is fair.
parts.working: 1 mark: a correct variable such as temperature; 1 mark: keeps the test fair so only pH affects the result.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme works best at about pH 2?
A salivary amylase in the mouth
B pepsin in the stomach
C lipase in the small intestine
D trypsin in the small intestine
parts.answer: B pepsin in the stomach
parts.working: The stomach contains hydrochloric acid, and pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. Trypsin (D) is a protease too but works in the alkaline small intestine.

practice.stem:
Amylase and starch were mixed with buffer solutions of different pH at 35 °C. The time for the starch to disappear (iodine test) was recorded.
pH: 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9
Time / s: 360 | 150 | 75 | 60 | 110 | 290

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate, 60 ÷ time, at pH 6. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.80 per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why buffer solutions were used.
parts.answer: To keep the pH of each mixture constant at the chosen value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the results to state the optimum pH and explain how you decided.
parts.answer: pH 7 – it had the shortest time (60 s) / highest rate (1.00 per minute).
parts.working: B1 pH 7; B1 shortest time / fastest rate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables, other than pH, that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature; volume/concentration of starch; volume/concentration of amylase; time between iodine tests.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Trypsin in the duodenum works best at about pH 8. Which description of the duodenum is most accurate?
A strongly acidic, about pH 1
B exactly neutral, pH 7
C slightly alkaline, because pancreatic juice and bile contain alkaline sodium hydrogencarbonate
D the same as the stomach
parts.answer: C slightly alkaline, because pancreatic juice and bile contain alkaline sodium hydrogencarbonate
parts.working: Acid from the stomach is neutralised in the duodenum by alkaline secretions, so the duodenum is slightly alkaline, suiting trypsin. The stomach is strongly acidic, so A and D are wrong, and B does not match the alkaline conditions.

practice.stem:
A student measured the time for a protease to clear a milk-protein solution at four pH values.
pH 4: 120 s
pH 6: 70 s
pH 8: 50 s
pH 10: 210 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate, 1000 ÷ time, at pH 6 and at pH 10. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the optimum pH shown by the results.
parts.answer: pH 8
parts.working: The shortest clearing time, 50 s, is at pH 8.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why salivary amylase stops working when food reaches the stomach.
parts.answer: The stomach pH is about 2, far below the optimum of about pH 7 for salivary amylase; the acid changes the shape of the active site, so the enzyme denatures and can no longer bind starch.
parts.working: 1 mark: stomach pH far from optimum; 1 mark: acid changes the active site shape; 1 mark: enzyme denatured, cannot bind starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would prepare solutions at different pH values and set up a fair test to compare an enzyme's activity at each pH.
parts.answer: Use buffer solutions of different known pH values; use the same volume and concentration of enzyme and substrate for each; keep the temperature constant; measure the time for the reaction to finish at each pH; repeat and calculate averages.
parts.working: 1 mark: buffer solutions of known pH; 1 mark: same volumes and concentrations, constant temperature; 1 mark: measure time or rate at each pH and repeat.

practice.stem: During a meal of chicken karahi with naan, food passes from the mouth to the stomach and then to the duodenum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pepsin has an optimum pH of about 2. Explain why pepsin stops digesting protein when food passes into the duodenum.
parts.answer: The duodenum is alkaline (bile and pancreatic juice neutralise the acid); the change in pH alters the shape of pepsin's active site / denatures it; protein no longer fits, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: B1 duodenum alkaline/neutral (bile, pancreatic juice); B1 active site shape altered / denatured; B1 substrate cannot bind.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Salivary amylase digests starch in the mouth. Suggest what happens to its activity when food reaches the stomach, and why.
parts.answer: It stops working because the stomach is very acidic (about pH 2), far from its optimum near pH 7, so it is denatured.
parts.working: B1 stops / activity falls; B1 acid pH denatures it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An enzyme's activity is 50 % of its maximum at both pH 5 and pH 9. (i) State whether the optimum pH can be found exactly from this information, and explain. (ii) Explain why the activity could be the same at pH 5 and pH 9.
parts.answer: (i) No: the optimum is not necessarily halfway between 5 and 9 unless the curve is symmetrical; more readings are needed. (ii) Both pH values partly change the shape or charge of the active site, so the same fraction of enzyme molecules can bind substrate on either side of the optimum.
parts.working: (i) 1 mark: cannot find exactly; 1 mark: the curve may not be symmetrical or more data needed. (ii) 1 mark: the active site is partly changed at each pH; 1 mark: same proportion of effective enzyme molecules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why changing the pH can affect the substrate as well as the enzyme.
parts.answer: Some substrate molecules have groups that gain or lose hydrogen ions; their charge changes with pH, which can change the substrate's shape, so it may no longer bind to the active site.
parts.working: 1 mark: groups in the substrate can gain or lose H⁺ ions; 1 mark: charge or shape changes with pH; 1 mark: substrate may no longer fit the active site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The maximum rate of a reaction is 2.4 cm³ per minute at the optimum pH. At pH 5.5 the activity is 62 % of the maximum. Calculate the rate at pH 5.5, in cm³ per minute, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 1.49 cm³ per minute
parts.working: 2.4 × 0.62 = 1.488, so 1.49 cm³/min. 1 mark for method, 1 mark for answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which conditions are needed for the germination of most seeds?
A light, water and warmth
B water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
C carbon dioxide, water and light
D oxygen, light and soil
parts.answer: B water, oxygen and a suitable temperature
parts.working: Seeds need water, oxygen (for aerobic respiration) and a suitable temperature (for enzymes). Light (A) is not needed because the seed uses stored food.

practice.stem: A tomato plant in a kitchen garden in Quetta has been pollinated and fertilised.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After fertilisation, state what each of these structures develops into.
(i) ovule
(ii) ovary
parts.answer: (i) seed; (ii) fruit

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the petals after fertilisation.
parts.answer: They wither and fall off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name of the cell formed when a male nucleus fuses with a female nucleus.
parts.answer: zygote

practice.stem:
Crushed maize grains were tested on the day they were soaked and after 4 days of germination.
Day 0: iodine test – blue-black; Benedict's test – blue
Day 4: iodine test – brown with a few black spots; Benedict's test – orange

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the results change from day 0 to day 4.
parts.answer: Starch decreases (iodine less blue-black) and reducing sugar increases (Benedict's changes from blue to orange).
parts.working: B1 less starch; B1 more reducing sugar.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme responsible for these changes.
parts.answer: amylase

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the germinating grain uses the sugar for.
parts.answer: Respiration to release energy for growth (or to build cellulose for new cells).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After fertilisation, what does the wall of the ovule (the integuments) develop into?
A the testa (seed coat)
B the fruit wall
C the cotyledons
D the plumule
parts.answer: A the testa (seed coat)
parts.working: The integuments of the ovule harden to form the testa, which protects the seed. B is wrong because the fruit wall develops from the ovary wall, not the ovule.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which part of a bean seed grows to form the first root of the seedling?
A plumule
B radicle
C cotyledon
D testa
parts.answer: B radicle
parts.working: The radicle is the embryonic root and is the first structure to emerge. The plumule (A) is the embryonic shoot.

practice.stem:
Twenty radish seeds were placed in each of four tubes and left for 5 days.
A: dry cotton wool, 25 °C – 0 germinated
B: moist cotton wool, 25 °C – 18 germinated
C: seeds under boiled and cooled water with a layer of oil on top, 25 °C – 0 germinated
D: moist cotton wool, in a refrigerator at 4 °C – 3 germinated

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination in each tube.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 two or three correct (n ÷ 20 × 100).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which condition was missing in tube C and explain why it is needed for germination.
parts.answer: Oxygen (boiling removed dissolved oxygen and the oil stops more dissolving); needed for aerobic respiration to release energy for growth.
parts.working: B1 oxygen; B1 aerobic respiration / energy for growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a few seeds in tube D germinated but many fewer than in tube B.
parts.answer: At 4 °C the enzymes in the seeds work very slowly (low kinetic energy), so germination is slow; it is not stopped completely.
parts.working: B1 low temperature slows enzymes; B1 slow (not zero) metabolism / respiration.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the control tube.
parts.answer: B

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the events that take place from the moment a pollen grain lands on a stigma until fertilisation.
parts.answer: A pollen tube grows from the pollen grain down through the style; it enters the ovary and passes through the micropyle into an ovule; the male nucleus travels down the tube; it fuses with the female nucleus (egg cell) in the ovule.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 4: pollen tube grows; down style; through micropyle into ovule; male nucleus moves down tube; fuses with female nucleus/egg nucleus = fertilisation.

practice.stem:
Thirty mung bean seeds were placed on moist paper in each of four dishes at different temperatures. The number that had germinated after 4 days was counted.
Temperature / °C: 10 | 20 | 30 | 40
Number germinated: 6 | 21 | 28 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination at each temperature. Give each answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Five seedlings at 30 °C had radicle lengths of 18, 22, 20, 25 and 15 mm. Calculate the mean radicle length.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fewer seeds germinated at 40 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.answer: 40 °C is above the optimum for the seeds' enzymes; some enzymes are denatured, so less stored food is broken down and respiration is slower.
parts.working: B1 above optimum / enzymes start to denature; B1 less food broken down / less energy for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why seeds need water to germinate.
parts.answer: Water activates enzymes / allows stored food to be broken down and transported in solution; it makes cells swell so the testa splits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why seeds need oxygen to germinate.
parts.answer: For aerobic respiration, which releases energy for cell division and growth of the embryo.
parts.working: B1 aerobic respiration; B1 energy for growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers in Punjab sow wheat seeds in moist, loose soil rather than in waterlogged soil. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil has little air, so the seeds would not get enough oxygen.

practice.stem: A pea pod picked from a vegetable plot in Peshawar is opened. It contains 7 fully developed seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the minimum number of pollen grains that must have produced pollen tubes to make this pod. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 7; each seed comes from a separate ovule, and each ovule is fertilised by a male nucleus from its own pollen grain/pollen tube.
parts.working: 1 mark: 7; 1 mark: one pollen tube (male gamete) needed per ovule/seed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the part of the flower that develops into the pod.
parts.answer: The ovary (wall)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the pod also contains two small, shrivelled structures that are not seeds.
parts.answer: These ovules were not fertilised (no pollen tube reached them); so they did not develop into seeds.
parts.working: 1 mark: unfertilised ovules; 1 mark: not enough pollen / pollen tube did not reach them, so no embryo developed.

practice.stem: A student split open a soaked broad bean seed and made a large drawing. The length of the bean on the drawing was 84 mm. The actual length of the bean was 21 mm. She labelled the testa, cotyledons, plumule and radicle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of: (i) the testa; (ii) the cotyledons; (iii) the radicle.
parts.answer: (i) protects the seed (embryo); (ii) store food for the embryo during germination; (iii) grows into the root.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student measured the bean after soaking it overnight. Suggest why the soaked bean was larger than a dry bean.
parts.answer: It absorbed water (by osmosis), so its cells swelled.

practice.stem:
A student soaked mung bean seeds for different times before placing 20 seeds of each group on moist cotton wool at 25 °C. After 3 days she counted the germinated seeds and measured the radicle lengths of five seedlings from each group.
Soaking time / h: 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 24
Number germinated (out of 20): 9 | 14 | 18 | 19 | 11
Radicle lengths for 8 h / mm: 12, 15, 11, 14, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination after 8 hours of soaking and after 24 hours of soaking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean radicle length for the seeds soaked for 8 hours. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why soaking the seeds for up to 12 hours increased the number that germinated.
parts.answer: The seeds absorb water, which activates their enzymes so stored food (starch) is broken down and transported to the embryo; it also makes the seed swell and the testa split.
parts.working: B1 water absorbed / enzymes activated; B1 stored food broken down and transported for growth / testa splits.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why fewer seeds germinated after 24 hours of soaking.
parts.answer: Seeds kept under water for a long time get too little oxygen, so aerobic respiration cannot release enough energy (some embryos may die).
parts.working: B1 lack of oxygen when submerged / less aerobic respiration.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat with more dishes (or more seeds) for each soaking time and calculate means.
parts.working: B1 repeats / larger sample and mean.

practice.stem: You are given mung bean seeds, Petri dishes, cotton wool, water, incubators that can be set to different temperatures, and a refrigerator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of temperature on the germination of mung bean seeds.
parts.answer: A plan with a range of temperatures, controlled variables, a measured outcome, repeats and a conclusion method.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: at least 4 temperatures (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40 °C) using incubators/refrigerator/water baths; same number of seeds (e.g. 20) per dish, same type and age; same volume of water / moist cotton wool kept moist; same time (e.g. 4 days); same light conditions; count number germinated (radicle visible) and calculate percentage; repeat with three dishes per temperature and find mean; plot percentage against temperature.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Germinating pea seeds were kept in the dark on moist cotton wool. Their total dry mass decreased over 6 days. What is the main reason?
A The seeds lost water by evaporation.
B Stored food was used in respiration, releasing carbon dioxide.
C Starch was changed into sugars.
D The seedlings were photosynthesising.
parts.answer: B Stored food was used in respiration, releasing carbon dioxide.
parts.working: Dry mass excludes water, so A is wrong. Respiration breaks down stored food and the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, so dry mass falls. Converting starch to sugar (C) does not change dry mass much.

practice.stem:
Some farmland in Sindh has salty soil. A student placed 40 wheat grains on filter paper soaked in salt solutions of different concentrations, kept at 25 °C. After 5 days she counted the number of grains that had germinated.
Salt concentration / mmol/dm³: 0 | 50 | 100 | 150 | 200
Number germinated (out of 40): 38 | 35 | 26 | 14 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination at each salt concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of salt concentration on germination.
parts.answer: As salt concentration increases, percentage germination decreases; the decrease is small from 0 to 50 mmol/dm³ and steep above 50 mmol/dm³ (95 % to 12.5 %).
parts.working: 1 mark: negative trend; 1 mark: use of data / steeper fall at higher concentrations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your knowledge of osmosis to explain the effect.
parts.answer: Salt solution has a lower water potential than the seed cells; less water (or no water) enters the seed by osmosis; without water, enzymes are not activated / stored food is not mobilised / cells cannot expand, so the seed does not germinate.
parts.working: 1 mark each: lower water potential outside; less water uptake by osmosis; water needed to activate enzymes / for growth.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature; volume of solution; type/variety of seed; number of seeds; time; light; oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of the anther?
A to make pollen grains
B to receive pollen during pollination
C to attract insects
D to make ovules
parts.answer: A to make pollen grains
parts.working: Anthers produce pollen. The stigma (B) receives pollen.

practice.stem: A student looked at a hibiscus flower from her garden in Hyderabad.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the function of each part of a flower.
(i) sepal
(ii) petal
(iii) stigma
(iv) ovary
parts.answer: (i) protects the flower in bud; (ii) attracts insects (pollinators); (iii) receives pollen; (iv) contains ovules / develops into the fruit.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure connects the stigma to the ovary?
A filament
B style
C anther
D sepal
parts.answer: B style
parts.working: The style is the stalk of the carpel that holds the stigma up and joins it to the ovary; the pollen tube grows down it. The filament (A) supports the anther.

practice.stem: A student examines a yellow mustard flower from a field near Multan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two parts that make up a stamen.
parts.answer: Anther and filament.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three parts that make up a carpel.
parts.answer: Stigma, style and ovary.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which part of the flower contains the ovules.
parts.answer: Ovary

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define pollination.
parts.answer: The transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two agents that can carry out pollination.
parts.answer: Insects (or other animals such as birds) and wind.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage to a plant of self-pollination.
parts.answer: Advantage: pollination does not depend on insects, wind or another plant being nearby, so it is reliable. Disadvantage: less genetic variation in the offspring, so the population is less able to survive a new disease or a change in conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: reliable / no pollinator or second plant needed; 1 mark: less variation / less able to adapt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Grass pollen grains are small, light and smooth. Sunflower pollen grains are larger and covered in spikes. Explain how each type of pollen is suited to the way the plant is pollinated.
parts.answer: Grass: small, light, smooth pollen is easily carried long distances by the wind. Sunflower: spikes help the pollen stick to the hairy bodies of insects that carry it to another flower.
parts.working: 1 mark: grass pollen light/smooth so carried by wind; 1 mark: sunflower spikes hook/stick onto insects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many people get hay fever when grass pollen is in the air in spring. Suggest why grasses cause more hay fever than insect-pollinated flowers.
parts.answer: Grass pollen is released into the air in very large amounts; so it is easily breathed in. Insect-pollinated pollen is heavier/sticky and stays on the flower or the insect.
parts.working: 1 mark: large amounts of airborne pollen; 1 mark: insect pollen is sticky/heavy and not carried in air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four ways in which a wind-pollinated flower such as wheat differs from an insect-pollinated flower such as mustard.
parts.answer: Wind: small/dull or no petals (insect: large, brightly coloured); no scent or nectar (insect: scent and nectar); anthers hang outside the flower on long filaments (insect: inside); large feathery stigmas outside (insect: small sticky stigma inside); large amounts of small, light, smooth pollen (insect: less, larger, sticky/spiky pollen).
parts.working: 1 mark for each comparative point, max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why wind-pollinated plants produce large amounts of pollen.
parts.answer: Pollen is carried randomly by wind, so most is wasted and never reaches a stigma.

practice.stem: A student removed the parts of a flower and counted them: 5 sepals, 5 petals, 10 stamens and 1 carpel. In a photograph taken through a microscope, a pollen grain from this flower is 18 mm across. Its actual diameter is 0.03 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether this flower is from a monocotyledon or a dicotyledon. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Dicotyledon – the flower parts are in multiples of five.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the pollen grain photograph.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The pollen grains are large with spiky surfaces. Suggest how this flower is pollinated. Give a reason.
parts.answer: By insects – spiky pollen sticks to the insect's body.
parts.working: B1 insects; B1 spiky/sticky pollen attaches to insects.

practice.stem: A student drew a petal of a periwinkle (sadabahar) flower at a magnification of ×3. The length of the petal in her drawing is 75 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the petal.
parts.answer: 25 mm
parts.working: M1 actual = drawing length ÷ magnification = 75 ÷ 3; A1 25 mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two rules the student should follow when making a biological drawing of the flower.
parts.answer: Any two: use a sharp pencil; clear, continuous single lines (no sketching); no shading; draw large enough to fill the space; correct proportions; label lines drawn with a ruler and not crossing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student counted 5 petals and 5 sepals. Suggest how she could tell the sepals from the petals.
parts.answer: Sepals are the outer ring, usually green and smaller; they enclosed the bud.

practice.stem: Maize is wind-pollinated. The male flowers form a tassel at the top of the stem. The female flowers are on the cob lower down; each has a long thread called a silk, which hangs outside the leaves that wrap the cob.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the silks are adapted for wind pollination.
parts.answer: They are long and feathery / sticky and hang outside the leaves; giving a large surface area exposed to the wind to catch pollen.
parts.working: 1 mark: long/feathery/exposed; 1 mark: large surface area to trap airborne pollen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the tassel is adapted for wind pollination.
parts.answer: It is at the top of the plant and the anthers hang outside on long filaments; so pollen is easily shaken out and blown away by the wind.
parts.working: 1 mark: anthers exposed/hanging on long filaments at top of plant; 1 mark: pollen released into the wind.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why maize is planted in square blocks of several rows rather than in one very long single row.
parts.answer: Pollen blown in any direction is more likely to land on silks of other plants; in a single row, wind blowing across the row would carry most pollen away from the crop.
parts.working: 1 mark: more plants near each other in all directions; 1 mark: higher chance of pollen landing on silks / more cobs fully filled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a honeybee transfers pollen from one sunflower to another.
parts.answer: The bee is attracted by the bright petals/scent and lands to feed on nectar; sticky pollen from the anthers sticks to its hairy body; when it visits another sunflower some pollen rubs off onto the stigma.
parts.working: 1 mark each: attracted by petals/scent/nectar; pollen sticks to bee body; pollen rubbed onto stigma of another flower.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In some regions the number of bees has fallen because of pesticide use. Suggest the effect on farmers who grow sunflowers for seed oil.
parts.answer: Fewer flowers are pollinated, so fewer seeds/fruits form; lower yield of oil and less income.
parts.working: 1 mark: less pollination/fertilisation; 1 mark: fewer seeds/lower yield.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define cross-pollination.
parts.answer: Transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.
parts.working: B1 different plant of same species.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In some flowers the anthers release pollen several days before the stigma of the same flower is ready. Suggest the advantage of this to the plant.
parts.answer: It prevents self-pollination, so cross-pollination happens; this increases genetic variation in the offspring.
parts.working: B1 prevents self-pollination / promotes cross-pollination; B1 more variation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why genetic variation can help a population of plants survive if the climate changes.
parts.answer: Some individuals may have features better suited to the new conditions; they survive and reproduce, passing on these features.
parts.working: B1 some better adapted; B1 survive and reproduce / pass on alleles.

practice.stem: Date palms in Khairpur are either male trees or female trees. Only female trees produce dates. Farmers cut flower stalks from male trees and tie them among the flowers of female trees. Pollen from one male tree is enough for about 50 female trees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the minimum number of male trees a farmer needs to pollinate an orchard of 600 female trees.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why farmers pollinate the flowers by hand instead of relying on wind.
parts.answer: Wind pollination is unreliable / much pollen is wasted; hand pollination makes sure pollen reaches every female flower cluster, so more fruits set and yield is higher; fewer male trees need to be grown.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: wind unreliable/wasteful; ensures pollination of all female flowers; higher yield; fewer male trees needed / more space for fruiting trees.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Date palms are usually grown from offshoots taken from the base of a female tree with good fruit. Explain why the farmer does not grow new trees from the seeds of the dates.
parts.answer: Seeds come from sexual reproduction, so offspring show variation and may not have the good fruit qualities; about half the seedlings would be male and produce no fruit; offshoots are genetically identical to the parent female tree.
parts.working: 1 mark each: seeds show variation / not identical; about half the seedlings would be male; offshoots are clones of the good female tree.

practice.stem:
A student placed drops of sucrose solution of different concentrations on microscope slides and sprinkled pollen from a tomato flower onto each drop. After 2 hours at 25 °C she looked at 50 grains on each slide and counted how many had grown a pollen tube.
Sucrose concentration / %: 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20
Number of grains with a pollen tube (out of 50): 4 | 18 | 31 | 22 | 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of pollen grains that germinated at each concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sucrose concentration that gave the most germination.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why very few pollen grains germinated in distilled water (0 %).
parts.answer: There is no sugar to supply energy (by respiration) for pollen tube growth; and/or water enters by osmosis and the grains may burst.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: no sugar for energy/respiration; water enters by osmosis; grains burst.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why germination was low at 20 % sucrose.
parts.answer: The solution has a low water potential; water leaves the pollen grains by osmosis, so they cannot grow tubes.
parts.working: 1 mark: low water potential / concentrated; 1 mark: water lost by osmosis.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest what the sucrose solution on the slide represents in a flower.
parts.answer: The sugary fluid on the stigma (stigma surface).

practice.stem: A plant breeder wants to cross tomato plant X, which resists a fungal disease, with tomato plant Y, which has large fruit. Tomato flowers normally self-pollinate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps the breeder should take so that the seeds come only from the cross she wants.
parts.answer: Choose a flower on plant X before its anthers are ripe (bud stage) and remove its anthers; cover it with a paper/muslin bag to keep out insects/other pollen; when the stigma is ready, collect ripe pollen from plant Y with a clean brush and dust it on the stigma; re-cover with the bag and label it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: remove anthers of X before they release pollen; bag the flower; transfer pollen from Y with brush when stigma ready; re-bag/label (or sterilise brush).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the anthers must be removed before they release pollen.
parts.answer: To prevent self-pollination of plant X with its own pollen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seedlings grown from these seeds are not all identical.
parts.answer: They come from sexual reproduction; each seed forms from a different pollen grain (male gamete) and ovule (female gamete), which carry different combinations of alleles (from meiosis).
parts.working: 1 mark: sexual reproduction / fusion of gametes; 1 mark: gametes differ genetically.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes asexual reproduction?
A Two parents produce offspring that show variation.
B One parent produces offspring that are genetically identical to it.
C Gametes fuse to form a zygote.
D Offspring are produced only from seeds.
parts.answer: B One parent produces offspring that are genetically identical to it.
parts.working: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gametes, giving genetically identical offspring. C describes sexual reproduction (fertilisation).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of asexual reproduction?
A A pollen grain fertilises an ovule of a mango tree.
B Sprouts grow from the "eyes" of a potato tuber and form new plants.
C Two goats mate and produce a kid.
D A sperm fertilises an egg in a fish.
parts.answer: B Sprouts grow from the "eyes" of a potato tuber and form new plants.
parts.working: A new potato plant from a tuber is produced from one parent without gametes, so it is asexual. A, C and D all involve the fusion of gametes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by asexual reproduction.
parts.answer: A process resulting in the production of genetically identical offspring from one parent (no gametes / no fertilisation).
parts.working: 1 mark: one parent (no fusion of gametes); 1 mark: offspring genetically identical to the parent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of nuclear division used to make the new cells in asexual reproduction.
parts.answer: Mitosis

practice.stem: In warm, cooked rice left out of a fridge, one kind of bacterium can divide into two every 25 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of times the bacteria divide in 5 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of bacteria after 5 hours, starting from one bacterium.
parts.working: M1 2 raised to the power 12; A1 4096.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why all the bacteria are genetically identical.
parts.answer: They are produced by asexual reproduction (binary fission) from one parent, with no fusion of gametes.

practice.stem: Some onion plants form small new bulbs (offsets) at the base of the parent bulb. These separate and grow into new plants.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of cell division that produces new cells in a growing onion bulb offset.
parts.answer: Mitosis

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why offsets from one onion are genetically identical to the parent.
parts.answer: Mitosis produces cells with exactly the same chromosomes/genes as the parent cell; no gametes or fertilisation are involved, so no new combinations of alleles.
parts.working: 1 mark: mitosis copies chromosomes exactly; 1 mark: no fusion of gametes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature of the offspring of sexual reproduction that is different.
parts.answer: They show genetic variation (not identical to each other or to the parents).

practice.stem: Farmers in Sindh grow new sugarcane plants by planting pieces of stem cut from a high-yielding crop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages to the farmer of growing sugarcane from stem cuttings rather than from seeds.
parts.answer: All plants identical to a high-yielding parent; faster growth/quicker crop; no pollination or seed needed; uniform crop ripens at the same time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of this method.
parts.answer: No variation, so all plants could be killed by the same disease or change in conditions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of cell division that produces the cells of the new plants.
parts.answer: mitosis

practice.stem: Strawberry plants growing in hill gardens in Swat produce runners. A runner is a long side stem that grows along the ground; where it touches the soil it forms roots and a new plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two advantages to a wild strawberry plant of reproducing by runners.
parts.answer: Any two: quick way to spread/colonise nearby ground; no need for pollinators or a mate; young plants are fed by the parent until rooted; offspring keep all the parent's alleles that suit the local conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage to the strawberry population of reproducing only by runners.
parts.answer: No genetic variation, so if conditions change or a disease arrives, all plants may be affected / overcrowding and competition near the parent.

practice.stem: A student compares asexual reproduction with sexual reproduction.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the comparison by writing the answer for each method.
(i) number of parents needed
(ii) gametes produced (yes/no)
(iii) genetic variation in offspring (yes/no)
(iv) which method usually produces offspring faster
parts.answer: (i) asexual: one; sexual: usually two. (ii) asexual: no; sexual: yes. (iii) asexual: no; sexual: yes. (iv) asexual.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly completed row.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding. State what happens to a bud.
parts.answer: A small outgrowth grows from the parent cell, receives a nucleus made by mitosis, and separates as a new cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: bud grows from parent and separates (with copy of nucleus).

practice.stem:
A student took five stem cuttings, each 10 cm long with two leaves, from one money plant (pothos) and placed them in jars of water on a windowsill. After 3 weeks she counted the roots on each cutting.
Cutting: 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
Number of roots: 6 | 9 | 7 | 8 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of roots per cutting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the new plants are genetically identical to the parent plant.
parts.answer: They are produced from one parent by asexual reproduction; the new cells are made by mitosis, which produces genetically identical cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: asexual / one parent; 1 mark: mitosis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Use more cuttings / repeat the investigation and find a mean.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one variable that should be controlled.
parts.answer: Any one: length of cutting; number of leaves; temperature; light; volume of water; time.

practice.stem:
A student grew five plants of one hibiscus variety from cuttings of one parent and five plants from seeds of the same parent. All were grown in the same compost under the same conditions. Heights after 8 weeks:
From cuttings / cm: 52, 54, 53, 55, 51
From seeds / cm: 38, 61, 47, 70, 44

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of heights for each group.
parts.answer: cuttings: 4 cm; seeds: 32 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in the ranges.
parts.answer: Plants from cuttings are genetically identical (asexual), so they vary only because of small differences in the environment; plants from seeds come from sexual reproduction, so each has a different combination of alleles; this genetic variation gives a much wider range of heights.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cuttings genetically identical; seeds from sexual reproduction / fusion of gametes; seedlings genetically different.

practice.stem: Most bananas grown for sale are produced asexually from suckers, so all the plants in a large plantation are genetically identical.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a fungal disease can destroy a whole plantation of bananas grown asexually.
parts.answer: The plants are genetically identical (clones); if one is not resistant, none are; so the disease can spread to and kill every plant.
parts.working: B1 genetically identical / no variation; B1 none has resistance; B1 disease spreads through all.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how sexual reproduction could help produce bananas resistant to the disease.
parts.answer: It produces offspring with genetic variation; some may be resistant, and these can be selected and bred.
parts.working: B1 variation; B1 resistant individuals selected.

practice.stem: Wild potato plants reproduce asexually by tubers and also produce flowers and seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the advantage to a wild potato plant of producing tubers.
parts.answer: Tubers store food (starch) so the plant survives cold/dry seasons; new plants grow quickly from the store in the next season, without needing pollination.
parts.working: 1 mark: food store / survival over unfavourable season; 1 mark: rapid growth of new plants / no need for pollinators.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the advantage to the same wild plant of also producing flowers and seeds.
parts.answer: Sexual reproduction produces genetic variation; some offspring may survive new diseases or changes in the environment / allows adaptation (natural selection); seeds can be dispersed far from the parent, reducing competition and colonising new areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each: variation; survival if conditions change/disease; dispersal to new areas / less competition.

practice.stem: Kinnow (mandarin) orchards in Sargodha are planted with grafted trees. A shoot (scion) cut from a high-quality kinnow tree is joined onto the stem and roots (rootstock) of a young seedling of a hardy citrus variety. The scion then grows to form the fruiting part of the tree.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why every fruit from the grafted trees has the same flavour and size.
parts.answer: The fruiting part (scion) of every tree comes from the same parent tree by asexual means; so all have the same genes (clones), and in the same conditions grow the same fruit.
parts.working: 1 mark: scions are clones / genetically identical; 1 mark: same genes give same fruit features.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the scion is grafted onto a rootstock rather than grown from a cutting with its own roots.
parts.answer: The rootstock may have a strong/resistant root system (resists soil disease or drought, tolerates poor soil); trees become established and fruit sooner.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible reasons.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rootstocks are grown from seeds. Suggest why the rootstocks differ from each other while the fruit on every tree is the same.
parts.answer: Seeds come from sexual reproduction, so each rootstock has a different combination of alleles (genetic variation); the fruit is produced by the scion, which carries the genes of the one parent kinnow tree, so its features are the same on every tree.
parts.working: 1 mark: rootstocks from sexual reproduction / genetically different; 1 mark: fruit features controlled by the scion's (identical) genes.

practice.stem: A nursery in Lahore takes 400 stem cuttings from one prize rose plant. 85 % of the cuttings form roots. Of the rooted cuttings, 5 % die before they can be sold.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of plants that survive to be sold.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Before they form roots, the cuttings are kept in a closed, humid, shaded propagator. Explain why.
parts.answer: The cuttings have no roots, so they cannot absorb water to replace water lost from the leaves; high humidity and shade reduce transpiration, so the cuttings do not wilt or die before roots grow.
parts.working: 1 mark: no roots / cannot take up water; 1 mark: humidity/shade reduce transpiration (water loss), preventing wilting.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a risk of selling only these plants to gardeners across a whole city.
parts.answer: They have no genetic variation, so one disease or pest could damage all of them.

practice.stem: In a plant laboratory, a banana shoot tip is grown on a sterile jelly containing nutrients and plant hormones. Every 4 weeks each shoot divides into 4 new shoots, which are separated and placed on fresh jelly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of plantlets produced from one shoot tip after 16 weeks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two advantages to a farmer of buying banana plantlets made in this way.
parts.answer: Any two: very large numbers produced quickly; all identical with known good fruit; disease-free (grown in sterile conditions); can be produced at any time of year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this method is a form of asexual reproduction.
parts.answer: Only one parent plant is used; new cells are made by mitosis; no gametes / no fertilisation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a 28-day menstrual cycle, state the days on which menstruation (bleeding) usually happens.
parts.answer: days 1–5

parts.label: b
parts.text: State on which day ovulation usually happens.
parts.answer: about day 14

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the hormone made by the ovary that causes the lining of the uterus to thicken (repair) after menstruation.
parts.answer: oestrogen

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the hormone that keeps the uterus lining thick after ovulation.
parts.answer: progesterone

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone stimulates a follicle containing an egg to develop in the ovary?
A FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone)
B progesterone
C testosterone
D insulin
parts.answer: A FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone)
parts.working: FSH from the pituitary gland causes a follicle (and its egg) to develop. Progesterone (B) maintains the uterus lining after ovulation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gland that secretes FSH and LH.
parts.answer: Pituitary gland

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that secretes oestrogen and progesterone.
parts.answer: Ovary

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the name given to the release of an egg from the ovary.
parts.answer: Ovulation

parts.label: d
parts.text: State where in the female reproductive system an egg travels after it is released.
parts.answer: Into the oviduct (fallopian tube)

practice.stem: In a typical 28-day menstrual cycle, day 1 is the first day of menstruation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the lining of the uterus during days 1 to 5.
parts.answer: It breaks down and is lost through the vagina with some blood (menstruation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to the lining between day 6 and day 14.
parts.answer: It is repaired and becomes thicker (builds up again).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lining stays thick from day 14 to about day 26.
parts.answer: Progesterone keeps the lining thick and with a good blood supply; ready for a fertilised egg/embryo to implant.
parts.working: 1 mark: progesterone maintains it; 1 mark: ready for implantation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the female sex hormone that causes the development of female secondary sexual characteristics at puberty.
parts.answer: Oestrogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two secondary sexual characteristics that develop in girls.
parts.answer: Any two: breasts develop; hips widen; pubic and underarm hair grows; menstrual cycle begins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the hormone that causes secondary sexual characteristics in boys and the organ that secretes it.
parts.answer: Testosterone; testes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which hormone causes ovulation to take place?
A oestrogen
B progesterone
C LH (luteinising hormone)
D testosterone
parts.answer: C LH (luteinising hormone)
parts.working: A surge of LH from the pituitary gland triggers the release of an egg. Oestrogen (A) rises before ovulation but does not itself release the egg.

practice.stem:
Blood samples were taken from a woman during one 28-day cycle. The pattern of three hormones is described below.
Hormone W: low until day 6, rises to a peak on day 12, falls, then rises a little again around day 21.
Hormone X: low for most of the cycle but rises very sharply to a short peak on day 13–14.
Hormone Y: low until day 14, rises to a peak around day 21, then falls to a low level by day 28.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify hormones W, X and Y. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: W is oestrogen – it rises as the follicle develops and peaks before ovulation; X is LH – it has a sudden sharp peak just before/at ovulation (day 14); Y is progesterone – it is high after ovulation (from the corpus luteum) and falls before menstruation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the hormone with a matching reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why menstruation starts on about day 28 if no egg is fertilised.
parts.answer: The level of progesterone (and oestrogen) falls; without progesterone the uterus lining is not maintained, so it breaks down.
parts.working: 1 mark: progesterone falls; 1 mark: lining no longer maintained / breaks down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the structure in the ovary that secretes progesterone after ovulation.
parts.answer: Corpus luteum (the empty follicle) – accept "the follicle after ovulation".

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two effects of progesterone in the menstrual cycle.
parts.answer: Any two: maintains the thick uterus lining; keeps the lining supplied with blood; inhibits FSH and LH so no new follicle develops.

parts.label: c
parts.text: If an egg is fertilised and implants, menstruation does not happen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Progesterone stays high (from the corpus luteum, then the placenta); so the uterus lining is maintained and not shed.
parts.working: 1 mark: progesterone remains high; 1 mark: lining kept / not shed.

practice.stem: A woman has a regular menstrual cycle of 30 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ovulation usually happens about 14 days before the next period starts. Calculate the day of her cycle on which she is most likely to ovulate.
parts.answer: Day 16

parts.label: b
parts.text: Her latest period started on 5 June (day 1). Predict the date on which she is most likely to ovulate.
parts.answer: 20 June
parts.working: A1 day 1 = 5 June, so day 16 = 5 + 16 − 1 = 20 June.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a woman can become pregnant after sexual intercourse a few days before ovulation.
parts.answer: Sperm can survive in the female reproductive system for several days; so sperm may still be alive in the oviduct when the egg is released.
parts.working: 1 mark: sperm survive several days; 1 mark: still present when ovulation happens.

practice.stem:
The thickness of the uterus lining of a woman was measured by ultrasound scan on several days of one 28-day cycle.
Day: 1 | 5 | 10 | 14 | 21 | 28
Thickness / mm: 4 | 1 | 3 | 5 | 7 | 4.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the day on which the lining was thinnest and suggest why.
parts.answer: Day 5; the lining has been shed during menstruation (days 1–5).
parts.working: 1 mark: day 5; 1 mark: menstruation / lining lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in thickness between day 5 and day 21, in mm per day.
parts.answer: 0.375 mm per day (accept 0.38)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the hormone mainly responsible for the increase in thickness between day 5 and day 14.
parts.answer: Oestrogen

practice.stem: A woman recorded the lengths of five of her menstrual cycles: 27, 29, 30, 28 and 26 days.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length of the five cycles.
parts.answer: 28.0 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Her last period started on 3 March. Use the mean cycle length to predict the date her next period will start.
parts.answer: 31 March

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the lining of the uterus breaks down if the egg is not fertilised.
parts.answer: The corpus luteum (yellow body) in the ovary breaks down; so less progesterone is made; progesterone no longer maintains the lining, so it breaks down (menstruation).
parts.working: B1 corpus luteum breaks down; B1 progesterone falls; B1 lining no longer maintained → menstruation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Name the gland that releases FSH and state one effect of FSH.
parts.answer: Pituitary gland; FSH causes an egg (follicle) to develop in the ovary / stimulates oestrogen release.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a combined contraceptive pill containing oestrogen and progesterone prevents pregnancy.
parts.answer: The high levels of oestrogen and progesterone inhibit the secretion of FSH and LH by the pituitary gland; without FSH no follicle develops; without the LH surge there is no ovulation, so no egg is available to be fertilised.
parts.working: 1 mark each: inhibits FSH/LH from pituitary; no follicle/egg matures; no ovulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The pill is taken for 21 days and then not taken for 7 days. Suggest why bleeding happens during the 7 days.
parts.answer: Hormone levels in the blood fall when the pill is stopped; the uterus lining is no longer maintained and breaks down.
parts.working: 1 mark: hormone (progesterone) levels fall; 1 mark: lining breaks down.

practice.stem: Some women who are not ovulating are given injections of FSH as a fertility treatment. In one clinic, 25 % of pregnancies after this treatment were twins, compared with about 1.5 % of pregnancies in the general population.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the FSH injections can lead to the release of more than one egg.
parts.answer: FSH stimulates follicles to develop; a large dose stimulates several follicles at once, so several eggs may mature and be released.
parts.working: 1 mark: FSH causes follicle development; 1 mark: high dose → several follicles/eggs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more likely twins are in this clinic than in the general population. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 16.7 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the twins born after this treatment are usually not identical.
parts.answer: They develop from two different eggs fertilised by two different sperm; each egg and sperm has a different combination of alleles (from meiosis).
parts.working: 1 mark: two eggs + two sperm; 1 mark: different genetic information.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a woman does not have menstrual cycles while she is pregnant.
parts.answer: The placenta (and corpus luteum) secretes progesterone, so progesterone stays high; this keeps the uterus lining in place; and inhibits FSH (and LH) secretion, so no new follicles develop and no ovulation happens.
parts.working: 1 mark each: high progesterone from placenta; lining maintained; FSH/LH inhibited so no ovulation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a fall in progesterone near the end of pregnancy may be linked to the start of birth.
parts.answer: Progesterone keeps the uterus muscle relaxed / maintains the lining; when it falls, the muscles of the uterus wall can start to contract.
parts.working: 1 mark: progesterone maintains pregnancy; 1 mark: fall allows contractions to begin.

practice.stem:
A woman measured her body temperature each morning before getting up.
Day of cycle: 11 | 12 | 13 | 14 | 15 | 16 | 17 | 18
Temperature / °C: 36.3 | 36.2 | 36.3 | 36.1 | 36.6 | 36.7 | 36.7 | 36.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the day on which ovulation most likely happened. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Day 14 (accept day 14–15); temperature is lowest on day 14 and rises to a higher level from day 15 onwards, after ovulation.
parts.working: 1 mark: day 14 (or 14–15); 1 mark: the rise in temperature begins after it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rise in temperature is caused by a hormone that increases after ovulation. Name this hormone.
parts.answer: Progesterone

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the highest temperature recorded on days 15–18 and the lowest temperature recorded on days 11–14.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this method can only show that ovulation has already happened and cannot be used to predict it in the same cycle.
parts.answer: The temperature rises only after ovulation (when progesterone is secreted); so by the time the rise is seen, the egg has already been released.
parts.working: 1 mark: rise follows ovulation; 1 mark: no change before ovulation to warn in advance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the amniotic fluid.
parts.answer: Protects the fetus from mechanical shock / bumps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the umbilical cord.
parts.answer: Carries blood vessels linking the fetus to the placenta.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens during birth.
parts.answer: Muscles of the uterus wall contract; the cervix widens (dilates); the amniotic sac breaks; the baby is pushed out through the vagina head first; the placenta is pushed out afterwards.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one advantage of breast-feeding a baby.
parts.answer: Contains antibodies / right balance of nutrients / free and sterile / bonding.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where in the female reproductive system fertilisation usually takes place.
parts.answer: Oviduct

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the zygote does as it travels towards the uterus.
parts.answer: It divides by mitosis to form a ball of cells (embryo).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process in which the embryo sinks into the lining of the uterus.
parts.answer: Implantation

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two functions of the placenta.
parts.answer: Any two: exchange of substances between mother and fetus (oxygen, nutrients in; carbon dioxide, urea out); secretes hormones (progesterone); acts as a barrier to some pathogens and toxins; keeps the two blood systems separate.

practice.stem: A health worker in a rural clinic gives advice to a pregnant woman.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pregnant woman is advised not to smoke.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried by her blood, and nicotine/other chemicals cross the placenta; so the fetus gets less oxygen and may grow less (low birth mass / premature).
parts.working: 1 mark: harmful substances (carbon monoxide/nicotine) reach the fetus; 1 mark: less oxygen / low birth mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why she is advised not to drink alcohol.
parts.answer: Alcohol crosses the placenta; it can damage the development of the fetus (especially the brain).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why her diet should contain extra iron.
parts.answer: To make extra haemoglobin/red blood cells for herself and the fetus.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these events in the correct order, starting with the earliest:
birth; implantation; ovulation; fertilisation; development of the placenta
parts.answer: ovulation → fertilisation → implantation → development of the placenta → birth
parts.working: 2 marks for all in the correct order; 1 mark if one pair is swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the approximate length of a human pregnancy in weeks.
parts.answer: About 40 weeks (accept 38–40).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the bag of fluid that surrounds the fetus.
parts.answer: Amniotic sac (amnion)

parts.label: a
parts.text: At the start of birth, the muscles in the wall of the uterus begin to contract. State the effect of these contractions.
parts.answer: They push the baby out of the uterus, through the cervix and vagina.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the cervix at the start of birth.
parts.answer: It widens (dilates).

parts.label: c
parts.text: After birth the umbilical cord is clamped and cut. Explain why the baby must start to breathe straight away.
parts.answer: The baby no longer receives oxygen from the mother's blood through the placenta and umbilical cord; it must take in oxygen through its own lungs for respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: no more oxygen from the placenta/cord; 1 mark: lungs must now supply oxygen for respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two substances that pass from the mother's blood to the fetus across the placenta and one that passes from the fetus to the mother.
parts.answer: To fetus: any two of oxygen, glucose, amino acids, water, mineral ions, antibodies; to mother: carbon dioxide or urea.
parts.working: B1 B1 to fetus; B1 to mother.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The blood of the mother and the fetus do not mix. Suggest one reason why this is important.
parts.answer: Mother's higher blood pressure could damage the fetus's vessels / blood groups may be incompatible / reduces passage of some pathogens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature of the placenta that helps exchange of substances.
parts.answer: Large surface area (villi) / thin barrier / good blood supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The placenta has many finger-like villi. Explain how this helps the exchange of substances.
parts.answer: The villi give a very large surface area; so more substances diffuse (or are transported) across per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: large surface area; 1 mark: faster exchange.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a thin barrier between the maternal blood and the fetal blood is important.
parts.answer: Short diffusion distance; so oxygen and nutrients diffuse quickly to the fetus and wastes diffuse to the mother.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the fetal blood must flow quickly through the placenta.
parts.answer: Blood that has collected oxygen/nutrients is carried away and replaced with blood low in them; this keeps a steep concentration gradient for diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood replaced continuously; 1 mark: maintains concentration gradient.

practice.stem:
The table shows the typical mass of a human fetus at different stages of pregnancy.
Week of pregnancy: 12 | 20 | 28 | 36 | 40
Mass / g: 14 | 300 | 1000 | 2600 | 3400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in mass between week 28 and week 36, in g per week.
parts.answer: 200 g per week

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two substances the fetus must obtain from the mother to increase its mass in this way.
parts.answer: Any two: glucose; amino acids; fatty acids/lipids; minerals such as calcium or iron; water; vitamins; oxygen (for respiration).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a baby born at week 28 may need help to breathe.
parts.answer: Its lungs are not fully developed (alveoli not mature).

practice.stem:
Blood samples were taken from the two kinds of blood vessel in the umbilical cord of a baby just after birth. Vessel P carries blood from the fetus to the placenta; vessel Q carries blood from the placenta to the fetus.
Glucose / mg per 100 cm³: P 60 | Q 85
Urea / mg per 100 cm³: P 28 | Q 22
Oxygen / cm³ per 100 cm³: P 11 | Q 16

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the data to state which substances the fetus gains from the placenta and which it loses to the placenta.
parts.answer: Gains glucose and oxygen (higher in Q, the blood going to the fetus); loses urea (higher in P, the blood leaving the fetus).
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose and oxygen gained; 1 mark: urea lost, with reference to the higher value in P or Q.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the concentration of urea is higher in vessel P than in vessel Q.
parts.answer: The fetus makes urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids (in its liver); urea diffuses from the fetal blood across the placenta into the mother's blood, so blood returning to the fetus contains less.
parts.working: 1 mark: urea is a waste made by the fetus; 1 mark: it diffuses into the mother's blood in the placenta / mother excretes it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the oxygen concentration in vessel Q is lower than in the mother's arteries.
parts.answer: Oxygen moves by diffusion, which needs a concentration gradient, so the fetal blood can only reach a lower concentration than the mother's blood (and the placenta itself uses some oxygen for respiration).
parts.working: 1 mark: diffusion down a gradient / placenta respires.

practice.stem: Some babies are born early, at about 30 weeks of pregnancy, and are cared for in a neonatal unit in a hospital in Karachi.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why a baby born at 30 weeks is kept in a warm incubator.
parts.answer: It has little fat under the skin / a large surface area to volume ratio and an immature temperature control; so it loses heat quickly and could become too cold.
parts.working: 1 mark: loses heat easily (little fat / large SA:V); 1 mark: cannot control body temperature well.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the baby may need to be given extra oxygen.
parts.answer: Its lungs are not fully developed / alveoli not mature; so not enough oxygen diffuses into the blood.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Before birth the baby did not need to breathe. Explain how it obtained oxygen.
parts.answer: Oxygen diffused from the mother's blood across the placenta into its blood.

practice.stem: A hospital survey found that the mean birth mass of babies born to mothers who did not smoke was 3.4 kg, and of babies born to mothers who smoked during pregnancy was 3.1 kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the mean birth mass of babies of smokers is lower than that of non-smokers. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how smoking during pregnancy can reduce the growth of the fetus.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide from smoke enters the mother's blood and combines with haemoglobin; less oxygen is carried across the placenta to the fetus; less aerobic respiration/energy for growth (nicotine also crosses the placenta).
parts.working: B1 carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin; B1 less oxygen to fetus; B1 less respiration / growth (or harmful chemicals cross placenta).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one pathogen that can cross the placenta.
parts.answer: HIV (or rubella virus)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Antibodies from the mother cross the placenta into the fetus. Explain how this protects the newborn baby.
parts.answer: The baby has antibodies against pathogens the mother has met; these destroy/neutralise those pathogens if the baby is infected in the first months (passive immunity).
parts.working: 1 mark: ready-made antibodies against specific pathogens; 1 mark: passive immunity / immediate protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this protection lasts only a few months.
parts.answer: The antibodies are not made by the baby's own lymphocytes / no memory cells are formed; they are broken down over time and not replaced.
parts.working: 1 mark: no memory cells / not made by baby; 1 mark: antibodies broken down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why breast-feeding continues this protection.
parts.answer: Breast milk contains antibodies from the mother.

practice.stem: Near the end of pregnancy, 300 cm³ of fetal blood flows through the placenta each minute. Blood entering the placenta from the fetus contains 12 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³; blood returning to the fetus contains 16 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the blood vessel in the umbilical cord that carries this oxygen-rich blood to the fetus.
parts.answer: Umbilical vein

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen the fetus receives from the placenta each minute, and each hour.
parts.answer: 12 cm³ per minute; 720 cm³ per hour
parts.working: M1 increase = 16 − 12 = 4 cm³ per 100 cm³; M1 300 × 4 ÷ 100 = 12 cm³/min; A1 × 60 = 720 cm³/h.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how oxygen passes from the mother to the fetus although the two bloods do not mix.
parts.answer: The concentration of oxygen in the maternal blood is higher than in the fetal blood; oxygen diffuses across the thin placental barrier into the fetal capillaries.
parts.working: 1 mark: concentration gradient; 1 mark: diffusion across thin placenta.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how identical twins are formed.
parts.answer: One egg is fertilised by one sperm; the zygote/early embryo splits into two, and each part develops into a baby.
parts.working: 1 mark: one egg and one sperm; 1 mark: embryo splits into two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how non-identical twins are formed.
parts.answer: Two eggs are released at the same time; each is fertilised by a different sperm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why identical twins can share one placenta but non-identical twins each have their own.
