parts.text: Suggest two advantages of blood from the gut passing through the liver before reaching the rest of the body.
parts.answer: Excess glucose can be stored as glycogen, so blood glucose stays steady; excess amino acids are deaminated; toxins such as alcohol are broken down.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the liver also needs blood from the hepatic artery.
parts.answer: Blood in the hepatic portal vein has already given up much of its oxygen in the gut; the hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood at higher pressure for the liver cells' respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: portal blood low in oxygen; 1 mark: artery supplies oxygen for respiration of liver cells.

practice.stem:
The volume of oxygen in 100 cm³ of blood was measured in four vessels.
vessel | W | X | Y | Z
oxygen / cm³ per 100 cm³ blood | 19.5 | 14.5 | 19.5 | 14.5
W is the aorta and X is the vena cava.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Y and Z are the pulmonary artery and the pulmonary vein. Identify Y and Z and explain your answer.
parts.answer: Y pulmonary vein (oxygenated, coming from lungs); Z pulmonary artery (deoxygenated, going to lungs)
parts.working: 1 mark for both identified; 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen given up to the body tissues by every 100 cm³ of blood.
parts.answer: 5.0 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: At rest the heart pumps 5000 cm³ of blood to the body each minute. Calculate the volume of oxygen used by the body tissues each minute.
parts.answer: 250 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Plasma transports many substances. Complete each line by naming where the substance is carried from and to.
(i) glucose
(ii) urea
(iii) carbon dioxide
(iv) insulin
parts.answer: (i) small intestine (via liver) to body cells / respiring tissues; (ii) liver to kidneys; (iii) respiring cells to lungs; (iv) pancreas to liver (and other target cells).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other substances carried in plasma.
parts.answer: Any two of: amino acids, mineral ions (e.g. sodium), plasma proteins (e.g. fibrinogen, antibodies), water, vitamins, fatty acids, other hormones, heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the red pigment in red blood cells.
parts.answer: haemoglobin

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the mineral element that this pigment contains.
parts.answer: iron

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the compound formed when the pigment combines with oxygen in the lungs.
parts.answer: oxyhaemoglobin

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one deficiency disease caused by a lack of the mineral element in the diet and one symptom.
parts.answer: anaemia; tiredness / breathlessness / pale skin

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of white blood cell that produces antibodies.
parts.answer: lymphocyte

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an antibody that attaches to the measles virus does not attach to the polio virus.
parts.answer: Antibodies are specific; each has a shape that is complementary to (fits) only one particular antigen, and the polio virus has differently shaped antigens.
parts.working: 1 mark: specific / complementary shape; 1 mark: different antigen on polio virus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: they mark pathogens so phagocytes engulf them / they cause pathogens to stick together (clump) / they neutralise toxins

practice.stem:
These statements describe how a blood clot forms when a boy grazes his knee on a cricket pitch, but they are in the wrong order.
A a mesh of fibrin threads traps red blood cells
B the skin and blood vessels are damaged
C soluble fibrinogen in the plasma is changed into insoluble fibrin
D platelets at the wound release chemicals

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the letters in the correct order.
parts.answer: B, D, C, A
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark if B first and A last.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fibrinogen is always present in the plasma. Suggest why clots do not normally form inside undamaged blood vessels.
parts.answer: Fibrinogen is only changed into fibrin when platelets at damaged tissue release chemicals; in undamaged vessels this does not happen, so fibrinogen stays soluble.
parts.working: 1 mark: conversion to fibrin needs the trigger from platelets/damaged tissue at a wound.

practice.stem: A blood donor gives 450 cm³ of blood. The donor's body replaces the lost plasma in about 2 days, but it takes about 8 weeks to replace the lost red blood cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times longer it takes to replace the red blood cells than the plasma.
parts.answer: 28 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the red blood cells take much longer to replace than the plasma.
parts.answer: New red blood cells must be made by cell division in the bone marrow and filled with haemoglobin; plasma is mainly water, which is quickly absorbed from the gut.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two substances other than water found in plasma.
parts.answer: any two of: glucose, amino acids, urea, hormones, carbon dioxide / hydrogencarbonate ions, mineral ions, plasma proteins (fibrinogen), antibodies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the structure of a red blood cell is adapted to its function.
parts.answer: Contains haemoglobin which combines with oxygen; no nucleus, so more room for haemoglobin; biconcave shape gives a large surface area for diffusion of oxygen; small and flexible so it can squeeze through capillaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how haemoglobin picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it in an actively respiring muscle.
parts.answer: In the lungs oxygen concentration is high, so haemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin; in the muscle oxygen concentration is low (used in respiration), so oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen; oxygen diffuses into the muscle cells.
parts.working: B1 oxyhaemoglobin formed at high oxygen concentration; B1 releases oxygen where concentration low; B1 diffusion into cells.

practice.stem: Haemophilia is a condition in which one of the proteins needed for blood clotting is missing from the plasma.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person with haemophilia may bleed for a long time after a minor cut.
parts.answer: Without the protein, fibrinogen is not converted to fibrin (or only slowly), so no fibrin mesh / clot forms to seal the wound.
parts.working: 1 mark: fibrin not formed; 1 mark: no clot / wound not sealed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a person with haemophilia may also suffer bleeding into their joints after a fall, without any cut in the skin.
parts.answer: Small blood vessels inside the body are damaged and the bleeding does not stop because clots do not form.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Patients are given injections of the missing clotting protein. Suggest why these injections must be repeated regularly.
parts.answer: The protein is broken down / used up in the body and is not made by the patient.

practice.stem: A 14-year-old boy in Peshawar has appendicitis. His white blood cell count rises from 7000 per mm³ to 18 000 per mm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater his white blood cell count has become. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 2.57 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of white blood cell that engulfs the bacteria at the site of infection.
parts.answer: phagocyte

parts.label: c
parts.text: The surgeon removes the infected appendix. Suggest why the boy's white blood cell count returns to normal over the next week.
parts.answer: The source of the bacteria has been removed, so the remaining pathogens are destroyed; fewer white blood cells are then needed, so fewer are produced.
parts.working: 1 mark: source of infection removed / pathogens destroyed; 1 mark: fewer white cells made / needed.

practice.stem: Thalassaemia is an inherited condition, common in Pakistan, in which the body cannot make enough normal haemoglobin. Many children with thalassaemia need a blood transfusion every few weeks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a child with thalassaemia becomes tired and short of breath.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin, so less oxygen is carried to the tissues; less aerobic respiration in muscle cells; less energy released / more anaerobic respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the transfusions must be repeated regularly.
parts.answer: Donated red blood cells only survive a limited time (they are destroyed after about 120 days or less), and the child cannot make enough normal haemoglobin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why donated blood is tested before it is given to a patient.
parts.answer: to make sure it does not contain pathogens such as hepatitis viruses or HIV / that it is a suitable (matching) type

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plasma transports heat as well as dissolved substances. Explain how the blood carries heat from active muscles to the skin.
parts.answer: Muscles release heat during respiration, which warms the blood (plasma is mainly water and absorbs heat); the blood flows to the skin, where heat is lost to the surroundings.
parts.working: 1 mark: heat from respiration absorbed by blood; 1 mark: carried to skin and lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one protein carried in the plasma and state its function.
parts.answer: fibrinogen – blood clotting (or antibodies – destroy/mark pathogens)
parts.working: 1 mark for protein with matching function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the form in which most carbon dioxide is carried in the plasma.
parts.answer: as hydrogencarbonate ions
parts.working: 1 mark: hydrogencarbonate ions (accept 'dissolved in the plasma').

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ways in which blood protects the body against infection.
parts.answer: Clotting seals wounds so pathogens cannot enter; platelets and fibrin form the clot; phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens; lymphocytes produce antibodies; antibodies are specific to an antigen and cause pathogens to clump / be destroyed; some lymphocytes remain as memory cells for a faster response next time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 5.0 cm³ blood sample was spun in a centrifuge. Cells made up 45 % of the volume. Calculate the volume of plasma in cm³.
parts.answer: 2.75 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cells sank to the bottom of the tube.
parts.answer: Cells are denser than plasma.

practice.stem: One gram of haemoglobin can combine with 1.34 cm³ of oxygen. A healthy person has 15 g of haemoglobin in each 100 cm³ of blood; a person with anaemia has 9 g in each 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen carried by 100 cm³ of blood in each person. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: healthy 20.1 cm³; anaemic 12.1 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in oxygen-carrying capacity in the person with anaemia.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The anaemic person's resting heart rate is higher than the healthy person's. Explain why.
parts.answer: Each volume of blood carries less oxygen; the heart must pump blood round faster to deliver the same amount of oxygen to the tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: less oxygen per unit volume; 1 mark: faster circulation keeps oxygen supply up.

practice.stem:
A student looked at a blood smear under a microscope. An eyepiece graticule was calibrated so that 1 graticule division = 2.5 µm. The diameters of eight red blood cells were measured in graticule divisions:
3.0, 2.8, 3.0, 3.2, 2.9, 3.0, 3.1, 2.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter of the red blood cells in graticule divisions.
parts.answer: 2.95 divisions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert the mean diameter to micrometres. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 7.4 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: A white blood cell in the same smear measured 5 graticule divisions across. Calculate its diameter in µm.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the student measured eight cells rather than one.
parts.answer: Cells vary in size; a mean of several is more representative / reliable.

practice.stem: Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and no mitochondria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of having no mitochondria for a cell whose job is to carry oxygen.
parts.answer: The cell does not respire aerobically, so it does not use up the oxygen it is carrying; all of it is delivered to the tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: does not use oxygen itself; 1 mark: more oxygen delivered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how a red blood cell must release energy to stay alive.
parts.answer: by anaerobic respiration (of glucose)

parts.label: c
parts.text: After losing a lot of blood in an accident, a patient is given iron tablets. Explain why.
parts.answer: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; the new red blood cells being made need haemoglobin to carry oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: iron used to make haemoglobin; 1 mark: for new red blood cells / to restore oxygen transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Most carbon dioxide made in a respiring muscle is carried to the lungs as hydrogencarbonate ions in the plasma. Describe how carbon dioxide gets from a muscle cell into the plasma.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide diffuses out of the muscle cell, through the tissue fluid and across the capillary wall into the blood, down a concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark: diffusion down concentration gradient; 1 mark: through tissue fluid and capillary wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why carbon dioxide leaves the blood in the lungs.
parts.answer: The concentration of carbon dioxide in the alveoli is lower than in the blood (because breathing removes it), so it diffuses from the blood into the alveolar air.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower concentration in alveoli; 1 mark: ventilation maintains the gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a build-up of carbon dioxide in the blood is harmful.
parts.answer: It makes the blood more acidic / lowers pH, which affects enzymes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement about tissue fluid is true or false.
(i) It contains red blood cells.
(ii) It contains glucose.
(iii) It forms from plasma that leaks out of capillaries.
(iv) All of it returns into the blood capillaries.
parts.answer: (i) false (ii) true (iii) true (iv) false

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the fluid formed when tissue fluid enters lymph vessels.
parts.answer: lymph

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three substances that pass out of blood capillaries into tissue fluid.
parts.answer: any three of: water, glucose, oxygen, amino acids, mineral ions, hormones

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two components of blood that do not normally pass out of the capillaries, and give the reason.
parts.answer: red blood cells and large plasma proteins (platelets accepted); they are too large to pass through the gaps in the capillary wall
parts.working: 1 mark for two components; 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the vessels in a villus of the small intestine that absorb fats.
parts.answer: lacteals

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where lymph returns to the blood.
parts.answer: into large veins near the heart (in the neck / under the collarbone)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of white blood cell found in large numbers in lymph nodes.
parts.answer: lymphocyte

practice.stem: A student wrote: 'Lymph is the same as blood plasma.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways in which lymph is different from blood plasma.
parts.answer: Lymph contains less protein; contains more lymphocytes; after a meal lymph from the gut contains much more fat.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one function of the lymphatic system.
parts.answer: returns tissue fluid to the blood / transports fats from the gut / defence against infection (lymphocytes in nodes)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how tissue fluid is formed.
parts.answer: High blood pressure at the arterial end of a capillary forces plasma (water and small dissolved substances) out through the capillary wall; this fluid surrounds the cells.
parts.working: B1 pressure forces plasma out of capillaries; B1 fluid (without red cells / large proteins) bathes the cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two functions of tissue fluid.
parts.answer: It carries oxygen, glucose and other nutrients to cells; it carries carbon dioxide and other wastes away from cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe what happens to the tissue fluid that does not return to the capillaries.
parts.answer: It drains into lymph vessels and becomes lymph; it is returned to the blood in veins near the heart.
parts.working: B1 enters lymphatic vessels as lymph; B1 returned to blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The heart does not pump lymph. Describe how lymph is moved through the lymph vessels.
parts.answer: Lymph vessels are squeezed by the contraction of nearby skeletal muscles (and by breathing movements); valves in the lymph vessels prevent backflow, so lymph moves in one direction towards the heart.
parts.working: 1 mark: squeezed by muscle contraction; 1 mark: valves; 1 mark: one direction / towards the veins near the heart.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what would happen in the legs if the valves in the lymph vessels there were damaged.
parts.answer: Lymph would flow back down the vessels under gravity, so tissue fluid would not drain from the legs; fluid would collect and the legs would swell.
parts.working: 1 mark: backflow / lymph not moved upwards; 1 mark: tissue fluid builds up / swelling.

practice.stem: During a throat infection, a girl notices small painful swellings in her neck. The doctor tells her these are swollen lymph nodes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the lymph nodes in her neck have become swollen.
parts.answer: Pathogens from the infected throat are carried in the lymph to the nodes; lymphocytes in the nodes divide to make more cells; these produce antibodies / the node fills with white cells, so it enlarges.
parts.working: 1 mark: pathogens carried to nodes in lymph; 1 mark: lymphocytes multiply; 1 mark: antibody production / phagocytes destroy pathogens.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the swelling goes down after a week or two.
parts.answer: The pathogens have been destroyed, so fewer lymphocytes are needed / numbers fall.

practice.stem: In a capillary in a muscle, the pressure of the blood is 4.3 kPa at the arterial end and 2.0 kPa at the venous end.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why tissue fluid is forced out of the capillary at the arterial end.
parts.answer: The blood pressure there is high (higher than the pressure of the tissue fluid), so water and small solutes are squeezed out through the gaps in the capillary wall.
parts.working: 1 mark: high pressure at arterial end; 1 mark: fluid forced through capillary wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why much of the water re-enters the capillary at the venous end.
parts.answer: Pressure is lower there; the plasma proteins left in the blood make its water potential lower, so water returns by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: lower pressure; 1 mark: osmosis / lower water potential due to proteins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the fall in pressure along the capillary as a percentage of the pressure at the arterial end. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

practice.stem: After a 20-hour bus journey from Karachi to Lahore, a passenger finds that her ankles are swollen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why tissue fluid collected around her ankles.
parts.answer: She sat still, so leg muscles did not contract to squeeze lymph and veins; tissue fluid was not drained by the lymph vessels as fast as it formed; gravity pulls fluid down to the ankles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one thing she could do on the next journey to reduce the swelling.
parts.answer: walk around at stops / move or flex her legs and feet / raise her feet

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route by which an oxygen molecule passes from a red blood cell in a capillary to a mitochondrion in a muscle cell.
parts.answer: Oxygen is released from oxyhaemoglobin, diffuses through the plasma and the capillary wall into the tissue fluid, then across the cell membrane into the muscle cell (and to the mitochondrion).
parts.working: 1 mark: released from oxyhaemoglobin; 1 mark: through capillary wall into tissue fluid; 1 mark: across cell membrane by diffusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the oxygen moves in this direction.
parts.answer: Oxygen concentration is lower in the respiring muscle cell than in the blood, so it diffuses down the gradient.

practice.stem: In an adult, about 20 dm³ of fluid leaves the blood capillaries each day to form tissue fluid. About 17 dm³ of this returns directly into the capillaries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the fluid that returns to the blood through the lymphatic system each day.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a disease spread by mosquitoes, small worms block lymph vessels in the legs. The legs become very swollen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Tissue fluid cannot drain into the lymph vessels; fluid builds up in the tissues, causing swelling.
parts.working: B1 lymph cannot drain; B1 fluid accumulates in tissues.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Lymph passes through lymph nodes. State the function of the lymph nodes.
parts.answer: They contain lymphocytes (and phagocytes) that destroy pathogens / produce antibodies, filtering the lymph.
parts.working: B1 contain lymphocytes; B1 destroy pathogens / produce antibodies.

practice.stem: Kwashiorkor is a condition in young children whose diet contains very little protein. The children have swollen bellies and legs because a lot of tissue fluid collects. The concentration of proteins in their blood plasma is very low.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the low concentration of plasma proteins causes tissue fluid to collect.
parts.answer: Plasma proteins normally give the blood a lower water potential than the tissue fluid; with few proteins, the water potential of plasma is higher, so less water is drawn back into the capillaries by osmosis; more fluid stays in the tissues.
parts.working: 1 mark: proteins normally draw water back by osmosis; 1 mark: fewer proteins → less water returns; 1 mark: fluid accumulates faster than lymph drains it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why giving the children a diet rich in protein, such as lentils (daal), milk and eggs, cures the swelling.
parts.answer: Amino acids are used to make plasma proteins again, so water returns to the blood.

practice.stem: In an adult about 3 dm³ of lymph returns to the blood each day. The heart pumps about 5 dm³ of blood every minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of lymph returned to the blood each hour, in cm³.
parts.answer: 125 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the volume of blood pumped by the heart in one day, in dm³.
parts.answer: 7200 dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the lymph returned each day as a percentage of the blood pumped each day. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Although the volume is small, removing the lymph vessels would quickly cause serious problems. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Tissue fluid would not drain and would collect in tissues (swelling); proteins that leak out would not be returned; fats from the gut would not be absorbed / lymphocytes not circulated.

practice.stem:
The table shows the composition of three fluids from the leg of a healthy person.
substance | blood plasma | tissue fluid | lymph
protein / g per dm³ | 70 | 20 | 25
glucose / g per dm³ | 1.0 | 0.9 | 0.9
lymphocytes | few | very few | many

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the protein concentration of tissue fluid is much lower than that of plasma.
parts.answer: Most plasma proteins are too large to pass through the capillary walls, so they stay in the blood; only a small amount leaks out.
parts.working: 1 mark: proteins too large; 1 mark: remain in capillary.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the glucose concentration of tissue fluid is slightly lower than that of plasma.
parts.answer: Cells absorb glucose from the tissue fluid for respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why lymph contains many more lymphocytes than tissue fluid.
parts.answer: Lymph passes through lymph nodes, where lymphocytes are made/stored and enter the lymph.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the plasma protein concentration that is found in lymph.

practice.stem: Some patients have the lymph nodes in one armpit removed during surgery for cancer. Months later, the arm on that side may swell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the arm swells.
parts.answer: Lymph vessels from the arm drain through the armpit nodes; with these removed, lymph cannot drain well; tissue fluid builds up in the arm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the patient is advised to avoid cuts and insect bites on that arm.
parts.answer: Fewer lymph nodes/lymphocytes to filter the lymph from the arm, so infections spread more easily and are harder to fight.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer lymphocytes/nodes; 1 mark: greater risk of infection.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why gentle arm exercises help reduce the swelling.
parts.answer: Muscle contractions squeeze the remaining lymph vessels and move lymph along.

practice.stem: Blood vessels: aorta; coronary artery; hepatic artery; hepatic portal vein; hepatic vein; renal artery; renal vein; pulmonary vein

parts.label: a
parts.text:
From the list, name the blood vessel that:
(i) carries oxygenated blood to the liver
(ii) carries blood from the liver towards the heart
(iii) supplies the heart muscle
(iv) carries blood with the lowest concentration of urea away from an organ.
parts.answer: (i) hepatic artery (ii) hepatic vein (iii) coronary artery (iv) renal vein

parts.label: a
parts.text: Arteries divide into smaller vessels before they reach the capillaries. Name these smaller vessels.
parts.answer: arterioles

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the small vessels that carry blood from capillaries into veins.
parts.answer: venules

parts.label: c
parts.text: Put these vessels in the order that blood passes through them, starting from the heart: capillary, vein, arteriole, artery, venule.
parts.answer: artery → arteriole → capillary → venule → vein
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for one error.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Veins have a wide lumen and thin walls. Explain why these features are suitable for the job of a vein.
parts.answer: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so thick walls are not needed; a wide lumen lowers resistance so blood flows back to the heart easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: low pressure so thin wall enough; 1 mark: wide lumen gives less resistance to flow.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the blood in most veins is darker red than the blood in arteries.
parts.answer: It is deoxygenated / contains less oxyhaemoglobin.

practice.stem: When a blood sample is taken for a test at a laboratory in Faisalabad, the needle is placed in a vein on the inside of the elbow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a vein, not an artery, is used.
parts.answer: Veins are near the surface and easy to find; blood pressure is low so there is less bleeding afterwards; artery walls are thick/deeper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A tight band is placed around the upper arm before the needle goes in, which makes the vein swell. Explain why.
parts.answer: The band stops blood in the vein flowing back to the heart; blood from the arteries keeps arriving, so it collects in the vein below the band.
parts.working: 1 mark: return to heart blocked; 1 mark: blood builds up in vein.

practice.stem: Mean blood pressure in different vessels (kPa): aorta 13.3; large artery 12.0; capillary 4.0; vein 1.3; vena cava 0.3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in pressure between the aorta and the capillaries. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is important that pressure in the capillaries is much lower than in the arteries.
parts.answer: Capillary walls are very thin and would be damaged by high pressure; low pressure / slow flow gives time for exchange of substances.
parts.working: B1 thin walls would burst; B1 slow flow allows time for exchange.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Name the blood vessel that carries:
(i) blood rich in absorbed food from the small intestine to the liver
(ii) blood to the kidney
(iii) oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
parts.answer: (i) hepatic portal vein (ii) renal artery (iii) pulmonary vein

parts.label: a
parts.text: List two substances that pass from the capillaries into the cells of the liver and two that pass from the liver cells into the capillaries.
parts.answer: into liver cells: oxygen, glucose, amino acids, (alcohol/toxins); out of liver cells: carbon dioxide, urea, (glucose when blood glucose is low)
parts.working: 1 mark each for two into and two out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the walls of capillaries, but not of arteries, allow this exchange.
parts.answer: Capillary walls are one cell thick with gaps, giving a short diffusion distance; artery walls are thick (muscle and elastic tissue), so substances cannot diffuse through them quickly.

practice.stem: A doctor measured a patient's blood pressure in the artery of the upper arm as 120/80 mm Hg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the two numbers represent.
parts.answer: 120 = the highest pressure, when the ventricles contract; 80 = the lowest pressure, when the ventricles relax.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the two pressures.
parts.answer: 40 mm Hg

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pressure in the artery does not fall to zero between heartbeats.
parts.answer: The stretched elastic wall of the artery recoils and keeps pushing on the blood; the semilunar valve stops blood flowing back into the ventricle.

practice.stem:
Blood glucose concentration was measured in two vessels of a person one hour after a meal of rice and bread, and again six hours after the meal.
vessel | 1 hour after meal / mg per 100 cm³ | 6 hours after meal / mg per 100 cm³
hepatic portal vein | 180 | 75
hepatic vein | 110 | 85

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the glucose concentration in the hepatic portal vein is high one hour after the meal.
parts.answer: Starch in rice/bread has been digested to glucose, which is absorbed into the capillaries of the villi and carried in the hepatic portal vein.
parts.working: 1 mark: digestion of starch to glucose; 1 mark: absorbed into blood from small intestine.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two vessels one hour after the meal.
parts.answer: The liver removes excess glucose and stores it as glycogen (stimulated by insulin), so blood leaving in the hepatic vein has less glucose.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose taken in by liver; 1 mark: converted to glycogen / insulin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the hepatic vein has more glucose than the hepatic portal vein six hours after the meal.
parts.answer: The liver breaks down glycogen and releases glucose into the blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the blood in the renal artery and the renal vein. For each substance, state whether its concentration is higher in the artery or the vein, and give a reason: (i) urea (ii) oxygen (iii) carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: (i) urea higher in artery – kidneys remove it into urine; (ii) oxygen higher in artery – kidney cells use it for respiration; (iii) carbon dioxide higher in vein – produced by kidney cell respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the vessel that brings blood to the kidney.
parts.answer: renal artery

practice.stem:
A student did this demonstration on a friend's forearm, where veins can be seen under the skin.
1 She pressed one finger on a vein near the wrist end of the forearm.
2 With another finger she pushed the blood along the vein towards the elbow, then lifted the second finger. The vein stayed empty between the two fingers.
3 She then pressed on the vein near the elbow and tried to push the blood along the vein towards the wrist. A small bulge appeared at one point along the vein, and the blood would not move past it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the vein stayed empty in step 2.
parts.answer: Blood could not flow back down towards the wrist because a valve closed; blood from the wrist was blocked by the first finger.
parts.working: 1 mark: valve prevents backflow; 1 mark: first finger stopped blood entering from below.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the small bulge in step 3 shows.
parts.answer: It shows the position of a valve; blood pushed the wrong way collects behind the closed valve.
parts.working: 1 mark: valve position; 1 mark: blood held back by closed valve.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the direction in which blood normally flows in the forearm veins.
parts.answer: towards the elbow / towards the heart

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood in the veins of the legs must travel upwards to the heart at low pressure. Explain how this happens.
parts.answer: Veins have valves that stop blood flowing backwards; contracting leg (skeletal) muscles squeeze the veins and push blood along; the valves make sure it moves only towards the heart; wide lumen gives low resistance to flow.
parts.working: B1 valves prevent backflow; B1 skeletal muscles squeeze veins; B1 one-way flow towards heart; B1 wide lumen / low resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A soldier standing still on guard duty for a long time on a hot day may faint. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Without leg muscle movement, blood collects in the leg veins; less blood returns to the heart, so less is pumped to the brain; the brain receives less oxygen (and glucose), causing fainting.
parts.working: B1 leg muscles not squeezing veins / blood pools in legs; B1 less returned to heart / pumped to brain; B1 less oxygen to brain.

practice.stem: In the summer in Jacobabad, air temperatures can reach 50 °C. The arterioles supplying the skin capillaries have muscle in their walls.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain what happens to the arterioles in the skin when the body temperature rises.
parts.answer: The muscle in the arteriole walls relaxes, so the arterioles widen (vasodilation); more blood flows through the skin capillaries near the surface; more heat is lost by radiation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a cold winter night the same person's skin becomes pale. Explain how the arterioles in the skin reduce heat loss.
parts.answer: The muscle in the arteriole walls contracts so the arterioles narrow (vasoconstriction); less blood flows through the skin capillaries near the surface, so less heat is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: arterioles narrow / vasoconstriction; 1 mark: less blood near skin surface so less heat lost.

practice.stem: At rest, about 1.2 dm³ of the 5.0 dm³ of blood pumped by the heart each minute flows to the two kidneys. The kidneys make up only 0.5 % of the body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the blood flow that goes to the kidneys.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater this percentage is than the kidneys' share of body mass.
parts.answer: 48 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the kidneys receive such a large blood flow.
parts.answer: The whole blood volume must be filtered many times a day to remove urea and other wastes and to control water/salt content; this needs a large flow at high pressure.
parts.working: 1 mark: filtering / removing urea from blood; 1 mark: regulating water and ions / blood is cleaned many times.

practice.stem:
The number of capillaries in each mm² of cross-section was counted in three tissues.
tissue | capillaries per mm²
heart muscle | 3000
leg muscle | 600
skin of the forearm | 150

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more capillaries there are in heart muscle than in leg muscle.
parts.answer: 5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why heart muscle has so many capillaries.
parts.answer: It contracts continuously and never rests, so it needs a constant, large supply of oxygen and glucose for aerobic respiration; it cannot rely on anaerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous contraction / high respiration rate; 1 mark: needs much oxygen/glucose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a blockage in a coronary artery is more serious than a blockage in a small artery of the forearm skin.
parts.answer: Heart muscle cells die quickly without oxygen and the heart may stop pumping blood to the whole body; skin has a lower demand and other vessels can supply it.

practice.stem: In a coronary bypass operation, a surgeon removes a length of vein from the patient's leg and joins it to the aorta and to the coronary artery beyond a blockage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the bypass helps the heart muscle.
parts.answer: Blood flows from the aorta through the new vessel, round the blockage, to the heart muscle beyond it, bringing oxygen and glucose.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood bypasses the blockage; 1 mark: oxygen reaches the heart muscle.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The leg vein must now carry blood at artery pressure. Suggest one problem this may cause and why.
parts.answer: The thin vein wall may stretch/bulge or leak because it has little muscle and elastic tissue; valves in the vein may obstruct flow if placed the wrong way round.
parts.working: 1 mark: problem; 1 mark: linked to thin wall / valves.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why removing a short length of leg vein does not harm the leg.
parts.answer: There are many other veins in the leg to carry blood back to the heart.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student views a cheek cell with a light microscope. The image of the cell is 36 mm wide and the magnification is ×400. What is the actual width of the cell?
A 0.09 µm
B 9 µm
C 90 µm
D 900 µm
parts.answer: C 90 µm
parts.working: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 36 mm ÷ 400 = 0.09 mm = 90 µm (× 1000). A (0.09 µm) forgets to convert mm to µm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which equation is correct for an image seen through a microscope?
A actual size = image size × magnification
B magnification = actual size ÷ image size
C image size = actual size × magnification
D image size = magnification ÷ actual size
parts.answer: C image size = actual size × magnification
parts.working: magnification = image size ÷ actual size, so image size = actual size × magnification. B is the formula upside down, which gives a value less than 1 for an enlargement.

practice.stem: A student peeled the thin inner layer from an onion scale leaf, stained it with iodine solution and drew one cell as seen with a light microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Line XY across the drawing of one cell measures 96 mm. The drawing has a magnification of ×120. Calculate the actual length of the cell in mm. Show your working.
parts.answer: 0.8 mm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification = 96 ÷ 120; A1 0.8 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to (a) into micrometres (µm).
parts.answer: 800 µm

practice.stem: Paramecium is a single-celled organism found in pond water in Lahore. A specimen is 0.18 mm long. Its image in a field guide is 54 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the image. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Express the actual length of the Paramecium in µm.
parts.answer: 180 µm

practice.stem: A student in Peshawar wants to look at onion epidermis cells with a light microscope.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student should prepare a slide of onion epidermis so that cells can be seen clearly.
parts.answer: Peel a thin layer; place flat in a drop of water or iodine on the slide; lower a coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle; remove excess liquid with paper towel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: peel a thin (one cell thick) layer of epidermis with forceps; place it flat on a clean slide; add a drop of water / iodine solution; lower coverslip at an angle / from one side using a mounted needle; to avoid air bubbles; blot excess liquid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why iodine solution is added.
parts.answer: It stains structures (e.g. the nucleus and cytoplasm) so they are easier to see.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the layer of tissue must be very thin.
parts.answer: So that light can pass through it / cells do not overlap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formula that links magnification, image size and actual size.
parts.answer: magnification = image size ÷ actual size

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chloroplast is 5 µm long. In a diagram it is drawn 20 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the diagram.

practice.stem: A student draws a root hair cell from a radish seedling at a magnification of ×40. The drawing of the cell, including its hair, is 18 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the root hair cell in mm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the actual length in µm.
parts.answer: 450 µm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which length is the same as 0.045 mm?
A 0.45 µm
B 4.5 µm
C 45 µm
D 450 µm
parts.answer: C 45 µm
parts.working: 1 mm = 1000 µm, so 0.045 × 1000 = 45 µm. B comes from multiplying by 100 instead of 1000.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A chloroplast-containing alga cell is 25 µm long. In a textbook photograph the same cell is 50 mm long. What is the magnification of the photograph?
A ×2
B ×200
C ×2000
D ×20 000
parts.working: Convert to the same units: 50 mm = 50000 µm. Magnification = 50000 ÷ 25 = ×2000. B (×200) comes from a wrong conversion (1 mm = 100 µm).

practice.stem: A photomicrograph shows a sunflower pollen grain at a magnification of ×850. The diameter of the pollen grain on the photograph is 34 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the pollen grain in µm. Show your working.
parts.answer: 40 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student makes a large drawing of the same pollen grain with a diameter of 68 mm. Calculate the magnification of the student's drawing.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why a magnification has no units.
parts.answer: It is a ratio of two lengths measured in the same units, so the units cancel.

practice.stem: A mosquito larva collected from a water tank is 12 mm long. A student makes a drawing of the larva that is 132 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another student got an answer of ×0.09. Explain how you know this answer must be wrong.
parts.answer: The drawing is larger than the larva, so the magnification must be greater than 1 (the student divided actual size by drawing size).
parts.working: B1 enlargement must be > 1 / divided the wrong way round

practice.stem: A highly magnified image of a rod-shaped bacterium from yoghurt is 60 mm long. The magnification of the image is ×30000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the bacterium in µm. Show your working.
parts.answer: 2 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many of these bacteria, placed end to end, would fit across a line 1 mm long?

practice.stem: A student measured the lengths of five cheek cells on a photograph taken at ×1000. The image lengths were: 58 mm, 62 mm, 55 mm, 61 mm, 64 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean image length.
parts.answer: 60 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your mean to calculate the actual length of a typical cheek cell in µm.
parts.answer: 60 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the student measured five cells rather than one.
parts.answer: Cells vary in size, so a mean of several is more representative / reliable.

practice.stem: A student wants to draw a fish egg that is 0.8 mm in diameter at a magnification of ×50.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how long the student's drawing of the egg should be.
parts.answer: 40 mm
parts.working: M1 image = actual × magnification = 0.8 × 50; A1 40 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of a good biological drawing that the student should include.
parts.answer: Clear continuous outline lines / no shading / correct proportions / drawing large enough / labels with ruled lines.

practice.stem: A photograph of a liver cell taken with a microscope has a scale bar beside it. The scale bar line is 25 mm long and is labelled 10 µm. On the photograph the nucleus of the cell is 15 mm across and the whole cell is 95 mm long.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the scale bar to calculate the magnification of the photograph.
parts.working: M1 convert 25 mm to 25 000 µm; A1 25 000 ÷ 10 = ×2500 (no units).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the nucleus, in µm.
parts.answer: 6 µm
parts.working: M1 15 mm = 15 000 µm; A1 15 000 ÷ 2500 = 6 µm. Allow error carried forward from (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the whole cell, in µm.
parts.answer: 38 µm

parts.label: d
parts.text: The photograph is later printed at twice the size in a revision book. Explain why the scale bar still gives correct results but a printed '×2500' label would not.
parts.answer: The scale bar is enlarged by the same amount as the cell, so the ratio stays correct; the written magnification no longer matches the new image size.
parts.working: 1 mark each: scale bar and image are enlarged by the same factor / ratio unchanged; the printed magnification would now be ×5000 so the label would be wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A red blood cell has a diameter of 7.5 µm. It is drawn in a revision poster at a magnification of ×6000. What is the diameter of the drawing?
A 4.5 mm
B 45 mm
C 450 mm
D 800 mm
parts.answer: B 45 mm
parts.working: Image size = actual size × magnification = 7.5 µm × 6000 = 45000 µm = 45 mm. A divides by 10 000 instead of 1000; D divides magnification by size.

practice.stem: A student draws a section through a mango leaf. The actual thickness of the leaf is 0.25 mm. On the drawing the thickness is 75 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On the same drawing one palisade mesophyll cell is 21 mm long. Use your answer to (a) to calculate the actual length of this cell in µm.
parts.answer: 70 µm

parts.label: c
parts.text: The student's calculated value is larger than the value given in a textbook. Suggest one reason, other than a calculation error, for this difference.
parts.answer: The drawing was not drawn exactly to scale / the cells were drawn too large in proportion to the leaf thickness, or the leaf used was thicker / different cells vary in size.

practice.stem: Two cells were photographed. Cell P (a cheek cell) has an image 45 mm long at ×1500. Cell Q (a plant cell) has an image 30 mm long at ×600.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of each cell in µm.
parts.answer: Cell P: 30 µm; cell Q: 50 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says that cell P is bigger because its image is bigger. Use your answers to explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Cell Q is actually larger, by 20 µm; image size depends on magnification as well as actual size.
parts.working: B1 Q is larger (by 20 µm); B1 P was magnified more so its image is larger even though the cell is smaller

practice.stem: A human egg cell has a diameter of about 70 µm. A photograph shows an egg cell with an image diameter of 42 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the magnification of the photograph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The same photograph is enlarged on a classroom screen so that the image of the cell becomes 210 mm long. Calculate the new magnification.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain whether enlarging the photograph lets you see more detail of the cell.
parts.answer: No — enlarging the photograph only makes the same image bigger; no new detail is revealed (resolution does not change).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student draws a guard cell. Drawing X of the cell is 30 mm long and has a magnification of ×600. A second drawing, Y, of the same cell is made at a magnification of ×1500. How long is drawing Y?
A 12 mm
B 45 mm
C 75 mm
D 750 mm
parts.answer: C 75 mm
parts.working: Actual length = 30 ÷ 600 = 0.05 mm. Drawing Y = 0.05 × 1500 = 75 mm. A comes from 30 × 600 ÷ 1500, i.e. using the ratio the wrong way round.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both plant cells and animal cells?
A cell wall
B chloroplast
C large permanent vacuole
D ribosome
parts.answer: D ribosome
parts.working: Ribosomes (protein synthesis) occur in all plant and animal cells. Cell walls, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole are found in plant cells only.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table by writing 'present' or 'absent' in each space.
Structure | palisade mesophyll cell | liver cell
cell wall | ? | ?
chloroplasts | ? | ?
nucleus | ? | ?
cell membrane | ? | ?
parts.answer: cell wall: present / absent; chloroplasts: present / absent; nucleus: present / present; cell membrane: present / present

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the cell membrane.
parts.answer: Controls what enters and leaves the cell (partially permeable).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the main substance from which a plant cell wall is made.
parts.answer: Cellulose

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the cell wall and the cell membrane in how substances pass through.
parts.answer: The cell wall is fully permeable (lets most substances through); the cell membrane is partially permeable (controls what passes).
parts.working: B1 wall fully / freely permeable; B1 membrane partially permeable

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one function of the cell wall.
parts.answer: Gives the cell a fixed shape / support / stops the cell bursting when it takes in water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which part of a cell controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell?
A cell membrane
B cell wall
C cytoplasm
D nucleus
parts.answer: A cell membrane
parts.working: The partially permeable cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. The cell wall (B) is fully permeable, so it does not control movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the cell structure that:
(i) contains chromosomes
(ii) is where photosynthesis takes place
(iii) contains cell sap
(iv) is where aerobic respiration takes place.
parts.answer: (i) nucleus (ii) chloroplast (iii) (large permanent) vacuole (iv) mitochondrion
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'cytoplasm' for (iv).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one structure from your answers to (a) that is never found in a human cell.
parts.answer: chloroplast or large permanent vacuole containing cell sap
parts.working: B1 either; humans do not photosynthesise / have no permanent sap vacuole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two structures present in a palisade mesophyll cell of a mango leaf that are not present in a human liver cell.
parts.answer: cell wall; chloroplasts (also accept large permanent vacuole)

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each structure you named in (a), state its function.
parts.answer: cell wall – gives strength/support, stops the cell bursting; chloroplast – absorbs light for photosynthesis; vacuole – stores cell sap, keeps cell turgid
parts.working: 1 mark per correct function matched to the structures given in (a).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one structure found in both cells and state its function.
parts.answer: e.g. nucleus – controls the cell's activities / contains genetic material; mitochondria – aerobic respiration; ribosomes – protein synthesis; cell membrane – controls entry/exit

practice.stem: A student gently scraped the inside of her cheek with a clean cotton bud, smeared the cells onto a slide, added a drop of methylene blue stain and a cover slip, and looked at the slide with a light microscope at ×400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the methylene blue stain is added to the cheek cells.
parts.answer: To make the nucleus (and cell parts) visible / give contrast.
parts.working: B1 stains cell structures so they can be seen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two structures the student would be able to see in a cheek cell with the light microscope.
parts.answer: nucleus and cytoplasm
parts.working: 1 mark each. The cell membrane is too thin to be seen as a separate structure with a light microscope.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Ribosomes are present in cheek cells but the student could not see them. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Ribosomes are too small to be seen with a light microscope (need an electron microscope).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a cotton bud that had been used should be put straight into disinfectant.
parts.answer: To kill any pathogens from the saliva/mouth so infections are not spread.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell from a leaf is treated so that its mitochondria stop working. Which process in the cell stops first?
A aerobic respiration
B photosynthesis
C diffusion of carbon dioxide
D protein synthesis on ribosomes
parts.answer: A aerobic respiration
parts.working: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration. Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, so B is wrong; diffusion needs no energy from respiration.

practice.stem: Lactobacillus is a bacterium used to make yoghurt (dahi). Its cell has a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, a loop of circular DNA and small plasmids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two structures that are found in this bacterial cell but are not found in a human cheek cell.
parts.answer: Cell wall; plasmids (also accept circular DNA free in cytoplasm).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: cell wall, plasmid(s), circular DNA

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the genetic material of a bacterium differs from that of a plant cell.
parts.answer: Bacterium: a single circular DNA loop free in the cytoplasm (plus plasmids), not inside a nucleus. Plant cell: DNA in chromosomes inside a nucleus.
parts.working: B1 no nucleus / DNA free in cytoplasm; B1 circular DNA / plasmids vs chromosomes in nucleus

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the structures in the bacterium where proteins are made.
parts.answer: Ribosomes

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the nucleus.
parts.answer: Contains genetic material (DNA / chromosomes) that controls the activities of the cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of ribosomes.
parts.answer: Protein synthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the function of the large permanent vacuole in a plant cell.
parts.answer: Stores cell sap (water, sugars, salts); when full it presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall, keeping the cell turgid and supporting the plant.
parts.working: B1 stores cell sap; B1 maintains turgor / support

practice.stem: Cell R was found in a water sample from a pond in Murree. It has a nucleus, a cell wall, a cell membrane, several chloroplasts and a large vacuole full of cell sap.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify whether cell R is a plant cell, an animal cell or a bacterial cell. Give two reasons from the description.
parts.answer: Plant cell: it has chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole, and it has a cell wall as well as a nucleus.
parts.working: B1 plant; 1 mark each for any two of: chloroplasts; large (permanent) vacuole containing cell sap; nucleus together with a cell wall (bacteria have a cell wall but no nucleus; animal cells have no cell wall)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cell S has a nucleus, cell membrane and many mitochondria but no cell wall. Name the type of cell.
parts.answer: Animal cell

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student wrote that cells from the inside of a potato tuber contain a cell wall, nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria and a large vacuole. Identify the mistake and explain it.
parts.answer: Potato tuber cells do not contain chloroplasts, because the tuber grows underground with no light, so it does not photosynthesise.
parts.working: B1 chloroplasts wrong; B1 no light underground / tuber does not photosynthesise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The tuber cells contain many starch grains. Suggest where the carbohydrate stored in these grains was made, and how it reached the tuber.
parts.answer: Made by photosynthesis in the leaves (as sugar); carried as sucrose in the phloem to the tuber, then stored as starch.
parts.working: B1 leaves/photosynthesis; B1 transported (as sucrose) in phloem.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the structure in tuber cells that releases energy from the stored starch after it is broken down to glucose.
parts.answer: mitochondria

practice.stem:
The table shows estimates of the mean number of mitochondria in some human cells.
cell type | mean number of mitochondria per cell
heart muscle cell | 5000
liver cell | 2000
skin cell | 200
mature red blood cell | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more mitochondria a heart muscle cell contains than a skin cell.
parts.answer: 25 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why heart muscle cells contain so many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Heart muscle contracts continuously; contraction needs a lot of energy; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases this energy.
parts.working: 1 mark each: continuous/frequent contraction; needs much energy; aerobic respiration in mitochondria releases energy.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mature human red blood cells contain no mitochondria. Suggest one advantage to the body of red blood cells not using aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: They do not use up the oxygen they are carrying, so more oxygen reaches the tissues.
parts.working: B1 they do not use the oxygen they transport / more room for haemoglobin.

practice.stem: Yeast is a single-celled fungus used in baking naan. Lactobacillus is a bacterium used to make yoghurt. A yeast cell has a cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, a nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes and a vacuole.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two structures found in both the yeast cell and the bacterial cell.
parts.answer: any two of: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two differences between the genetic material of the yeast cell and that of the bacterial cell.
parts.answer: Yeast DNA is in chromosomes inside a nucleus; bacterial DNA is a single circular loop free in the cytoplasm; the bacterium also has plasmids.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: nucleus vs no nucleus; linear chromosomes vs circular DNA; plasmids in bacterium.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Yeast cells contain mitochondria. Name the process that takes place in them.
parts.answer: aerobic respiration

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why sperm cells have many mitochondria in the middle region.
parts.answer: To carry out a lot of aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the tail to move / swim to the egg.
parts.working: B1 aerobic respiration releases energy; B1 for tail movement / swimming

parts.label: b
parts.text: Root hair cells do not have chloroplasts. Explain why.
parts.answer: They are underground so receive no light; photosynthesis cannot occur, so chloroplasts would be of no use.
parts.working: B1 no light underground; B1 so no photosynthesis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why cells in the pancreas that make digestive enzymes have many ribosomes.
parts.answer: Enzymes are proteins, and ribosomes are where proteins are made.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where in the cell the chemical reactions of aerobic respiration take place.
parts.answer: Mitochondria

parts.label: b
parts.text: Muscle cells in a sprinter's legs contain more mitochondria than skin cells. Explain why.
parts.answer: Muscle contraction needs a lot of energy; more mitochondria allow more aerobic respiration to release this energy.
parts.working: B1 more aerobic respiration; B1 more energy (released) for contraction

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the part of the cell where most chemical reactions of the cell take place, and state what it contains.
parts.answer: Cytoplasm; contains water, dissolved substances / enzymes and organelles.
parts.working: B1 cytoplasm; B1 any one valid content

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cell has a cell wall, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a loop of DNA, but no nucleus. Which other structure is it most likely to contain?
A chloroplasts
B mitochondria
C plasmids
D a large permanent vacuole
parts.answer: C plasmids
parts.working: No nucleus and a loop (circular) DNA means a bacterial cell; bacteria also contain small rings of DNA called plasmids. Bacteria have no mitochondria (B), which are found only in cells with a nucleus.

practice.stem: Streptomycin is an antibiotic. It attaches to the ribosomes of bacteria and stops them working.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why stopping bacterial ribosomes from working stops the bacteria from growing and reproducing.
parts.answer: Ribosomes make proteins; so the bacteria cannot make enzymes / structural proteins; so metabolism, growth and cell division cannot take place.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis; no enzymes/proteins made; so no growth/division.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why this antibiotic does little harm to human cells.
parts.answer: Human ribosomes are different (larger) from bacterial ribosomes, so the antibiotic does not affect them.
parts.working: B1 human ribosomes differ in structure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this antibiotic would not cure a viral infection such as influenza.
parts.answer: Viruses do not have their own ribosomes / are not cells; they use the host cell's ribosomes, which the antibiotic does not affect.
parts.working: 1 mark each: viruses have no ribosomes/cell structures; they use host cell machinery.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the vacuole and the cell wall work together to make a plant cell firm (turgid).
parts.answer: Water enters the vacuole by osmosis; the vacuole swells and pushes the cytoplasm against the cell wall; the strong cell wall resists further expansion, so pressure builds and the cell becomes firm.
parts.working: 1 mark each: water enters vacuole by osmosis; vacuole/cell contents push outwards on wall; wall is strong/inelastic and resists so cell is turgid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how turgid cells support the leaves of a non-woody plant such as a coriander (dhania) plant.
parts.answer: Turgid cells press against each other, making the tissues rigid, which holds the leaves and stem upright / spread out to catch light.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cells press on each other; tissue firm so leaves held out/upright.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why coriander leaves on a market stall in hot sun soon droop.
parts.answer: Cells lose water (by evaporation/osmosis), vacuoles shrink, cells become flaccid and the plant wilts.
parts.working: B1 loss of water so cells lose turgor.

practice.stem:
A table shows which structures are present (✓) or absent (✗) in four cells, P, Q, R and S.
cell | cell wall | nucleus | plasmid | large permanent vacuole | mitochondria
P | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗
Q | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓
R | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓
S | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify cell P and give a reason for your answer.
parts.answer: bacterium – it has no nucleus and has a plasmid/cell wall
parts.working: B1 bacterium; B1 no nucleus with plasmid.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cell Q has no chloroplasts. Suggest where in a plant it came from, and explain why.
parts.answer: From a root (or other underground/non-green part); there is no light there so chloroplasts would be no use.
parts.working: B1 root; B1 no light so no photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify cell R and cell S.
parts.answer: R: animal cell (e.g. cheek or liver cell); S: (mammalian) red blood cell

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how the lack of a nucleus is linked to the function of cell S.
parts.answer: More space for haemoglobin, so it can carry more oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list is in order of increasing level of organisation?
A cell → organ → tissue → organ system
B cell → tissue → organ → organ system
C tissue → cell → organ → organism
D organ → tissue → organ system → organism
parts.answer: B cell → tissue → organ → organ system
parts.working: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems. A puts organ before tissue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each of the following, state whether it is a cell, a tissue, an organ or an organ system: (i) the heart (ii) xylem (iii) a neurone (iv) the stomach, intestines and liver working together.
parts.answer: (i) organ (ii) tissue (iii) cell (iv) organ system

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define the term organ.
parts.answer: A group of tissues working together to perform specific functions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is an organ?
A a leaf
B a red blood cell
C muscle tissue
D the digestive system
parts.answer: A a leaf
parts.working: A leaf is made of several tissues (epidermis, mesophyll, xylem, phloem) working together, so it is an organ. The digestive system (D) is an organ system, a group of organs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of cell that lines the trachea and has tiny hair-like structures on its surface.
parts.answer: ciliated (epithelial) cell

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how these cells help to keep the lungs free of dust and bacteria.
parts.answer: Mucus (from goblet cells) traps dust and bacteria; the cilia beat/wave to move the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mucus traps particles; cilia beat to sweep mucus up/away from lungs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features of a red blood cell and explain how each one helps it to carry oxygen.
parts.answer: biconcave disc shape – large surface area for oxygen to diffuse in/out; no nucleus – more space for haemoglobin; contains haemoglobin – combines with oxygen; small and flexible – squeezes through capillaries close to tissues
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three feature + explanation pairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the level of organisation of blood.
parts.answer: tissue

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these in order from the simplest to the most complex level of organisation:
heart, cardiac muscle tissue, human, muscle cell, circulatory system
parts.answer: muscle cell → cardiac muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → human
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark if one pair is swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by an organ system.
parts.answer: a group of organs that work together to carry out a particular function

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other organ that is part of the circulatory system.
parts.answer: a blood vessel such as the aorta (accept artery/vein)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the specialised cell that:
(i) absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil
(ii) carries oxygen in the blood
(iii) carries impulses from the spinal cord to a muscle
(iv) swims to fertilise an egg cell
parts.answer: (i) root hair cell (ii) red blood cell (iii) motor neurone (iv) sperm cell

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to show one feature of each cell and how it helps the cell's function.
Cell | function | feature | how the feature helps
ciliated cell | ? | ? | ?
red blood cell | ? | ? | ?
parts.answer: Ciliated cell: moves mucus (and trapped particles) in the trachea/bronchi; cilia beat to move mucus. Red blood cell: transports oxygen; contains haemoglobin which binds oxygen / no nucleus so more room / biconcave shape gives large surface area.
parts.working: Ciliated: B1 function (move mucus), B1 feature + explanation (cilia beat / sweep). RBC: B1 function (carry oxygen), B1 feature + explanation (haemoglobin / no nucleus / biconcave)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the meaning of the term tissue.
parts.answer: A group of cells with similar structures, working together to perform a shared function.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row correctly matches a specialised cell, one of its features and how that feature helps it?
A red blood cell – no nucleus – more space for haemoglobin
B root hair cell – many chloroplasts – makes food for the root
C sperm cell – flagellum – stores energy for the embryo
D palisade mesophyll cell – few chloroplasts – lets light through to lower cells
parts.answer: A red blood cell – no nucleus – more space for haemoglobin
parts.working: A red blood cell has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen. A sperm's flagellum (C) is for swimming, not storing energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table with one difference between a human sperm cell and a human egg cell.
feature | sperm cell | egg cell
size | ... | ...
ability to move | ... | ...
parts.answer: size: sperm very small / egg much larger; movement: sperm swims using a flagellum / egg cannot move by itself

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the sperm cell has many mitochondria.
parts.answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the flagellum to beat/swim to the egg.
parts.working: 1 mark each: respiration releases energy; for swimming/flagellum movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the function of the energy store in the cytoplasm of the egg cell.
parts.answer: to supply energy/materials for the early cell divisions of the embryo after fertilisation

practice.stem: A student estimated the surface area of the roots of a radish seedling. Without its root hairs, the surface area of the root was estimated as 50 cm². Including the root hairs, it was 240 cm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in surface area produced by the root hairs.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this increase is important to the plant.
parts.answer: More surface area for absorbing water by osmosis and mineral ions (by active transport/diffusion); so faster uptake.
parts.working: 1 mark each: larger area for absorption; of water and mineral ions.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Seedlings pulled out of a nursery bed and replanted often wilt for a few days. Use the data to suggest why.
parts.answer: Many root hairs are torn off when the seedling is pulled up; surface area for water uptake falls (towards 50 cm²) so less water is absorbed than is lost by transpiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each: root hairs damaged/lost; less water absorbed than lost.

practice.stem:
Mean numbers of chloroplasts in cells from a leaf of a mango tree:
cell type | mean number of chloroplasts
palisade mesophyll cell | 60
spongy mesophyll cell | 20
upper epidermis cell | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the mean number of chloroplasts in a palisade cell to the mean number in a spongy mesophyll cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why palisade cells contain more chloroplasts than spongy mesophyll cells.
parts.answer: Palisade cells are near the upper surface where most light falls; more chloroplasts absorb more light so more photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark each: nearer upper surface/most light; more light absorbed for photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the cells of the upper epidermis contain no chloroplasts.
parts.answer: So they are transparent and light passes through them to the palisade layer.

practice.stem: The wall of the stomach contains muscle tissue, glandular tissue that releases gastric juice, and a lining of epithelial tissue.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the stomach is described as an organ.
parts.answer: It is made of several different tissues; which work together to carry out a function (digestion).
parts.working: 1 mark each: several tissues; working together for a function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ system the stomach belongs to, and one other organ in that system.
parts.answer: digestive system; e.g. small intestine, oesophagus, pancreas, liver

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest the job of the muscle tissue in the stomach wall.
parts.answer: Contracts to churn food and mix it with gastric juice (physical digestion).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood is described as a tissue. Suggest why.
parts.answer: It is a group of cells (with similar origin) working together to carry out a function such as transport.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two types of cell found in blood and state the function of each.
parts.answer: red blood cell – carries oxygen; phagocyte – engulfs/ingests pathogens; lymphocyte – makes antibodies; (platelets – clotting, accept as cell fragments)
parts.working: For each of two: B1 name, B1 function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the shape of a root hair cell helps it to absorb water and mineral ions.
parts.answer: The long hair-like extension gives a large surface area, so more water and ions can be absorbed at a time.
parts.working: B1 long extension / hair; B1 large surface area for absorption

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a palisade mesophyll cell is adapted for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: It contains many chloroplasts to absorb light; it is long/column-shaped and near the upper surface so it receives more light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: many chloroplasts; near upper surface; elongated shape packed closely; large vacuole pushes chloroplasts to edge

parts.label: c
parts.text: A motor neurone can be over 1 m long. Suggest how this length is an advantage.
parts.answer: It carries impulses over long distances (from the spinal cord to muscles) quickly without needing synapses along the way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of a motor neurone.
parts.answer: carries electrical impulses from the central nervous system to an effector (muscle or gland)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of a motor neurone and explain how each suits its function.
parts.answer: long axon/fibre – carries impulses over long distance to muscles without many junctions; branched endings – connect with many muscle fibres; insulating (myelin) sheath – speeds up impulses; many dendrites – receive impulses from many other neurones
parts.working: For each of two features: B1 feature, B1 matched explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why damage to the motor neurones in the spinal cord can cause paralysis of the legs even though the leg muscles are not damaged.
parts.answer: Impulses can no longer reach the leg muscles, so they cannot contract.

practice.stem:
A student looked at three cells with a light microscope and made notes.
cell A: has a cell wall, a long thin extension pushing out from one side, no chloroplasts
cell B: tall and column-shaped, has a cell wall and many chloroplasts close to the cell edge
cell C: no cell wall, many tiny hair-like projections on one surface, many mitochondria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify cell A and cell B.
parts.answer: A: root hair cell; B: palisade mesophyll cell

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cell C came from the lining of the trachea. Suggest why it contains many mitochondria.
parts.answer: The cilia beat continuously; this needs energy released by aerobic respiration in mitochondria.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cilia movement needs energy; mitochondria release energy by respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Cells like C are found side by side with mucus-secreting cells. Name the level of organisation formed by a group of cells like C, and describe what this group does in the trachea.
parts.answer: a tissue (ciliated epithelium); cilia beat to sweep mucus with trapped dust and pathogens up and away from the lungs
parts.working: B1 tissue; B1 cilia move mucus away from lungs/towards throat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A test shows that most of a man's sperm cells have a short, weak flagellum. Explain why this may stop him from fathering a child.
parts.answer: The sperm cannot swim (far/fast enough) through the uterus to the oviduct; so they do not reach the egg and fertilisation does not happen.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cannot swim; do not reach egg so no fertilisation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another man's sperm have normal flagella but very few mitochondria. Explain why this could also reduce fertility.
parts.answer: Little aerobic respiration, so little energy released; the flagellum cannot beat for long enough to reach the egg.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less energy from respiration; less/no movement of flagellum.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why millions of sperm are released for each egg.
parts.answer: Most sperm die or fail to reach the egg, so large numbers raise the chance that one fertilises it.

practice.stem: A human egg cell is about 0.1 mm in diameter. The head of a human sperm cell is about 5 µm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times wider a human egg cell is than the head of a sperm cell.
parts.answer: 20 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the egg cell is so much larger than the sperm cell.
parts.answer: The egg contains a store of energy/nutrients in its cytoplasm; to supply the dividing cells of the embryo until it implants; the sperm needs to be small to swim.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what happens to the jelly coat of the egg after one sperm has entered.
parts.answer: It changes/hardens so that no other sperm can enter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single-celled Amoeba in a pond carries out all life processes in one cell. Explain why a large multicellular organism such as a human needs specialised cells, tissues and organs.
parts.answer: Its cells are far from the surface, so diffusion alone is too slow; specialised cells/organs can carry out particular jobs (e.g. gas exchange, transport) more efficiently; division of labour.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: small surface area to volume ratio; diffusion too slow over large distances; needs transport/exchange organs; specialised cells efficient at one job / division of labour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage to an organism of having highly specialised cells.
parts.answer: Cells depend on each other; failure of one organ (e.g. kidneys) can kill the whole organism; specialised cells may not be able to divide/replace themselves.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast?
A lactic acid only
B alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide
C carbon dioxide and water
D lactic acid and carbon dioxide
parts.answer: B alcohol (ethanol) and carbon dioxide
parts.working: Yeast respires glucose anaerobically to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Lactic acid (A) is made by human muscle, not yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for anaerobic respiration in human muscle cells.
parts.answer: glucose → lactic acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: State when muscle cells respire anaerobically.
parts.answer: During vigorous exercise, when oxygen cannot be supplied fast enough for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: B1 vigorous exercise / not enough oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose molecule than aerobic respiration. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Glucose is only partly broken down; lactic acid still contains a lot of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three differences between aerobic respiration and anaerobic respiration in human muscle.
