parts.answer: Aerobic needs oxygen, anaerobic does not; aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water, anaerobic produces lactic acid; aerobic releases much more energy per glucose; aerobic is a complete breakdown of glucose, anaerobic is incomplete.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three comparative differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which humans use anaerobic respiration by yeast.
parts.answer: Bread making (carbon dioxide makes dough rise); making ethanol/alcohol for biofuel or drinks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the gas produced by yeast that makes bread rise.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What builds up in muscle cells during vigorous exercise when oxygen supply cannot keep up with demand?
A ethanol
B carbon dioxide only
C lactic acid
D glycogen
parts.answer: C lactic acid
parts.working: Muscle cells respire anaerobically when oxygen is short and make lactic acid. Ethanol is the anaerobic product of yeast, not muscle, so A is the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the substance that builds up in muscles during anaerobic respiration.
parts.answer: lactic acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to deal with this substance.
parts.answer: oxygen debt
parts.working: B1 oxygen debt (repaying the oxygen debt)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why breathing stays fast for some time after exercise has stopped.
parts.answer: to supply the extra oxygen needed to break down the lactic acid (in aerobic respiration) and to restore the body to its normal state
parts.working: B1 extra oxygen needed; B1 to break down or remove lactic acid

parts.label: a
parts.text:
After a race, lactic acid is removed from the blood. In which organ is most of it broken down using oxygen?
A kidney
B liver
C lungs
D stomach
parts.answer: B liver
parts.working: Blood carries lactic acid from the muscles to the liver, where it is broken down by aerobic respiration (paying back the oxygen debt). The kidneys (A) do not remove lactic acid this way.

practice.stem: A baker in Multan mixed flour, water, sugar and yeast to make 50 cm³ of dough. After 1 hour in a warm place the dough had a volume of 120 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in volume of the dough.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dough rises.
parts.answer: Yeast respires anaerobically, producing carbon dioxide gas; the bubbles are trapped in the dough, so it expands.
parts.working: B1 yeast respiration produces carbon dioxide; B1 gas trapped / bubbles make dough expand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dough was left in a warm place rather than a refrigerator.
parts.answer: Warmth increases the activity of the yeast's enzymes, so respiration and carbon dioxide production are faster; in the cold enzymes work slowly.
parts.working: B1 enzymes work faster at warm temperature (near optimum); B1 faster respiration / more gas.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State what happens to the alcohol made by the yeast when the dough is baked.
parts.answer: It evaporates (boils off) in the oven heat.

practice.stem: An athlete in Islamabad ran a 400 m race. At the end of the race her blood lactic acid concentration was 12.0 mmol per dm³. After resting for 45 minutes it was 3.0 mmol per dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate at which the lactic acid concentration fell during the 45 minutes. Give your answer in mmol per dm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 0.2 mmol per dm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lactic acid built up in the athlete's blood during the race.
parts.answer: Muscles needed more energy than aerobic respiration could supply; oxygen could not reach them fast enough, so they respired anaerobically, producing lactic acid.
parts.working: B1 not enough oxygen to muscles; B1 anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the oxygen debt is repaid after the race.
parts.answer: Heart rate stays high to carry lactic acid in the blood from the muscles to the liver; breathing stays fast and deep to supply oxygen; lactic acid is broken down by aerobic respiration in the liver.
parts.working: B1 fast heart rate transports lactic acid to liver; B1 deep/fast breathing supplies extra oxygen; B1 aerobic respiration of lactic acid in liver.

practice.stem:
Yeast was mixed with sugar solutions of different concentrations at 30 °C. Each tube was connected by a delivery tube to a tube of water, and the bubbles of gas were counted for one minute, three times.
Sugar concentration / %: 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8
Bubbles per minute, count 1: 0 | 8 | 17 | 25 | 26
Bubbles per minute, count 2: 0 | 10 | 19 | 24 | 27
Bubbles per minute, count 3: 0 | 9 | 18 | 26 | 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute for each sugar concentration.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of sugar concentration on the rate of respiration of the yeast.
parts.answer: Rate increases as sugar concentration increases from 0 % to 6 %, then levels off between 6 % and 8 %.
parts.working: B1 increase; B1 levels off with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the bubbles at 0 % sugar were zero.
parts.answer: There is no glucose (substrate) for the yeast to respire, so no carbon dioxide is made.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why counting bubbles is not an accurate way to measure the volume of gas, and suggest a better method.
parts.answer: Bubbles are different sizes; collect the gas in a gas syringe or an inverted measuring cylinder over water and measure its volume.
parts.working: B1 bubbles vary in size / may be missed; B1 gas syringe / measuring cylinder.

practice.stem:
Equal samples of bread dough, each 20 cm³, were placed in measuring cylinders in water baths at different temperatures. The volume was read after 30 minutes.
Temperature / °C: 15 | 25 | 35 | 45 | 60
Volume after 30 min / cm³: 24 | 31 | 40 | 34 | 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in volume of the dough at each temperature.
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 three or four correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in volume at 35 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dough at 60 °C did not rise.
parts.answer: The high temperature denatured the yeast's enzymes / killed the yeast, so no respiration and no carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 enzymes denatured / yeast killed; B1 no carbon dioxide produced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same.
parts.answer: Any two: starting volume of dough; mass of yeast; mass of sugar; type of flour; time (30 minutes); diameter of measuring cylinder.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Compared with aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule, anaerobic respiration of glucose in muscle
A releases more energy, because lactic acid is produced
B releases the same energy, because the same substances are made
C releases less energy, because glucose is only partly broken down
D releases less energy, because oxygen is made
parts.answer: C releases less energy, because glucose is only partly broken down
parts.working: Anaerobic respiration does not break glucose down fully, so much of the chemical energy stays in the lactic acid. A is wrong: the energy yield is lower, not higher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A baker mixes yeast with flour, warm water and sugar. Name the gas that makes the dough rise.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for the anaerobic respiration of glucose by yeast.
parts.answer: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 glucose as reactant; B1 ethanol and carbon dioxide as products

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dough rises more slowly in a refrigerator at 4 °C than at 30 °C.
parts.answer: the yeast enzymes work more slowly at low temperature, so fewer glucose molecules are respired and less carbon dioxide is made
parts.working: B1 enzymes work more slowly / fewer collisions at low temperature; B1 less carbon dioxide produced per minute

practice.stem:
A student used yeast and sugar solution at four temperatures and measured the volume of gas (cm³) produced in 10 minutes. Each value is the mean of three trials.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50
Volume of gas in 10 minutes / cm³: 2.1, 5.0, 9.6, 3.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of gas production at 40 °C in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 0.96 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the volume of gas produced changes from 20 °C to 40 °C.
parts.answer: it increases from 2.1 to 9.6 cm³ in 10 minutes; the gas volume is about 4.6 times greater at 40 °C
parts.working: B1 increases with temperature; B1 quoting values or the ratio (9.6 ÷ 2.1 ≈ 4.6)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why less gas is produced at 50 °C.
parts.answer: the enzymes in the yeast denature at 50 °C, so respiration slows down
parts.working: B1 enzymes denature / active site changes shape; B1 less respiration, so less carbon dioxide

practice.stem: Relative molecular masses: glucose = 180, ethanol = 46, carbon dioxide = 44.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the balanced chemical equation for anaerobic respiration in yeast.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of ethanol produced when 90 g of glucose is completely respired anaerobically by yeast.
parts.working: M1 90 ÷ 180 = 0.5 mol glucose → 1.0 mol ethanol; A1 1.0 × 46 = 46 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced from the same 90 g of glucose.

practice.stem:
A flask of glucose solution and yeast, closed with a cotton wool plug, was placed on a top-pan balance at 30 °C.
Time / min: 0 | 15 | 30 | 45 | 60
Mass of flask / g: 250.00 | 249.86 | 249.62 | 249.36 | 249.12
Assume that all the mass lost is carbon dioxide released by anaerobic respiration of the yeast.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of carbon dioxide lost in 60 minutes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of mass loss over the 60 minutes, in g per minute, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.0147 g per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the equation C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ to calculate the mass of glucose respired. (Mr: glucose 180, CO₂ 44)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the cotton wool plug was used instead of a rubber bung.
parts.answer: It lets the carbon dioxide escape, so the loss in mass can be measured; it still keeps out microorganisms (and limits air movement), while a bung would trap the gas (and could be forced out by the pressure).
parts.working: B1 lets carbon dioxide escape (mass loss measured); B1 keeps out microorganisms / bung would trap gas and build up pressure.

practice.stem: At a distillery near a sugar mill in Sindh, molasses (a sugary waste from sugar cane) is diluted and mixed with yeast in closed tanks to make ethanol, which is sold as a fuel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why air is kept out of the fermentation tanks.
parts.answer: With oxygen, yeast would respire aerobically, producing carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol; without oxygen it respires anaerobically and makes ethanol.
parts.working: B1 aerobic respiration with oxygen gives no ethanol; B1 anaerobic conditions make ethanol.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the tanks is controlled at about 30–35 °C.
parts.answer: This is near the optimum for yeast enzymes, so respiration is fast; higher temperatures would denature the enzymes / kill the yeast.
parts.working: B1 optimum for enzymes; B1 high temperature denatures / kills yeast.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fermentation stops after some days even though the yeast is still present. Suggest two reasons.
parts.answer: The sugar is used up; the ethanol concentration becomes high enough to poison/kill the yeast.
parts.working: B1 sugar used up; B1 ethanol toxic to yeast (or pH falls).

practice.stem:
A student's breathing rate was recorded at rest and after 3 minutes of skipping.
At rest: 14 breaths per minute
End of exercise: 38
2 minutes after: 30
5 minutes after: 22
10 minutes after: 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in breathing rate from rest to the end of the exercise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the breathing rate stayed above the resting rate for several minutes after exercise.
parts.answer: An oxygen debt built up because muscles respired anaerobically and made lactic acid; extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid by aerobic respiration (in the liver); so fast, deep breathing continues until the lactic acid is removed.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration / lactic acid formed; B1 oxygen debt; B1 extra oxygen used to break down lactic acid (aerobically, in liver).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sprinter's blood lactic acid concentration rose from 1.0 mmol/dm³ at rest to 9.0 mmol/dm³ one minute after a race. Calculate the increase in concentration and the percentage increase.
parts.answer: increase 8.0 mmol/dm³; percentage increase 800 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lactic acid is still present in the blood some time after the race has finished.
parts.answer: lactic acid is removed slowly; it must be carried to the liver and converted back to glucose or broken down aerobically, which needs oxygen
parts.working: B1 removal is slow / needs oxygen; B1 carried to liver or broken down aerobically

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sprinter's muscles can only respire anaerobically for a short time.
parts.answer: anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose, so the muscle cannot meet its energy demand; lactic acid builds up in the muscle and causes fatigue
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration releases much less energy per glucose; B1 lactic acid builds up and causes muscle fatigue

parts.label: a
parts.text: Yeast ferments 1.80 g of glucose completely: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Using relative formula masses glucose 180 and ethanol 46, calculate the mass of ethanol produced.
parts.working: M1 moles of glucose = 1.80 ÷ 180 = 0.0100 mol, so 0.0200 mol ethanol; A1 0.0200 × 46 = 0.92 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced in the same reaction. Relative formula mass of CO₂ is 44.
parts.working: M1 0.0200 mol CO₂ (2 mol per mol of glucose); A1 0.0200 × 44 = 0.88 g

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to show that the mass is conserved in this reaction.
parts.answer: 0.92 + 0.88 = 1.80 g, the mass of glucose used
parts.working: B1 products add up to the starting mass

practice.stem:
Two vacuum flasks were set up with a thermometer in each.
Flask A: germinating peas – 21.0 °C at the start, 26.5 °C after 3 days
Flask B: boiled peas – 21.0 °C at the start, 21.0 °C after 3 days

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the temperature rise in flask A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature in flask A increased.
parts.answer: The germinating peas respire, releasing energy, some as heat; the vacuum flask stops the heat escaping.
parts.working: B1 respiration releases energy as heat; B1 flask insulates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the purpose of flask B.
parts.answer: A control: boiled peas are dead and do not respire, showing the heat comes from respiration of living peas.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Both sets of peas were rinsed in dilute disinfectant. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To kill microorganisms (bacteria, fungi) on the peas, whose respiration would also release heat.

practice.stem:
Air was drawn slowly through two tubes and then bubbled through limewater.
Tube X: germinating peas
Tube Y: the same volume of glass beads

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the limewater in tube X.
parts.answer: It turns milky (cloudy).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a).
parts.answer: The germinating peas respire and release carbon dioxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why glass beads were used in tube Y.
parts.answer: As a control with the same volume of solid but no living material.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which observation shows that carbon dioxide is present?
A limewater turns milky
B hydrogencarbonate indicator turns from red to purple
C blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink
D iodine solution turns blue-black
parts.answer: A limewater turns milky
parts.working: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. Cobalt chloride paper (C) tests for water, and indicator going purple (B) shows less carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A respirometer contains germinating seeds and soda lime. A second tube contains glass beads instead of seeds. What is the purpose of this control tube?
A to show that the seeds produce carbon dioxide
B to allow for changes in temperature and air pressure
C to absorb the oxygen released by the seeds
D to show that glass beads respire
parts.answer: B to allow for changes in temperature and air pressure
parts.working: Glass beads do not respire, so any movement of the liquid in the control tube is caused by temperature or pressure changes, not by respiration. The seeds' movement can then be corrected.

practice.stem: A respirometer contains 20 germinating peas and soda lime. The capillary tube has an internal radius of 0.80 mm. The coloured drop moves 15.0 mm towards the peas in 10 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen taken in during the 10 minutes, in mm³. Use volume = πr² × distance and give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 30.2 mm³
parts.working: M1 π × 0.80² × 15.0 = 30.16 mm³; A1 30.2 mm³ to 3 significant figures

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 3.02 mm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why soda lime is placed in the respirometer.
parts.answer: it absorbs the carbon dioxide released, so the change in gas volume is due to oxygen uptake
parts.working: B1 absorbs carbon dioxide so only oxygen uptake changes the volume

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student could collect the gas given off by yeast and show that it is carbon dioxide.
parts.answer: pass the gas through a delivery tube into limewater; the limewater turns milky (cloudy), which shows carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 gas passed into limewater through a delivery tube; B1 limewater turns milky/cloudy; B1 this identifies carbon dioxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one control used in this investigation.
parts.answer: boiled yeast, or a tube with sugar solution and no yeast
parts.working: B1 any suitable control (boiled yeast / no yeast)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a respirometer containing germinating seeds and soda lime, a drop of coloured liquid in the capillary tube moves towards the seeds. Why?
A The seeds produce carbon dioxide, which pushes the liquid.
B The seeds take in oxygen and the carbon dioxide they release is absorbed by the soda lime.
C The soda lime releases oxygen, which the seeds absorb.
D The seeds release water vapour, which condenses.
parts.answer: B The seeds take in oxygen and the carbon dioxide they release is absorbed by the soda lime.
parts.working: Oxygen is used and the carbon dioxide released is absorbed, so the gas volume falls and the drop moves towards the seeds. A is wrong because the carbon dioxide is removed by the soda lime.

practice.stem: Eight woodlice were placed in a respirometer containing soda lime, kept in a water bath at 25 °C. The coloured drop in the capillary tube (internal radius 0.5 mm) moved 24 mm in 5 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen used in 5 minutes. Use volume = πr²l, where l is the distance moved. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 18.8 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen use in mm³ per minute, to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 3.77 mm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the role of the soda lime.
parts.answer: It absorbs the carbon dioxide released by the woodlice.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the apparatus was left for 10 minutes in the water bath before the readings were started.
parts.answer: To let the temperature of the air inside reach that of the water bath, so expansion/contraction of air does not move the drop.

practice.stem:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red in normal air, yellow when carbon dioxide concentration is high and purple when it is low. Four sealed tubes, kept in the dark, each contained 5 cm³ of red indicator and a gauze platform holding:
A: ten maggots
B: glass beads
C: germinating mung bean seeds
D: boiled mung bean seeds

parts.label: a
parts.text: Predict the colour of the indicator in each tube after 2 hours.
parts.answer: A yellow; B red; C yellow; D red

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the colour in tube C.
parts.answer: Germinating seeds respire, releasing carbon dioxide, which makes the indicator more acidic, so it turns yellow.
parts.working: B1 respiration releases carbon dioxide; B1 acidic → yellow.

practice.stem:
Yeast in glucose solution was connected to a gas syringe at 35 °C.
Time / min: 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10
Volume of gas / cm³: 0 | 6 | 14 | 22 | 27 | 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of gas production between 2 and 6 minutes, in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 4.0 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the rate changes after 6 minutes and suggest why.
parts.answer: The rate slows (only 8 cm³ in the last 4 minutes) because the glucose is being used up / ethanol builds up.
parts.working: B1 rate decreases with data; B1 substrate used up / product inhibits.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the gas collected.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide

practice.stem:
Students placed 10 woodlice into each of two tubes containing hydrogencarbonate indicator. The indicator is red at normal carbon dioxide levels and turns yellow when carbon dioxide increases.
Tube A: woodlice at 20 °C. Red to yellow in 25 minutes.
Tube B: woodlice at 10 °C. Red to yellow in 52 minutes.
Tube C: no woodlice, at 20 °C. Still red after 60 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why tube C was included in the experiment.
parts.answer: it is a control: with no woodlice there is no respiration, so it shows the colour change is caused by carbon dioxide from the woodlice
parts.working: B1 control to show the change is due to the animals; B1 no colour change without animals means CO₂ comes from respiration

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in time from tube A to tube B.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the result for tube B.
parts.answer: at 10 °C the enzymes in the woodlice work more slowly, so they respire more slowly and produce carbon dioxide more slowly
parts.working: B1 lower temperature slows enzyme-controlled respiration; B1 less CO₂ per minute so the colour change takes longer

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a gas syringe can be used to measure the rate of respiration of yeast at a fixed temperature.
parts.answer: yeast and sugar solution in a flask kept at a fixed temperature in a water bath, joined to a gas syringe; read the volume of gas at set times (e.g. every 5 minutes); repeat and calculate the mean; rate = volume ÷ time
parts.working: B1 yeast and sugar in flask at fixed temperature; B1 gas syringe connected; B1 volume read at timed intervals; B1 repeat, mean and rate = volume ÷ time

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same in this investigation.
parts.answer: temperature; mass or amount of yeast; volume and concentration of sugar solution

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the temperature must be kept constant in a respirometer experiment.
parts.answer: a change in temperature expands or contracts the air and moves the liquid drop falsely; the rate of respiration depends on temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: false movement from gas expansion; respiration rate changes with temperature; enzymes are affected

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the measurement of the movement more accurate.
parts.answer: use a capillary tube with a narrower bore (or a finer scale on the syringe)
parts.working: B1 narrower tube / finer scale / measure over a longer time

parts.label: a
parts.text: In an investigation of the effect of sugar concentration on the gas produced by yeast, identify the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: independent variable: sugar concentration; dependent variable: volume of gas produced (per minute)
parts.working: B1 independent variable is sugar concentration; B1 dependent variable is volume (or rate) of gas

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one variable that must be controlled and explain why.
parts.answer: temperature; so that any change in gas volume is caused only by the change in sugar concentration
parts.working: B1 names a suitable variable (temperature, yeast mass, volume); B1 explains it keeps the test fair

practice.stem:
A respirometer with 2 g of fly larvae and soda lime was placed in water baths at different temperatures. The distance moved by the drop in 10 minutes was recorded.
Temperature / °C: 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30
Distance in 10 min / mm: 6 | 11 | 17 | 9 | 34

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and suggest a reason for it.
parts.answer: 25 °C (9 mm) – expected about 23–25 mm; a leak in the apparatus / the larvae were not at the bath temperature / fewer larvae used.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the drop at 30 °C in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 3.4 mm per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the distance was at 30 °C than at 10 °C, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the rate of respiration increased with temperature.
parts.answer: Respiration is controlled by enzymes; higher temperature gives molecules more kinetic energy so more collisions / enzyme–substrate complexes, until the optimum.
parts.working: B1 enzymes; B1 more kinetic energy / collisions.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest two improvements to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each temperature three times and calculate means; use the same mass of larvae; leave to equilibrate before timing; use a thermostatic water bath.

practice.stem: You are provided with dried yeast, 5 % glucose solution, boiling tubes with delivery tubes, gas syringes, water baths, thermometers, a stopwatch and vegetable oil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find the effect of temperature on the rate of anaerobic respiration of yeast.
parts.answer: A plan with at least 5 temperatures, a measured product, controlled variables, repeats and a fair way to compare.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 6: use water baths at e.g. 20, 30, 40, 50, 60 °C; same mass of yeast and same volume and concentration of glucose solution; leave to reach temperature before mixing; a layer of oil on top (or sealed) to keep oxygen out; measure carbon dioxide volume in a gas syringe (or count bubbles) for a fixed time, e.g. 10 min; repeat three times and calculate mean; rate = volume ÷ time; control of boiled yeast; risk: hot water / care with glassware.

practice.stem: Twenty wheat grains had a total dry mass of 5.40 g. Twenty similar grains were germinated in the dark for 6 days, then dried in an oven; their dry mass was 4.32 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in dry mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dry mass decreased.
parts.answer: The seeds respire, breaking down stored food (starch) to release energy; carbon dioxide (and water) is lost, and in the dark no photosynthesis replaces the food.
parts.working: B1 respiration uses stored food; B1 carbon lost as CO₂ / no photosynthesis in dark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why dry mass, rather than fresh mass, was measured.
parts.answer: Fresh mass changes with the amount of water taken up, which does not show the change in food/organic material.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two yeast tubes with sugar solution are kept at 30 °C. Tube A has living yeast. Tube B has yeast that was boiled for 5 minutes before the start. Tube A gives off gas and tube B gives none. Which conclusion is best supported?
A sugar is not needed for yeast to respire
B boiling produces oxygen, which stops the respiration
C living yeast cells with working enzymes are needed to produce the gas
D boiled yeast contains more sugar than living yeast
parts.answer: C living yeast cells with working enzymes are needed to produce the gas
parts.working: Heat denatures the yeast enzymes, so the boiled yeast cannot respire. Boiling does not produce oxygen (B), and the sugar is the same in both tubes, so D is wrong.

practice.stem: Germinating seeds of mass 2.6 g were placed in a respirometer with soda lime. The gas syringe reading fell from 10.0 cm³ to 7.4 cm³ in 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 0.13 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate per gram of seeds, in cm³ per minute per gram.
parts.answer: 0.05 cm³ per minute per gram

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the gas syringe reading fell.
parts.answer: the seeds take in oxygen for aerobic respiration and the carbon dioxide they give out is absorbed by the soda lime, so the total gas volume falls
parts.working: B1 oxygen used in aerobic respiration; B1 carbon dioxide absorbed by soda lime so the volume falls

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a gas syringe with seedlings. Describe one limitation of this method for measuring the respiration of seedlings.
parts.answer: the syringe measures a small volume and may leak; seedlings also photosynthesise in light and change the gas volume
parts.working: B1 leaks / small volume gives a large error; B1 photosynthesis in light affects the gas volume (so use dark conditions)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an improvement that would make the investigation more reliable.
parts.answer: keep the apparatus in the dark and repeat the readings for a mean
parts.working: B1 dark conditions or repeat readings with a mean

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which part of a cell does most aerobic respiration take place?
A nucleus
B mitochondria
C ribosomes
D cell membrane
parts.answer: B mitochondria
parts.working: Aerobic respiration releases energy in the mitochondria. Ribosomes (C) make proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process uses energy released by respiration in a plant?
A diffusion of oxygen into a leaf
B active transport of mineral ions into root hair cells
C osmosis of water into a root hair cell
D transpiration of water from a leaf
parts.answer: B active transport of mineral ions into root hair cells
parts.working: Active transport needs energy from respiration because ions move against a concentration gradient. Diffusion and osmosis are passive and transpiration is a physical process driven by evaporation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas needed for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organelle in which aerobic respiration takes place.
parts.answer: mitochondrion (mitochondria)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two products of aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide and water

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cells of a plant root need aerobic respiration during the night.
parts.answer: roots cannot photosynthesise, so they need energy from respiration to actively take up mineral ions and to grow
parts.working: B1 no photosynthesis in roots / no light at night; B1 energy for active transport or growth

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaf in darkness takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide. Explain why.
parts.answer: aerobic respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide; there is no photosynthesis in darkness to use the carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂; B1 no photosynthesis in the dark

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process in the human body does NOT need energy from respiration?
A contraction of muscles
B active transport of glucose in the small intestine
C diffusion of oxygen into the blood in the alveoli
D building proteins from amino acids
parts.answer: C diffusion of oxygen into the blood in the alveoli
parts.working: Diffusion is passive and needs no energy from respiration. Active transport (B) needs energy, so it is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four uses of the energy released by respiration in the human body.
parts.answer: Any four: muscle contraction; protein synthesis; cell division; active transport; growth; passage of nerve impulses; maintaining a constant body temperature.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: The chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules (glucose) to release energy.
parts.working: B1 uses oxygen; B1 breaks down nutrients/glucose to release energy (in cells).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Muscle cells in the legs of a cyclist contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
parts.answer: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration; muscle contraction needs a lot of energy, so many mitochondria release more energy.
parts.working: B1 aerobic respiration in mitochondria; B1 lots of energy needed for contraction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The middle piece of a sperm cell is packed with mitochondria. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To release energy for the tail (flagellum) to move the sperm.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the two substances that the blood must bring to muscle cells for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: glucose and oxygen

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released when one molecule of glucose is completely broken down by aerobic respiration?
A 2
B 6
C 12
D 1
parts.answer: B 6
parts.working: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O: each glucose has six carbon atoms, and each one leaves as one molecule of carbon dioxide. Two or twelve do not match the balanced equation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of moles of glucose in 18.0 g. Relative formula mass of glucose is 180.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen needed to respire this mass of glucose completely.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of aerobic respiration increases during exercise, and how the breathing rate and heart rate respond.
parts.answer: muscles need more energy, so more oxygen is used and more carbon dioxide is produced; breathing rate and heart rate increase to bring more oxygen to the muscles and remove carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 muscles need more energy; B1 more oxygen used and more carbon dioxide made; B1 breathing and heart rate increase to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why liver cells contain many mitochondria.
parts.answer: liver cells carry out many energy-demanding processes, such as making proteins and converting ammonia into urea; aerobic respiration in the many mitochondria releases the energy needed
parts.working: B1 many energy-using processes (e.g. making proteins, converting ammonia to urea); B1 aerobic respiration in the mitochondria releases the energy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why aerobic respiration releases more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration.
parts.answer: glucose is broken down completely into carbon dioxide and water in aerobic respiration, whereas anaerobic respiration only partly breaks it down
parts.working: B1 complete breakdown in aerobic respiration; B1 partial breakdown in anaerobic respiration

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how oxygen reaches the cells in the interior of a leaf for aerobic respiration.
parts.answer: oxygen enters through stomata and diffuses through the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll to the cells, where it dissolves and diffuses into the cells
parts.working: B1 enters through stomata; B1 diffuses through air spaces to cells

practice.stem:
Relative molecular masses: glucose 180, oxygen 32, carbon dioxide 44, water 18.
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of oxygen needed to respire 36 g of glucose completely. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 36 ÷ 180 = 0.2 mol glucose needs 1.2 mol O₂; A1 1.2 × 32 = 38.4 g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that mass is conserved in this reaction.
parts.working: B1 water = 1.2 × 18 = 21.6 g and totals equal (74.4 g).

practice.stem: For this question, assume that aerobic respiration releases 16.0 kJ per gram of glucose and anaerobic respiration in muscle releases 0.8 kJ per gram of glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy is released per gram of glucose by aerobic respiration than by anaerobic respiration.
parts.answer: 20 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of glucose needed to release 400 kJ by (i) aerobic respiration and (ii) anaerobic respiration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use these figures to explain why muscles cannot rely on anaerobic respiration for long periods.
parts.answer: Anaerobic respiration releases far less energy per gram, so glucose would be used up very quickly; lactic acid also builds up and causes fatigue.
parts.working: B1 little energy / glucose used rapidly; B1 lactic acid accumulates / oxygen debt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose releases 2870 kJ per mole in aerobic respiration (value given for this question). Calculate the energy released by 9.0 g of glucose. Relative formula mass of glucose is 180.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Anaerobic respiration of one mole of glucose in yeast releases 210 kJ (value given for this question). Calculate this energy as a percentage of the aerobic value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Muscle tissue was placed in a water bath. Oxygen uptake was 0.30 cm³ per minute at 20 °C and 0.55 cm³ per minute at 30 °C. Calculate the percentage increase in oxygen uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the increase in oxygen uptake.
parts.answer: a higher temperature gives the enzymes more kinetic energy, so respiration is faster and more oxygen is used
parts.working: B1 more kinetic energy / more successful collisions; B1 faster enzyme-controlled respiration uses more oxygen

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a green plant needs both photosynthesis and aerobic respiration. Describe how the energy flows through the plant.
parts.answer: photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy in glucose; aerobic respiration releases this energy in mitochondria for growth and active processes; at night the plant respires but cannot photosynthesise; oxygen made in photosynthesis is used in respiration
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: light energy stored in glucose; respiration releases energy; energy used for growth and active transport; respiration continues at night; gases exchanged between the two processes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student measures the rate of photosynthesis of a plant at increasing light intensities, with temperature kept at 25 °C. The rate rises at first and then stays the same however bright the light becomes. Which factor is most likely to be limiting the rate once it stops rising?
A light intensity
B carbon dioxide concentration
C oxygen concentration
D humidity of the air
parts.answer: B carbon dioxide concentration
parts.working: Once more light no longer increases the rate, something other than light is in short supply; with temperature fixed, carbon dioxide concentration is the likely limiting factor. A is wrong because extra light has no effect on the plateau.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three environmental factors that can limit the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Light intensity; carbon dioxide concentration; temperature
parts.working: 1 mark each: light intensity; carbon dioxide concentration; temperature

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a limiting factor.
parts.answer: The factor that is in shortest supply; increasing it increases the rate of the process.
parts.working: B1 factor in shortest supply / that restricts the rate; B1 increasing it increases the rate

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Pondweed is kept in water baths at different temperatures. The rate of bubbling increases from 10 °C to 35 °C but falls sharply above 45 °C. What is the best explanation for the fall?
A enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured
B the pondweed closes its stomata
C carbon dioxide becomes more soluble in warm water
D the lamp gives out less light
parts.answer: A enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured
parts.working: High temperatures change the shape of the active sites of photosynthesis enzymes, so the rate falls. C is wrong: gases are less soluble, not more, in warmer water, and this would not explain a sharp fall.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A plant is in bright light at its optimum temperature. Which change is most likely to increase its rate of photosynthesis?
A lower the temperature to 5 °C
B remove the chlorophyll from the leaves
C increase the carbon dioxide concentration around the leaves
D move the plant into darkness
parts.answer: C increase the carbon dioxide concentration around the leaves
parts.working: With light and temperature no longer limiting, carbon dioxide is the next factor that can limit the rate. Lowering the temperature slows enzymes, and removing chlorophyll or using darkness stops photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two factors that a greenhouse owner can control to increase the rate of photosynthesis of tomato plants.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide concentration; temperature (or artificial light)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why adding more heat stops increasing the rate of photosynthesis above a certain temperature.
parts.answer: above the optimum temperature the enzymes denature, so photosynthesis slows down
parts.working: B1 enzymes denature above the optimum; B1 shape of the active site changes so fewer enzyme-substrate collisions

practice.stem:
A student placed a piece of pondweed in a test tube of water containing sodium hydrogencarbonate. A lamp was placed at different distances from the tube, and a beaker of water was placed between the lamp and the tube. After 5 minutes at each distance, the student counted the bubbles released in one minute, three times.
Distance / cm: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Trial 1: 52, 38, 22, 14, 8
Trial 2: 48, 35, 25, 12, 7
Trial 3: 50, 35, 22, 13, 9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute at 20 cm and at 40 cm.
parts.answer: 20 cm: 36; 40 cm: 13 bubbles per minute
parts.working: M1 add the three readings and divide by 3; A1 both means correct (36 and 13)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the distance of the lamp and the rate of bubbling.
parts.answer: As the distance increases the number of bubbles per minute decreases; from 50 per minute at 10 cm to 8 per minute at 50 cm.
parts.working: B1 further lamp → fewer bubbles (inverse relationship); B1 quotes paired data with units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate of bubbling changes as the lamp is moved further away.
parts.answer: Light intensity falls with distance; light is the limiting factor, so less photosynthesis and less oxygen is released.
parts.working: B1 lower light intensity further away; B1 less photosynthesis so less oxygen (gas) produced / light is limiting

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that the student should keep the same.
parts.answer: Any two of: temperature of water; carbon dioxide (hydrogencarbonate) concentration; same piece/length of pondweed; same lamp/bulb power; time allowed to acclimatise.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid controlled variables

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest why the student placed a beaker of water between the lamp and the test tube.
parts.answer: To absorb heat from the lamp so the temperature of the pondweed stays constant.
parts.working: B1 acts as a heat shield / keeps temperature constant

practice.stem: A grower near Murree produces tomatoes in a glasshouse during winter. Paraffin heaters are burned inside the glasshouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how burning paraffin in the heaters can increase the yield of tomatoes.
parts.answer: Burning releases heat, raising the temperature towards the optimum for photosynthesis enzymes; it also releases carbon dioxide, a raw material; so photosynthesis is faster and more sugar is made for growth.
parts.working: B1 raises temperature (enzymes work faster); B1 adds carbon dioxide (raw material/limiting factor); B1 faster photosynthesis → more glucose/growth/yield

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the grower switches on extra lamps on cloudy winter days.
parts.answer: Light intensity is low, so light is the limiting factor; lamps increase the rate of photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 light limiting on cloudy days

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the grower does not keep increasing the carbon dioxide concentration in the glasshouse.
parts.answer: Above a certain concentration another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting so yield does not increase further; the extra cost would then be wasted.
parts.working: B1 another factor becomes limiting / rate levels off; B1 extra cost gives no extra profit

practice.stem:
Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red when in equilibrium with air, yellow when carbon dioxide concentration rises and purple when it falls. Four tubes were set up and left for 3 hours:
Tube A: leaf, bright light
Tube B: leaf, tube covered in black paper
Tube C: no leaf, bright light
Tube D: leaf, tube covered with thin gauze (dim light)
All tubes started red. After 3 hours the indicator in tube D was still red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of the indicator in tubes A, B and C after 3 hours.
parts.answer: A purple; B yellow; C red (unchanged)
parts.working: 2 marks all three correct; 1 mark for two correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the colour in tube A and in tube B.
parts.answer: A: the leaf photosynthesised faster than it respired, taking in carbon dioxide, so CO₂ fell and the indicator turned purple. B: in the dark there is no photosynthesis; respiration released carbon dioxide so the indicator turned yellow.
parts.working: B1 A photosynthesis > respiration; B1 CO₂ removed → purple; B1 B only respiration, CO₂ added → yellow

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why tube C was set up.
parts.answer: As a control, to show that the leaf caused the colour change (light alone does not change the indicator).
parts.working: B1 control to show the change is due to the leaf

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the indicator in tube D stayed the same colour.
parts.answer: In dim light the rate of photosynthesis equalled the rate of respiration, so there was no net change in carbon dioxide concentration.
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis rate = respiration rate (compensation point); B1 no net uptake or release of CO₂

practice.stem:
A student measured the number of oxygen bubbles released by pondweed in one minute at a fixed distance of 20 cm from a lamp, using different concentrations of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.
Concentration / %: 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6
Bubbles per minute: 6, 11, 18, 22, 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable in this investigation.
parts.answer: concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution (carbon dioxide)
parts.working: B1 concentration of the hydrogencarbonate solution

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship between concentration and the rate of bubble production.
parts.answer: the rate increases as concentration rises from 0.1 % to 0.8 %, then levels off at 22 bubbles per minute from 0.8 % to 1.6 %
parts.working: B1 rate rises with concentration; B1 rate levels off after 0.8 %

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the rate does not increase between 0.8 % and 1.6 %.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide is no longer the limiting factor; light intensity or temperature is now limiting
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide no longer in short supply; B1 another factor (light or temperature) limits the rate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed, using bubble counts. Include the set-up, what you would change and what you would measure.
parts.answer: place pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution at a fixed distance from a lamp; keep the solution in a water bath at a set temperature; count bubbles per minute at each temperature; repeat and calculate the mean
parts.working: B1 pondweed in hydrogencarbonate at fixed light distance; B1 water bath to set and vary temperature; B1 count bubbles per minute; B1 repeat and calculate means

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: light intensity (distance from lamp); concentration of hydrogencarbonate solution; time of counting / length of pondweed

practice.stem: In a pondweed investigation, relative light intensity is calculated using the formula: relative light intensity = 10 000 ÷ d², where d is the distance of the lamp from the plant in cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the relative light intensity at 25 cm and at 50 cm.
parts.answer: 25 cm: 16.0 units; 50 cm: 4.0 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many times greater the light intensity is at 25 cm than at 50 cm.
parts.answer: 4 times
parts.working: B1 16 ÷ 4 = 4 (halving the distance gives four times the light)

parts.label: c
parts.text: The volume of oxygen collected at 25 cm was only 2.5 times the volume collected at 50 cm. Suggest why it was not 4 times greater.
parts.answer: At the higher light intensity another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, was limiting, so the rate could not rise in proportion to light.
parts.working: B1 another factor limiting at high light (CO₂ / temperature named); B1 so rate is not proportional to light intensity / light no longer the only limiting factor

practice.stem:
The rate of photosynthesis of a crop plant (arbitrary units) was measured at 25 °C.
Light intensity / units: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10
Rate at 0.04% CO₂: 0, 12, 20, 24, 24, 24
Rate at 0.10% CO₂: 0, 12, 24, 34, 40, 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the factor limiting the rate at a light intensity of 2 units for both concentrations of carbon dioxide. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Light intensity; the rate is the same at both carbon dioxide concentrations (and rises when light increases).
parts.working: B1 light intensity; B1 same rate at both CO₂ levels

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the factor limiting the rate at 0.04% carbon dioxide and a light intensity of 8 units. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide concentration; increasing CO₂ to 0.10% raises the rate, while more light does not.
parts.working: B1 carbon dioxide concentration; B1 higher CO₂ gives higher rate / plateau with more light

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in rate at a light intensity of 8 units when the carbon dioxide concentration is raised from 0.04% to 0.10%. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one factor that could be limiting the rate at 0.10% carbon dioxide and a light intensity of 10 units.
parts.answer: Temperature (or amount of chlorophyll / number of chloroplasts / enzymes).
parts.working: B1 temperature or another valid internal factor; not light or CO₂

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis of pondweed. Your plan should include the apparatus, the method, the variables to control and how the results would be recorded.
parts.answer: Pondweed in a boiling tube of hydrogencarbonate solution placed in water baths at a range of temperatures (e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C); acclimatise 5 minutes; count bubbles or collect gas volume in a set time (e.g. 1 minute); keep light intensity (lamp at fixed distance), CO₂ concentration and the same piece/length of pondweed constant; repeat 3 times and calculate a mean; record in a table of temperature against bubbles per minute; plot rate against temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: water baths/thermostatic control; at least 5 temperatures with a stated range; acclimatisation time; measure bubbles/gas volume in fixed time; light at fixed distance/same lamp; same CO₂/hydrogencarbonate concentration; same plant/length of pondweed; repeats and mean; results table with units / graph

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A pondweed gives 40 bubbles per minute at 10 cm from a lamp. Assume the rate of photosynthesis is proportional to light intensity, and that light intensity falls with the square of distance. How many bubbles per minute would be expected at 20 cm?
A 20
B 10
C 5
D 40
parts.working: Doubling the distance cuts the intensity to a quarter: 40 ÷ 4 = 10 bubbles per minute. A (20) assumes the rate halves, which is the wrong relationship.

practice.stem:
Leaf discs were placed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solutions of different concentrations. The time taken for half of the discs to float was recorded.
Concentration of hydrogencarbonate / %: 0.2, 0.8, 1.6, 3.2
Time for half the discs to float / min: 22.0, 8.0, 6.5, 6.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate 1 ÷ time for the 0.8 % and 3.2 % solutions, giving each answer to 3 significant figures. Give units.
parts.answer: 0.125 min⁻¹ and 0.159 min⁻¹

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the time hardly changes between 1.6 % and 3.2 %.
parts.answer: another factor (light or temperature) is now limiting, so more carbon dioxide has no further effect
parts.working: B1 another factor limits the rate

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: repeat each concentration and calculate a mean time
parts.working: B1 repeats and mean; or use more discs

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Magnesium ions taken up by a plant are needed to make
A chlorophyll
B protein
C cellulose
D starch
parts.answer: A chlorophyll
parts.working: Magnesium is part of the chlorophyll molecule. Protein (B) needs nitrogen from nitrate ions, not magnesium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why plants need nitrate ions.
parts.answer: To make amino acids (and so proteins).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two visible signs of nitrate ion deficiency in a plant.
parts.answer: Stunted (poor) growth; yellowing of the (older, lower) leaves.
parts.working: 1 mark each: stunted/weak growth; yellow leaves

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecule in a plant cell needs phosphate ions taken up from the soil?
A starch
B cellulose
C DNA
D glucose
parts.answer: C DNA
parts.working: Phosphate is part of nucleic acids such as DNA. Starch, cellulose and glucose contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two features of root hair cells that help them take up mineral ions.
parts.answer: a long projection giving a large surface area; many mitochondria that release energy for active transport
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: large surface area; many mitochondria; thin cell wall (short diffusion path)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the roots of a plant growing in waterlogged soil may absorb mineral ions less well.
parts.answer: waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so the roots cannot respire aerobically; less energy is released for active transport of mineral ions
parts.working: B1 little oxygen in waterlogged soil; B1 roots cannot respire aerobically; B1 less energy for active transport of ions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a plant growing in soil that lacks magnesium ions grows slowly.
parts.answer: Magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; less chlorophyll is made, so leaves turn yellow; less light is absorbed so the rate of photosynthesis falls; less glucose is available for respiration and for making new materials (e.g. cellulose, proteins) for growth.
parts.working: B1 Mg for chlorophyll; B1 less chlorophyll/yellow leaves; B1 less light absorbed/less photosynthesis; B1 less glucose for growth/energy/new cells

practice.stem:
Maize seedlings were grown for 4 weeks in jars of different solutions.
Solution 1: complete nutrient solution – mean height 32 cm, dark green leaves
Solution 2: no nitrate – mean height 11 cm, pale yellow older leaves
Solution 3: no magnesium – mean height 18 cm, yellow between the leaf veins
Solution 4: distilled water – mean height 6 cm, very pale leaves

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which solution acts as the control.
parts.answer: Solution 1 (complete nutrient solution)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean height of seedlings in solution 2 as a percentage of the mean height in solution 1. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the appearance of the seedlings in solution 3.
parts.answer: No magnesium so less chlorophyll is made; leaves turn yellow (between the veins) and less photosynthesis means slower growth.
parts.working: B1 no Mg → little chlorophyll / yellow leaves; B1 less photosynthesis → less growth

parts.label: d
parts.text: Air was bubbled through each jar. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To supply oxygen to the roots for aerobic respiration; this releases energy for active transport (uptake) of ions.
parts.working: B1 oxygen for root respiration; B1 energy for active uptake of mineral ions

parts.label: e
parts.text: Each jar was covered with black paper. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To stop algae growing in the solution (algae would compete for ions).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Root hair cells take up mineral ions from dilute soil solution by active transport. Which statement explains why this process needs energy?
A the ions move down a concentration gradient
B the ions move from a lower to a higher concentration
C water moves into the cell by osmosis
D the ions are too large to pass through the membrane
parts.answer: B the ions move from a lower to a higher concentration
parts.working: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, which needs energy from aerobic respiration. A describes diffusion, which needs no energy.

practice.stem:
Maize plants were grown for four weeks in solutions containing different concentrations of nitrate ions. The dry mass of the shoots was measured at the end.
Nitrate concentration / mg per dm³: 0, 50, 100, 200
Mean dry mass of shoots / g: 0.42, 0.78, 1.10, 1.14

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean dry mass of shoots between 0 and 100 mg per dm³ nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of nitrate concentration on the dry mass of shoots.
parts.answer: dry mass increases as nitrate concentration rises from 0 to 100 mg per dm³; above 100 mg per dm³ dry mass levels off
parts.working: B1 increases with nitrate up to 100 mg per dm³; B1 levels off because nitrate is no longer limiting

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one change to the investigation that would show more precisely where the dry mass stops increasing.
parts.answer: test more nitrate concentrations between 100 and 200 mg per dm³, and repeat each one to calculate a mean
parts.working: B1 extra concentrations between 100 and 200 mg per dm³; B1 repeat each concentration and calculate a mean

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bag of fertiliser has a mass of 25 kg and is labelled 15 % nitrogen by mass. Calculate the mass of nitrogen in the bag.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the ion that plants take up as their main source of nitrogen from the soil.
parts.answer: nitrate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to set up a fair experiment to compare the growth of cress seedlings in a complete nutrient solution with distilled water.
parts.answer: same number and size of seedlings in each container; same volume of solution, light and temperature; measure height or dry mass after the same time; repeat and calculate the mean
parts.working: B1 same number/size of seedlings; B1 same light, temperature, volume; B1 measure growth after the same time; B1 repeat and mean

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrate ions are often at a higher concentration inside root hair cells than in the soil water. Explain how root hair cells absorb nitrate ions.
parts.answer: By active transport; ions move against the concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration) using carrier proteins in the membrane; energy is released by respiration in the root cells.
parts.working: B1 active transport; B1 against the concentration gradient; B1 energy from respiration (carrier proteins)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a crop growing in waterlogged soil absorbs fewer nitrate ions.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen (air spaces filled with water); root cells carry out less aerobic respiration; so less energy is released for active transport of ions.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen in soil; B1 less aerobic respiration in roots; B1 less energy for active transport

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how adding nitrate fertiliser increases the yield of a wheat crop.
parts.answer: Nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins; these are needed for growth of new cells (e.g. enzymes, more leaves), so the plant grows larger and produces more grain.
parts.working: B1 amino acids/proteins made; B1 more growth / more leaves / more photosynthesis → greater yield

practice.stem:
A farmer in Punjab tested different amounts of nitrate fertiliser on wheat.
Fertiliser / kg per ha: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
Yield / tonnes per ha: 2.8, 4.1, 5.0, 5.4, 5.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in yield for each of these steps: 0 to 50 kg/ha, and 150 to 200 kg/ha.
parts.answer: 0 to 50: 1.3 tonnes/ha; 150 to 200: 0.1 tonnes/ha
parts.working: M1 subtraction from table; A1 both values

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield when the fertiliser is raised from 0 to 150 kg/ha. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farmer decides to use 150 kg/ha rather than 200 kg/ha. Suggest two reasons for this decision.
parts.answer: The extra 50 kg gives very little extra yield, so the cost of the fertiliser is greater than the value of the extra crop; excess fertiliser may be washed (leached) into rivers and cause eutrophication.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: small extra yield; cost not repaid/profit; leaching/run-off; eutrophication/water pollution; another factor now limiting

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that mineral ions enter root hair cells by osmosis. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: osmosis is the movement of water only, down a water potential gradient; mineral ions move by active transport against a concentration gradient, using energy from respiration
parts.working: B1 osmosis moves water, not ions; B1 ions move by active transport against the concentration gradient, which needs energy from aerobic respiration

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why magnesium deficiency first shows as yellowing on the older leaves.
parts.answer: magnesium is mobile in the phloem and is moved from the older leaves to the younger, growing leaves
parts.working: B1 magnesium is mobile / moved in the phloem; B1 older leaves lose it first

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which tissue of a leaf do the cells contain the most chloroplasts?
A upper epidermis
B palisade mesophyll
C spongy mesophyll
D xylem
parts.answer: B palisade mesophyll
parts.working: Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface where light is brightest. Spongy mesophyll (C) has fewer chloroplasts and more air spaces.

practice.stem:
A student describes a section through a leaf, from top to bottom:
W – a thin, waxy layer with no cells
X – a single layer of transparent cells with no chloroplasts
Y – tall, column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts
Z – rounded, loosely packed cells with large air spaces between them
The lowest layer of cells contains many small pores, each surrounded by a pair of bean-shaped cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name layers W, X, Y and Z.
parts.answer: W cuticle; X upper epidermis; Y palisade mesophyll; Z spongy mesophyll

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pores in the lower layer and the cells on either side of each pore.
parts.answer: Stomata; guard cells

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which layer of a leaf are most of the stomata found?
A upper epidermis
B lower epidermis
C palisade mesophyll
D xylem
parts.answer: B lower epidermis
parts.working: Most stomata are on the lower epidermis, which is shaded and cooler, reducing water loss. The palisade layer contains chloroplasts but no stomata.

practice.stem:
A student describes a leaf cross-section from top to bottom:
P: thin, waxy and transparent, with no cells
Q: a single layer of flattened, transparent cells
R: tall, column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts
S: rounded cells with large air spaces between them
T: a single layer of cells with stomata

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the layers P, Q, R, S and T.
parts.answer: P cuticle; Q upper epidermis; R palisade mesophyll; S spongy mesophyll; T lower epidermis

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the waxy layer P.
parts.answer: reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two tissues in a vascular bundle and the substances each transports.
parts.answer: xylem carries water and mineral ions up the plant; phloem carries sugars (sucrose) and amino acids, in both directions
parts.working: B1 xylem; B1 water and mineral ions up; B1 phloem; B1 sugars and amino acids

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how palisade mesophyll cells are adapted for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: They contain many chloroplasts to absorb light; they are near the upper surface where light intensity is greatest; they are tall/closely packed, so many fit in the layer and absorb most light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: many chloroplasts; near upper surface; closely packed/column shape; thin walls/large vacuole pushes chloroplasts to edge

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll.
parts.answer: Allow gases (carbon dioxide and oxygen) to diffuse quickly through the leaf to and from the cells; provide a large surface area for gas exchange.
parts.working: B1 diffusion of CO₂ to cells / O₂ away; B1 large surface area for gas exchange

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the upper epidermis has no chloroplasts and is transparent.
parts.answer: So that light passes through to the palisade cells below.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the pathway taken by a carbon dioxide molecule from the air outside a leaf to a chloroplast in a palisade cell.
parts.answer: Through an open stoma; diffuses through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll; dissolves in the film of water on the cell surface and diffuses through the cell wall and membrane into the chloroplast.
parts.working: B1 enters via stoma; B1 through air spaces; B1 dissolves in moisture / through cell wall and membrane into chloroplast

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf during the day.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is used up in photosynthesis, so its concentration inside the leaf is lower than in the air; it diffuses down the concentration gradient.
parts.working: B1 used in photosynthesis; B1 lower concentration inside / down concentration gradient

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does the spongy mesophyll have large air spaces between its cells?
A to store starch
B to allow gases to diffuse quickly to and from the cells
C to hold water for transpiration
D to protect the leaf from pests
parts.answer: B to allow gases to diffuse quickly to and from the cells
parts.working: The air spaces let carbon dioxide and oxygen diffuse rapidly to the cells and away from them. Water is held in cell walls, not in the air spaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of a leaf is adapted for gas exchange. Give four points.
parts.answer: stomata let carbon dioxide and oxygen diffuse in and out; air spaces in the spongy mesophyll let gases reach every cell; the leaf is thin, so gases diffuse a short distance; cell surfaces are moist, so gases dissolve before entering the cells
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: stomata; air spaces; thin leaf (short diffusion distance); moist cell surfaces; gases dissolve in cell walls; many stomata give a large exchange area

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a desert plant's leaf reduces water loss. Give three features.
parts.answer: a thick waxy cuticle; sunken stomata in pits; fewer stomata; hairs on the leaf that trap humid air; rolled leaves

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaf has an area of 6.0 cm². The lower surface has 180 stomata per mm². Calculate the number of stomata on the lower surface. (1 cm² = 100 mm²)
parts.answer: 108 000 stomata

practice.stem:
A student painted clear nail varnish on both surfaces of a hibiscus leaf, peeled it off and counted stomata in five fields of view under a microscope. The diameter of the field of view was 0.4 mm.
Lower surface: 22, 25, 19, 24, 20
Upper surface: 3, 5, 4, 2, 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of stomata per field of view for each surface.
parts.answer: Lower: 22; upper: 4

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the area of the field of view in mm². Use area = πr². Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the number of stomata per mm² on the lower surface. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: 175 stomata per mm²

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why there are more stomata on the lower surface of this leaf.
parts.answer: The lower surface is shaded and cooler; so less water is lost by transpiration/evaporation than if stomata were on the upper surface.
parts.working: B1 lower surface cooler/out of direct sunlight; B1 reduces water loss

practice.stem:
A student measured leaves from the top (sunny) and the lower (shaded) branches of a mango tree.
Sun leaves: palisade layer 120 µm thick, mean leaf area 42 cm²
Shade leaves: palisade layer 60 µm thick, mean leaf area 68 cm²

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of the palisade thickness of sun leaves to shade leaves.
parts.answer: 2 : 1 (twice as thick)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest an advantage to the tree of having a thicker palisade layer in sun leaves.
parts.answer: More layers of palisade cells / more chloroplasts; so more of the bright light is absorbed and used, giving more photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 more palisade cells/chloroplasts; B1 absorb more light → more photosynthesis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why shade leaves have a larger surface area.
parts.answer: Light is dim in the shade; a larger area traps more of the limited light for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 low light intensity in shade; B1 larger area absorbs more light

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why shade leaves are thinner.
parts.answer: Little light reaches deep layers, so extra layers of cells would not photosynthesise much (and would use materials/respire).
parts.working: B1 little light penetrates / thick leaf not needed

practice.stem: A student measures a palisade cell in a microscope image. The image is 42 mm long and the magnification is × 400.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual length of the palisade cell in micrometres. Use 1 mm = 1000 µm.
parts.answer: 105 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the magnification of a microscope image must be known before a length can be found.
parts.answer: to convert the measured length of the image into the actual length of the cell
parts.working: B1 to convert the image size into the actual size

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the function of the cuticle on the upper epidermis.
parts.answer: a waterproof wax layer that reduces water loss by evaporation through the upper surface
parts.working: B1 waterproof / reduces water loss; B1 by evaporation from the upper surface

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stomata open in light and close in darkness.
parts.answer: in light, guard cells take in water and become turgid, so the stomata open to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis; in darkness, there is no photosynthesis, so the guard cells lose water and the stomata close to save water
parts.working: B1 guard cells turgid in light; B1 open to let CO₂ in for photosynthesis; B1 in the dark guard cells lose water and stomata close

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis?
A 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
B 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
C C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
D CO₂ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂
parts.answer: A 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
parts.working: A has 6 C, 18 O and 12 H on each side. C is the equation for aerobic respiration, the reverse of photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the source of energy for photosynthesis and name the substance that absorbs it.
parts.answer: Light (from the Sun); chlorophyll

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where water used in photosynthesis enters the plant.
parts.answer: Through the root hair cells (roots)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas is released by a plant during photosynthesis in bright light?
A carbon dioxide
B oxygen
C nitrogen
D hydrogen
parts.answer: B oxygen
parts.working: Photosynthesis splits water and releases oxygen. Carbon dioxide is taken in, not given out, when photosynthesis is faster than respiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two products of photosynthesis.
parts.answer: glucose and oxygen

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the gas that aerobic respiration needs but that is released by photosynthesis, not made by respiration.
parts.answer: oxygen
parts.working: B1 oxygen: respiration uses it to release energy from glucose; photosynthesis releases it

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four ways in which a plant uses the glucose made in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Any four of: respiration to release energy; converted to starch for storage; cellulose for cell walls; sucrose for transport in phloem; amino acids/proteins (with nitrate ions); fats and oils for storage (e.g. in seeds); nectar to attract insects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why glucose is converted to starch for storage in leaf cells.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble; so it does not affect the water potential of the cell / cause osmosis (and does not diffuse out of the cell).
parts.working: B1 starch insoluble; B1 no effect on osmosis / water potential, or compact and stays in cell

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define photosynthesis.
parts.answer: The process by which plants make carbohydrates (glucose) from raw materials (carbon dioxide and water) using energy from light.
parts.working: B1 makes carbohydrates/glucose from CO₂ and water; B1 using light energy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy; and transfers it into chemical energy (for making carbohydrates).
parts.working: B1 absorbs light; B1 converts/transfers it to chemical energy

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two things that can happen to the oxygen made in a palisade cell.
parts.answer: Used in respiration in the plant's own cells; diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata into the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Using the balanced equation 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, calculate the mass of oxygen released from 90 g of water. Assume all the water reacts. (Mr of water = 18, of oxygen = 32)
parts.working: M1 90 ÷ 18 = 5 mol water, so 5 mol O₂; A1 5 × 32 = 160 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose made in leaves is often converted to starch for storage. Explain why the plant stores starch rather than glucose.
parts.answer: starch is insoluble, so it does not affect the water potential of cells or diffuse out; glucose is soluble and would draw in water and be lost
parts.working: B1 starch is insoluble / does not change water potential; B1 glucose is soluble and would be transported or lost

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other uses of the glucose made in photosynthesis.
parts.answer: respiration to release energy; making cellulose for cell walls; making proteins with nitrogen from nitrate

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the word equations for photosynthesis and aerobic respiration. State what the products of photosynthesis are for the reactants of respiration.
parts.answer: the glucose and oxygen made in photosynthesis are the reactants of aerobic respiration; the carbon dioxide and water from respiration are the reactants of photosynthesis
parts.working: B1 glucose and oxygen used in respiration; B1 carbon dioxide and water used in photosynthesis

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the energy change that takes place during photosynthesis.
parts.answer: light energy is absorbed by chlorophyll and converted into chemical energy stored in the glucose made
parts.working: B1 light energy absorbed by chlorophyll; B1 converted to chemical energy in glucose

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a test to show that oxygen is produced by pondweed in bright light.
parts.answer: collect the gas given off in a test tube; put a glowing wooden splint into the tube; the splint relights, showing oxygen
parts.working: B1 collect gas and insert a glowing splint; B1 relights, showing oxygen

practice.stem: A maize crop was kept in a sealed chamber with 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness. In the light, the crop took in carbon dioxide at a rate of 30 units per hour. In the dark, it released carbon dioxide at a rate of 6 units per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the net uptake of carbon dioxide by the crop over the whole 24 hours.
parts.answer: 288 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the crop releases carbon dioxide at night.
parts.answer: There is no light so no photosynthesis; respiration continues all the time and releases carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 no photosynthesis in dark; B1 respiration releases CO₂

parts.label: c
parts.text: The measured uptake of 30 units per hour in the light is less than the true rate of photosynthesis. Explain why.
parts.answer: During the day the plant also respires; some of the carbon dioxide used in photosynthesis comes from respiration inside the plant, so the measured uptake = photosynthesis − respiration.
parts.working: B1 respiration also happens in the light; B1 CO₂ from respiration used, so uptake underestimates gross photosynthesis

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A plant absorbs 36 molecules of carbon dioxide during photosynthesis. Assuming every carbon dioxide molecule is used, how many glucose molecules could be made?
A 6
B 1
C 12
D 36
parts.answer: A 6
parts.working: The equation 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ needs six carbon dioxide molecules per glucose. 36 ÷ 6 = 6 glucose molecules.

parts.label: a
