parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide needed and the mass of oxygen produced when 9.0 g of glucose is made by photosynthesis. Relative formula masses: glucose 180, CO₂ 44, O₂ 32.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide 13.2 g; oxygen 9.6 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sealed flask containing a plant is kept in bright light. Over several hours the carbon dioxide in the flask falls and the mass of the plant increases. Explain both observations using the equation for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose, so the carbon dioxide level falls; glucose is stored in the plant as starch or cellulose, increasing its dry mass; respiration uses some of the glucose but photosynthesis is faster overall; the water is taken from the sealed system
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: CO₂ used in photosynthesis; glucose builds up as dry mass; photosynthesis faster than respiration; glucose stored or used to make cellulose

practice.stem: A leaf was destarched by keeping the plant in the dark for 48 hours. Half of the leaf was covered with black card. The plant was then kept in bright light for 6 hours and the leaf was tested for starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of the uncovered part of the leaf after the iodine test.
parts.answer: blue-black

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the covered part of the leaf would show, and explain why.
parts.answer: no colour change (it stays orange-brown); the covered part got no light, so no photosynthesis took place and no starch was made
parts.working: B1 orange-brown / no starch; B1 no light so no photosynthesis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Half of the leaf was covered with black card, rather than cutting the leaf in two. Explain why covering part of one leaf is a better method.
parts.answer: both parts come from the same leaf, so they have the same age and history; the card only blocks light, so the covered and uncovered parts are compared fairly
parts.working: B1 both halves are from the same leaf, so the comparison is fair; B1 the card blocks light only, all other conditions being the same

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of boiling the leaf in water before the test.
parts.answer: kills the cells and breaks down the membranes so that the iodine can reach the starch

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaf is heated in ethanol in a water bath rather than over a Bunsen burner.
parts.answer: ethanol is flammable, so a naked flame is dangerous; a water bath heats it safely
parts.working: B1 ethanol is flammable; B1 water bath avoids a naked flame

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of the ethanol.
parts.answer: it removes the chlorophyll so that the colour change is easier to see

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of iodine solution before and after it reacts with starch.
parts.answer: orange-brown before; blue-black after

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the leaf is spread on a white tile before iodine is added.
parts.answer: so that the colour change is easy to see
parts.working: B1 colour change easy to see

practice.stem:
A student tests a leaf for starch.
Step 1: the leaf is placed in boiling water for 1 minute.
Step 2: the leaf is placed in a tube of ethanol in a hot water bath until it turns white.
Step 3: the leaf is dipped into warm water.
Step 4: the leaf is spread on a white tile and covered with iodine solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the reason for each of steps 1 to 4.
parts.answer: 1: kills the cells / stops reactions and breaks down membranes so iodine can enter; 2: removes the chlorophyll (decolourises the leaf) so the colour change can be seen; 3: softens the brittle leaf (and removes ethanol); 4: tests for starch.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ethanol is heated in a water bath and not directly over a Bunsen burner.
parts.answer: Ethanol is flammable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the colour seen if the leaf contains starch and if it contains no starch.
parts.answer: Starch present: blue-black; no starch: orange-brown (colour of iodine).

practice.stem: A variegated plant has leaves with green patches and white patches. The plant was destarched in the dark and then kept in light for 6 hours. When the leaf was tested, only the green patches turned blue-black.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the white patches of the leaf did not turn blue-black.
parts.answer: white patches have no chlorophyll, so no photosynthesis takes place and no starch is made
parts.working: B1 no chlorophyll; B1 no photosynthesis so no starch

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the independent variable and one variable that must be kept the same.
parts.answer: independent variable: presence of chlorophyll (green or white tissue); kept the same: the light intensity / time in the light
parts.working: B1 presence of chlorophyll; B1 light or time kept the same

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use the results below to conclude which two factors are needed for starch to be made in a leaf.
Leaf 1: in light, with carbon dioxide: blue-black
Leaf 2: in light, carbon dioxide absorbed by soda lime: orange-brown
Leaf 3: in darkness, with carbon dioxide: orange-brown
Leaf 4: in light, with carbon dioxide: blue-black
parts.answer: light and carbon dioxide
parts.working: B1 light is needed (leaf 3 has no starch); B1 carbon dioxide is needed (leaf 2 has no starch)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these steps into the correct order: add iodine; boil the leaf in water; dip the leaf in warm water; heat the leaf in ethanol in a water bath.
parts.answer: boil the leaf in water; heat in ethanol in a water bath; dip in warm water; add iodine
parts.working: B1 boiling first and ethanol second; B1 warm water dip before the iodine

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaf has an area of 12.0 cm². After the test, 7.5 cm² of the leaf was blue-black. Calculate the percentage of the leaf area that was blue-black.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the leaf is dipped into warm water after the ethanol step.
parts.answer: the leaf becomes soft and easier to handle, and the warm water rehydrates it so that the iodine can penetrate
parts.working: B1 softens the leaf / removes ethanol; B1 rehydrates the leaf so iodine can enter

practice.stem:
A potted plant with variegated leaves (green areas with chlorophyll and white areas without) was kept in the dark for 48 hours. A strip of aluminium foil was then fixed across part of one leaf and the plant was placed in sunlight for 6 hours. The leaf was then tested for starch.
Region P: green, not covered
Region Q: white, not covered
Region R: green, covered by foil

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plant was kept in the dark for 48 hours before the experiment.
parts.answer: To destarch the leaves; the plant uses up its stored starch (converted to sugar and respired/translocated), so any starch found later must have been made during the experiment.
parts.working: B1 removes starch / destarching; B1 so starch present must come from photosynthesis during the experiment

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the colour after the iodine test in each of regions P, Q and R. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: P (green, uncovered): blue-black – it had chlorophyll and light so photosynthesised and made starch. Q (white, uncovered): orange-brown – no chlorophyll so no photosynthesis. R (green, covered): orange-brown – no light reached it so no photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 P blue-black; B1 Q orange-brown; B1 R orange-brown; B1 Q explained (no chlorophyll); B1 R explained (no light)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which two regions show that light is needed for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: P and R

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's leaf turned blue-black all over, including the area covered by black card. Suggest two reasons for this error.
parts.answer: the plant was not destarched properly before the test; light leaked under the card; iodine was left on the leaf
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible errors

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the reason the leaf must be decolourised before testing.
parts.answer: chlorophyll is green and hides the blue-black colour; ethanol removes it so the colour change can be seen
parts.working: B1 chlorophyll hides the colour; B1 ethanol removes it

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that Benedict's solution can be used instead of iodine to show starch in a leaf. Explain why this would not work.
parts.answer: Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars, not for starch; starch is a large non-reducing molecule, so the test would give no colour change
parts.working: B1 Benedict's tests for reducing sugar; B1 starch is non-reducing, so no colour change

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two safety precautions when heating ethanol for the starch test.
parts.answer: use a water bath rather than a naked flame; keep the ethanol away from any flames
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: water bath, not a naked flame; ethanol is flammable, so keep it away from flames; wear eye protection

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student reported that starch was present in a leaf because the leaf turned brown with iodine. Identify the error and give the correct colour for a positive result.
parts.answer: brown or orange is the colour of iodine alone, so no reaction happened; a positive test turns blue-black
parts.working: B1 brown is the colour of iodine alone / no reaction; B1 positive result is blue-black

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a control test to check that the iodine solution itself is working.
parts.answer: add a few drops of iodine to a starch solution; a blue-black colour shows that the iodine works
parts.working: B1 iodine added to a known starch solution; B1 blue-black shows the reagent is working

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the arrangement of tissues in a leaf allows as much light as possible to be absorbed.
parts.answer: Leaf is broad/flat with large surface area; thin so light reaches all cells; upper epidermis and cuticle are transparent; palisade layer with most chloroplasts is just below the upper surface; spongy cells also contain chloroplasts to absorb light passing through.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: large surface area; thin; transparent cuticle/epidermis; palisade near top; many chloroplasts in palisade; chloroplasts can move/spongy layer absorbs remaining light

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how guard cells control the opening of a stoma during the day and explain why this is important for photosynthesis.
parts.answer: In light, guard cells take in water and become turgid; this makes them curve apart and the stoma opens; carbon dioxide can then diffuse in for photosynthesis.
parts.working: B1 guard cells absorb water/turgid; B1 stoma opens; B1 CO₂ enters for photosynthesis (O₂ leaves)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path of water from the xylem in a vein to the air outside a leaf.
parts.answer: water leaves the xylem and moves into the mesophyll cells; it evaporates from the cell walls into the air spaces; it diffuses out through open stomata into the air
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: leaves xylem by osmosis or diffusion; moves through mesophyll cell walls; evaporates into air spaces; diffuses out through open stomata

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how humidity and wind speed affect the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: high humidity lowers the water vapour concentration gradient, so transpiration slows; wind removes water vapour from around the stomata, keeping the gradient steep, so transpiration speeds up; stomata may close in very windy or dry conditions
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: humidity lowers the gradient; high humidity slows; wind removes vapour; steeper gradient; faster transpiration; wind can cause stomata to close

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how guard cells open a stoma.
parts.answer: guard cells take in water by osmosis and become turgid; their thin inner walls bend apart, opening the stoma; the uneven thickness of the walls causes the bending
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: water enters by osmosis; turgid; uneven wall thickness; walls bend apart; stoma opens

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a plant in a dry habitat reduces water loss, using the stomata and the leaf surface.
parts.answer: stomata close in the heat of the day to reduce evaporation; fewer or sunken stomata reduce the air movement at the surface; hairs trap a layer of moist air; a thick cuticle reduces evaporation through the surface; rolled leaves trap humid air
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between a leaf grown in full sun and a leaf grown in deep shade.
parts.answer: a sun leaf is thicker and smaller; a shade leaf is larger and thinner; a sun leaf has more palisade layers; a shade leaf has more chloroplasts per cell
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four sensible contrasts

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why shade leaves are larger and thinner, and contain more chlorophyll.
parts.answer: a larger surface area helps capture the little light available; a thin leaf lets more light reach the cells; more chlorophyll absorbs more of the scarce light; these are adaptations to low light
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: large area for low light; thin; more chlorophyll; more light absorbed; adaptive response; less water loss not the main factor

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the distribution of stomata on the upper and lower surfaces of a floating pond-lily leaf with a land plant leaf.
parts.answer: a floating leaf has stomata only on the upper surface, which is in air; a land leaf has more stomata on the lower surface, which is shaded; both surfaces of a land leaf may have stomata
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparisons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the advantage of this difference for the floating leaf.
parts.answer: the upper surface is exposed to air so gases can diffuse in and out there; the lower surface is in water so stomata there would not work and would let water in; this lets the leaf photosynthesise and exchange gases efficiently
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the cuticle and the stomata of a leaf from a plant in a dry habitat with those of a tomato leaf. Give four points.
parts.answer: the dry-habitat leaf has a thicker, waxier cuticle; the tomato leaf has a thin cuticle; the dry-habitat leaf has fewer stomata (or sunken stomata); the tomato leaf has more stomata on its surface
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four contrasts

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the thickness of the cuticle affects the rate of water loss, and why a plant from a dry habitat benefits from a thick cuticle.
parts.answer: a thicker cuticle slows the evaporation of water through the leaf surface, so the rate of water loss is lower; this helps the plant survive when little water is available
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points: thick cuticle slows evaporation; lower water loss; waxy layer is waterproof; survives dry conditions

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table shows the number of stomata per mm² on the upper and lower surfaces of two leaves.
Leaf X: upper 20, lower 120
Leaf Y: upper 5, lower 90
Describe the difference between the two leaves.
parts.answer: leaf X has more stomata on both surfaces; leaf X has a much higher upper surface count (20 against 5); the difference is greatest on the lower surface (120 − 90 = 30, against 20 − 5 = 15 on the upper surface); both leaves have more stomata on the lower surface
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparisons with figures

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest and explain which leaf is better adapted to a dry environment.
parts.answer: leaf Y, because it has fewer stomata on the upper surface where the air is hot and dry; fewer stomata reduce water loss by transpiration; the lower surface is shaded
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the vascular bundles in a leaf support photosynthesis and transport its products.
parts.answer: Xylem brings water (a raw material) and mineral ions such as magnesium to the mesophyll; phloem carries sucrose (and amino acids) made in photosynthesis away from the leaf to other parts of the plant; the network of veins means every cell is close to a vein; xylem also helps to support the leaf so it is held out flat to the light.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: xylem supplies water; xylem supplies mineral ions; phloem removes sucrose/amino acids; translocation to growing/storage parts; branching veins close to all cells; support/lignin keeps blade spread

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why most leaves are thin.
parts.answer: Short diffusion distance for gases (CO₂ in, O₂ out) to and from all cells; light can reach all the cells.
parts.working: B1 short diffusion distance for gases; B1 light penetrates to all cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a leaf has a waxy cuticle even though this reduces gas exchange through the surface.
parts.answer: It reduces water loss by evaporation; gases can still enter through the stomata.
parts.working: B1 reduces water loss (gases use stomata)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of the palisade and spongy mesophyll layers and their functions.
parts.answer: palisade cells are tall and packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface to absorb most light; spongy cells are loosely packed with air spaces for gas exchange; spongy cells also contain some chloroplasts
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: palisade near top; many chloroplasts; spongy with air spaces; gas exchange; some chloroplasts in spongy

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how carbon dioxide reaches the palisade cells.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide enters through stomata in the lower epidermis; it diffuses through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll; it dissolves into the moist cell walls; it diffuses across the cell membranes into the palisade cells; a concentration gradient is maintained by photosynthesis using the carbon dioxide
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: stomata; air spaces; dissolves in moist cell walls; diffuses into cells; concentration gradient; used up by photosynthesis

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a method for counting stomata using clear nail varnish and a microscope.
parts.answer: paint nail varnish on the leaf and leave it to dry; peel off the impression and place it on a slide; count the stomata in a field of view on the microscope; repeat in several fields of view and calculate the mean
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: nail varnish impression; peel and mount; count in one field; repeat and mean

parts.label: b
parts.text: In one investigation, the mean number of stomata in a field of view of area 0.5 mm² was 60. Calculate the number of stomata per mm². Give one source of error in the method.
parts.answer: 120 stomata per mm²; source of error: counting the same stomata twice, or missing stomata at the edge of the field of view
parts.working: M1 60 ÷ 0.5; A1 120 stomata per mm²; B1 one sensible source of error (counting twice, missing stomata at the edge, or nail varnish not peeling cleanly)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a chloroplast and state its role.
parts.answer: a double membrane surrounds stacks of thylakoids (grana) and a fluid stroma; the thylakoids contain chlorophyll; the chloroplast is the site of photosynthesis
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: double membrane; thylakoids/grana; chlorophyll in thylakoids; stroma; site of photosynthesis

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a plant with a magnesium deficiency is pale and cannot make enough glucose, and why a leaf with few chloroplasts photosynthesises less.
parts.answer: magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll; without it, less light is absorbed; with fewer chloroplasts there is less surface for light absorption and fewer sites for photosynthesis; so less glucose is made and growth slows
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: Mg needed for chlorophyll; less light absorbed; fewer chloroplasts; less photosynthesis; less glucose; slower growth

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path of light through a typical leaf.
parts.answer: light passes through the transparent cuticle and upper epidermis; it reaches the palisade cells, which absorb most of it; the remaining light passes through the spongy mesophyll, which also absorbs some
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: cuticle; upper epidermis; palisade absorbs most; spongy absorbs remainder

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the leaves of most plants are broad and flat, and why the arrangement of chloroplasts is important.
parts.answer: a broad flat leaf presents a large surface area to the Sun so more light is absorbed; chloroplasts near the upper surface are where light is strongest; chloroplasts can move within the cell to avoid strong light; so photosynthesis is efficient
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of xylem vessels and state their function.
parts.answer: dead cells with no cytoplasm or end walls, forming continuous tubes; strengthened by lignin; they carry water and mineral ions up the plant
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: dead cells; no end walls; lignin strengthening; carry water and ions upwards

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how xylem vessels allow a leaf to keep transpiring during a hot day.
parts.answer: water is pulled up the xylem by transpiration pull; the continuous water column is held by cohesion; the lignin stops the vessels collapsing under tension; water loss from the leaf replaces water taken up by the roots
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: transpiration pull; cohesion; column of water; no collapse due to lignin; replaces water lost; continuous flow

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaf is approximately rectangular, 8.0 cm long and 5.0 cm wide. Calculate its area in cm² and in mm². (1 cm² = 100 mm²)
parts.answer: 40 cm²; 4000 mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a larger leaf may not always photosynthesise faster than a smaller one.
parts.answer: a larger leaf needs more water and loses more water by transpiration; the leaf may not receive the same light in the middle of the canopy; diffusion of carbon dioxide into the centre of the leaf may be slower; a larger leaf may shade lower leaves
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the adaptations of a leaf and a root hair cell as exchange surfaces.
parts.answer: both have a large surface area; both have a thin wall or membrane for a short diffusion distance; both maintain a steep concentration gradient; leaves have stomata for gases, while root hairs take in water and mineral ions
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four comparisons

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a plant needs exchange surfaces that are large and thin.
parts.answer: a large, thin surface gives a short diffusion distance and a large area for exchange; gases and water exchange quickly; a steep concentration gradient is maintained, increasing the rate of diffusion; this supports photosynthesis and root absorption
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six sensible points

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student adds biuret solution to a sample of liquid egg white and shakes the tube. What colour shows that protein is present?
A blue-black
B brick red
C purple
D cloudy white
parts.answer: C purple
parts.working: Biuret solution is blue and turns purple (violet) with protein. Blue-black is the iodine result for starch, so A is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which food test must be carried out in a hot water bath?
A Benedict's test for reducing sugar
B biuret test for protein
C ethanol emulsion test for fat
D iodine test for starch
parts.answer: A Benedict's test for reducing sugar
parts.working: Benedict's solution only reacts with reducing sugar when heated (about 80 °C water bath). The iodine test is done cold, so D is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the reagent used to test a food for starch.
parts.answer: iodine solution
parts.working: B1 iodine (solution); accept iodine in potassium iodide

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour of the reagent before the test and the colour seen if starch is present.
parts.answer: before: orange-brown (yellow-brown); with starch: blue-black

parts.label: c
parts.text: A potato slice gives a positive result. Suggest why a slice of ripe mango gives only a weak result.
parts.answer: most of the starch in ripe mango has been converted to sugars
parts.working: B1 starch broken down/converted to (reducing) sugar during ripening

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how you would test a sample of ground peanuts for fat using the ethanol emulsion test.
parts.answer: Mix/shake the crushed peanut with ethanol; pour the ethanol (liquid) into a tube of water (or add water); a cloudy white emulsion shows fat.
parts.working: B1 shake sample with ethanol; B1 add (decant) the ethanol into water; B1 cloudy/milky white emulsion = fat present

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the test tube and sample must be kept away from a Bunsen flame.
parts.answer: ethanol is flammable

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the food substance detected by each of these tests.
Test 1: iodine solution
Test 2: Benedict's solution
Test 3: biuret solution
Test 4: ethanol emulsion
parts.answer: 1 starch; 2 reducing sugar; 3 protein; 4 fat (lipid)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which test needs heating?
parts.answer: Test 2 (Benedict's)

practice.stem:
Four food samples, P, Q, R and S, were tested. Results:
P: iodine blue-black; Benedict's blue; biuret purple; emulsion clear
Q: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's brick red; biuret blue; emulsion cloudy white
R: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's blue; biuret blue; emulsion cloudy white
S: iodine blue-black; Benedict's green; biuret blue; emulsion clear

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the substances present in sample P and in sample Q.
parts.answer: P: starch and protein; Q: reducing sugar and fat
parts.working: B1 P both correct; B1 Q both correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which sample could be a mixture of fruit juice and coconut milk? Give a reason.
parts.answer: Q, because fruit juice gives reducing sugar and coconut milk gives fat
parts.working: B1 Q; B1 reducing sugar (from juice) and fat (from coconut milk)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that should be kept the same when doing each test on the four samples.
parts.answer: volume of sample (or volume of reagent, temperature/time of heating for Benedict's)
parts.working: B1 any one sensible controlled variable

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the food test that uses copper(II) sulfate and sodium hydroxide.
parts.answer: biuret test

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the food test that turns brick red.
parts.answer: Benedict's test

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a food that gives a positive ethanol emulsion test.
parts.answer: e.g. butter, ghee, cooking oil, nuts

practice.stem:
Benedict's test was done on four samples heated for 4 minutes at 80 °C.
Tube 1 (sugarcane juice, diluted): yellow
Tube 2 (milk): green
Tube 3 (apple juice): brick red
Tube 4 (distilled water): blue

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which tube shows the most reducing sugar.
parts.answer: tube 3

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the control tube.
parts.answer: tube 4 (water)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why all tubes were heated for exactly the same time.
parts.answer: colour continues to change with time, so a fair comparison needs equal heating

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A crushed sample of a food gave these results.
iodine solution: stays orange-brown
Benedict's solution, heated: turns orange
biuret solution: stays blue
ethanol emulsion test: clear
Which food could it be?
A boiled rice
B grape juice
C cooking oil
D boiled egg white
parts.answer: B grape juice
parts.working: Only reducing sugar is present, which fits grape juice (glucose and fructose). Boiled rice would give blue-black with iodine, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to carry out the Benedict's test on a sample of honey dissolved in water. Include the safety precaution you would take.
parts.answer: Add an equal volume of Benedict's solution to the honey solution; heat in a water bath at about 80 °C for a few minutes; wear eye protection (goggles).
parts.working: B1 add Benedict's (equal volume); B1 heat in water bath (not direct flame), named time/temperature; B1 goggles/eye protection or use test-tube holder

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the colour change seen if a large amount of reducing sugar is present.
parts.answer: blue to brick red

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a negative result with Benedict's solution does not prove that a food contains no sugar at all.
parts.answer: some sugars, such as sucrose, are non-reducing and do not react with Benedict's solution
parts.working: B1 non-reducing sugar (sucrose) gives no colour change

parts.label: a
parts.text: A food technologist in Faisalabad tests a new flavoured milk drink. It gives a purple colour with biuret solution and a green colour with Benedict's solution. State what these results show.
parts.answer: protein present; small amount of reducing sugar present
parts.working: B1 protein; B1 (little/small amount of) reducing sugar

parts.label: b
parts.text: Biuret solution can be made by mixing two solutions. Name the two solutions.
parts.answer: sodium hydroxide (or potassium hydroxide) and copper(II) sulfate
parts.working: B1 sodium/potassium hydroxide; B1 copper sulfate

parts.label: c
parts.text: The technologist also tests plain water in the same way. Explain why.
parts.answer: it is a control, to show that the reagents alone do not give a colour change
parts.working: B1 control / to compare / show colour is due to the food

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: "Chapati gave a blue-black colour with iodine, so chapati contains only starch." Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: a positive iodine test only shows starch is present; other substances (protein, fat) may also be present and need their own tests
parts.working: B1 test only shows starch; B1 other nutrients need other tests / chapati also contains protein/fat

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find out whether the chapati also contains protein.
parts.answer: crush with water, add biuret solution (sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate); purple shows protein

practice.stem:
A student heated 2 cm³ of each of four drinks, A to D, with 2 cm³ Benedict's solution in a water bath at 80 °C. She recorded the time for the first appearance of green.
A: 85 s
B: 240 s
C: 40 s
D: 130 s

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the results to put the drinks in order of reducing sugar content, highest first.
parts.answer: C, A, D, B

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the time taken links to the reducing sugar concentration.
parts.answer: the higher the concentration, the shorter the time for the colour to change

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate a relative rate of colour change for drink A as 1000/time (arbitrary units), giving your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 1000 ÷ 85 = 11.8 (arbitrary units)

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the end point of the test more reliable.
parts.answer: compare against a colour standard/chart, or use the same observer, white tile behind the tube, or repeat and average

practice.stem:
A student crushed 2 g each of lentils (daal), boiled rice, chicken and banana with 10 cm³ water and tested them with biuret solution.
lentils: deep purple
boiled rice: very pale lilac
chicken: purple
banana: blue

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why each crushed sample was mixed with the same volume of water.
parts.answer: so that the comparison is fair / the concentration depends only on the food

parts.label: b
parts.text: Which food contained the most protein? Explain how you decided.
parts.answer: lentils, because they gave the deepest purple

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one hazard in this test and how to reduce it.
parts.answer: sodium hydroxide is corrosive/irritant: wear eye protection

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest an improvement so that the colours could be compared more objectively.
parts.answer: use a colorimeter, or compare with a colour chart of known protein standards

practice.stem:
Four unlabelled tubes, W, X, Y and Z, contain glucose solution, starch suspension, albumin (protein) solution and an oil-in-water mixture, in some order.
W: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's blue; biuret blue
X: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's brick red; biuret blue
Y: iodine blue-black; Benedict's blue; biuret blue
Z: iodine orange-brown; Benedict's blue; biuret purple

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the solution in each tube.
parts.answer: X: glucose; Y: starch; Z: albumin (protein)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what tube W must contain, and explain how you can tell from these results.
parts.answer: the oil-in-water mixture; W gave negative results in all three tests, and glucose, starch and albumin have already been identified in X, Y and Z, so W is the only one left (by elimination)
parts.working: B1 oil/fat; B1 negative for all three tests and the other three solutions identified (elimination)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest a further test to confirm that W is the oil-in-water mixture, and state the expected result.
parts.answer: ethanol emulsion test: cloudy white

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student in Lahore tests milk for fat by shaking it with ethanol and pouring into water. The result is cloudy. Explain why this result might be unreliable unless a control is used.
parts.answer: milk itself is cloudy/white, so the cloudiness may not be due to an emulsion; a control (milk + water without ethanol) is needed for comparison
parts.working: B1 milk already cloudy/opaque; B1 compare with control

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why fats form a cloudy emulsion in this test.
parts.answer: fat dissolves in ethanol but is insoluble in water, so it forms tiny droplets when the ethanol is added to water
parts.working: B1 fat insoluble in water, droplets form

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four glucose solutions of different concentrations were each heated with the same volume of Benedict's solution for 5 minutes. Which final colour shows the highest concentration of glucose?
A blue
B green
C yellow
D brick red
parts.answer: D brick red
parts.working: The more reducing sugar, the more precipitate forms and the colour moves blue → green → yellow → orange → brick red. Yellow (C) shows less sugar than brick red.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor suspects that a patient has diabetes. Explain how a Benedict's test on the patient's urine could support this diagnosis.
parts.answer: glucose is a reducing sugar; urine of a person with diabetes may contain glucose, so the test turns green/yellow/orange/red instead of staying blue
parts.working: B1 glucose present in urine of diabetic (not normally present); B1 positive (colour change from blue) result

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the Benedict's test is not used to measure exact blood glucose concentration in a hospital.
parts.answer: it is only semi-quantitative: the colours are judged by eye and only show a rough range; it does not give a number
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: colour judged subjectively; only rough/semi-quantitative; colours overlap; slow/needs heating; other reducing sugars also react

parts.label: a
parts.text: A seed is cut in half and one half is crushed with water, then filtered. Explain why the seed must be crushed before testing it for starch and protein.
parts.answer: crushing breaks open cells (cell walls) so the starch/protein is released and can mix with the reagent
parts.working: B1 breaks cells/cell walls; B1 releases contents / larger surface area for reagent to reach

parts.label: b
parts.text: The filtrate gives a blue-black colour with iodine but the solid residue on the filter paper gives an even darker colour. Suggest why.
parts.answer: starch is insoluble (large molecules), so most stayed in the residue; only a little passed through into the filtrate
parts.working: B1 starch insoluble/large molecules; B1 most starch remains in the residue

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the result you would expect with Benedict's solution if the seed has just started to germinate, and explain your answer.
parts.answer: orange/red (positive) because amylase breaks down starch into maltose, a reducing sugar
parts.working: B1 colour change from blue (green to red); B1 starch digested to maltose/reducing sugar by amylase

practice.stem: A student had a 10 % glucose stock solution and distilled water. She wanted to make 10 cm³ each of 2 %, 4 %, 6 % and 8 % glucose standards to compare with an unknown sample using Benedict's solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the stock solution and of distilled water needed to make 10 cm³ of each standard. Give the volumes for 2 %, 4 % and 6 %.
parts.answer: 2 %: 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water; 4 %: 4 cm³ stock + 6 cm³ water; 6 %: 6 cm³ stock + 4 cm³ water

parts.label: b
parts.text: The unknown sample went the same colour as the 4 % standard after the same heating time. State the glucose concentration of the unknown, and suggest how to make the estimate more precise.
parts.answer: about 4 %; make more standards with smaller intervals (e.g. 3.5 %, 4.5 %) around 4 %
parts.working: B1 4 % (between 3 and 5 %); B1 smaller intervals / use a colorimeter

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: volume of Benedict's solution; volume of sample; temperature of water bath; time of heating

practice.stem:
Starch solution and amylase were mixed at 35 °C. Every 2 minutes a drop of the mixture was added to a drop of iodine solution on a spotting tile.
0 min: blue-black
2 min: blue-black
4 min: dark brown
6 min: orange-brown
8 min: orange-brown

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the time when all the starch had been digested.
parts.answer: 6 minutes
parts.working: B1 first sample to stay orange-brown

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the colour of the iodine changed during the experiment.
parts.answer: amylase digested starch into maltose (reducing sugar); iodine stays orange-brown when no starch is left
parts.working: B1 amylase breaks down starch; B1 to maltose/sugar so no blue-black

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe a test you could do on the mixture at 8 minutes to show a product of the reaction, and state the expected result.
parts.answer: Benedict's test: heat with Benedict's in a water bath; brick red/orange (colour change from blue)
parts.working: B1 Benedict's + heat; B1 positive colour

parts.label: d
parts.text: Calculate the rate of starch digestion as 1/time in min⁻¹, to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare the reducing sugar content of three brands of orange juice using Benedict's solution. Include the variables you would control and how you would record results.
parts.answer: Same volume of each juice (e.g. 2 cm³) + same volume of Benedict's (2 cm³); heat in a water bath at the same temperature (80 °C) for the same time, or time until first colour change; compare colours with a range of glucose standards or record time; repeat three times and average; wear goggles; record in a table (brand, colour/time, repeats, mean).
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to six of: same volume juice; same volume Benedict's; water bath stated temp; same time / time to colour change; dilute juices equally if needed; standards of known glucose concentration; repeats and mean; safety (goggles); table with headings; conclusion: more sugar = redder / shorter time

parts.label: a
parts.text: A solution of the enzyme amylase is tested with biuret solution and with Benedict's solution. Predict both results and explain them.
parts.answer: biuret: purple, because amylase is a protein; Benedict's: stays blue, because there is no reducing sugar
parts.working: B1 purple + enzyme is protein; B1 Benedict's blue/negative

parts.label: b
parts.text: The amylase solution is mixed with starch suspension and left at 37 °C for 15 minutes. Predict the results of the iodine, Benedict's and biuret tests on the mixture. Explain each prediction.
parts.answer: iodine: orange-brown (starch digested); Benedict's: positive, green to brick red (maltose produced); biuret: purple (enzyme is still present, unchanged at the end of the reaction)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which molecules are joined together to form a protein?
A amino acids
B fatty acids
C glucose
D glycerol
parts.answer: A amino acids
parts.working: Proteins are chains of amino acids. Fatty acids and glycerol make fats, so B is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the smaller molecules that make up:
(i) starch
(ii) fats and oils
parts.answer: (i) glucose; (ii) fatty acids and glycerol
parts.working: B1 glucose; B1 fatty acids; B1 glycerol

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the chemical elements found in all carbohydrates.
parts.answer: carbon, hydrogen and oxygen

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which list shows all of the chemical elements found in fats and oils?
A carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
B carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen
C carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
D carbon, oxygen and sulfur
parts.answer: A carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
parts.working: Fats and oils contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (like carbohydrates, but with much less oxygen). Nitrogen (C) is found in proteins, not fats.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each substance is a carbohydrate, a protein or a fat (lipid):
(i) haemoglobin in red blood cells
(ii) the cellulose in a cotton shirt
(iii) cooking oil pressed from mustard seeds
(iv) insulin
parts.answer: (i) protein (ii) carbohydrate (iii) fat/lipid (iv) protein

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the smaller molecules that join together to make the substance in (a)(ii).
parts.answer: glucose

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each fat molecule is made from one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acid molecules. A sample containing 40 fat molecules is completely digested. Calculate the number of fatty acid molecules and the number of glycerol molecules produced.
parts.answer: 120 fatty acid molecules and 40 glycerol molecules

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme that digests fats.
parts.answer: lipase

parts.label: a
parts.text: From this list, name the two substances that are small enough to be absorbed into the blood without digestion: starch, glucose, protein, amino acid, fat.
parts.answer: glucose and amino acid

parts.label: b
parts.text: A child eats a piece of potato. Explain why the starch in the potato must be digested before the body can use it.
parts.answer: Starch is a large, insoluble molecule; it cannot pass through the gut wall into the blood, so it is broken down into small soluble glucose molecules that can be absorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: starch molecules too large / insoluble; must be broken down to glucose (small, soluble) to be absorbed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the substance described in each case:
(i) a polysaccharide made of glucose that is stored in the liver
(ii) a molecule made of glycerol and fatty acids
(iii) the building blocks of the enzyme amylase
(iv) a polysaccharide made of glucose that forms the walls of plant cells
parts.answer: (i) glycogen (ii) fat/lipid (iii) amino acids (iv) cellulose

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the polysaccharide stored in the liver and muscles of humans.
parts.answer: glycogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the polysaccharide that forms plant cell walls.
parts.answer: cellulose

parts.label: c
parts.text: Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all made of the same smaller molecule. Name it, and state one reason why starch is a good storage molecule.
parts.answer: glucose; insoluble so it does not affect osmosis (or compact, large)
parts.working: B1 glucose; B1 insoluble/does not affect water potential/compact

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sucrose is the sugar in sugarcane. Name the two simple sugars that make one sucrose molecule.
parts.answer: glucose and fructose

parts.label: b
parts.text: Maltose is made when starch is digested. State the simple sugar it is made of.
parts.answer: glucose (two glucose units)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which one of these carbohydrates is insoluble in water: glucose, cellulose, maltose.
parts.answer: cellulose
parts.working: B1 cellulose (a polysaccharide); glucose and maltose are soluble sugars

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of molecules are both polysaccharides made of glucose?
A glycogen and cellulose
B glucose and starch
C sucrose and glycogen
D maltose and cellulose
parts.answer: A glycogen and cellulose
parts.working: Glycogen, cellulose and starch are long chains of glucose. Glucose is a single sugar, and sucrose and maltose are made of only two sugar units, so B, C and D each contain a molecule that is not a polysaccharide.

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows the mass of three nutrients in 100 g of four foods eaten in Pakistan.
food | carbohydrate / g | protein / g | fat / g
boiled chickpeas (chana) | 27 | 9 | 3
ghee | 0 | 0 | 99.5
chapati | 46 | 8 | 4
boiled egg | 1 | 13 | 11

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which food in the table is mainly lipid.
parts.answer: ghee

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of protein in a 250 g serving of boiled chickpeas.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mass of protein in two boiled eggs of 50 g each, and state whether this is more or less protein than in (b).
parts.answer: 13 g; less than in (b)

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the element that is present in the protein of these foods but not in their carbohydrate.
parts.answer: nitrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mustard plant makes glucose by photosynthesis. Name three different carbohydrates that the plant can make from this glucose and state one use of each.
parts.answer: starch – energy store; cellulose – cell walls; sucrose – transport in phloem
parts.working: 1 mark each for a correct named carbohydrate with its use: starch (storage), cellulose (cell wall), sucrose (transport in phloem).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The plant also stores oil in its seeds. Name the two kinds of smaller molecule that make up oil.
parts.answer: fatty acids and glycerol

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the plant also needs to absorb nitrate ions from the soil before it can make proteins.
parts.answer: Proteins are made of amino acids, which contain nitrogen; glucose has no nitrogen, so nitrate supplies the nitrogen to make amino acids.
parts.working: 1 mark each: amino acids/proteins contain nitrogen; nitrate is the source of nitrogen (glucose contains only C, H, O).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A runner stores about 400 g of glycogen in her muscles and 100 g in her liver. Each gram of glycogen releases about 17 kJ when respired. Calculate the total energy available from these stores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the molecule that glycogen is broken down into before it is used in respiration.
parts.answer: glucose

parts.label: c
parts.text: Glycogen is a large, insoluble molecule. Suggest one advantage of storing glucose as glycogen rather than as glucose itself.
parts.answer: It is insoluble so it does not affect water potential / osmosis in the cells (and does not diffuse out of the cell).
parts.working: B1 insoluble so no osmotic effect / does not leave the cell; accept compact store.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what determines the shape of a protein molecule.
parts.answer: the sequence (order) of amino acids in the chain

parts.label: b
parts.text: In sickle-cell anaemia one amino acid in the haemoglobin chain is different. Suggest why this single change can stop haemoglobin working normally.
parts.answer: A different amino acid changes the shape of the protein, so it no longer carries oxygen normally.
parts.working: 1 mark each: change in sequence changes shape; shape is linked to function, so function (oxygen carrying) is affected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Antibodies are proteins. Explain why an antibody that fits the measles virus does not fit the polio virus.
parts.answer: Each antibody has a specific binding site shape that is complementary to one antigen; the polio antigen has a different shape so it does not fit.
parts.working: 1 mark each: binding site has specific shape; complementary to only one antigen shape.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one element found in proteins that is not found in carbohydrates or fats.
parts.answer: nitrogen (also sulfur in some)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Different enzymes have different shapes even though they are all made of amino acids. Explain why.
parts.answer: different sequence (order) of amino acids; this makes the chain fold into a different shape
parts.working: B1 sequence/order of amino acids; B1 folds into specific shape

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a person whose diet lacks protein may not be able to make some enzymes.
parts.answer: enzymes are proteins made from amino acids obtained from dietary protein

parts.label: a
parts.text: A camel's hump stores about 36 kg of fat. Fat releases about 39 kJ per gram and carbohydrate (glycogen) about 17 kJ per gram. Calculate the mass of glycogen that would store the same amount of energy as the fat. Give your answer in kg to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to suggest why animals that travel long distances store energy mainly as fat.
parts.answer: Fat stores more than twice as much energy per gram, so the same energy store is much lighter: the fat is about 46.6 kg lighter than the glycogen that would store the same energy, so it is less energy to carry.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more energy per gram / less mass for same energy; lighter to carry when moving (quote a figure for credit).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Proteins are built from 20 different kinds of amino acid. Calculate how many different chains of exactly three amino acids could be made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Most proteins contain hundreds of amino acids. Use your answer to (a) to explain why there are so many different proteins with different functions in living organisms.
parts.answer: The number of possible sequences rises enormously with chain length; each different sequence of amino acids folds into a different shape; the shape (e.g. active site, binding site) decides the function.
parts.working: 1 mark each: huge number of possible sequences; different sequence → different shape; shape determines function (e.g. enzyme active site / antibody binding site).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table.
molecule | elements present | smaller molecules it is made from
starch | ? | ?
protein | ? | ?
fat | ? | ?
parts.answer: starch: C, H, O – glucose; protein: C, H, O, N (some S) – amino acids; fat: C, H, O – fatty acids and glycerol

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says, 'If I eat enough fat I do not need protein, because both give me energy.' Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: The body needs amino acids to make its own proteins (enzymes, antibodies, muscle, growth and repair); fat contains no nitrogen, so the body cannot make amino acids from it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: proteins needed for growth/repair; to make enzymes/antibodies/haemoglobin; amino acids contain nitrogen; fats lack nitrogen so cannot be converted to amino acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sunflower seed has a mass of 60 mg and 45 % of this mass is oil. Oil releases 39 kJ per gram and starch 17 kJ per gram. Calculate the energy stored in the oil of one seed, in kJ.
parts.answer: 1.053 kJ (accept 1.05 kJ)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer harvests 2.5 kg of these sunflower seeds. Calculate the total mass of oil in the harvest, in kg.
parts.answer: 1.125 kg (accept 1.13 kg)
parts.working: M1 2.5 × 0.45 = 1.125 kg (oil is 45 % of the seed mass); A1 1.125 kg.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is an advantage for seeds that are carried by the wind to store oil rather than starch.
parts.answer: The seed is lighter for the same energy store (about 62 mg of starch v 27 mg of oil), so it is carried further by the wind.
parts.working: B1 lighter / smaller for same energy, so dispersed further.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starch and cellulose are both made of glucose. Humans can digest starch but not cellulose. Explain why, using your knowledge of enzymes.
parts.answer: Enzymes are specific: amylase fits the bonds/shape in starch but not in cellulose, and humans do not make an enzyme (cellulase) that digests cellulose.
parts.working: 1 mark each: enzymes are specific to the shape of their substrate; humans lack an enzyme that digests cellulose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cows can obtain energy from the cellulose in grass. Suggest how.
parts.answer: Microorganisms in their gut make enzymes that digest cellulose into glucose, which the cow can use.
parts.working: B1 microorganisms/bacteria in the gut digest cellulose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Although humans cannot digest it, cellulose in vegetables such as okra (bhindi) is an important part of the diet. State why.
parts.answer: It is dietary fibre (roughage): it adds bulk so food moves through the intestine by peristalsis and constipation is prevented.
parts.working: B1 fibre/roughage helps peristalsis / prevents constipation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which property of water makes it important for transporting substances in blood plasma and phloem?
A It is a solvent for many substances.
B It contains nitrogen.
C It is a source of energy.
D It is an enzyme.
parts.answer: A It is a solvent for many substances.
parts.working: Water dissolves many substances (glucose, ions, urea), so they can be carried in solution. Water provides no energy, so C is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which elements are present in a molecule of glucose?
A carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen
B carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
C carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
D carbon, oxygen and nitrogen
parts.answer: B carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
parts.working: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a carbohydrate and contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. C is the set for amino acids/proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the liquid in which each substance is transported dissolved in water:
(i) glucose in a human
(ii) mineral ions in a rice plant
(iii) sucrose in a sugarcane plant
parts.answer: (i) blood plasma (ii) xylem sap / water in xylem (iii) phloem sap

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other process in the human body in which water acts as a solvent.
parts.answer: digestion (food dissolved so enzymes can act / products absorbed) or excretion (urea removed in urine)

parts.label: a
parts.text: About 60 % of the mass of an adult human is water. Calculate the mass of water in a man of mass 70 kg.
parts.answer: 42 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: A lettuce leaf is about 95 % water but a dry wheat grain is only about 12 % water. Calculate the mass of water in a 40 g lettuce leaf.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a dry wheat grain can be stored for many months without germinating.
parts.answer: There is too little water for enzymes to work / for metabolism, so the grain stays dormant.
parts.working: B1 too little water for enzymes/reactions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy the table and write a tick (✓) where an element is always present in the molecule and a cross (✗) where it is not.
element | carbohydrate | fat | protein
carbon | | |
hydrogen | | |
oxygen | | |
nitrogen | | |
parts.answer: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen: ✓ in all three; nitrogen: ✗ carbohydrate, ✗ fat, ✓ protein

parts.label: a
parts.text: Apart from acting as a solvent, state two ways in which plants use water.
parts.answer: raw material for photosynthesis; keeps cells turgid to support the plant; transpiration cools leaves

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why animal cells need water in their cytoplasm.
parts.answer: Chemical reactions (metabolism) take place in solution / enzymes act in solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the element described in each case:
(i) present in all proteins but not in starch
(ii) a mineral element found in haemoglobin
(iii) a mineral element needed to make chlorophyll
parts.answer: (i) nitrogen (ii) iron (iii) magnesium

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Urea leaves the body in urine. Which role of water does this show?
A water as a coolant
B water as a solvent in excretion
C water as a raw material for photosynthesis
D water as a solvent in digestion
parts.answer: B water as a solvent in excretion
parts.working: Urea is a waste product that is removed dissolved in water, so water is acting as a solvent in excretion. D is about dissolving food in the gut, not removing waste.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Saliva is about 99 % water. A student puts a dry, salted cracker in his mouth. Explain why the water in saliva is important in the digestion of the cracker.
parts.answer: Water dissolves the food/sugars and moistens it; amylase can only act on starch in solution / the enzyme reactions happen in water.
parts.working: 1 mark each: dissolves/moistens food; enzymes (amylase) work in solution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the products of digestion must be dissolved in water before they are absorbed in the small intestine.
parts.answer: Only dissolved molecules can diffuse/be transported across the villus wall into the blood; they are then carried in solution in plasma.
parts.working: 1 mark each: dissolved molecules pass through the gut wall/cell membranes; carried in solution in blood plasma.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person excretes 30 g of urea dissolved in 1.5 dm³ of urine in a day. Calculate the concentration of urea in g per dm³.
parts.answer: 20 g per dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a hot day in Jacobabad the same person drank little water and produced only 0.8 dm³ of urine, still containing 30 g of urea. Calculate the new concentration.
parts.answer: 37.5 g per dm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the body cannot stop producing urine completely, even when short of water.
parts.answer: Urea is toxic and must be removed; it can only be excreted dissolved in water, so some water must be lost in urine.
parts.working: 1 mark each: urea toxic/must be excreted; needs water as a solvent to remove it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the tissue through which water carries mineral ions from the roots to the leaves.
parts.answer: xylem

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer's maize crop is growing in very dry soil. The soil contains plenty of magnesium, but the leaves are turning yellow. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: Mineral ions are only absorbed and transported when dissolved in water; with little soil water, little magnesium enters the roots/xylem; magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll, so leaves turn yellow.
parts.working: 1 mark each: ions must be dissolved to be absorbed/transported; little water so little Mg reaches leaves; Mg needed for chlorophyll.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child with cholera loses large volumes of watery faeces. State two substances, apart from water, that the child loses.
parts.answer: salts/ions such as sodium and chloride (also potassium)
parts.working: 1 mark each; accept named ions (sodium, chloride, potassium).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Doctors in Karachi give oral rehydration solution: clean water with salt and glucose dissolved in it. Explain why the child's blood needs enough water to carry out its functions.
parts.answer: Plasma is mostly water; water is the solvent in which glucose, ions, urea and hormones are transported; without it blood volume falls and transport/excretion fail.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two: plasma is mainly water; water is the solvent for transport of nutrients/ions; needed to carry urea to kidneys for excretion.

practice.stem:
A student found the water content of three foods. She weighed a fresh sample, dried it in an oven at 90 °C for two days, and weighed it again.
food | fresh mass / g | dry mass / g
cucumber | 50.0 | 2.4
potato | 50.0 | 10.2
cooked rice | 50.0 | 15.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of water in each food. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: cucumber 95.2 %; potato 79.6 %; cooked rice 68.4 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which food contained the greatest percentage of water.
parts.answer: cucumber

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the samples were dried in an oven at 90 °C and not over a Bunsen flame.
parts.answer: A flame would burn the food, so mass would also be lost as other substances, not only water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water is important as a solvent in living organisms. Give two examples.
parts.answer: many substances dissolve in water so they can be transported (e.g. glucose in plasma, sucrose in phloem) and so that chemical reactions (e.g. digestion, enzyme reactions) can take place in solution; urea removed in urine
parts.working: B1 substances dissolve so can be transported/react; 1 mark each for two examples: transport in blood/plasma, transport in phloem/xylem, digestion, excretion of urea in urine, reactions in cytoplasm

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says fats contain the same elements as carbohydrates. State whether this is correct and give one difference in their composition.
parts.answer: correct (C, H, O); fats have much less oxygen in proportion to carbon and hydrogen

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Three samples, X, Y and Z, were analysed for elements.
X: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur
Y: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
Z: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen
State which sample is a protein and give a reason.
parts.answer: X; it is the only one containing nitrogen (and sulfur).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Y and Z could each be a carbohydrate or a fat. Explain why analysing elements cannot tell them apart, and describe a test that would show which one is a fat.
parts.answer: Carbohydrates and fats both contain only C, H and O; ethanol emulsion test: shake with ethanol, pour into water – a cloudy white emulsion shows fat.
parts.working: B1 same elements; B1 shake with ethanol then add to water; B1 cloudy/milky white emulsion = fat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person has 3.0 dm³ of blood plasma. Plasma is about 92 % water by volume. Calculate the volume of water in the plasma.
parts.answer: 2.76 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Glucose and urea are carried dissolved in plasma, but most oxygen is carried by haemoglobin in red blood cells. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Glucose and urea are very soluble in water so plasma can carry enough; oxygen is only slightly soluble in water, so plasma alone could not carry enough for respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each: glucose/urea soluble; oxygen has low solubility so needs haemoglobin.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how water acting as a solvent links digestion, transport and excretion in the body.
parts.answer: Digested food dissolves in water in the gut and is absorbed; it is carried dissolved in plasma to cells; waste urea made in the liver is carried in plasma and excreted dissolved in urine.
parts.working: 1 mark each for digestion, transport and excretion each linked to water as solvent.

practice.stem:
A student dried 25.0 g of fresh spinach leaves in an oven at 80 °C and weighed them each day.
day | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4
mass / g | 25.0 | 7.9 | 4.1 | 3.3 | 3.3

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the water content of the leaves as a percentage of the fresh mass. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 uses constant dry mass 3.3 g: (25.0 − 3.3) ÷ 25.0 × 100; A1 86.8 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student kept drying the leaves until the mass stopped changing.
parts.answer: To make sure all the water had been removed; while the mass was still falling, water was still evaporating, so using an earlier mass would give too low a water content.
parts.working: 1 mark each: all water removed; constant mass shows this / earlier readings would underestimate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one source of error in this method and one improvement.
parts.answer: Leaves may absorb water vapour from the air while cooling before weighing – cool in a sealed container / weigh quickly; or only one sample – repeat with several samples and take a mean.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When maltose is digested, one water molecule is used to split each maltose into two glucose molecules. A starch chain of 500 glucose units is completely digested to glucose. Each bond broken uses one water molecule. Calculate how many water molecules are used.
parts.working: M1 500 units are joined by 499 bonds; A1 499 water molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this example to explain why water is needed in the gut for digestion, not just as a solvent.
parts.answer: Water is a reactant: it is used up in breaking (hydrolysing) the bonds of large molecules.
parts.working: B1 water takes part in the reaction / is used to break bonds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dry bean seed is soaked in water before it germinates. Suggest two reasons why the seed needs to take up water before germination can begin.
parts.answer: To activate enzymes / allow enzyme reactions in solution; to dissolve and transport stored food (e.g. sugars from starch) to the growing embryo; to make cells swell/turgid so the testa splits and cells expand.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stored starch in the seed must be converted to sugar before it can be moved to the growing shoot.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble so cannot be carried in water; it is digested to soluble sugar which dissolves and is transported to the shoot.
parts.working: 1 mark each: starch insoluble; sugar soluble so it can be transported in solution.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The table (figures for this question) shows daily water losses for a student in Lahore.
route of loss | volume / cm³
urine | 1500
sweat | 500
exhaled air | 350
faeces | 150
She gains 700 cm³ of water from food and 300 cm³ from respiration. Calculate the volume she must drink each day to stay in balance.
parts.answer: 1500 cm³
parts.working: M1 total loss 2500 cm³; A1 2500 − 700 − 300 = 1500 cm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On a very hot day her sweat loss rises to 1800 cm³. All other values stay the same. Calculate the new volume she must drink.
parts.answer: 2800 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why she continues to lose water in urine even when she drinks very little.
parts.answer: Urea must be excreted and needs water as a solvent.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme digests protein in the stomach?
A amylase
B lipase
C maltase
D pepsin
parts.answer: D pepsin
parts.working: Pepsin is the protease of the stomach and works in acid. Amylase digests starch, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by chemical digestion.
parts.answer: the breakdown of large insoluble molecules into small soluble molecules by enzymes
parts.working: B1 large insoluble → small soluble; B1 by enzymes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of physical (mechanical) digestion in the alimentary canal.
parts.answer: chewing by teeth; churning by the stomach muscles (also emulsification by bile)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how physical digestion helps chemical digestion.
parts.answer: it increases the surface area for enzymes to act on

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the following for each enzyme: the food it digests and the product(s).
(i) amylase
(ii) protease
(iii) lipase
parts.answer: (i) starch → maltose; (ii) protein → amino acids; (iii) fat → fatty acids and glycerol
parts.working: B1 each (substrate and product both needed)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme on the lining of the small intestine that completes the digestion of starch, and its product.
parts.answer: maltase; glucose

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of food and enzyme is correctly matched?
A starch and lipase
B protein and protease
C fat and amylase
D maltose and pepsin
parts.answer: B protein and protease
parts.working: Protease digests protein into amino acids. Lipase acts on fat, amylase acts on starch, and pepsin does not digest maltose, so A, C and D are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which the mouth carries out physical digestion of a chapati.
parts.answer: Teeth chew (mechanically break) the chapati into smaller pieces, increasing its surface area; the tongue mixes the food with saliva to form a soft bolus that can be swallowed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: teeth cut and grind the food into smaller pieces; this increases surface area; tongue mixes food with saliva; forms a bolus. Physical digestion involves no chemical change.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of bile in digestion?
A It breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
C It digests starch to maltose.
D It makes the small intestine acidic.
parts.answer: B It emulsifies fats into small droplets.
parts.working: Bile emulsifies fat (physical digestion), increasing surface area for lipase. Bile contains no enzyme, so A (the action of lipase) is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the roles of hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
parts.answer: kills bacteria/microorganisms in food; gives a low (acidic) pH which is the optimum for pepsin
parts.working: B1 kills pathogens/bacteria; B1 optimum pH for pepsin/enzymes in stomach

parts.label: b
parts.text: Trypsin is a protease made by the pancreas. Suggest why trypsin does not work well in the stomach.
parts.answer: its optimum pH is about 8 (alkaline); the acid of the stomach denatures it / it works slowly at low pH
parts.working: B1 optimum pH alkaline/neutral; B1 acid denatures / changes active site shape

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how the contents of the duodenum are made slightly alkaline.
parts.answer: bile (and pancreatic juice) neutralise the acid from the stomach

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of tooth used for:
(i) biting off pieces of naan
(ii) grinding food into smaller pieces
parts.answer: (i) incisors; (ii) molars (and premolars)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why food that is chewed well is digested faster.
parts.answer: chewing breaks food into smaller pieces with a larger surface area; enzymes (such as salivary amylase) can act on more of the food at once
parts.working: B1 larger surface area; B1 more contact with enzymes/faster enzyme action

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Lipase digests a fat (triglyceride) in the small intestine. Which products are formed?
A glucose and glycerol
B glycerol and fatty acids
C amino acids and glycerol
D glucose and fatty acids
parts.answer: B glycerol and fatty acids
parts.working: Lipase breaks each triglyceride into glycerol and fatty acids. Glucose comes from carbohydrate and amino acids from protein, so A, C and D each contain a product lipase does not make.

practice.stem: A 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm cube of cooked potato is cut into 1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm cubes, all the same size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of 1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm cubes that can be cut from the 1 cm cube.
parts.answer: 1000 cubes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of all the 1 mm cubes, in cm². Each 1 mm cube has a surface area of 6 mm².
parts.answer: 60 cm²
parts.working: 1000 × 6 mm² = 6000 mm²; 1 cm² = 100 mm², so 6000 ÷ 100 = 60 cm². 1 mark for method, 1 for answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the smaller pieces are digested more quickly by enzymes.
parts.answer: Larger total surface area, so more enzyme molecules can contact the food at the same time, giving more enzyme-substrate collisions per second.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area; 1 mark: more enzyme-food contact or collisions per unit time.

practice.stem:
Three tubes contained 5 cm³ milk, sodium carbonate solution and a pH indicator (pink in alkali, colourless at about pH 7).
Tube A: + 1 cm³ lipase + 1 cm³ bile salts
Tube B: + 1 cm³ lipase + 1 cm³ water
Tube C: + 1 cm³ boiled lipase + 1 cm³ bile salts
Time for the pink colour to disappear (three repeats):
A: 12, 14, 13 min
B: 25, 29, 27 min
C: no change after 60 min

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time for tube A and for tube B. Give your answers to the nearest minute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two results.
parts.answer: in A the fat was emulsified by bile into small droplets, giving a larger surface area for lipase, so it was digested faster
parts.working: B1 bile emulsifies; B1 larger surface area for lipase

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pH falls as the fat is digested.
parts.answer: fatty acids are produced

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the purpose of tube C.
parts.answer: control: shows that the pH fall is caused by lipase

parts.label: a
parts.text: A piece of boiled egg white is placed in a tube with pepsin and dilute hydrochloric acid at 37 °C. After 2 hours the cloudy egg white has become clear. Explain this observation.
parts.answer: pepsin digested the protein into smaller soluble molecules (peptides/amino acids), which dissolve so the liquid clears
parts.working: B1 protein digested by pepsin; B1 products soluble

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict and explain the result if the tube had been kept at 70 °C.
parts.answer: egg white stays cloudy: pepsin is denatured (active site changes shape), so no digestion
parts.working: B1 no change; B1 denatured / active site shape lost

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the egg white was cut into small cubes of equal size.
parts.answer: equal surface area so the comparison is fair / larger surface area for faster digestion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the products of chemical digestion must be small, soluble molecules.
parts.answer: so they can pass through the wall of the small intestine (be absorbed) into the blood/lymph
parts.working: B1 absorbed through intestine wall/membranes; B1 into blood/transported

parts.label: b
parts.text: People who have had their gall bladder removed are advised to eat less fat at each meal. Suggest why.
parts.answer: bile is not stored, so less bile is released at a meal; fat is less emulsified and is digested more slowly / poorly
parts.working: B1 less bile available (released) at once; B1 less emulsification, fat digested less

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the chemical digestion of starch from the mouth to the end of the small intestine. Name each enzyme, where it is made, and the final product.
parts.answer: Mouth: salivary amylase (made in the salivary glands) changes starch to maltose. In the stomach, the acid stops the amylase. In the duodenum, pancreatic amylase (made in the pancreas) changes the remaining starch to maltose. Maltase on the small intestine wall changes maltose to glucose, the final product.
parts.working: Any six: salivary amylase from salivary glands acts in the mouth; starch to maltose; acid in the stomach stops the amylase; pancreatic amylase from the pancreas acts in the duodenum; maltase on the intestine wall; maltose to glucose; glucose is the final product.

practice.stem: A student tests the digestion of boiled egg white by pepsin. She cuts the egg white into cubes of two sizes, 2 mm and 8 mm, using the same total mass (2 g) in each tube. Each tube has 5 cm³ of pepsin solution and 5 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid at 37 °C, and she records the time for the egg white to clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the independent variable and the dependent variable.
parts.answer: Independent: size (or surface area) of the egg white pieces. Dependent: time taken for the egg white to clear (or rate of digestion).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the same total mass of egg white was used in each tube.
parts.answer: To keep the amount of substrate the same, so that the size of the pieces is the only variable that changes (a fair test).
parts.working: 1 mark: keeps the amount of substrate constant; 1 mark: makes the size of the pieces the only variable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The 2 mm pieces cleared in 40 minutes and the 8 mm pieces cleared in 160 minutes. Calculate how many times faster the 2 mm pieces were digested.
parts.answer: 4 times faster (160 ÷ 40 = 4)
parts.working: 1 mark for the method (160 ÷ 40); 1 mark for the answer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain the difference in the times using the idea of surface area.
parts.answer: The 2 mm pieces have a larger total surface area, so more pepsin molecules contact the protein per unit time, so digestion is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: larger surface area; 1 mark: more enzyme-substrate contact per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which mineral is needed to make haemoglobin?
A calcium
B iodine
C iron
D nitrogen
parts.answer: C iron
parts.working: Iron is part of haemoglobin; lack causes anaemia. Calcium is needed for bones and teeth, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a balanced diet.
parts.answer: a diet with all the nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) in the correct amounts/proportions to meet the body's needs
parts.working: B1 all nutrients/food groups; B1 correct proportions/amounts

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the deficiency disease caused by a lack of vitamin C and state one symptom.
parts.answer: scurvy; bleeding gums (or slow wound healing)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one food rich in vitamin C.
parts.answer: citrus fruit such as oranges, lemons; guava; tomatoes

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which deficiency disease is caused by a lack of vitamin C?
A night blindness
B rickets
C scurvy
D goitre
parts.answer: C scurvy
parts.working: Scurvy (bleeding gums, slow wound healing) is caused by lack of vitamin C. Night blindness is caused by lack of vitamin A, rickets by lack of vitamin D, and goitre by lack of iodine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of fibre (roughage) in the diet.
parts.answer: Adds bulk to the faeces; stimulates peristalsis (keeps food moving through the gut); helps prevent constipation (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: adds bulk; stimulates peristalsis; prevents constipation; helps the gut work normally.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the table by naming the deficiency disease caused by the lack of each nutrient.
Nutrient lacking | Deficiency disease
vitamin A | (i)
iron | (ii)
vitamin D | (iii)
parts.answer: (i) night blindness; (ii) anaemia; (iii) rickets
parts.working: 1 mark each: vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness; iron deficiency causes anaemia (too few red blood cells or less haemoglobin); vitamin D deficiency causes rickets in children.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A child living indoors for long periods develops soft, bent leg bones. Which deficiency is most likely?
A vitamin C
B vitamin D
C iron
D fibre
parts.answer: B vitamin D
parts.working: Lack of vitamin D (made in skin in sunlight) reduces calcium absorption and causes rickets. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, not bent bones.

practice.stem: A lunch of rice and chicken korma contains 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 15 g fat. Energy values: carbohydrate 17 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g, fat 39 kJ/g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total energy in the meal in kJ.
parts.working: M1 multiply each mass by its energy value; A1 1945

parts.label: b
