parts.text: State which nutrient in the meal provides the most energy per gram.
parts.answer: fat

parts.label: c
parts.text: Fibre provides no usable energy. Explain why fibre is still needed in the diet.
parts.answer: it adds bulk, helping peristalsis (movement of food through the gut); prevents constipation

practice.stem: A woman in Karachi needs 18 mg of iron each day. A breakfast cereal contains 2.4 mg of iron per 100 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many grams of the cereal she would need to eat to get her daily iron requirement from cereal alone. Give your answer to the nearest gram.
parts.working: M1 18 ÷ 2.4 (= 7.5 portions of 100 g); A1 750 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why women of child-bearing age need more iron than men of the same age.
parts.answer: iron is lost in blood during menstruation; needed to make haemoglobin for new red blood cells (also for the fetus in pregnancy)
parts.working: B1 blood loss in menstruation (or pregnancy); B1 iron to make haemoglobin/red cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the condition caused by lack of iron.
parts.answer: anaemia

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A community living far from the sea has many people with an enlarged neck (goitre). Which nutrient is most likely lacking in their diet?
A iodine
B iron
C calcium
D protein
parts.answer: A iodine
parts.working: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; without it the thyroid gland enlarges. Iron deficiency causes anaemia, and calcium and protein deficiencies do not cause goitre.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A snack contains 25 g of fat, 40 g of carbohydrate and 6 g of protein. Use these energy values: fat 37 kJ/g, carbohydrate 16 kJ/g, protein 17 kJ/g. Calculate the energy from the fat, in kJ.
parts.answer: 925 kJ

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total energy in the snack, in kJ.
parts.working: 925 + (40 × 16 = 640) + (6 × 17 = 102) = 1667 kJ. 1 mark for the method, 1 for the answer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy that comes from fat. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.stem: A 50 g portion of a food contains 12 mg of calcium. The recommended daily intake (RI) of calcium is 800 mg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of calcium in a 250 g portion of the food.
parts.answer: 60 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the recommended daily intake (RI) given by the 250 g portion. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why the body needs calcium.
parts.answer: For strong bones and teeth (or for muscle contraction, or for blood clotting).
parts.working: Any one correct function of calcium.

practice.stem:
Daily energy needs of two men of the same age and mass:
office worker: 9 500 kJ
construction worker: 12 000 kJ

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in daily energy needed by the construction worker compared with the office worker. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the construction worker needs more energy.
parts.answer: more physical activity; more muscle contraction needs more respiration to release energy
parts.working: B1 more activity; B1 more respiration/energy for muscles

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two health risks if the office worker regularly eats 12 000 kJ a day.
parts.answer: obesity (weight gain, fat stored); coronary heart disease / type 2 diabetes / high blood pressure

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the effects of a diet with too much saturated fat over many years.
parts.answer: fat (cholesterol) deposits build up in artery walls, especially coronary arteries; arteries narrow / blood clots form; leads to coronary heart disease / heart attack; also obesity
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: cholesterol/fat deposits in arteries; narrowing of lumen; reduced blood flow/clot; coronary heart disease/heart attack; obesity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two changes to a typical festive meal of fried pakoras, mutton karahi and sweet halwa that would reduce this risk.
parts.answer: bake or grill instead of frying; use less ghee/oil; leaner meat or lentils/fish; more vegetables/fruit; less sugar
parts.working: 1 mark each for two sensible changes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a diet with no fruit or vegetables for several months can cause bleeding gums and slow wound healing. Refer to the role of vitamin C in making collagen.
parts.answer: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, a structural protein; collagen holds tissues such as gums, skin and blood vessel walls together. Without it, blood vessels become weak and fragile and bleed; new tissue cannot be formed properly, so wounds heal slowly.
parts.working: Any four: vitamin C needed to make collagen; collagen gives strength to tissues; gum and blood vessel walls weaken; capillaries become fragile and bleed; new tissue cannot form properly; wounds heal slowly.

practice.stem: A 45 g serving of a fortified breakfast cereal contains 7.2 mg of iron and 2.5 g of fibre. The RI for iron is 14 mg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the RI for iron given by one serving. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of fibre in 100 g of the cereal. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why a manufacturer might add iron to a cereal.
parts.answer: To help people whose diet is low in iron avoid anaemia.
parts.working: Any one: to supply iron, to prevent iron-deficiency anaemia, to meet RI.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which organ is most water absorbed from digested food?
A stomach
B small intestine
C large intestine
D oesophagus
parts.answer: B small intestine
parts.working: Most water is absorbed in the small intestine; the colon absorbs a smaller amount. The stomach absorbs little water, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put these parts in the order that food passes through them: small intestine, mouth, large intestine, stomach, oesophagus.
parts.answer: mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
parts.working: B2 all correct; B1 one adjacent pair swapped

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the oesophagus.
parts.answer: carries food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the organ that makes bile.
parts.answer: liver

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which organ produces bile?
A gall bladder
B liver
C pancreas
D small intestine
parts.answer: B liver
parts.working: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. The pancreas makes pancreatic juice and the gall bladder only stores bile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of each of the following: (i) salivary glands; (ii) oesophagus; (iii) gall bladder.
parts.answer: (i) produce saliva (containing amylase) to moisten food and start starch digestion; (ii) carry food from the mouth to the stomach by peristalsis; (iii) store bile.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where pancreatic juice enters the alimentary canal, and name one substance in pancreatic juice that is not an enzyme.
parts.answer: Duodenum (the first part of the small intestine); sodium hydrogencarbonate (an alkali).
parts.working: 1 mark for duodenum; 1 mark for sodium hydrogencarbonate, which neutralises acid from the stomach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the function of salivary amylase in the mouth, and name the food it digests.
parts.answer: Salivary amylase digests starch into maltose (a smaller sugar). The food digested is starch.
parts.working: 1 mark: changes starch to maltose; 1 mark: the food is starch.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how peristalsis moves food along the alimentary canal.
parts.answer: circular and longitudinal muscles in the wall contract and relax alternately; a wave of contraction behind the food pushes it along
parts.working: B1 muscle contraction (circular/longitudinal antagonistic); B1 wave squeezes/pushes food

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the anus and the name of the process that removes undigested food.
parts.answer: faeces leave the body through the anus; egestion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between egestion and excretion.
parts.answer: egestion removes undigested food that was never absorbed; excretion removes metabolic waste made by cells

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the stomach is correct?
A it absorbs most of the water from food
B it produces hydrochloric acid
C it produces bile
D most starch is digested in it
parts.answer: B it produces hydrochloric acid
parts.working: Stomach glands secrete hydrochloric acid and pepsin. Water absorption happens mainly in the intestines, bile comes from the liver, and most starch is digested in the small intestine by pancreatic amylase.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The inside of the stomach is lined with a layer of mucus. Explain why the stomach wall must be protected from its own acid and pepsin, and name the cells that secrete the mucus.
parts.answer: The stomach wall would be digested by its own pepsin and damaged by the acid, so the mucus forms a protective barrier that keeps the acid and pepsin away from the wall. Mucus is secreted by mucus-producing (goblet-type) cells in the stomach lining.
parts.working: 1 mark: wall would be digested or damaged; 1 mark: mucus forms a barrier to acid and pepsin; 1 mark: mucus secreted by cells of the stomach lining.

practice.stem: A teaching model of the alimentary canal has these lengths: oesophagus 25 cm; stomach 25 cm; small intestine 650 cm; large intestine 150 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total length of the alimentary canal in this model, in cm.
parts.answer: 850 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the total length that is the small intestine. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the small intestine is much longer than the stomach.
parts.answer: A long small intestine gives food more time in contact with enzymes and bile, so digestion is complete; it also gives a large surface area for absorption.
parts.working: 1 mark: more time for digestion or more contact with enzymes; 1 mark: large surface area for absorption.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pancreas releases its juice into the duodenum. Name three enzymes in pancreatic juice.
parts.answer: amylase, trypsin (protease), lipase

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient's pancreatic duct is blocked. Suggest and explain two effects on the patient's faeces and body mass.
parts.answer: faeces contain undigested fat (pale, fatty); weight loss because less food is digested and absorbed
parts.working: B1 more undigested food/fat in faeces; B1 weight loss / poor absorption

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path of a bolus of food from the mouth to the anus. Name the regions in order and state the role of the sphincter at the anus.
parts.answer: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus. Food is stored in the rectum before egestion; the anus is closed by a ring of muscle (sphincter) that controls release of faeces.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: correct order from the mouth to the stomach; small intestine then large intestine; rectum stores faeces; sphincter at the anus controls egestion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland. Explain what this means, giving one example of a substance released by each part.
parts.answer: Exocrine: the pancreas releases pancreatic juice (e.g. amylase, lipase or trypsin) through a duct into the duodenum. Endocrine: it releases hormones such as insulin or glucagon directly into the blood.
parts.working: 1 mark: exocrine means it releases secretions through a duct; 1 mark: endocrine means it releases hormones into the blood; 1 mark: correct example for each (any appropriate).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one enzyme made by each of the following, and give the substance it digests: (i) the stomach wall; (ii) the pancreas; (iii) the wall of the small intestine.
parts.answer: (i) pepsin, digests protein; (ii) lipase (or amylase), digests fat (or starch); (iii) maltase, digests maltose.
parts.working: 1 mark each: a correct enzyme with a correct substrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by absorption.
parts.answer: movement of small digested food molecules (and ions) from the small intestine into the blood/lymph

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of a villus that help absorption.
parts.answer: thin wall (one cell thick); microvilli give large surface area; rich capillary network; lacteal

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why do the villi have a rich network of capillaries?
A to make the villi move in and out of the intestine
B to carry absorbed food away quickly, keeping the concentration gradient steep
C to remove carbon dioxide from the intestine
D to make the villi waterproof
parts.answer: B to carry absorbed food away quickly, keeping the concentration gradient steep
parts.working: Blood capillaries carry away absorbed glucose and amino acids, so the concentration inside the villus stays low and absorption continues. A is wrong because villi do not move, C is wrong because the villi do not remove carbon dioxide from the gut, and D is wrong because villi must let substances pass through.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a lacteal absorbs, and what happens to it after that.
parts.answer: A lacteal absorbs fatty acids and glycerol (the products of fat digestion). They pass into the lymphatic system (lymph vessels) and then enter the bloodstream.
parts.working: 1 mark: fatty acids and glycerol absorbed; 1 mark: pass into lymph vessels and then into the blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three ways in which the structure of the small intestine increases its surface area for absorption.
parts.answer: Folds in the inner wall; villi on the inner surface; microvilli on the surface of the epithelial cells (any three).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: folds (circular folds); villi; microvilli.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the wall of a villus is only one cell thick, and what this means for absorption.
parts.answer: It means the distance that substances must diffuse is short, so absorption into the blood is fast.
parts.working: 1 mark: short diffusion distance; 1 mark: faster absorption.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Into which structure in a villus are the products of fat digestion mainly absorbed?
A capillary
B lacteal
C microvillus
D vein
parts.answer: B lacteal
parts.working: Fatty acids and glycerol pass into the lacteal (lymph vessel). Glucose and amino acids enter the capillaries, so A is a distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the capillary network in each villus helps to keep absorption of glucose fast.
parts.answer: blood flow carries absorbed glucose away; keeps a steep concentration gradient between the intestine and the blood
parts.working: B1 carries glucose away; B1 maintains concentration gradient (for diffusion)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some glucose is absorbed by active transport. State why active transport is needed.
parts.answer: to absorb glucose against a concentration gradient (when concentration in the lumen is lower than in the cells/blood)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries absorbed food from the small intestine to the liver.
parts.answer: hepatic portal vein

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Glucose from the villi leaves the intestine in the blood. Which vessel carries glucose from the capillaries of the villi straight to the liver?
A hepatic vein
B hepatic portal vein
C vena cava
D pulmonary artery
parts.answer: B hepatic portal vein
parts.working: Blood from the small intestine drains into the hepatic portal vein, which carries it to the liver. The hepatic vein carries blood away from the liver, and the vena cava and pulmonary artery are not involved in this route.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Glucose may be absorbed into the epithelial cells of a villus even when its concentration in the lumen is lower than inside the cell. Explain how this is possible.
parts.answer: Glucose is moved by active transport against its concentration gradient, using energy from respiration and carrier proteins; sodium ions are often co-transported with glucose into the cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: active transport (against the gradient); 1 mark: uses energy from respiration (ATP); 1 mark: carrier protein or co-transport with sodium ions.

practice.stem: In an experiment, a 15 cm² piece of intestinal tissue absorbed 0.45 g of glucose in 30 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of absorption in g per minute per cm².
parts.answer: 0.001 g per minute per cm²
parts.working: 0.45 g ÷ 30 min ÷ 15 cm² = 0.001 g/min/cm². 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Convert your answer to mg per minute per cm².
parts.answer: 1.0 mg per minute per cm²

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a meal, water moves into the villi by osmosis. Explain why.
parts.answer: Absorbed solutes such as glucose and amino acids lower the water potential inside the villus cells and blood; this is lower than the water potential of the fluid in the lumen, so water moves in by osmosis.
parts.working: 1 mark: absorbed solutes lower water potential inside the villus; 1 mark: water potential in the lumen is higher; 1 mark: water moves by osmosis down the gradient.

practice.stem: In the small intestine, folds of the lining increase surface area by a factor of 3, villi by a further factor of 10, and microvilli by a further factor of 20.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the factor by which the surface area is increased by the folds, villi and microvilli together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answer to calculate the absorbing surface area of a small intestine with a smooth inner surface area of 0.5 m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: A disease in children flattens the villi. Suggest and explain two effects.
parts.answer: smaller surface area so less absorption of nutrients; leads to weight loss / poor growth / deficiency (e.g. anaemia)
parts.working: B1 reduced absorption due to smaller surface area; B1 named consequence

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient has inflamed intestine walls in which the villi are shortened and flattened. Explain why this reduces the absorption of digested food.
parts.answer: Flattened villi have a much smaller surface area; fewer epithelial cells and microvilli are in contact with the food; fewer capillaries are close to the surface, so less absorption can occur; less absorption takes place per unit time.
parts.working: Any four: smaller surface area; fewer epithelial cells in contact with food; fewer microvilli; fewer capillaries near the surface; less absorption per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path taken by a fatty acid molecule from the lumen of the small intestine to a muscle cell in the leg. Name each structure it passes through.
parts.answer: Lumen of the small intestine; epithelial cell of the villus; lacteal; lymph vessel (then the thoracic duct into a large vein near the heart); bloodstream/blood capillary; muscle cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four correct stages in order: epithelial cell; lacteal; lymph vessels and the thoracic duct into the blood; blood capillaries to the muscle cell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why most absorption of digested food occurs in the small intestine rather than in the stomach or the large intestine.
parts.answer: The small intestine is long and has villi and microvilli, giving a very large surface area and rich blood supply; the stomach lining does not absorb much digested food; the large intestine mainly absorbs water and minerals.
parts.working: 1 mark: large surface area from length, villi and microvilli; 1 mark: stomach does not absorb much; 1 mark: large intestine absorbs mainly water and minerals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by assimilation.
parts.answer: movement of digested food molecules into cells, where they are used and become part of the cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way the body uses absorbed amino acids.
parts.answer: to make proteins (e.g. enzymes, antibodies, new cells for growth/repair)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two substances stored in the liver.
parts.answer: Glycogen; vitamins (such as vitamin A or D); iron (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: glycogen; vitamin A; vitamin D; iron.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the small intestine to the liver, and the blood vessel that carries blood from the liver towards the heart.
parts.answer: Hepatic portal vein; hepatic vein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deamination takes place in the liver. Describe what happens during deamination, and name the substance formed from the nitrogen-containing part.
parts.answer: The amino group is removed from excess amino acids; the nitrogen is converted to ammonia, which the liver converts to urea.
parts.working: 1 mark: amino group removed; 1 mark: ammonia or urea formed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the liver does to excess glucose after a meal, and name the hormone that causes this.
parts.answer: The liver converts excess glucose into glycogen and stores it; the hormone is insulin.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose converted to glycogen and stored; 1 mark: insulin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a meal of rice, the glucose concentration of blood in the hepatic portal vein is higher than in the hepatic vein. Explain why.
parts.answer: the liver removes excess glucose from the blood and converts it to glycogen for storage
parts.working: B1 liver takes up glucose; B1 converted to/stored as glycogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the hormone that stimulates the liver to do this.
parts.answer: insulin

parts.label: a
parts.text: Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into lacteals and do not travel straight to the liver in the hepatic portal vein. Explain why.
parts.answer: The lacteals are lymph vessels; the fatty acids and glycerol travel in the lymph and enter the blood near the heart (via the thoracic duct), so they reach the body's tissues before passing through the liver.
parts.working: 1 mark: lacteals are lymph vessels, not blood capillaries into the portal vein; 1 mark: lymph carries them to the blood near the heart; 1 mark: they enter the general circulation before reaching the liver.

practice.stem:
The table shows the glucose concentration in the blood of two veins after a meal of boiled potatoes.
Time after meal (min) | Hepatic portal vein (mmol/dm³) | Hepatic vein (mmol/dm³)
0 | 4.8 | 4.6
30 | 6.9 | 5.2
60 | 7.4 | 5.8
120 | 5.2 | 4.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference in glucose concentration between the hepatic portal vein and the hepatic vein at 60 minutes.
parts.answer: 1.6 mmol/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the glucose concentration in the hepatic vein is lower than in the hepatic portal vein at 60 minutes.
parts.answer: The liver takes up glucose from the blood and converts it to glycogen for storage, so less glucose leaves the liver in the hepatic vein.
parts.working: 1 mark: liver removes glucose from the blood; 1 mark: converts it to glycogen (stores it).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the glucose concentration in both veins falls by 120 minutes.
parts.answer: Insulin causes the liver and body cells to store and use glucose, and less glucose is absorbed from the gut.
parts.working: Any one: insulin takes glucose into storage or cells; absorption from the gut has slowed; body cells use glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the body stores excess glucose as glycogen in the liver and in muscles, and state one reason glycogen is a suitable storage molecule.
parts.answer: Glucose molecules are joined together to form glycogen, a large branched polysaccharide, in liver and muscle cells. Glycogen is insoluble, so it does not change the osmotic potential of the cells, and it can be quickly broken down back to glucose.
parts.working: 1 mark: glucose joined to form glycogen in liver and muscles; 1 mark: glycogen is insoluble (does not affect osmosis); 1 mark: can be converted back to glucose quickly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two functions of the liver other than storage and deamination.
parts.answer: Making bile; making plasma proteins (e.g. albumin); breaking down toxins or alcohol; breaking down old red blood cells (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct functions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of the liver in dealing with excess amino acids absorbed after a high-protein meal.
parts.answer: deamination: amino group removed from excess amino acids; converted to urea; remaining part used for respiration / converted to glycogen or fat (stored)
parts.working: B1 deamination/removal of nitrogen-containing part; B1 urea formed (transported to kidneys); B1 rest used for energy/stored

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the hepatic portal vein carries blood to the liver before it reaches the rest of the body.
parts.answer: so the liver can process absorbed food first: store excess glucose, break down harmful substances (e.g. alcohol), deaminate excess amino acids

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the liver's production of urea is linked to the work of the kidneys.
parts.answer: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver; the nitrogen is converted into urea, which is released into the blood plasma; the kidneys filter the urea out of the blood; it is excreted in urine; without the kidneys, urea would build up in the blood.
parts.working: Any four: deamination in liver; urea made from the nitrogen; urea carried in the blood; kidneys filter urea from the blood; urea excreted in urine; urea would build up if the kidneys failed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person with severe liver damage may have a low blood glucose level between meals.
parts.answer: The liver normally breaks down its glycogen stores to release glucose into the blood between meals, and makes glucose from other substances; damaged liver cells cannot do this, so blood glucose falls.
parts.working: 1 mark: normally glycogen is broken down to release glucose; 1 mark: liver can make glucose from other substances; 1 mark: damaged liver cannot release glucose, so blood glucose falls.

practice.stem: A liver stores 100 g of glycogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy, in kJ, released by the glycogen in the liver. Use 17 kJ per gram.
parts.working: 100 g × 17 kJ/g = 1700 kJ. 1 mark for method, 1 for answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many hours a person could work at 850 kJ per hour using only this glycogen.
parts.answer: 2 hours

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route a glucose molecule takes from the small intestine to a muscle cell, and explain why this route allows the liver to control the blood glucose concentration.
parts.answer: Absorbed into a villus capillary; hepatic portal vein to the liver; liver takes up, stores or releases glucose; hepatic vein to the vena cava, the heart, the aorta and the body; capillary to muscle cell. The liver is the first organ after the intestine, so it can regulate glucose entering the rest of the body.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: villus capillary; hepatic portal vein; liver stores or releases glucose; hepatic vein to heart and body; muscle capillaries; the liver receives glucose before the rest of the body, so it can regulate the concentration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by malnutrition.
parts.answer: eating too little, too much, or the wrong proportions of nutrients

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Name the deficiency illness caused by a lack of each:
(i) vitamin D
(ii) iron
(iii) fibre
parts.answer: (i) rickets; (ii) anaemia; (iii) constipation

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors that increase a person's daily energy requirement.
parts.answer: High physical activity; growth (in children) or pregnancy; living in a cold environment; a larger body mass (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct factors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the disease caused by a lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine), and describe one symptom.
parts.answer: Beriberi; any one symptom: nerve damage, muscle weakness, or heart problems.
parts.working: 1 mark for beriberi; 1 mark for a correct symptom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one function each of protein, carbohydrate and fat in the body.
parts.answer: Protein: growth and repair of cells. Carbohydrate: energy for respiration. Fat: energy store, insulation or protection of organs.

practice.stem: A teenager needs 40 mg of vitamin C a day. Fresh kinnow juice contains 36 mg of vitamin C per 100 cm³. One glass holds 200 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the daily vitamin C requirement given by one glass of the juice. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The juice was left in an open jug in the sun for a day. Suggest why its vitamin C content fell.
parts.answer: vitamin C is destroyed by heat/light/oxidation by air

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why vitamin C must be eaten every day, while vitamin D can be stored.
parts.answer: vitamin C is water-soluble and excess is lost in urine (not stored); vitamin D is fat-soluble and stored in the liver/fat
parts.working: B1 vitamin C not stored/lost in urine; B1 vitamin D stored in liver/fat

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cooked rice dish contains 540 kJ per 100 g. Calculate the energy in a 150 g portion.
parts.answer: 810 kJ
parts.working: 150 ÷ 100 × 540 = 810 kJ. 1 mark for method, 1 for answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A vitamin tablet contains 500 mg of vitamin C. The RI for vitamin C is 45 mg per day. Calculate how many times the RI is in the tablet. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 11.1 times
parts.working: 500 ÷ 45 = 11.11, so 11.1 to 1 d.p. 1 mark method, 1 mark answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a child needs more energy per kilogram of body mass than an adult.
parts.answer: A child is growing and making new tissue, which uses energy; a child has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so loses heat faster; children are usually more active.
parts.working: Any three: growth and making new tissue; larger surface area to volume ratio so more heat loss; more activity; (energy per kg relates to body mass).

practice.stem: A 60 kg adult needs 0.8 g of protein per kg of body mass each day. A 25 g portion of lentils contains 6 g of protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the daily protein requirement of a 60 kg adult, in g.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of 25 g portions of lentils needed to supply this protein requirement, if each portion gives 6 g of protein.
parts.answer: 8 portions

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a diet low in fibre can cause constipation.
parts.answer: Less fibre means less bulk in the faeces; the muscles of the gut need bulk to stimulate peristalsis, so movement is slower; faeces stay longer in the colon, more water is absorbed, and the faeces become hard and difficult to pass.
parts.working: 1 mark: less bulk; 1 mark: less stimulation of peristalsis; 1 mark: faeces stay longer and become hard.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the differences in daily dietary needs between a pregnant woman and a woman of the same age who is not pregnant. Consider energy, protein, calcium and iron.
parts.answer: more energy (for the growing fetus and extra body mass); more protein for growth of fetal tissues and placenta; more calcium for fetal bones and teeth; more iron for haemoglobin in fetal blood and extra maternal blood volume; also vitamin D for calcium absorption
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to five of: extra energy + reason; extra protein + growth of fetus; extra calcium + bones/teeth; extra iron + haemoglobin/red cells; extra blood volume; vitamin D for calcium absorption

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why advice on diet during pregnancy should consider the woman's usual diet and activity.
parts.answer: needs depend on body size, activity and existing nutrient stores/deficiencies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why women planning a pregnancy are advised to take folic acid before and in the early stages of pregnancy.
parts.answer: Folic acid is needed for the healthy development of the nervous system; the neural tube forms very early, often before a woman knows she is pregnant; folic acid reduces the risk of neural tube defects such as spina bifida.
parts.working: 1 mark: needed for healthy development of the nervous system; 1 mark: neural tube forms early; 1 mark: reduces the risk of neural tube defects.

practice.stem: A village survey found that 42 of 150 children had stunted growth (too short for their age). The main food is rice, with very little meat, pulses, fruit or vegetables.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of children with stunted growth. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two dietary causes of stunting in this village.
parts.answer: Too little protein; too little iron, zinc or vitamin A; not enough total energy; little variety in the diet (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct causes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that could reduce stunting in this village.
parts.answer: Add protein sources such as pulses, eggs or milk; add fruit and vegetables; nutrition education; supplements for the mineral or vitamin lacking (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible actions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the effect of iodine deficiency on the thyroid gland and on the body's metabolic rate.
parts.answer: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; without enough iodine less thyroxine is made, so the thyroid gland enlarges (goitre) as it tries to produce more; the metabolic rate falls, causing tiredness and weight gain.
parts.working: 1 mark: iodine needed to make thyroxine; 1 mark: thyroid enlarges (goitre); 1 mark: metabolic rate falls.

practice.stem: A nutrition label gives these values per 100 g of a biscuit: protein 12 g, carbohydrate 60 g, fat 8 g. Use these energy values: protein 17 kJ/g, carbohydrate 16 kJ/g, fat 37 kJ/g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy in 100 g of the biscuit, in kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the energy that comes from fat. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of cell produces antibodies?
A red blood cell
B phagocyte
C lymphocyte
D platelet
parts.answer: C lymphocyte
parts.working: Lymphocytes produce antibodies. Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens but do not make antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an antigen.
parts.answer: A molecule (e.g. a protein) on the surface of a pathogen / cell that stimulates antibody production.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways in which antibodies help to destroy pathogens.
parts.answer: Bind to antigens and mark pathogens so phagocytes can engulf them; directly destroy pathogens / cause them to clump together.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between an antibody and an antibiotic.
parts.answer: An antibody is a protein made by lymphocytes in the body that binds to a specific antigen; an antibiotic is a drug (medicine) taken to kill bacteria (or stop their growth).
parts.working: B1 antibody: protein made by lymphocytes / body; B1 antibiotic: drug that kills bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat measles or influenza.
parts.answer: These diseases are caused by viruses; antibiotics only kill bacteria / do not affect viruses.
parts.working: B1 caused by virus; B1 antibiotics act on bacteria only

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a person develops active immunity after recovering from chickenpox.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes produced antibodies against the virus antigens during the infection; memory cells remain and give fast antibody production on re-infection.
parts.working: B1 antibodies made by own lymphocytes; B1 memory cells

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these gives a person active immunity?
A antibodies passed to a baby in breast milk
B an injection of ready-made antibodies against snake venom
C a vaccination against measles
D antibodies passing from mother to fetus across the placenta
parts.answer: C a vaccination against measles
parts.working: A vaccine makes the person's own lymphocytes produce antibodies and memory cells, which is active immunity. A, B and D supply ready-made antibodies, which is passive immunity.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what is meant by:
(i) active immunity
(ii) passive immunity
parts.answer: (i) defence against a pathogen by the body making its own antibodies (after infection or vaccination), with memory cells; (ii) short-term defence from antibodies made by another person/organism (no memory cells)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of how a person can gain each type of immunity.
parts.answer: active: being vaccinated / recovering from an infection; passive: antibodies from mother across placenta or in breast milk / injection of antibodies

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which type of immunity lasts longer.
parts.answer: active immunity

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A newborn baby receives antibodies from its mother in breast milk. Which statement is correct?
A This is active immunity and lasts for life.
B This is passive immunity and no memory cells are made.
C This is active immunity because the baby makes memory cells.
D This is passive immunity and lasts for life.
parts.answer: B This is passive immunity and no memory cells are made.
parts.working: Antibodies from another individual give passive immunity: short-term protection with no memory cells, so it does not last. A and D wrongly say lifelong.

practice.stem: Polio vaccination campaigns in Pakistan give drops of vaccine to young children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a vaccine contains.
parts.answer: Harmless / weakened / dead pathogen, or its antigens; which stimulate an immune response but do not cause the disease.
parts.working: B1 weakened / dead pathogen or antigens; B1 does not cause disease

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how vaccination protects a person against polio for a long time.
parts.answer: Antigens in the vaccine are recognised by lymphocytes; lymphocytes produce specific antibodies; memory cells are formed which stay in the blood; on later infection antibodies are made quickly before the person becomes ill.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person bitten by a snake may be given an injection containing ready-made antibodies against the venom. State the type of immunity this gives.
parts.answer: Passive immunity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this injection gives immediate protection, but only for a short time.
parts.answer: The antibodies are already made, so act at once without waiting for lymphocytes to respond; they are not made by the person's body and are broken down; no memory cells are produced.
parts.working: B1 antibodies ready to act at once; B1 broken down / not replaced; B1 no memory cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one natural way in which a fetus gains passive immunity.
parts.answer: Antibodies cross the placenta from the mother.

practice.stem:
Antibodies against measles that a baby received from its mother were measured (arbitrary units).
age / months | 0 | 3 | 6
antibody level | 100 | 25 | 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the mother's antibodies between birth and 3 months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the antibodies from the mother disappear from the baby's blood.
parts.answer: They are broken down / not replaced; the baby has no memory cells for them because it did not make them (passive immunity).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why babies are given their first vaccinations at about 6 weeks old.
parts.answer: Maternal antibodies are falling, so the baby needs its own protection; the vaccine makes the baby produce its own antibodies and memory cells (active immunity) before the mother's antibodies are gone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Polio vaccine contains weakened polio viruses. Explain why the vaccine must be kept cold from the factory until it is given to a child.
parts.answer: The antigens are proteins (on the virus) that can be damaged/denatured by heat; then they no longer have the right shape to stimulate the correct lymphocytes, so the vaccine does not work.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a child given a heat-damaged vaccine may still catch polio later.
parts.answer: No (or few) antibodies and memory cells against polio were made; so when the real virus enters, the response is too slow to stop it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does one type of antibody protect against only one type of pathogen?
A each antibody has a shape complementary to one specific antigen
B antibodies are made of carbohydrate
C each pathogen has the same antigens
D antibodies kill pathogens by digesting them
parts.answer: A each antibody has a shape complementary to one specific antigen
parts.working: Antibodies are proteins with a specific shape that fits one antigen. C is wrong: different pathogens carry different antigens.

practice.stem:
A child was given two doses of a hepatitis B vaccine, five weeks apart. Antibody concentration (arbitrary units) was measured each week after each dose.
week after dose | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5
after first dose | 0 | 2 | 8 | 12 | 6 | 3
after second dose | 3 | 40 | 90 | 85 | 70 | 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times higher the peak antibody concentration was after the second dose than after the first dose.
parts.answer: 7.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the response to the second dose is faster and greater.
parts.answer: The first dose caused memory cells to be made; memory cells recognise the antigen at once on second exposure; they rapidly produce many lymphocytes / large amounts of antibody.
parts.working: B1 memory cells made after first dose; B1 recognise antigen; B1 rapid / greater antibody production

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of immunity produced by vaccination.
parts.answer: Active (artificial) immunity

practice.stem: In one region, 9,120,000 out of 9,600,000 children under five were given measles vaccine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of children vaccinated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how vaccinating a large percentage of a population also protects people who are not vaccinated.
parts.answer: Most people are immune, so the pathogen cannot easily spread / there are few people to infect; an infected person is unlikely to meet a non-immune person; so the disease is controlled (herd immunity).
parts.working: B1 most people immune / cannot pass on; B1 less chance unvaccinated person meets an infected person; B1 spread controlled / herd immunity

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some children in a population might not be vaccinated.
parts.answer: Too young / medical condition / weak immune system / parents refuse / live in remote areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement correctly describes memory cells?
A They are lymphocytes that stay in the blood after an infection and quickly make antibodies if the same pathogen enters again.
B They are phagocytes that remember the shape of a pathogen and engulf it faster next time.
C They are antibodies that stay in the blood for life.
D They are lymphocytes that make antibodies against any pathogen that enters the body.
parts.answer: A They are lymphocytes that stay in the blood after an infection and quickly make antibodies if the same pathogen enters again.
parts.working: Memory cells are lymphocytes that respond rapidly to the same antigen. Antibodies themselves (C) do not last for life, and each lymphocyte is specific to one antigen, so D is wrong.

practice.stem: Rabies is a viral disease passed on in the saliva of an infected animal, usually by a bite. A person bitten by a stray dog is given an injection of ready-made antibodies against rabies and also a course of rabies vaccine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the injection of ready-made antibodies is given immediately.
parts.answer: The antibodies act at once against the virus; the person's own immune response (from the vaccine) would take days/weeks to make enough antibodies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a course of vaccine is also given.
parts.answer: The vaccine stimulates the person's lymphocytes to make their own antibodies and memory cells; giving long-lasting (active) protection after the injected antibodies have been broken down.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why rabies vaccine works even though it is given after the virus has entered the body.
parts.answer: The virus spreads slowly to the brain (long incubation), so there is time for the body to make antibodies first.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a pathogen?
A any microorganism
B a disease-causing organism
C a chemical that kills bacteria
D a protein made by white blood cells
parts.answer: B a disease-causing organism
parts.working: A pathogen is a disease-causing organism. A is wrong because most microorganisms are harmless or useful.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transmissible disease.
parts.answer: A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table to give one example of each method of transmission.
method | example of how pathogen is passed
direct contact | ?
contaminated food | ?
animal (vector) | ?
parts.answer: Direct contact: through blood / body fluids (e.g. sharing needles, hepatitis B). Food: eating undercooked meat or eggs, or food handled with unwashed hands (e.g. Salmonella food poisoning, typhoid). Vector: mosquito bite (malaria / dengue) or houseflies carrying pathogens from faeces to food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways in which hepatitis B virus can be passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Infected blood (e.g. sharing needles / razors, unsterilised equipment); sexual contact; from mother to baby at birth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why barbers are advised to use a new blade for each customer.
parts.answer: A used blade could carry blood containing the virus into a cut on the next customer.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is an example of indirect transmission of a pathogen?
A receiving a transfusion of infected blood
B eating food on which houseflies have landed
C a fetus being infected across the placenta
D sharing a used syringe needle with an infected person
parts.answer: B eating food on which houseflies have landed
parts.working: Houseflies carry pathogens from faeces to food, so the pathogen passes indirectly. A, C and D involve direct contact with the body fluids of an infected person.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how washing hands with soap and water before eating reduces the spread of disease.
parts.answer: Removes (and kills) pathogens picked up from surfaces/faeces; so they are not swallowed with food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one disease whose spread is reduced by handwashing.
parts.answer: e.g. cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea/food poisoning, influenza

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why hands should be washed after using the toilet.
parts.answer: Hands may carry pathogens from faeces, which could reach food or other people.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of pathogen that causes each disease:
(i) cholera
(ii) influenza
(iii) malaria
(iv) athlete's foot
parts.answer: (i) bacterium (ii) virus (iii) protoctist (single-celled organism) (iv) fungus

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which disease is transmitted mainly through contaminated drinking water?
A cholera
B influenza
C tuberculosis
D measles
parts.answer: A cholera
parts.working: Cholera bacteria are passed on in water contaminated with faeces. Influenza, tuberculosis and measles are spread mainly by droplets in the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each of the following reduces the spread of disease: (i) treating sewage (ii) proper disposal of household rubbish (iii) washing hands before preparing food.
parts.answer: (i) removes / kills pathogens in faeces before water is returned to rivers (ii) prevents breeding sites for flies / rats that carry pathogens (iii) removes pathogens that could enter food

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why outbreaks of diarrhoeal disease often follow floods.
parts.answer: Floods mix sewage with drinking water supplies; people drink water containing pathogens.
parts.working: B1 sewage contaminates water; B1 pathogens ingested

parts.label: a
parts.text: Malaria is caused by a single-celled organism and transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes. Explain what is meant by a vector.
parts.answer: An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways people in rural Sindh can reduce the spread of malaria.
parts.answer: Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets; remove standing water where mosquitoes breed; use insect repellent; spray insecticides; cover water containers.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which action most directly reduces the spread of disease by houseflies?
A covering food and collecting rubbish in closed bins
B boiling drinking water
C vaccinating children against measles
D wearing a face mask in crowded places
parts.answer: A covering food and collecting rubbish in closed bins
parts.working: Flies breed in rubbish and carry pathogens onto uncovered food. Boiling water (B) kills water-borne pathogens but does not stop flies.

practice.stem: A restaurant in Faisalabad prepares chicken karahi and rice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why cooked food should be kept in a refrigerator at below 5 °C.
parts.answer: Low temperature slows bacterial enzymes; so bacteria reproduce very slowly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why raw meat should be kept away from cooked food.
parts.answer: Raw meat may carry pathogens; they could transfer to cooked food that will not be heated again.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why chicken must be cooked until the centre is very hot.
parts.answer: High temperature kills pathogens (e.g. Salmonella) throughout the meat.

practice.stem: A plate of cooked rice is left in a warm kitchen. It contains 50 bacteria, which divide every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many bacteria there would be after 4 hours if none died.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use this information to explain why food such as cooked rice should not be left in a warm kitchen for hours.
parts.answer: Bacteria (pathogens) reproduce very quickly at warm temperatures; large numbers can build up and cause food poisoning when eaten.
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction in warmth; B1 enough to cause disease

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which food can be stored to slow down bacterial growth.
parts.answer: Refrigerate / freeze / cover it / reheat thoroughly before eating.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a bacterium that is spread in droplets when an infected person coughs. Suggest why TB spreads more quickly in crowded housing.
parts.answer: People are close together, so droplets are more likely to be breathed in by others; often poor ventilation so droplets stay in the air.
parts.working: B1 close contact; B1 poor ventilation / more droplets inhaled

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important for TB patients to complete their full course of antibiotics.
parts.answer: If the course is stopped early, some bacteria survive; the survivors may be resistant and multiply, spreading resistant TB.
parts.working: B1 not all bacteria killed; B1 resistant bacteria survive / spread

practice.stem: In a simple model of an outbreak of a disease spread in the air, each infected person passes the pathogen to 3 new people, and this happens in rounds. One infected person starts the outbreak (round 0), so there are 3 new cases in round 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of new cases in the 5th round of infection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of people infected in the first five rounds, not counting the first person.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how vaccinating most of the population would slow the spread.
parts.answer: Most contacts of an infected person are immune; so each case infects fewer than one new person on average and the outbreak dies out (herd immunity).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one other measure that would reduce the number of people each case infects.
parts.answer: isolating infected people / ventilation / masks / handwashing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how an open rubbish dump close to houses can increase the spread of disease.
parts.answer: Houseflies breed in rotting rubbish; flies carry pathogens on their bodies/feet to food; rats are attracted and can carry pathogens; rainwater collecting in rubbish/containers lets mosquitoes breed; liquid from the dump can contaminate water supplies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why burning the rubbish is not a good long-term solution.
parts.answer: Produces smoke that harms lungs/air pollution; releases carbon dioxide and toxic gases; does not reduce rubbish produced; may not burn wet waste fully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of organism that causes cholera.
parts.answer: Bacterium

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how cholera is usually spread.
parts.answer: Drinking water (or eating food) contaminated with faeces containing the bacteria.
parts.working: B1 contaminated water / food; B1 with faeces from an infected person

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways a city can reduce cholera outbreaks.
parts.answer: Treat / chlorinate drinking water; proper sewage treatment / sanitation; boil water; hand washing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the main symptom of cholera.
parts.answer: severe watery diarrhoea

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cholera can kill a person quickly.
parts.answer: Large amounts of water and ions/salts are lost from the body; causing severe dehydration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the main treatment given to a person with cholera.
parts.answer: oral rehydration therapy (drinking a solution of salts and glucose in water) / intravenous fluids

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways a family without piped water can make its drinking water safe from cholera bacteria.
parts.answer: boil the water; add chlorine/water-purifying tablets; (filtering alone is not enough)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cholera is more common where sewage is not treated.
parts.answer: Cholera bacteria are in the faeces of infected people; untreated sewage contaminates drinking water sources.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table.
disease | type of pathogen | main way it is spread | can antibiotics treat it?
cholera | ... | ... | ...
influenza | ... | ... | ...
parts.answer: cholera: bacterium; contaminated water/food; yes. influenza: virus; droplets in the air (coughs/sneezes); no
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct pair of cells (pathogen type ×2, spread ×2); antibiotics column needed for the last mark with both correct.

practice.stem: A recipe for oral rehydration solution uses 2.6 g of salt (sodium chloride) and 13.5 g of glucose in 1000 cm³ of water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of salt and the mass of glucose needed to make 250 cm³ of the solution. Give each answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: salt 0.65 g; glucose 3.38 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the water used to make the solution should be boiled and cooled first.
parts.answer: To kill any pathogens in the water so the child is not infected again.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a child with cholera can die within a day if not treated.
parts.answer: Very rapid loss of water and salts in diarrhoea; severe dehydration (low blood volume) stops organs working.
parts.working: B1 rapid water / ion loss; B1 dehydration leads to organ failure / shock

parts.label: a
parts.text: Dengue fever is caused by a virus carried by Aedes mosquitoes. Explain why antibiotics are not given to treat dengue.
parts.answer: Antibiotics do not kill viruses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Aedes mosquitoes breed in small amounts of clean standing water. Suggest two actions a school in Rawalpindi could take to reduce dengue during the monsoon.
parts.answer: Empty / cover water containers, flower pots, old tyres; clear blocked drains; use repellents / long sleeves; fit window screens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Typhoid is caused by a bacterium spread in food and water contaminated by faeces. State one symptom that typhoid and cholera may both cause, and explain why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: Diarrhoea (or fever / vomiting); causes dehydration / loss of water and salts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person who has recovered from cholera can still pass the disease on.
parts.answer: They may still carry the bacteria in their gut / faeces for some time; these can contaminate water or food.
parts.working: B1 still carries bacteria; B1 in faeces → water / food

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The toxin made by cholera bacteria makes cells lining the small intestine secrete large amounts of one type of ion. Which ion is it?
A chloride ions
B calcium ions
C iron ions
D nitrate ions
parts.answer: A chloride ions
parts.working: The toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the intestine, which lowers the water potential there so water follows by osmosis. The other ions are not involved in this process.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Put these statements in the correct order to explain how cholera causes diarrhoea. Start with C.
A Water moves out of the cells into the intestine by osmosis.
B Large volumes of watery faeces are produced.
C Cholera bacteria in the small intestine release a toxin.
D The water potential in the intestine falls.
E Cells lining the intestine release chloride ions into the intestine.
parts.answer: C → E → D → A → B
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for one pair swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the person becomes dehydrated even though they drink water.
parts.answer: Water is lost into the gut faster than it is absorbed; the water potential gradient keeps drawing water out of the blood/tissues into the intestine.

practice.stem:
Records from a cholera outbreak (illustrative figures):
group | number of patients | number who died
not treated | 400 | 120
treated with oral rehydration solution | 2500 | 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of patients who died in each group.
parts.answer: untreated: 30 %; treated: 0.8 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how oral rehydration solution reduces deaths.
parts.answer: Replaces water and ions lost in diarrhoea; so blood volume and ion balance are kept up / prevents dehydration.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why giving oral rehydration solution is especially useful in remote villages.
parts.answer: It is cheap, simple, does not need a hospital/injections and can be given by family members.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does cholera cause severe watery diarrhoea?
A The bacterium digests the wall of the large intestine.
B A toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine, and water follows by osmosis.
C The bacterium uses up water in the gut for its respiration.
D A toxin stops the kidneys reabsorbing water.
parts.answer: B A toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the small intestine, and water follows by osmosis.
parts.working: The cholera toxin causes chloride ions to be released into the small intestine. This lowers the water potential of the gut contents, so water moves out of the blood into the gut by osmosis. D wrongly blames the kidneys.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain, using the term water potential, how cholera bacteria in the small intestine cause dehydration.
parts.answer: Bacteria release a toxin; toxin causes chloride ions to be secreted into the lumen of the small intestine; this lowers the water potential of the intestinal contents; water moves from the blood / tissues into the gut by osmosis; lost as watery diarrhoea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why oral rehydration solution contains salts as well as water.
parts.answer: Salts (ions) are lost in the diarrhoea and must be replaced; they help the body absorb and keep water.
parts.working: B1 replace lost ions / salts; B1 help water absorption

practice.stem:
Reported cholera cases in one district:
year | number of cases
2019 | 1240
2020 | 860
2021 | 610
2022 | 2950
2023 | 720

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in cases from 2021 to 2022, to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heavy floods occurred in this district in 2022. Suggest why this explains the change.
parts.answer: Floods contaminated drinking water with sewage; people drank water containing cholera bacteria / sanitation broke down.
parts.working: B1 sewage mixes with drinking water; B1 bacteria ingested / sanitation failure

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the trend from 2019 to 2021 and suggest one reason for it.
parts.answer: Cases fell each year (1240 → 610); e.g. better water treatment / sanitation / vaccination / hygiene campaigns.
parts.working: B1 trend with figures; B1 reason

practice.stem:
During a cholera outbreak in one district of a city, investigators recorded where each household got its drinking water. All the households were in the same area.
water source | number of households | number of cholera deaths
pump A | 500 | 90
other pumps and wells | 1200 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of deaths per 100 households for each group, and how many times greater the rate was for pump A.
parts.answer: pump A: 18; other sources: 1; 18 times greater

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these data support the idea that cholera is spread in water, not through bad-smelling air.
parts.answer: Deaths are concentrated among people using one water source; households in the same district (breathing the same air) using other water had few deaths.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one action the city should take immediately.
parts.answer: Close/disable pump A and supply safe (boiled/chlorinated) water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient with severe cholera loses 15 dm³ of fluid in one day. The total water in their body is 42 dm³. Calculate the fluid lost as a percentage of the body's water, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this loss would be fatal if the fluid were not replaced.
parts.answer: Blood volume falls, so the heart cannot pump enough blood to tissues (circulation fails); cells lose water by osmosis and cannot function / ion balance is upset.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics alone are not enough to save a patient with severe cholera.
parts.answer: Antibiotics kill the bacteria but do not replace the water and ions already lost; rehydration is still needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a chemical barrier against pathogens?
A hairs in the nose
B hydrochloric acid in the stomach
C the skin
D phagocytosis
parts.answer: B hydrochloric acid in the stomach
parts.working: Stomach acid kills many pathogens in food, so it is a chemical barrier. Nose hairs and skin are mechanical barriers; phagocytosis is a cell defence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how each of the following helps to prevent pathogens entering the body: (i) skin (ii) mucus in the airways (iii) hairs in the nose.
parts.answer: (i) forms a barrier that pathogens cannot pass through (ii) traps pathogens (which are then removed by cilia / swallowed) (iii) trap dust and pathogens in inhaled air

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a deep cut increases the risk of infection.
parts.answer: The skin barrier is broken, so pathogens can enter the blood / tissues.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sort these defences into the correct groups: skin, hairs in the nose, lysozyme in tears, stomach acid, phagocytosis, antibody production.
mechanical barrier | chemical barrier | cells
parts.answer: mechanical: skin, hairs in the nose; chemical: lysozyme in tears, stomach acid; cells: phagocytosis, antibody production

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the skin prevents pathogens from entering the body.
parts.answer: It forms a tough, continuous outer layer (of dead cells) that pathogens cannot pass through.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two main types of white blood cell.
parts.answer: phagocytes; lymphocytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how each type helps defend the body.
parts.answer: phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis); lymphocytes produce antibodies

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why breathing in through the nose helps to protect the lungs from infection more than breathing in through the mouth.
parts.answer: Hairs in the nose trap larger particles/dust carrying pathogens; mucus in the nose traps pathogens; cilia move the mucus to the throat to be swallowed (into the stomach acid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium.
parts.answer: The phagocyte moves towards / is attracted to the bacterium; it engulfs the bacterium (surrounds it with its cytoplasm / membrane); it digests it with enzymes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other way in which white blood cells defend the body.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes produce antibodies.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How does hydrochloric acid in the stomach help to protect the body against disease?
A It kills most bacteria swallowed with food.
B It makes antibodies against bacteria.
C It traps bacteria in mucus.
D It helps phagocytes engulf bacteria.
parts.answer: A It kills most bacteria swallowed with food.
parts.working: The very low pH of stomach acid kills most pathogens in food and drink. Antibodies (B) are made by lymphocytes, not by the stomach.

practice.stem: A blood test on a healthy person showed 7000 white blood cells per mm³. During a bacterial chest infection the same person had 15 000 white blood cells per mm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in white blood cells during the infection. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the number of white blood cells increases during an infection.
parts.answer: More phagocytes are needed to engulf pathogens; more lymphocytes (that recognise the antigen) divide to make antibodies.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a doctor might use a white blood cell count to help diagnose an infection.
parts.answer: A high count shows that the body is fighting an infection.

practice.stem:
Equal numbers of a harmless bacterium were kept in liquids at different pH for 30 minutes, and the surviving bacteria were then grown and counted as colonies.
pH | 7 | 4 | 2
number of colonies | 300 | 120 | 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of bacteria killed at pH 2 compared with pH 7. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the results to explain how the stomach protects the body from pathogens in food.
parts.answer: The stomach contains hydrochloric acid with a pH of about 2; most bacteria swallowed with food are killed before reaching the intestine.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a few bacteria still survived at pH 2.
parts.answer: Some bacteria are more resistant to acid / were protected inside clumps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phagocytes can change shape and contain many digestive enzymes. Explain how each of these features helps a phagocyte to destroy bacteria.
parts.answer: Changing shape lets it surround/engulf the bacteria (and squeeze out of capillaries into tissues); enzymes digest the bacteria inside the cell.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how phagocytes and lymphocytes work together during an infection.
parts.answer: Lymphocytes make antibodies that attach to pathogens / clump them together; this makes it easier for phagocytes to recognise and engulf them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smoking damages the cilia lining the trachea. Explain why smokers get more chest infections.
parts.answer: Cilia normally beat to move mucus containing trapped pathogens up to the throat; damaged cilia cannot do this; mucus and pathogens collect in the lungs and cause infection.
parts.working: B1 cilia move mucus; B1 mucus traps pathogens; B1 mucus / pathogens stay in lungs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how blood clotting at a wound helps defend against disease.
parts.answer: The clot seals the wound; preventing pathogens from entering (and blood loss).
parts.working: B1 seals / blocks wound; B1 stops entry of pathogens

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some people take antacid tablets every day for many months to reduce indigestion. These raise the pH of the stomach. Suggest and explain why these people may get food poisoning more often.
parts.answer: Antacid neutralises some stomach acid so pH rises; fewer swallowed bacteria are killed; more reach the intestine and multiply, causing infection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other body defence that would still help protect them against swallowed pathogens.
parts.answer: white blood cells (phagocytes/antibodies) / mucus lining the gut

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some people the mucus in the airways is much thicker and stickier than normal. Explain why these people suffer from many chest infections.
parts.answer: Cilia cannot move the thick mucus; mucus with trapped bacteria stays in the airways/lungs; bacteria multiply there and cause infection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why physiotherapy that helps these people cough up mucus reduces the number of infections.
parts.answer: It removes mucus and the trapped pathogens from the lungs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A disease destroys a person's lymphocytes. Explain why this person catches many infections that are normally harmless.
parts.answer: Without lymphocytes no antibodies are made; pathogens are not marked/neutralised so phagocytes are less effective; pathogens multiply and cause disease (no memory cells either).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why vaccines would not protect this person.
parts.answer: Vaccines work by stimulating lymphocytes to make antibodies and memory cells; with no lymphocytes there is no response.

practice.stem:
Numbers of bacteria and phagocytes in a small infected cut on a person's hand were estimated each day.
day | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
bacteria / arbitrary units | 10 | 60 | 90 | 50 | 15 | 2 | 0
phagocytes / arbitrary units | 5 | 15 | 40 | 75 | 80 | 40 | 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the changes in the number of bacteria.
parts.answer: Bacteria increase rapidly to a peak on day 2 (reproducing in the wound); then fall to zero by day 6; because phagocytes engulf and digest them (and antibodies are made).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of phagocytes reaches its peak after the number of bacteria peaks.
parts.answer: Phagocytes are attracted to the wound in response to the bacteria, so they arrive/increase after the bacteria have multiplied; it takes time for many phagocytes to collect.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the number of phagocytes falls after day 4.
parts.answer: Most bacteria have been destroyed, so fewer phagocytes are needed (phagocytes die).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what is meant by:
(i) a pathogen
(ii) a transmissible disease
parts.answer: (i) a disease-causing organism; (ii) a disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe, with examples, the different ways in which pathogens can be passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Direct contact with blood or other body fluids (e.g. hepatitis B by shared needles/razors, blood transfusion); indirectly in contaminated water (e.g. cholera, typhoid); in contaminated food (e.g. food poisoning bacteria); in droplets in the air from coughs and sneezes (e.g. influenza, TB); on contaminated surfaces/hands; by animal vectors such as mosquitoes (malaria, dengue) or houseflies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five; at least two named examples needed for full marks.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why diseases spread more quickly where many people live close together.
parts.answer: More contact between people; droplets/air shared in crowded rooms; sanitation and clean water may be harder to provide; so each infected person passes the pathogen to more people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the body's barriers stop pathogens from entering.
parts.answer: Skin is a tough barrier; hairs in the nose trap particles; mucus in the airways traps pathogens; cilia sweep mucus away to the throat; stomach acid kills pathogens in food; blood clots seal cuts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how good food hygiene in the home reduces the spread of disease.
parts.answer: Wash hands before preparing food; keep food covered from flies; store perishable food in a refrigerator; keep raw and cooked food apart; cook food thoroughly; wash fruit/vegetables in clean water; clean utensils and surfaces; do not reheat food more than once.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain how each of these personal habits reduces the transmission of disease:
(i) covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing
(ii) washing hands after using the toilet
(iii) not sharing razors or toothbrushes
parts.answer: (i) traps droplets containing pathogens so fewer reach the air/other people (e.g. influenza, TB); (ii) removes pathogens from faeces so they do not reach food/mouths (e.g. cholera, typhoid); (iii) avoids contact with blood from small cuts, which can contain blood-borne viruses (e.g. hepatitis B)
parts.working: 2 marks for each: B1 how it stops transfer, B1 named route or disease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens in the body when bacteria enter through a cut in the skin.
parts.answer: Blood clots to seal the cut; phagocytes move to the area and engulf/digest the bacteria; lymphocytes make antibodies specific to the bacteria's antigens; antibodies clump bacteria/mark them for phagocytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain how each of the following reduces the risk of water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid:
(i) adding chlorine to the town water supply
(ii) boiling drinking water at home
(iii) covering water storage containers
(iv) building latrines well away from wells
(v) washing fruit and salad in clean water
parts.answer: (i) chlorine kills bacteria in the water; reaches everyone who uses the supply; (ii) high temperature kills pathogens; makes water safe even if the source is contaminated; (iii) stops flies, dust and dirty hands contaminating the water; and stops mosquitoes breeding; (iv) stops faeces/sewage seeping through the soil into the well water; (v) removes pathogens from soil, manure or dirty water on the surface; because these foods are eaten raw (not cooked).
parts.working: 2 marks for each (B1 action, B1 explanation).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how malaria is passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Malaria is caused by a single-celled protoctist (Plasmodium); a female Anopheles mosquito bites an infected person and takes in the pathogen with blood; the pathogen develops in the mosquito; when the mosquito bites another person the pathogen is injected (in saliva) into their blood.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the methods that can be used to reduce the spread of malaria.
parts.answer: Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets – prevents bites at night; drain or cover standing water – removes breeding sites for larvae; spray insecticide in houses – kills adult mosquitoes; put larva-eating fish in ponds/tanks – kills larvae; wear long sleeves/use repellent – fewer bites; treat infected people with antimalarial drugs – fewer people carry the pathogen for mosquitoes to pick up.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six; method alone 1 mark only if explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why untreated sewage can cause outbreaks of disease.
parts.answer: Sewage contains faeces with pathogens (e.g. cholera, typhoid bacteria); it can leak into rivers, wells or water pipes; people drink the water or use it to wash food; flies can carry pathogens from sewage to food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a town can reduce disease by treating sewage and disposing of waste properly.
parts.answer: Build closed sewers that carry sewage away from houses; treat sewage in treatment works so pathogens are removed/killed (by microorganisms/settling) before release; keep sewage separate from drinking water; chlorinate drinking water; collect household rubbish regularly in covered bins; landfill/incinerate rubbish away from homes; reduce fly and rat breeding sites.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the ways in which pathogens carried in blood, such as the hepatitis B virus, can be passed from one person to another.
parts.answer: Shared or reused needles/syringes; transfusion of unscreened infected blood; from mother to baby at birth; contact with blood through cuts, e.g. shared razors, unsterilised dental or barber's tools.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the precautions that hospitals and clinics take to stop blood-borne pathogens spreading.
parts.answer: Use each needle once and dispose of it in a sealed sharps box; sterilise reusable instruments (heat/autoclave) to kill pathogens; screen all donated blood before transfusion; staff wear gloves to avoid contact with blood; cover cuts; vaccinate health workers against hepatitis B; clean blood spills with disinfectant.

practice.stem:
A disease spread by droplets broke out in a boarding school with 400 students. Sick students were isolated in a separate building from the end of week 3.
week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
new cases | 2 | 8 | 20 | 12 | 5 | 1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of students infected and the percentage of the 400 students in the school.
parts.answer: 48 students; 12 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern of new cases over the six weeks.
parts.answer: New cases rise from 2 to a peak of 20 in week 3; then fall each week to 1 in week 6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest and explain how isolating sick students from the end of week 3 affected the outbreak.
parts.answer: New cases fell after isolation; sick students no longer in contact with healthy students; so fewer people were exposed to the pathogen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why there were still some new cases in weeks 4 and 5.
parts.answer: Some students had already been infected before isolation and became ill later (incubation period); some infected students had no symptoms and were not isolated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why international travel helps diseases to spread between countries.
parts.answer: People can travel across the world in less time than the incubation period of many diseases; they may carry pathogens without showing symptoms; they mix with many people in airports/aircraft; diseases reach countries where people have no immunity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain measures that countries use to reduce the spread of transmissible diseases by travellers.
