parts.answer: Require vaccination certificates (e.g. polio or yellow fever) so travellers are immune; screen arriving passengers for symptoms such as fever; quarantine/isolate people who may be infected until the incubation period has passed; check imported food/animals; give health information to travellers (e.g. use mosquito nets, drink safe water); share outbreak information between countries.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how influenza spreads from person to person, and suggest three measures that could reduce its spread in a school.
parts.answer: Spread: infected person coughs / sneezes droplets containing the virus, which are breathed in by others (or touched on surfaces then transferred to mouth/nose). Measures: cover mouth when coughing / wear masks; wash hands regularly; keep sick pupils at home; ventilate classrooms; vaccination.
parts.working: B1 droplets from coughing / sneezing; B1 inhaled / via surfaces; 1 mark each for three measures

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a new influenza vaccine is needed most years.
parts.answer: The virus changes (mutates) and its antigens change; antibodies / memory cells from the old vaccine no longer fit the new antigens.
parts.working: B1 virus mutates / antigens change; B1 old antibodies / memory cells do not recognise it

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why diseases such as cholera and typhoid are much more common where there is no clean water supply or sewage system.
parts.answer: Faeces from infected people contain pathogens; without sewage treatment these get into rivers / wells used for drinking; people drink untreated water and are infected; flies may carry pathogens from faeces to food.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A village in Balochistan gets a new well and a simple filter-and-chlorine system. Explain how each part reduces disease.
parts.answer: Filter removes particles / some microorganisms; chlorine kills remaining pathogens.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the body's own defences protect against swallowed bacteria.
parts.answer: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills many bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After the severe floods in Sindh in 2022, the number of cases of diarrhoea, malaria and skin infections rose sharply. Explain why floods increase each of these diseases.
parts.answer: Diarrhoea: floodwater mixes with sewage and contaminates drinking water; latrines and water pipes damaged; people forced to drink unsafe water. Malaria: large areas of standing water left behind are breeding sites for mosquitoes; people sleep outdoors without nets. Skin infections: people wade in dirty water; cannot wash with clean water; crowded camps help spread.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for each disease (max 6).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest four actions that relief workers should take to reduce disease in flood camps.
parts.answer: Supply clean/chlorinated drinking water or purification tablets; build temporary latrines away from water; give out mosquito nets and repellent; vaccinate (e.g. measles, cholera); provide soap for handwashing; provide oral rehydration solution; remove standing water / rubbish.

practice.stem:
A health survey in a large city recorded new tuberculosis (TB) cases per 100 000 people per year in homes with different numbers of people per room (illustrative figures).
people per room | 1–3 | 4–6 | more than 6
TB cases per 100 000 | 120 | 310 | 590

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between crowding and TB cases, and calculate how many times more common TB was in the most crowded homes than in the least crowded homes. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: TB cases increase as the number of people per room increases; 4.9 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why TB spreads more easily in crowded homes.
parts.answer: TB bacteria are spread in droplets coughed into the air; in crowded rooms people breathe the same air and are close together; poor ventilation means droplets stay in the air longer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest four ways the number of TB cases could be reduced in this city.
parts.answer: Better housing/less crowding and good ventilation; finding and treating infected people with a full course of antibiotics; isolating infectious patients; vaccinating children (BCG); improving nutrition so defences are stronger; covering coughs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how houseflies can spread pathogens such as those causing typhoid and diarrhoea.
parts.answer: Flies breed and feed on faeces, rubbish or rotting material; pathogens stick to their hairy legs/bodies; flies land on uncovered food; they may vomit/excrete onto food while feeding; people eat the contaminated food and are infected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rabies is caused by a virus in the saliva of infected dogs. Explain how it is transmitted to people and why vaccinating stray dogs reduces the number of human cases.
parts.answer: Transmitted when an infected dog bites (or licks a wound of) a person, passing the virus into the body; vaccinated dogs make antibodies/memory cells and do not become infected; so they cannot pass the virus on; fewer infected dogs means fewer bites carrying the virus; vaccinating most dogs breaks the chain of transmission.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to compare how well three methods of cleaning hands (water only, soap and water, alcohol hand gel) remove bacteria. Include safety precautions.
parts.answer: Use sterile nutrient agar plates; a volunteer touches one plate with a fingertip after each method (and an unwashed control); same finger, same pressure and time; wash for the same time with same volume/temperature of water; seal lids with tape and label; incubate at 25 °C (not 37 °C) for 2–3 days; count colonies; repeat with several volunteers and find means; never open plates after incubation; dispose of plates by autoclaving.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six, including a control and at least one safety precaution.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the results and explain how the investigation shows why handwashing reduces disease.
parts.answer: Fewest colonies after alcohol gel or soap and water; most with unwashed/water only; soap/alcohol remove or kill bacteria; fewer bacteria on hands means fewer pathogens transferred to food or mouth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which set of conditions will a sunflower plant lose water vapour fastest?
A cool, humid, still air
B warm, humid, windy
C warm, dry, windy
D cool, dry, still air
parts.answer: C warm, dry, windy
parts.working: High temperature increases evaporation, low humidity gives a steep water vapour concentration gradient and wind removes water vapour from around the leaf. B is humid, which reduces the gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term transpiration.
parts.answer: Loss of water vapour from the leaves (by evaporation of water at the surfaces of the mesophyll cells) followed by diffusion of water vapour through the stomata.
parts.working: B1 loss of water vapour from leaves / aerial parts; B1 evaporation from mesophyll cell surfaces and diffusion out through stomata

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the pores in the leaf through which most water vapour leaves.
parts.answer: Stomata

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which transpiration is useful to a plant.
parts.answer: Pulls water and mineral ions up the xylem / cools the leaves / supplies water for photosynthesis and support.

practice.stem: A student uses a potometer in which the leafy shoot is fixed into a rubber bung, a capillary tube with a scale is attached and a water reservoir with a tap is connected to the tube.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the joints of the potometer were sealed with petroleum jelly.
parts.answer: To make them airtight / stop air leaking in or water leaking out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how the student could return the bubble to the start of the scale between readings.
parts.answer: Open the tap of the water reservoir / syringe to push water in.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student waited 5 minutes after changing conditions before starting a new reading.
parts.answer: To let the shoot adjust to the new conditions so the rate is steady.

practice.stem:
Transpiration rate of a rubber plant at different relative humidities (temperature kept at 25 °C).
relative humidity / % | rate of transpiration / arbitrary units
30 | 8.4
45 | 6.9
60 | 5.1
75 | 3.2
90 | 1.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of relative humidity on the rate of transpiration. Use figures from the table.
parts.answer: As humidity increases, rate decreases: from 8.4 at 30 % to 1.6 at 90 %.
parts.working: B1 inverse trend; B1 data quote with units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the decrease in rate between 30 % and 90 % humidity.
parts.answer: 6.8 arbitrary units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the rate at 100 % humidity and explain your prediction.
parts.answer: Very close to zero (but probably not zero); the air is saturated, so there is almost no concentration gradient for water vapour to diffuse out.
parts.working: B1 near zero / below 1.6; B1 no / tiny concentration gradient

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A potometer is used to measure the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. What does the potometer actually measure?
A the volume of water evaporating from the leaves
B the rate of water uptake by the shoot
C the rate of photosynthesis
D the number of open stomata
parts.answer: B the rate of water uptake by the shoot
parts.working: The bubble moves as the shoot takes up water. Most of this water is lost in transpiration, but some is used in photosynthesis or kept in cells, so A is not exactly what is measured.

practice.stem:
A student set up a bubble potometer with a leafy shoot of a guava plant. A small electric fan was placed 50 cm from the shoot. The distance moved by the air bubble was recorded in 4 minutes at each fan setting.
Fan setting | distance moved by bubble / mm | time / min
off | 12 | 4
low | 27 | 4
high | 44 | 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of bubble movement in mm per minute for each fan setting.
parts.answer: off: 3 mm/min; low: 6.75 mm/min; high: 11 mm/min
parts.working: B2 all three correct (B1 for two correct)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain the effect of wind speed on the rate of transpiration shown by these results.
parts.answer: As wind speed increases, the rate increases (3.0 → 11.0 mm/min). Wind blows away water vapour near the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient, so water vapour diffuses out of stomata faster.
parts.working: B1 trend with figures; B1 wind removes water vapour from around leaf / reduces humidity near leaf; B1 steeper gradient so faster diffusion through stomata

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two variables that must be kept constant.
parts.answer: Light intensity; temperature (also: same shoot / humidity / distance of fan).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration increases when the temperature rises.
parts.answer: Water molecules gain kinetic energy, so more water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces and water vapour diffuses out faster.
parts.working: B1 more evaporation / molecules move faster; B1 faster diffusion of water vapour out of stomata

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of transpiration decreases on a humid day in Karachi.
parts.answer: The air outside the leaf already contains much water vapour, so the concentration gradient between the air spaces and the outside air is smaller and diffusion is slower.
parts.working: B1 high water vapour concentration outside; B1 smaller concentration gradient so slower diffusion

practice.stem: A potted chilli plant was watered and its pot and soil surface were sealed in a plastic bag. It was placed on a balance in a sunny courtyard. At 9 am its mass was 412.0 g. At 3 pm its mass was 397.6 g.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of water lost in 6 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the starting mass that was lost. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of water loss in g per hour.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the pot and soil were covered with a plastic bag.
parts.answer: So that mass lost is due to transpiration from the plant only, not evaporation from the soil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing light intensity on the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Rate increases (up to a point).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain your answer to (a).
parts.answer: In light the stomata open (wider), so more water vapour can diffuse out of the leaf.
parts.working: B1 stomata open in light; B1 more water vapour diffuses out

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a plant transpires very little at night.
parts.answer: Stomata are closed in the dark (and it is cooler).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would increase the rate of transpiration from a leafy shoot?
A moving it from a bright window into a dark cupboard
B raising the relative humidity of the room
C placing a fan close to the shoot
D moving it into a cooler room
parts.answer: C placing a fan close to the shoot
parts.working: A fan removes water vapour from around the leaves, keeping the concentration gradient steep so diffusion through the stomata continues quickly. Darkness closes stomata, higher humidity reduces the gradient and a cooler room slows evaporation, so A, B and D each reduce transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Four similar leaves were treated with petroleum jelly, which is waterproof, and hung up for two days. Leaf 1: no jelly. Leaf 2: jelly on the upper surface. Leaf 3: jelly on the lower surface. Leaf 4: jelly on both surfaces. Apart from leaf 4, which leaf lost the least mass?
A leaf 1
B leaf 2
C leaf 3
D all three lost the same mass
parts.answer: C leaf 3
parts.working: Most stomata are on the lower surface of a typical dicot leaf, so blocking the lower surface stops most water vapour loss. Leaf 2 still loses water through the many lower stomata.

practice.stem: In a potometer the air bubble moved 36 mm along a capillary tube in 4 minutes. The radius of the capillary bore is 0.5 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of water taken up by the shoot in mm³. Use the formula volume = πr²l. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 28.3 mm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ per minute, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 7.07 mm³/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the cut end of the shoot was cut under water before it was put in the potometer.
parts.answer: To prevent air entering the xylem vessels, which would block the water column and stop water being drawn up.
parts.working: B1 stops air entering xylem; B1 air bubble would block water flow / break water column

practice.stem: On a very hot afternoon in Multan in June, a farmer notices that his cotton plants have drooping leaves, even though the soil is slightly damp. By the next morning the plants look normal again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the plants wilted.
parts.answer: Water was lost by transpiration faster than it was absorbed by the roots; cells lost water and became flaccid (lost turgor); so the leaves and stems were no longer supported.
parts.working: B1 transpiration rate greater than water uptake; B1 cells lose turgor / become flaccid; B1 loss of support

parts.label: b
parts.text: When wilting occurs, the stomata close. Give one advantage and one disadvantage to the plant of closing its stomata.
parts.answer: Advantage: reduces water loss. Disadvantage: less carbon dioxide enters, so less photosynthesis (also less cooling / less mineral transport).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how temperature affects the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot. Your plan should include what you would change, measure and keep the same.
parts.answer: Use a potometer; vary temperature (e.g. 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 °C in a temperature-controlled room or incubator, checked with a thermometer); measure distance bubble moves in a fixed time; calculate rate; keep light intensity, humidity, air movement and same shoot constant; allow time to adjust; repeat and calculate mean.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: potometer / mass loss method; at least 5 temperatures stated with range; how temperature is controlled (heater / room / incubator, check with thermometer); dependent variable: bubble distance in fixed time (or mass lost); calculate rate; same shoot / same leaf area; constant light intensity; constant humidity / wind; acclimatise before timing; repeat at each temperature and find mean

practice.stem: A cactus growing in the Thar Desert has leaves reduced to spines, a thick waxy cuticle and stomata sunk in pits in a thick green stem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest how each feature reduces water loss: (i) leaves reduced to spines (ii) a thick waxy cuticle (iii) stomata sunk in pits.
parts.answer: (i) smaller surface area for transpiration (ii) waterproof layer reduces evaporation from the surface (iii) humid air is trapped in the pit, reducing the concentration gradient

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the cactus stem is green.
parts.answer: The stem carries out photosynthesis instead of the leaves (contains chloroplasts).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the correct pathway taken by water as it moves through a plant?
A root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
B root hair cell → phloem → root cortex cells → mesophyll cells
C xylem → root hair cell → mesophyll cells → stomata
D root cortex cells → root hair cell → xylem → mesophyll cells
parts.answer: A root hair cell → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
parts.working: Water enters root hair cells, crosses the cortex to the xylem, travels up in the xylem and then enters mesophyll cells. B is wrong because water moves in xylem, not phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State where root hairs are found on a root.
parts.answer: Just behind the root tip.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seedlings that are pulled out and replanted often wilt. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Root hairs are damaged / torn off when the seedlings are pulled up; so the surface area for water absorption is reduced.
parts.working: B1 root hairs damaged; B1 less surface area / less water absorbed

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how a gardener can reduce wilting when moving seedlings.
parts.answer: Move them with a ball of soil around the roots / water well / move in the evening.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of a root hair cell increases its surface area for absorption?
A a nucleus
B a long, thin, hair-like extension
C many chloroplasts
D a thick cellulose wall
parts.answer: B a long, thin, hair-like extension
parts.working: Root hairs are long, thin outgrowths of epidermal cells, which increase the surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions. Root cells are underground and have no chloroplasts, and a thick wall does not increase surface area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue in the root that carries water up to the stem, and give one feature of its cells that helps it carry water.
parts.answer: Xylem; the vessels are dead and hollow, with lignified walls and no cell contents (or no end walls) so water flows freely.
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem; 1 mark: dead, hollow lignified vessels with no cell contents.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why root hairs are found only in a short zone just behind the root tip, and not on the older, woody part of the root.
parts.answer: Root hairs are short-lived, and the older part of the root is covered by a protective corky layer (bark) instead of root-hair-bearing epidermis; new root hairs form in the young growing zone just behind the root tip.
parts.working: 1 mark: root hairs are short-lived or the older part has no root hairs (corky bark); 1 mark: new root hairs form in the young zone just behind the tip.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how water moves from the soil into a root hair cell.
parts.answer: By osmosis; from a higher water potential in the soil (dilute solution) to a lower water potential in the cell sap; through the partially permeable cell membrane.
parts.working: B1 osmosis; B1 higher to lower water potential (soil → cell); B1 partially permeable membrane

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why root hair cells are able to absorb a lot of water.
parts.answer: Many long root hairs give a large surface area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Nitrate ions are absorbed by root hair cells even when their concentration in the soil is lower than in the cell. Name this process.
parts.answer: Active transport

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the root hair cells need oxygen for this process.
parts.answer: Active transport needs energy; energy is released by aerobic respiration, which uses oxygen.
parts.working: B1 needs energy; B1 from (aerobic) respiration

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plants in waterlogged soil take up fewer mineral ions.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil has little oxygen (air spaces filled with water), so root cells respire less aerobically and release less energy for active transport.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen in soil; B1 less respiration / energy for active transport

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Water moves into a root hair cell by osmosis. Which statement is correct?
A the cell sap has a higher water potential than the soil water
B the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water
C the soil water and cell sap have equal water potential
D water moves out of the cell into the soil
parts.answer: B the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water
parts.working: Water moves by osmosis from higher water potential (soil water) to lower water potential (cell sap containing dissolved solutes). A and D reverse the direction, and C would mean no net movement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A root hair cell has a solute concentration of 0.30 mol/dm³ and the soil water has a solute concentration of 0.10 mol/dm³. Explain which way water moves and why.
parts.answer: Water moves from the soil into the root hair cell by osmosis. The cell has a higher solute concentration, so a lower water potential than the soil water, and water moves down this water potential gradient across the cell membrane.
parts.working: 1 mark: water moves into the root hair cell; 1 mark: cell has lower water potential (higher solute concentration); 1 mark: water moves by osmosis down the water potential gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two adaptations of a root hair cell and explain how each helps the uptake of water.
parts.answer: Long, thin extension: increases the surface area in contact with soil water, so more water enters per unit time. Large vacuole with concentrated cell sap: lowers the water potential inside the cell, so water enters by osmosis more readily. (Any two adaptations, each with an explanation.)
parts.working: 1 mark per adaptation named (2) and 1 mark per correct explanation (2). Accept: many root hairs per root (large total surface area); a large vacuole lowering water potential.

practice.stem: A farmer in Faisalabad added far too much fertiliser to a field of young wheat plants. A few days later the plants wilted, although the soil was moist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the term water potential to explain why the plants wilted.
parts.answer: The fertiliser made the soil solution very concentrated, with a lower water potential than the root cells; water moved out of the root cells into the soil by osmosis; so less water reached the leaves and cells lost turgor.
parts.working: B1 soil water potential lower than root cells; B1 water leaves root cells by osmosis / cannot enter; B1 cells / plant lose turgor

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest what the farmer should do to help the plants recover.
parts.answer: Water the field heavily to dilute the fertiliser.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how water moves from the root hair cell to the xylem.
parts.answer: By osmosis from cell to cell across the root cortex, down a water potential gradient (each cell has a lower water potential than the one before).
parts.working: B1 through cortex cells; B1 osmosis / water potential gradient

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how water moves up the xylem to the leaves.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from mesophyll cells and is lost by transpiration; this creates a pull (tension) on the water in the xylem; water molecules stick together (cohesion) so a continuous column is drawn up.
parts.working: B1 transpiration / evaporation at leaves; B1 creates pull / suction; B1 water molecules stick together / continuous column

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chemical that stops aerobic respiration is added to the root hair cells of a plant. Explain why the uptake of water by osmosis continues, but the uptake of mineral ions falls.
parts.answer: Water enters by osmosis down a water potential gradient, which needs no energy. Mineral ions are taken up by active transport, which needs energy (ATP) from aerobic respiration; with respiration stopped there is less energy, so fewer mineral ions are taken up.
parts.working: 1 mark: osmosis is passive and needs no energy; 1 mark: active transport of mineral ions needs energy from aerobic respiration; 1 mark: with respiration stopped, less energy is released so fewer ions are taken up.

practice.stem: Two plants have different numbers of root hairs. Plant A has 120 root hairs and absorbs 36 mm³ of water per day. Plant B has 90 root hairs and absorbs 24 mm³ of water per day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average volume of water absorbed per day by one root hair on plant A and on plant B. Give each answer to 2 decimal places, in mm³.
parts.answer: Plant A: 0.30 mm³; plant B: 0.27 mm³ (per root hair per day)
parts.working: A: 36 ÷ 120 = 0.30; B: 24 ÷ 90 = 0.267, so 0.27. 1 mark for method, 1 mark for both values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the value for plant B differs from the value for plant A.
parts.answer: Root hairs are not the only factor: root hair length, the soil water, or the rate of transpiration of each plant may differ.
parts.working: Any one sensible factor that affects water uptake other than root hair density.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate of water uptake by a plant is higher on a hot, dry, sunny day than on a cool, humid, still day. Use the ideas of water potential and transpiration.
parts.answer: Transpiration increases as the leaves lose water vapour faster, lowering the water potential of the leaf cells; this draws water up the xylem from the roots; the root cells then have a lower water potential than the soil, so water enters the root hairs faster by osmosis.
parts.working: Any four: more transpiration on a hot dry day; leaf water potential falls; water pulled up xylem; root cell water potential falls below soil; more osmosis into root hairs.

practice.stem: A celery stalk with leaves was stood in water containing red dye. After some time, a thin slice was cut across the stalk and viewed with a hand lens. Small red spots were seen in a ring near the outside of the stalk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the tissue that the dye travelled through.
parts.answer: Xylem

parts.label: b
parts.text: The dye moved 84 mm up the stalk in 30 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of movement in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 2.8 mm/min

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could make the dye travel faster.
parts.answer: Place it in a warm / bright / windy place, or near a fan, to increase transpiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which pair of cell types makes up phloem tissue?
A dead, lignified vessels with no cell contents
B sieve tube elements with companion cells
C tracheids with bordered pits
D root hair cells
parts.answer: B sieve tube elements with companion cells
parts.working: Phloem is made of living sieve tube elements (with sieve plates) and companion cells. Xylem vessels and tracheids are dead and lignified (A and C), and root hairs are not part of phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Xylem vessels have walls strengthened with lignin. State two reasons why this strengthening is needed.
parts.answer: It supports the plant (the stem and leaves stay upright); it stops the vessel collapsing when water is pulled up under tension.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: support of the plant; prevents collapse under tension or pressure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one function of companion cells.
parts.answer: They provide energy (ATP from respiration) for active loading of sugars into the sieve tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the group of tissues that forms a vascular bundle in a dicot stem, and the layer between xylem and phloem in that bundle.
parts.answer: Vascular bundle; cambium.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which description of xylem vessels is correct?
A living cells with sieve plates
B dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin
C living cells with many chloroplasts
D dead cells with cross walls full of pores
parts.answer: B dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin
parts.working: Xylem vessels are dead cells joined end to end with no cross walls, forming hollow tubes with lignified walls. A describes phloem sieve tubes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two functions of xylem.
parts.answer: Transports water and mineral ions; provides support.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how two features of xylem vessels are related to their functions.
parts.answer: No cross walls / hollow (no cytoplasm), so water flows freely as a continuous column; lignin in walls makes them strong, giving support and stopping collapse under tension; narrow tubes help the water column hold together.
parts.working: For each of two features: B1 feature, B1 linked function

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature of xylem vessels allows water to move sideways between neighbouring vessels?
A lignin in the walls
B pits in the lignified walls
C sieve plates
D companion cells
parts.answer: B pits in the lignified walls
parts.working: Pits are gaps in the lignified walls where lignin is absent, so water can pass between vessels. Lignin strengthens the walls, sieve plates are in phloem, and companion cells are also phloem cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a sieve tube element, and state how it is linked to a companion cell.
parts.answer: Sieve tube elements are living cells joined end to end to form a tube; they have no nucleus; their end walls have sieve plates with pores; the cytoplasm is continuous. Each element is linked to a companion cell that contains a nucleus and provides the energy.
parts.working: 1 mark: living cells joined end to end; 1 mark: no nucleus, sieve plates with pores; 1 mark: linked to a companion cell which has a nucleus and gives energy.

practice.stem: A student stood a leafy stem in a dye solution. The dye moved 120 mm up the xylem in 40 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average rate of movement of the dye in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 3.0 mm per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the distance the dye would travel in 1 hour at this rate.
parts.answer: 180 mm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare xylem and phloem by stating: (i) whether the cells are alive or dead; (ii) one substance transported by each tissue; (iii) the direction of transport.
parts.answer: (i) xylem: dead; phloem: living. (ii) xylem: water and mineral ions; phloem: sucrose and amino acids. (iii) xylem: upwards from roots to leaves; phloem: up or down, from sources to sinks.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of the three correct comparisons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the positions of xylem and phloem in (i) a transverse section of a dicot stem and (ii) a transverse section of a dicot root.
parts.answer: (i) Stem: vascular bundles in a ring near the outside; xylem towards the centre (inside), phloem towards the outside. (ii) Root: xylem in the centre (often star / X shaped); phloem in groups between the arms of the xylem.
parts.working: Stem: B1 bundles in a ring, B1 xylem inner, phloem outer. Root: B1 xylem central, B1 phloem between xylem arms

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to the strand containing xylem and phloem in a leaf.
parts.answer: Vein / vascular bundle

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the arrangement of xylem and phloem: (i) in a dicot leaf vein, as seen in cross section; (ii) in a monocot stem.
parts.answer: (i) Xylem lies towards the upper surface of the leaf and phloem towards the lower surface. (ii) The xylem and phloem are grouped into separate vascular bundles scattered through the ground tissue of the stem.
parts.working: 1 mark each: xylem towards the upper surface; phloem towards the lower surface; monocot stem has scattered vascular bundles; each bundle contains both xylem and phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why xylem vessels are dead, whereas sieve tube elements must remain living to do their job.
parts.answer: Dead xylem vessels have no cytoplasm or end walls, so water flows freely in a continuous column. Sieve tube elements need living cytoplasm, with companion cells providing energy, to load and move sugars actively through the phloem.
parts.working: 1 mark: dead vessels have no obstructions so water flows freely; 1 mark: sieve tubes need living contents to move sugars; 1 mark: companion cells supply energy for active transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the vascular cambium in a growing dicot stem.
parts.answer: The vascular cambium is a meristem that divides to produce new xylem and phloem; it thickens the stem and increases the transport capacity as the plant grows.
parts.working: 1 mark: meristem or cell division; 1 mark: produces new xylem and phloem; 1 mark: increases the stem's thickness or transport capacity.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is translocation?
A movement of water from roots to leaves in xylem
B movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks
C loss of water vapour from leaves
D movement of mineral ions into root hairs by active transport
parts.answer: B movement of sucrose and amino acids in phloem from sources to sinks
parts.working: Translocation is the movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from regions of production or release (sources) to regions of storage or use (sinks). A is water transport in xylem.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sugar is the main form in which carbohydrate is transported in phloem?
A glucose
B sucrose
C starch
D maltose
parts.answer: B sucrose
parts.working: Sucrose is soluble and less reactive than glucose, so it is transported in phloem. Starch is insoluble and used for storage, glucose is used in respiration, and maltose is a digestion product.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two roles of translocation in a plant.
parts.answer: Moves sucrose from sources (leaves) to sinks (roots, growing regions, fruits, storage organs); moves amino acids and other substances to where they are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct roles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two substances, other than sugars, that are translocated in phloem.
parts.answer: Amino acids; plant hormones; mineral ions (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct substances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one sink in a plant during growth and one sink used for storage.
parts.answer: Growing shoot tip (or developing flower, fruit or seed) for growth; storage root, tuber or bulb for storage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any correct growing sink and any correct storage sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the terms source and sink.
parts.answer: Source: part of the plant that releases sucrose / amino acids (e.g. where they are made). Sink: part where they are used or stored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In sugar cane, sucrose is stored in the stem. State the source and the sink in a sugar cane plant during growth.
parts.answer: Source: leaves (photosynthesis). Sink: stem (storage) — also accept growing tips / roots.
parts.working: B1 source leaves; B1 sink stem

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tissue in which sucrose is moved.
parts.answer: Phloem

parts.label: a
parts.text: In spring a stored potato tuber starts to sprout new shoots. Explain why the tuber acts as a source at this time.
parts.answer: Stored starch is broken down to sucrose; the sucrose is transported in phloem to the growing shoots (sinks), which cannot yet photosynthesise enough.
parts.working: B1 starch → sucrose released; B1 transported to growing shoots / sinks

parts.label: b
parts.text: Later in summer the potato plant forms new tubers. Explain why the new tubers are sinks.
parts.answer: Sucrose from the leaves is transported to them and converted to starch for storage.
parts.working: B1 receive sucrose from leaves; B1 stored as starch

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why translocation can occur in both directions in a plant, unlike water transport.
parts.answer: Sources and sinks can be above or below each other (and change with season), so phloem carries substances up and down.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sucrose is loaded into the sieve tubes at a source leaf by which process?
A osmosis alone
B simple diffusion
C active transport
D evaporation
parts.answer: C active transport
parts.working: Sucrose is moved into the sieve tubes against a concentration gradient by active transport, using energy from respiration in companion cells. Osmosis and diffusion only move water or substances down a gradient, and evaporation loses water from leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the direction of movement of substances in xylem and in phloem. State where the substances move from and to in each tissue.
parts.answer: Xylem moves water and minerals in one direction only, upwards from the roots to the leaves. Phloem moves sugars and other substances in both directions (up and down), from a source (where sugar is made or stored) to a sink (where it is used or stored).
parts.working: 1 mark: xylem one direction, upwards; 1 mark: phloem moves in both directions; 1 mark: source to sink described correctly.

practice.stem: A plant moves sucrose from a source leaf to a sink fruit. The sucrose concentration in the sieve tube is 0.80 mol/dm³ at the source and 0.20 mol/dm³ at the sink.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the sucrose concentration is at the source than at the sink.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why sucrose moves from the source to the sink.
parts.answer: The sucrose concentration is higher at the source than at the sink, so sucrose moves down this concentration gradient; the sink uses or stores sucrose, which keeps the gradient steep.
parts.working: 1 mark: movement down a concentration gradient; 1 mark: sink uses or removes sucrose, maintaining the gradient.

practice.stem: A leaf makes 12 g of sucrose per day. 25 % of this sucrose is used by the leaf for respiration. Of the sucrose that remains, 60 % is sent to a storage root.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sucrose left in the leaf after respiration.
parts.answer: 9 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of sucrose sent to the storage root per day.
parts.working: 9 g × 0.60 = 5.4 g. 1 mark for method, 1 for answer.

practice.stem: A ring of bark, including the phloem, was carefully removed all the way round the trunk of a young apple tree. After some weeks the bark just above the ring had swollen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the bark above the ring swelled.
parts.answer: The ring removed the phloem (which is in the bark); sucrose moving down from the leaves could not pass the ring; sucrose built up above the ring, and the extra sugar caused water to enter / extra growth, so the bark swelled.
parts.working: B1 phloem removed; B1 sucrose transport (down from leaves) blocked; B1 accumulation above ring

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the leaves above the ring did not wilt for several weeks.
parts.answer: The xylem, which is deeper in the stem (wood), was not removed, so water still reached the leaves.
parts.working: B1 xylem intact / inside the bark; B1 water still transported up

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict what would happen to the roots after a long time, and explain.
parts.answer: The roots would die; they receive no sucrose for respiration, so they cannot release energy (and eventually the whole tree dies).
parts.working: B1 roots die / stop growing; B1 no sugar for respiration

parts.label: a
parts.text: An aphid feeds by pushing its feeding tube (stylet) into a sieve tube. When the stylet is cut, sap flows out for hours. Explain why this sap is evidence that sugars move in phloem.
parts.answer: The sieve tube contents are under pressure, so sap flows out of the cut stylet; the sap contains a high concentration of sucrose, which the aphid feeds on; sampling the sap shows that sugars are carried in the phloem.
parts.working: 1 mark: sieve tube contents are under pressure so sap flows; 1 mark: sap contains sugar (sucrose); 1 mark: shows sugar is transported in phloem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sugar in a potato tuber is stored as starch rather than as sucrose.
parts.answer: Starch is insoluble, so it does not raise the solute concentration of the cells; sucrose in high concentration would lower the water potential and draw water into the cells. Starch can be converted back into sucrose and translocated when the plant needs it.
parts.working: 1 mark: starch is insoluble; 1 mark: high sucrose would lower water potential/ draw water in; 1 mark: starch can be converted back to sucrose when needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a single stem can have sugar moving upwards in phloem in one part and downwards in another part.
parts.answer: Sugar moves from a source to a sink, so the direction depends on which parts are sources and which are sinks; leaves higher on the stem may send sugar up to a growing shoot tip while leaves lower on the stem send sugar down to the roots.
parts.working: 1 mark: direction depends on the position of source and sink; 1 mark: sugar goes up to growing shoot tips; 1 mark: sugar goes down to roots or storage organs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two conditions in which the rate of transpiration is lowest.
parts.answer: Cool; humid (high relative humidity); still air; dark (stomata closed) (any two).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two correct conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the openings on a leaf through which most water vapour is lost, and the cells that control their opening.
parts.answer: Stomata; guard cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why the capillary tube of a potometer must be completely filled with water, with no air bubbles, before the shoot is used.
parts.answer: Air bubbles would break the continuous water column, so the bubble movement would not measure water uptake correctly.
parts.working: Any one correct reason: continuous water column; an air bubble would block or distort the measurement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the unit for the rate of movement of the air bubble if the distance is measured in mm and the time in minutes, and describe how the rate is found from the readings.
parts.answer: mm per minute (mm/min); rate = distance moved ÷ time taken.
parts.working: 1 mark for the unit mm/min; 1 mark for rate = distance ÷ time.

practice.stem: A potometer records the distance moved by an air bubble. At 25 °C the bubble moved 15 mm in 5 minutes. At 35 °C it moved 27 mm in 5 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the rate of movement of the bubble at each temperature, in mm per minute.
parts.answer: 25 °C: 3.0 mm/min; 35 °C: 5.4 mm/min

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the rate between 25 °C and 35 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Leaf P has an area of 40 cm² and loses 8.0 cm³ of water per hour. Leaf Q has an area of 25 cm² and loses 6.0 cm³ of water per hour. Calculate the water loss per cm² per hour for each leaf, to 2 decimal places, and state which leaf loses more water per cm².
parts.answer: Leaf P: 0.20 cm³ per cm² per hour; leaf Q: 0.24 cm³ per cm² per hour; leaf Q loses more per cm².
parts.working: 1 mark each for P and Q values (8.0 ÷ 40 = 0.20; 6.0 ÷ 25 = 0.24); 1 mark for stating Q.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student covers a shoot with a plastic bag and records a lower water loss. Explain why the bag reduces the water loss.
parts.answer: The bag traps water vapour around the leaves, so the water vapour concentration outside the leaves rises; this reduces the concentration gradient between the leaf and the air, so less vapour diffuses out through the stomata.
parts.working: 1 mark: traps water vapour; 1 mark: gradient between leaf and air is reduced; 1 mark: less diffusion out of stomata.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leafy shoot loses half of its leaves, and all other conditions are kept the same. Describe and explain the effect on the rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: The rate of transpiration falls. With fewer leaves there are fewer stomata and less leaf surface area for water vapour to diffuse out, so less water is lost per unit time.
parts.working: 1 mark: rate decreases; 1 mark: fewer stomata or less leaf surface area; 1 mark: less water vapour diffuses out per unit time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why transpiration has a cooling effect on the plant.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells inside the leaf; evaporation takes in heat energy from the leaf, so the leaf cools.
parts.working: 1 mark: evaporation of water; 1 mark: takes in heat energy from the leaf.

practice.stem: A student hung a cut leafy shoot of a neem tree from a balance with its cut end in a sealed flask of water (the water surface was covered with oil). She recorded the mass every hour, first in still air and then with a fan blowing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the student's results could be used to show the effect of the fan.
parts.answer: Compare the mass lost per hour with and without the fan; the rate with the fan is higher.
parts.working: B1 compare rates / mass loss; B1 under the same other conditions

parts.label: b
parts.text: Without the fan the shoot lost 1.8 g in 3 hours. With the fan it lost 3.3 g in 3 hours. Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of water loss caused by the fan.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain fully how water moves from the xylem in a leaf to the air outside, and why moving air speeds this up.
parts.answer: Water passes from xylem into mesophyll cells by osmosis; it evaporates from the surfaces of mesophyll cells into air spaces; water vapour diffuses out through stomata down a concentration gradient; moving air removes water vapour near the stomata, keeping the gradient steep.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four: osmosis into mesophyll; evaporation from cell surfaces into air spaces; diffusion of water vapour through stomata; down a concentration gradient; wind removes water vapour / maintains gradient

practice.stem: Measurements on a rice plant in a field in Punjab on a clear summer day showed that water loss rose from 8 am to a peak at 2 pm and then fell. Water uptake by the roots followed a similar pattern but reached its peak about an hour later.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why water loss from the plant is greater at 2 pm than at 8 am.
parts.answer: Higher light intensity, so more stomata open wider; higher temperature, so faster evaporation and diffusion; lower humidity at midday, so steeper concentration gradient.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: more light so stomata open wider; higher temperature, more evaporation; molecules have more kinetic energy / diffuse faster; lower humidity / steeper gradient

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the rate of water uptake by roots lags behind the rate of transpiration in the early afternoon.
parts.answer: Water is first lost from the leaves, creating the pull; it takes time for the pull to be transmitted down the xylem and for water to cross the root, so uptake reaches its peak later.
parts.working: B1 loss from leaves comes first / drives uptake; B1 time for pull to travel / delay in uptake

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways in which a hot, dry climate could be a problem for a crop such as rice, which needs a lot of water.
parts.answer: Plants may wilt / lose turgor; stomata close so less photosynthesis and lower yield; more irrigation water needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation, using a potometer and a fan, to find how wind speed affects the rate of transpiration. Include: the independent and dependent variables; two control variables; how you would measure the rate; and one precaution to make the results accurate.
parts.answer: Independent variable: fan speed (or distance from fan). Dependent variable: distance moved by the air bubble per minute (rate). Controls: temperature, light intensity, humidity, the same shoot or leaf area. Measure: distance moved by the bubble in set time, repeated and averaged. Precaution: keep the capillary tube full of water and cut the shoot under water.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: independent variable; dependent variable; two controls (1 each); method for measuring the rate; one precaution. Accept any sensible equivalent.

practice.stem: Three shoots were tested in a potometer for one hour. Shoot W: leaf area 60 cm², water loss 1.8 cm³. Shoot X: leaf area 30 cm², water loss 1.2 cm³. Shoot Y: leaf area 120 cm², water loss 5.0 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the water loss per cm² of leaf area for each shoot, to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: W: 0.0300 cm³ per cm²; X: 0.0400 cm³ per cm²; Y: 0.0417 cm³ per cm² (per hour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why transpiration is much slower at night than at midday in most plants.
parts.answer: Most stomata close at night, so less water vapour diffuses out of the leaf; temperature is lower, so less water evaporates; less light means less stomatal opening, so the gradient is smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark: stomata close at night; 1 mark: lower temperature means less evaporation; 1 mark: smaller concentration gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a potometer measures water uptake rather than the exact rate of transpiration.
parts.answer: Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis and for growth, so it is not lost; some is retained in the cells to keep them turgid; so the uptake measured is slightly greater than the loss by transpiration.
parts.working: 1 mark: water used in photosynthesis or growth; 1 mark: water retained in the plant; 1 mark: uptake is greater than the loss measured.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which measure helps to keep a fish population sustainable?
A using nets with a smaller mesh size
B fishing all year round
C setting a maximum catch (quota) for each boat
D catching the largest number of young fish
parts.answer: C setting a maximum catch (quota) for each boat
parts.working: A quota limits how many fish are removed so enough remain to breed. A smaller mesh (A) would catch more young fish before they breed, which harms the stock.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why it is important to conserve endangered species.
parts.answer: To maintain biodiversity; plants or animals may provide future medicines or foods; to keep food chains / webs stable; for ecotourism and income; for future generations / moral reasons; to preserve genetic variety for breeding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods used to conserve endangered species.
parts.answer: Protecting habitats in national parks or reserves; captive breeding programmes and release; laws against hunting / trade; seed banks for plants; education.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes a sustainable resource?
A a resource that is produced as rapidly as it is removed from the environment, so it does not run out
B a resource that can never be used up however much is taken
C a resource that is only found in protected areas
D a resource such as coal that forms naturally over millions of years
parts.answer: A a resource that is produced as rapidly as it is removed from the environment, so it does not run out
parts.working: A sustainable resource is replaced as fast as it is used (e.g. managed forest, fish stocks with quotas). Coal (D) is non-renewable on a human time scale; B is wrong because any living resource can be over-used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how treating sewage before releasing it into a river helps to conserve water resources.
parts.answer: Treatment removes harmful bacteria and organic matter, so the river water stays clean enough to be used again downstream for drinking or irrigation, and aquatic life is not harmed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: removes pathogens/organic waste; water can be reused / river ecosystem protected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which water can be conserved on a farm or in a home.
parts.answer: Any two: drip irrigation instead of flooding fields; mending leaking pipes and taps; collecting rainwater; reusing treated waste water; covering water tanks to reduce evaporation.

practice.stem: The Indus river dolphin is an endangered species found mainly in the Indus river in Pakistan. In one stretch of the river, surveys counted 1250 dolphins in an early survey and 1820 in a later survey (figures for this question).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in the number of dolphins counted. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three threats to the Indus river dolphin.
parts.answer: Barrages divide the river into separate sections, isolating populations; less water in the river when it is taken for irrigation; accidental capture in fishing nets; pollution from farms, factories and sewage; dolphins trapped in irrigation canals.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two actions that may have helped the population to increase.
parts.answer: Hunting banned / legal protection; a protected reserve; rescuing dolphins trapped in canals; educating fishing communities; monitoring by surveys.

practice.stem:
The catch of one species of fish by boats along a stretch of coast (thousand tonnes):
2000: 52; 2005: 61; 2010: 70; 2015: 48; 2020: 31

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in catch between 2010 and 2020. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the catch fell after 2010 even though more boats were fishing.
parts.answer: Overfishing: fish were removed faster than they could reproduce; too few adult fish were left to breed.
parts.working: B1 overfishing; B1 breeding stock reduced.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe three ways to make fishing in this area sustainable.
parts.answer: Quotas limiting catch; larger mesh size so young fish escape; closed seasons during breeding; no-fishing protected areas; limit the number of boats / licences; fish farming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a sustainable resource.
parts.answer: A resource that is produced as fast as it is used, so it does not run out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how forests can be managed so that timber is a sustainable resource.
parts.answer: Replant trees to replace those cut down; selective felling (only some trees cut); leave areas protected; limit felling to the rate of regrowth; education / certification schemes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how recycling paper helps to conserve forests.
parts.answer: Fewer new trees need to be cut down to make paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hingol National Park in Balochistan protects a large area of desert, mountains, coast and river habitats. Explain why protecting a large area of habitat conserves more species than a captive breeding programme for one species.
parts.answer: The whole ecosystem is protected, including the plants, insects and other organisms in the food webs; many species are conserved at the same time; populations stay large and keep their genetic variation and natural behaviour.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: whole ecosystem / habitat protected; many species at once (incl. food sources); large populations / genetic variation kept; natural behaviour kept / no need to release animals later.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two problems in protecting wildlife in a very large national park.
parts.answer: Illegal hunting or tree-cutting is hard to detect over a large area; local people may need the land for grazing, fuel or farming; paying enough rangers is expensive.

practice.stem: A national seed bank stores seeds of wild plants and old crop varieties. To check one stored batch of chickpea seeds, 50 seeds were sown and 41 germinated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination in this test.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Seeds in the bank are dried and stored at about −20 °C. Explain why.
parts.answer: Low water content and low temperature slow the seed's respiration and enzyme activity (and stop mould growth), so the seeds stay alive for many years.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reduces respiration / enzyme activity; seeds remain viable for longer / no decay by fungi.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the seed bank tests a sample of each type of seed every few years.
parts.answer: To check that the seeds are still alive; if germination falls, new seeds are grown to replace the stock.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two advantages of conserving plant species as stored seeds rather than as growing plants in a botanic garden.
parts.answer: Seeds take up very little space, so many species and varieties can be stored; they stay alive for many years with little care; they are safe from pests, diseases and bad weather.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: little space / many samples; long storage life / low cost; protected from disease, pests or natural disasters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by artificial insemination and how it can be used in a captive breeding programme for a rare species of antelope.
parts.answer: Sperm is collected from a male and placed into the female's reproductive tract without mating; sperm can be transported or frozen and sent between zoos instead of moving animals, so more males contribute offspring.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sperm collected and inserted into female without mating; sperm transported/frozen instead of moving animals; allows unrelated / more males to father young.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why captive-bred animals are usually kept in large enclosures that resemble their natural habitat before release.
parts.answer: So they learn natural behaviour such as finding food and avoiding predators, which increases their chance of surviving after release.
parts.working: 1 mark each: learn natural behaviour; better survival after release.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A zoo runs a captive breeding programme for a rare species of leopard, starting with only eight animals. Explain why a population that has become very small is at risk even if it is protected.
parts.answer: Little genetic variation remains; inbreeding increases the chance of harmful recessive conditions; the population may be unable to adapt to new diseases or environmental change; a single disaster could wipe it out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how zoos can reduce this risk.
parts.answer: Exchange animals between zoos in different countries; keep breeding records (studbooks) to avoid breeding close relatives; use frozen sperm / artificial insemination.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a seed bank is a useful way of conserving plant species.
parts.answer: Seeds can be stored dry and cold for many years in a small space; they keep a wide range of genetic variety and can be grown if the species dies out in the wild.
parts.working: B1 long-term storage in small space; B1 keeps genetic variety / allows replanting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Markhor are wild goats living in the mountains of northern Pakistan. Their numbers fell because of hunting. In some areas, a small number of permits are now sold each year to foreign hunters to shoot an old male, and most of the fee goes to the local community. Suggest how this scheme can help the markhor population to increase.
parts.answer: Local people earn money from living markhor, so they protect them and stop illegal hunting; only a few old males are shot, which have already bred; money is used for wildlife guards / habitat protection / community projects.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one argument against this scheme.
parts.answer: Killing animals is ethically wrong; risk of corruption or too many permits; the strongest males may be removed from the gene pool.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how scientists could check whether the scheme is working.
parts.answer: Carry out regular surveys / counts of markhor in the same areas; compare numbers over years and with areas that do not have the scheme.
parts.working: B1 repeated population surveys; B1 comparison over time / with control area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Haleji Lake, a wetland in Sindh, is a protected area for wintering water birds. Discuss reasons why conservation programmes such as this one are important. Your answer should refer to species, ecosystems and people.
parts.answer: Points: reduce extinction of species (migratory birds, fish); protect vulnerable ecosystems; maintain food webs and ecosystem functions such as nutrient cycling and water purification; keep genetic resources and biodiversity; resources for people (fish, reeds, clean water, possible medicines); tourism and education; flood control.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point up to 6; for full marks the answer must refer to species, ecosystems and people.

practice.stem: Scientists estimate that the stock of one kind of fish in the Arabian Sea is 50 000 tonnes and that, without fishing, it would increase by 12 % each year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of fish that can be caught each year without reducing the stock.
parts.answer: 6000 tonnes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The fishing fleet actually catches 9000 tonnes each year. Calculate the stock at the end of the first year and at the end of the second year, assuming the growth rate stays at 12 %.
parts.answer: end of year 1: 47 000 tonnes; end of year 2: 43 640 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the stock may fall even faster than your calculation suggests.
parts.answer: As the stock falls there are fewer breeding adults, so fewer young are produced and the growth in tonnes is smaller; the fleet may also catch more young fish when adults are scarce.
parts.working: 1 mark each: fewer breeding adults / fewer young produced; growth not a fixed amount / more young fish caught.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Villagers next to a protected forest in the hills depend on it for firewood and grazing. Discuss how the forest could be used sustainably while still meeting the villagers' needs.
parts.answer: Allow only some trees to be cut (selective felling) and replant at least as many as are removed; limit grazing to certain areas or seasons; give the villagers other fuels such as biogas or solar cookers; let the community manage the forest and earn money from ecotourism.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: selective felling / quotas; replanting; controlled grazing; alternative fuels (biogas, solar, fuel-efficient stoves); community management / income from ecotourism; education.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why conservation schemes that involve local people are more likely to succeed.
parts.answer: Local people benefit from the forest, so they protect it and report illegal cutting; they are less likely to break rules they helped to make, and they have local knowledge of the area.
parts.working: 1 mark each: people gain benefits so protect it / less illegal use; local knowledge / cooperation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Fertiliser washes from farmland into a lake. Which sequence of events follows?
A algae grow rapidly → plants below die from lack of light → bacteria decompose dead plants → oxygen falls → fish die
B fish die → bacteria decompose fish → oxygen rises → algae grow rapidly → plants die
C algae grow rapidly → oxygen rises → bacteria die → fish die from too much oxygen
D plants die from lack of nitrate → algae die → fish die from lack of food → bacteria increase
parts.answer: A algae grow rapidly → plants below die from lack of light → bacteria decompose dead plants → oxygen falls → fish die
parts.working: Extra nitrate and phosphate cause an algal bloom; algae block light so plants die; decomposing bacteria increase and use up oxygen in aerobic respiration, so fish die. B gets the order wrong, starting with fish death.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Much of the litter on beaches near Karachi is plastic. State what is meant by saying that plastic is non-biodegradable.
parts.answer: It cannot be broken down by decomposers (bacteria and fungi), so it stays in the environment for a very long time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways in which plastic waste in the sea can harm marine animals.
parts.answer: Animals such as turtles swallow plastic bags, which block the gut and they starve; animals get tangled in nets and plastic, and drown or are injured; small pieces of plastic (microplastics) enter food chains.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways to reduce plastic pollution of the sea.
parts.answer: Use reusable cloth bags; recycle plastic; ban single-use plastic bags; proper waste collection; beach clean-ups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by eutrophication.
parts.answer: Enrichment of water with nutrients (nitrate and phosphate ions), leading to rapid growth of algae.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two sources of the nitrate or phosphate ions that cause eutrophication.
parts.answer: Fertiliser washed off farmland; untreated sewage; detergents.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one visible sign that a pond is undergoing eutrophication.
parts.answer: Green layer of algae (algal bloom) on the surface; or dead fish.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why farmers should not spread fertiliser on their fields just before heavy rain is forecast.
parts.answer: The rain would wash (leach) the fertiliser off the field into rivers or lakes, wasting money and causing eutrophication.
parts.working: 1 mark each: washed off / run-off / leached; causes water pollution / eutrophication or is wasted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some farmers leave a strip of grass and trees between their fields and a river. Suggest how this reduces water pollution.
parts.answer: The plants in the strip absorb nitrate and phosphate ions from water running off the field before it reaches the river; their roots also hold soil in place.
parts.working: 1 mark each: plants take up the ions; reduce run-off / soil erosion into river.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Untreated sewage and fertiliser run-off can both pollute a lake. State two ways in which their effects on the lake are similar.
parts.answer: Both add nitrate and phosphate ions, causing rapid growth of algae (eutrophication); both lead to more decomposition by bacteria, which uses up dissolved oxygen so fish die.
parts.working: 1 mark each: both add nutrients / cause algal growth (eutrophication); both cause oxygen loss / fish death through decomposition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one harm caused by untreated sewage that is not caused by fertiliser.
parts.answer: It contains pathogens that spread diseases such as cholera or typhoid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how untreated sewage entering a river can cause the death of fish several hundred metres downstream.
parts.answer: Sewage contains organic matter and nutrients (nitrate / phosphate); nutrients cause rapid growth of algae; algae block light so water plants cannot photosynthesise and die; bacteria (decomposers) multiply and break down sewage and dead plants; bacteria use oxygen in aerobic respiration; oxygen concentration falls so fish cannot respire and die.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Untreated sewage is also a danger to people who use the river water. Explain why.
parts.answer: It contains pathogens (e.g. bacteria causing cholera or typhoid) that can cause disease if the water is drunk.

practice.stem:
A housing estate releases untreated sewage into a river at an outlet (0 m). Samples were taken upstream (−100 m) and downstream.
distance / m: -100, 0, 200, 500, 1000, 2000
oxygen / mg/dm³: 9.2, 8.8, 4.1, 2.3, 5.0, 8.5
bacteria (relative numbers): 10, 120, 300, 260, 90, 20

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the oxygen concentration changes downstream of the outlet.
parts.answer: It falls from 8.8 mg/dm³ at the outlet to a lowest value of 2.3 mg/dm³ at 500 m; then rises again to 8.5 mg/dm³ at 2000 m.
parts.working: B1 falls to minimum at 500 m; B1 recovers further downstream (data quoted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in oxygen concentration from the upstream site (−100 m) to the lowest value. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use the data on bacteria to explain the change in oxygen concentration between 0 and 500 m.
parts.answer: Bacteria numbers increase greatly as they feed on the sewage; their aerobic respiration uses up oxygen from the water.
parts.working: B1 more bacteria feeding on sewage; B1 respiration uses oxygen.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the oxygen concentration recovers further downstream.
parts.answer: The sewage has been broken down so bacteria numbers fall; oxygen dissolves from the air / is made by photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During eutrophication of a lake, which organisms use up most of the dissolved oxygen that causes fish to die?
A aerobic bacteria decomposing dead algae and plants
B algae photosynthesising at the surface
C fish respiring faster because of the extra food
D plants growing on the bottom of the lake
parts.answer: A aerobic bacteria decomposing dead algae and plants
parts.working: Dead algae and plants are broken down by aerobic bacteria, whose population grows and respires rapidly, using up the oxygen. B is wrong: photosynthesis by algae adds oxygen rather than removing it.

practice.stem:
Dissolved oxygen was measured in a fish pond near Muzaffargarh that had a thick growth of algae.
time: 06:00, 12:00, 18:00, 24:00
dissolved oxygen / mg/dm³: 2.1, 9.8, 11.4, 5.6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the range of dissolved oxygen concentrations over the day.
parts.answer: 9.3 mg/dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the oxygen concentration is high at 18:00 and low at 06:00.
parts.answer: During the day the algae photosynthesise and release more oxygen than all organisms use; at night there is no photosynthesis, but the algae, bacteria and fish keep respiring, so oxygen falls to its lowest by dawn.
parts.working: 1 mark each: photosynthesis in light adds oxygen; rate of photosynthesis greater than respiration in day; no photosynthesis at night; respiration of algae/bacteria/fish uses oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fish farmers often switch on aerators in the early morning.
parts.answer: Oxygen is lowest at dawn, so fish are most likely to suffocate then.

practice.stem: Water downstream of a factory that discharged waste containing mercury was studied. Mercury concentrations (parts per million) were: plankton 0.02, small fish 0.3, large predatory fish 2.4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the mercury concentration is in the large fish than in the plankton, and in the small fish than in the plankton.
parts.answer: large fish 120 times; small fish 15 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the concentration increases along the food chain.
parts.answer: Each consumer eats many organisms from the level below; mercury is not broken down or excreted, so it builds up in its body.
parts.working: 1 mark each: eats large numbers of prey; mercury stored / not excreted / accumulates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why people living near the river are advised not to eat large fish caught there.
parts.answer: Large fish (top consumers) have the highest concentration of the toxic metal, which can harm people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A power station takes water from a river for cooling and returns it 8 °C warmer. Suggest how this could affect the fish downstream of the outlet.
parts.answer: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen; fish are cold-blooded so their respiration rate rises in warm water and they need more oxygen; some fish may die or move away; species needing cool, oxygen-rich water are replaced.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less dissolved oxygen in warm water; higher respiration / oxygen demand of fish; fish die or leave; change in species present / enzymes may be affected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the power station could reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Cool the water in cooling towers or ponds before returning it to the river.

practice.stem:
Students counted two kinds of animal in kick samples from four sites on a stream below a farm. Stonefly nymphs need water with a high oxygen concentration. Bloodworms (midge larvae) contain haemoglobin.
site: A (upstream), B, C, D (furthest downstream)
stonefly nymphs: 24, 2, 0, 11
bloodworms: 1, 30, 52, 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the differences in the numbers of the two animals between site A and site C.
parts.answer: Stonefly nymphs fall from 24 at A to 0 at C; bloodworms increase from 1 at A to 52 at C.
parts.working: B1 stonefly decrease; B1 bloodworm increase (data).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the information to explain these differences.
parts.answer: Site C has the least oxygen because of pollution (bacteria decomposing waste); stonefly nymphs need high oxygen so cannot survive there; bloodworms have haemoglobin, so they can obtain enough oxygen and survive with less competition.
parts.working: B1 low oxygen at polluted site; B1 stonefly need high oxygen; B1 bloodworm haemoglobin allows survival in low oxygen.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest which site, B or D, is cleaner. Give a reason.
parts.answer: D: it has more stonefly nymphs (11 v 2) and fewer bloodworms (12 v 30).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using living organisms rather than a single chemical test to monitor pollution.
parts.answer: Organisms show the effect of pollution over a long period, not just at the moment of sampling.

practice.stem:
Farmers around a lake increased the amount of nitrate fertiliser used each year. The mean nitrate concentration in the lake water was recorded.
fertiliser / kg per hectare: 50, 100, 150, 200
nitrate in lake / mg/dm³: 2.0, 4.5, 8.0, 13.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the nitrate concentration was in the year with 200 kg/ha than in the year with 50 kg/ha.
parts.answer: 6.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why nitrate in the lake increased more than in proportion to the fertiliser applied.
parts.answer: Crops can absorb only a limited amount; once their need is met, extra fertiliser is not taken up and more of it is washed (leached) into the lake.
parts.working: B1 crops take up limited amount; B1 excess leached / runs off.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe three ways in which farmers and local councils could reduce eutrophication of the lake.
parts.answer: Apply only the amount of fertiliser crops need; avoid spreading before heavy rain; leave a strip of uncultivated land / trees along the lake edge; use organic manure that releases nutrients slowly; treat sewage before release.

practice.stem:
Ten duckweed fronds were placed in each of five beakers of water containing different concentrations of nitrate ions. After 14 days the number of fronds was counted.
nitrate / mg/dm³: 0, 5, 10, 20, 40
number of fronds: 14, 26, 41, 58, 60

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each beaker started with 10 fronds. Calculate the percentage increase in the number of fronds in the beaker with 20 mg/dm³ nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of nitrate concentration on the growth of duckweed.
parts.answer: Growth increases as nitrate concentration increases up to 20 mg/dm³; above this there is little further increase (58 to 60 fronds).
parts.working: 1 mark for increase; 1 mark for levelling off with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State three variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Light intensity; temperature; volume of solution; number/size of starting fronds; other mineral ions; time.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain how these results help to explain why water bodies near heavily fertilised fields often develop thick plant growth.
parts.answer: Nitrate washed in from fields acts like a fertiliser for water plants and algae, increasing their growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how phosphate from detergents in waste water can lead to the death of plants growing on the bottom of a lake.
parts.answer: Phosphate causes rapid growth of algae at the surface (algal bloom); the algae block light; plants on the bottom cannot photosynthesise and die.
parts.working: 1 mark each: algal growth/bloom; blocks light; bottom plants cannot photosynthesise and die.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Continue the explanation to show how the death of these plants leads to the death of fish.
parts.answer: Dead plants and algae are decomposed by aerobic bacteria; the bacteria increase in number and use up dissolved oxygen in respiration; fish cannot get enough oxygen and die.
parts.working: 1 mark each: decomposed by (aerobic) bacteria; bacteria respire using oxygen / oxygen falls; fish suffocate.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some countries have banned phosphates in washing powders.
parts.answer: To reduce eutrophication of rivers and lakes from household waste water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas released by burning coal is the main cause of acid rain?
A carbon dioxide
B methane
C oxygen
D sulfur dioxide
parts.answer: D sulfur dioxide
parts.working: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water in clouds to form acidic solutions that fall as acid rain. Carbon dioxide (A) is mainly linked to the enhanced greenhouse effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two greenhouse gases and give one human source of each.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide: burning fossil fuels / deforestation. Methane: cattle (digestion) / rice paddy fields / rubbish in landfill sites.
parts.working: B1 each gas; B1 each correct source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two things a family could do to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide they produce.
parts.answer: Use public transport, walk or cycle; use solar panels; switch off lights and appliances; use energy-efficient bulbs; plant trees.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes the enhanced greenhouse effect?
A extra carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere absorb more of the heat radiated from the Earth's surface, so the Earth becomes warmer
B a hole in the ozone layer lets more heat from the Sun reach the Earth
C sulfur dioxide forms acid rain, which warms the oceans
D greenhouse gases reflect sunlight away from the Earth, so the Earth becomes warmer
parts.answer: A extra carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere absorb more of the heat radiated from the Earth's surface, so the Earth becomes warmer
