parts.working: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared (heat) radiated from the Earth and re-emit some back, trapping heat; more gas traps more heat. B confuses ozone depletion with the greenhouse effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the gas, released by burning coal and oil that contain sulfur, which causes acid rain.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two effects of acid rain on living organisms.
parts.answer: Any two: damages leaves and kills trees; lowers the pH of lakes, killing fish and other aquatic animals; releases toxic aluminium ions from soil; makes soil nutrients wash away.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why acid rain can fall in a country far from the factories that cause it.
parts.answer: The gases are carried long distances by wind before dissolving in rain.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two fossil fuels.
parts.answer: Any two of: coal, oil (petrol/diesel), natural gas.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how burning fossil fuels increases the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Fossil fuels contain carbon from organisms that died millions of years ago; combustion releases this carbon as carbon dioxide faster than photosynthesis can remove it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: carbon in fuels / combustion produces CO₂; released faster than it is removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which farming activity releases large amounts of methane?
A growing rice in flooded paddy fields
B planting trees along field edges
C spraying insecticide on cotton
D harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
parts.answer: A growing rice in flooded paddy fields
parts.working: Bacteria in the waterlogged, anaerobic soil of flooded paddy fields produce methane (cattle are another major source). Planting trees (B) removes carbon dioxide and does not release methane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how increasing amounts of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere lead to global warming.
parts.answer: Heat (infrared) radiation from the Earth's surface is absorbed by greenhouse gases; more greenhouse gases trap more heat; the mean temperature of the Earth rises (enhanced greenhouse effect).
parts.working: B1 Earth radiates heat / infrared; B1 absorbed / trapped by greenhouse gases; B1 more gas → more heat retained → temperature rises.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three possible effects of climate change.
parts.answer: Melting glaciers and ice caps; sea level rise and flooding of coastal areas; more extreme weather (heatwaves, floods, droughts); changes in rainfall affecting crops; species extinction or migration; spread of insect-borne diseases.

practice.stem:
Carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere measured at a remote mountain observatory (values rounded to the nearest ppm):
year: 1960, 1980, 2000, 2020
carbon dioxide / ppm: 317, 339, 370, 414

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in carbon dioxide concentration, in ppm per year, between 1960 and 1980, and between 2000 and 2020.
parts.answer: 1960–1980: 1.1 ppm per year; 2000–2020: 2.2 ppm per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in carbon dioxide concentration from 1960 to 2020. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two human activities that have caused this increase.
parts.answer: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) in vehicles, power stations and factories; deforestation / burning forests, so less carbon dioxide is absorbed by photosynthesis.

practice.stem: A dairy farm keeps 50 buffaloes. Assume that each animal releases 100 kg of methane per year and that 1 kg of methane has the same warming effect as 28 kg of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total mass of methane produced by the herd each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the carbon dioxide equivalent of this methane, in tonnes. (1 tonne = 1000 kg)
parts.answer: 140 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why methane released by livestock contributes to climate change.
parts.answer: Methane is a greenhouse gas; it absorbs heat radiated from the Earth and traps it in the atmosphere, increasing the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.
parts.working: 1 mark each: greenhouse gas; traps heat / absorbs infrared radiation leading to warming.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why flooded rice fields release large amounts of methane.
parts.answer: The waterlogged soil contains very little oxygen; organic matter is decomposed by bacteria that respire anaerobically; these bacteria release methane.
parts.working: 1 mark each: little oxygen in flooded soil; anaerobic decomposition by bacteria; methane produced.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some farmers now drain their rice fields for a few days at a time during the growing season. Suggest how this reduces methane production.
parts.answer: Air (oxygen) enters the soil, so methane-producing anaerobic bacteria are less active and decomposition becomes aerobic.
parts.working: 1 mark each: oxygen enters soil; fewer/less active methane-producing (anaerobic) bacteria.

practice.stem:
Sodium metabisulfite releases sulfur dioxide gas. Fifty cress seeds were placed on damp cotton wool in each of five sealed containers, each with a small dish holding a different mass of sodium metabisulfite. The number of seeds that germinated after 4 days was counted.
mass of sodium metabisulfite / g: 0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0
number germinated: 47, 40, 31, 12, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage germination for each mass of sodium metabisulfite.
parts.working: Each value = number ÷ 50 × 100. 3 marks all five; 2 marks four; 1 mark three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State a conclusion from these results.
parts.answer: As the concentration of sulfur dioxide increases, germination of cress seeds decreases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one variable that should be kept constant and one safety precaution.
parts.answer: Number/type of seeds, volume of water, temperature, time; precaution: do not breathe the gas / open in a fume cupboard (sulfur dioxide is harmful to people with asthma).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how these results relate to crops growing near a brick kiln that burns high-sulfur coal.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide from the kiln could reduce germination and growth of nearby crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Every winter, cities in Punjab such as Lahore suffer from heavy smog. Sources include vehicle exhaust, burning of crop stubble and coal-burning factories and brick kilns. Explain how sulfur dioxide from these sources can damage lakes and forests far from the city.
parts.answer: Sulfur dioxide is carried by wind; it dissolves in rainwater to form acid rain; acid rain lowers the pH of lakes, killing fish and other aquatic organisms (aluminium released from soil); it damages leaves and roots of trees / leaches minerals from soil, so trees die.
parts.working: B1 carried by wind; B1 forms acid rain; B1 effect on lakes; B1 effect on trees / soil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three ways to reduce sulfur dioxide pollution.
parts.answer: Use low-sulfur fuels; remove sulfur dioxide from chimney gases (scrubbers / flue-gas desulfurisation); use renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric); improve kiln technology; ban burning of crop stubble.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Measurements of carbon dioxide at an observatory in the northern hemisphere rise every year, but within each year the concentration falls between May and September. What is the best explanation for this fall?
A more photosynthesis by plants in the northern hemisphere during its summer
B less respiration by animals during the summer
C less fossil fuel is burned in winter
D carbon dioxide dissolves less in warm sea water
parts.answer: A more photosynthesis by plants in the northern hemisphere during its summer
parts.working: In the northern summer, the large area of land plants photosynthesises much more, removing carbon dioxide faster than it is released. C is wrong because burning in winter is usually higher, and D would raise, not lower, atmospheric carbon dioxide.

practice.stem:
The mean summer temperature in one city was recorded each decade.
year: 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020
mean summer temperature / °C: 32.1, 32.4, 32.9, 33.3, 33.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in temperature per decade between 1980 and 2020. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.45 °C per decade

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways in which this warming could affect wild species in the region.
parts.answer: Any two: species move to cooler areas or higher altitude; species that cannot move or adapt may become extinct; breeding or flowering times change; food chains disrupted; spread of pests and diseases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says the data prove that burning fossil fuels caused the warming. Explain why the data alone do not show this.
parts.answer: The data show only a correlation over time from one city; they do not measure carbon dioxide or other causes (e.g. city growth or concrete heating), so a cause cannot be proved.
parts.working: 1 mark each: correlation not cause / no CO₂ data; other factors could be responsible (e.g. urban heat, one location).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how climate change could reduce food production in Pakistan.
parts.answer: Any five: higher temperatures and heatwaves damage crops such as wheat and reduce yield; changes in monsoon rainfall cause droughts or floods; glaciers melt faster, first increasing floods and later reducing river water for irrigation; more evaporation and soil salinity; sea level rise floods coastal farmland in the Indus delta; pests and diseases spread to new areas; livestock suffer heat stress.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point, up to 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways farmers could adapt to these changes.
parts.answer: Grow heat- or drought-tolerant varieties; change sowing dates; use drip irrigation / store water; plant trees as windbreaks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why humans destroy natural habitats.
parts.answer: To clear land for farming / grazing; building houses and cities; building roads; extracting natural resources (mining, quarrying, timber); building dams; dumping waste.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why destroying a habitat can cause a species to become extinct.
parts.answer: The species loses its food, shelter and breeding sites; if it lives only in that habitat, the population falls until none are left.
parts.working: B1 loss of food / shelter / breeding sites; B1 population falls / cannot move elsewhere.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is a direct effect of deforestation on the carbon cycle?
A less carbon dioxide is removed from the air by photosynthesis
B more oxygen is released into the air
C more carbon is stored in the wood of trees
D less carbon dioxide is produced by decomposers
parts.answer: A less carbon dioxide is removed from the air by photosynthesis
parts.working: Fewer trees means less photosynthesis, so less carbon dioxide is absorbed; burning or decay of the cleared trees adds more. B and C are the opposite of what happens.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four undesirable effects of deforestation.
parts.answer: Extinction / loss of species and biodiversity; loss of soil by erosion; flooding; increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere (also: loss of habitats, reduced rainfall locally, landslides).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a forest, minerals are returned to the soil when leaves fall and decay. Explain why soil becomes poor in minerals a few years after the forest is cleared for farming.
parts.answer: There is no leaf litter to decompose and return minerals; rain washes (leaches) minerals out of the bare soil; crops are harvested and removed so minerals are not returned.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no leaf litter/decomposition; leaching by rain; minerals removed in harvested crops.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Large areas of forest on a hillside are cut down. Which effect is most likely in the following years?
A more transpiration from the hillside
B less soil erosion during heavy rain
C more flooding in valleys below
D more carbon dioxide absorbed from the air
parts.answer: C more flooding in valleys below
parts.working: Without trees, less rain is intercepted and absorbed by roots, so water runs off quickly and floods valleys (with soil erosion). B is wrong: erosion increases because roots no longer hold the soil.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hillside forests in northern Pakistan have been cut for timber and firewood. Explain how deforestation can increase the risk of floods and landslides.
parts.answer: Fewer trees intercept rainfall; fewer roots to absorb water, so more runs off the surface quickly into rivers; roots no longer hold soil, so soil is washed away (erosion) and slopes become unstable; eroded soil fills river beds, so rivers overflow more easily.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how deforestation contributes to an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Fewer trees to remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis; burning or decay of cut trees releases carbon dioxide.
parts.working: B1 less photosynthesis; B1 burning / decomposition releases CO₂.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mangrove forests grow along the coast of the Indus delta. Large areas have been cut down for firewood and to make space for shrimp farms. Suggest two effects of this on fish populations in the area.
parts.answer: Young fish and shrimps lose the sheltered nursery areas among mangrove roots; less food (leaf litter, small animals); so fish populations and catches fall.
parts.working: B1 loss of breeding / nursery habitat; B1 loss of food / fewer fish.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why losing mangroves can lead to more damage to coastal villages during storms.
parts.answer: Mangrove roots trap sediment and slow down waves; without them the coast erodes and storm waves reach further inland.
parts.working: B1 roots hold soil / reduce erosion; B1 waves no longer slowed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Large mangrove replanting projects have taken place on the Sindh coast. Give one benefit of replanting other than for fish.
parts.answer: Mangroves absorb carbon dioxide; protect the coastline; provide habitats for birds and other wildlife; sustainable wood supply.

practice.stem: Scientists measured soil loss from two hillside plots in the Swat valley during the monsoon. Soil loss from the forested slope was 0.4 tonnes per hectare per year; soil loss from a nearby slope cleared of trees was 18.6 tonnes per hectare per year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more soil was lost from the cleared slope.
parts.answer: 46.5 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why more soil was lost from the cleared slope.
parts.answer: Without trees, roots no longer hold the soil together; leaves and leaf litter no longer protect the soil surface from heavy rain; rainwater runs off quickly over the surface carrying soil away.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no roots binding soil; no canopy/leaf litter to break impact of rain; faster run-off washes soil away.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one effect of this soil loss on a reservoir downstream.
parts.answer: Silt fills the reservoir, reducing the water it can store (and making water muddy).

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a wetland, reeds are eaten by ducks and by insects. Insects are eaten by frogs, and frogs are eaten by herons. The wetland is drained to build houses. Explain the effects on the animals in this food web.
parts.answer: Draining removes the reeds (producers) and water; insects and ducks lose their food and habitat and decline; frogs lose their food and breeding water; herons lose their food, so all populations fall or move away; some may become locally extinct.
parts.working: 1 mark each: loss of producers/reeds; loss of habitat/breeding sites; effects passed along the food chain to frogs and herons; animals die or migrate / local extinction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Wetlands are often used by migratory birds. Suggest why destroying one wetland can affect bird populations in other countries.
parts.answer: Migratory birds rest and feed there on their journey or spend the winter there; without it they may not survive the journey or breed, so populations fall where they breed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: stopover / wintering site for food and rest; fewer survive to breed elsewhere.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mixed natural forest is cut down and replaced by a plantation of a single fast-growing tree species. Explain why the number of animal species in the area decreases.
parts.answer: Only one kind of producer is present, so fewer kinds of food; fewer layers/habitats and nesting sites; animals that depend on particular plants lose their food and leave or die.
parts.working: 1 mark each: one plant species / less food variety; fewer habitats / niches; specialised animals lose food/shelter.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one advantage to people of the plantation.
parts.answer: Fast supply of timber or fuel wood, reducing cutting of other natural forest.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term habitat.
parts.answer: The place where an organism lives.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how habitat destruction can lead to the extinction of a species.
parts.answer: The organisms lose their food, shelter and breeding sites; population falls as many die or fail to reproduce; if the species lives only in that habitat (and cannot move elsewhere) it may die out completely.
parts.working: 1 mark each: loss of food/shelter/breeding sites; population decreases; species found nowhere else / cannot migrate so extinct.

practice.stem: Satellite images showed that the forest cover in one district was 4800 km² in 1990 and 3360 km² in 2020.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of forest lost between 1990 and 2020.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean area of forest lost per year.
parts.answer: 48 km² per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how this loss of forest could reduce rainfall in the region.
parts.answer: Fewer trees means less transpiration; less water vapour enters the air, so fewer clouds form and less rain falls.
parts.working: B1 less transpiration; B1 less water vapour / cloud formation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the loss of forest reduces biodiversity.
parts.answer: Many species lose their habitats, food sources and breeding sites; species that depend on them in food webs are also affected, so the number of different species falls.
parts.working: B1 habitat / food loss; B1 effects through food webs / extinction / fewer species.

practice.stem:
Bird species were counted in forest patches of different sizes.
area of forest patch / ha: 1, 10, 100, 1000
number of bird species: 8, 17, 31, 44

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the area of a forest patch and the number of bird species found.
parts.answer: As the area increases the number of species increases, but not in proportion: a 1000-fold increase in area gives only 5.5 times as many species (each tenfold increase adds only about 9–14 species).
parts.working: 1 mark positive relationship; 1 mark for detail with data, e.g. not proportional / each tenfold increase adds only 9–14 species.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more bird species are found in the 1000 ha patch than in the 1 ha patch.
parts.answer: 5.5 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: A large forest is split into many small patches by new roads and farms. Use the data to explain why many species may be lost even if the total area of forest left is quite large.
parts.answer: Each small patch can support few species; species needing large territories or deep forest cannot survive; small isolated populations cannot move between patches to breed or find food, so they die out.
parts.working: 1 mark each: small patches hold fewer species; large animals/territories not supported; isolation prevents movement / breeding.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way of reducing this effect.
parts.answer: Leave strips of forest (wildlife corridors) connecting the patches.

practice.stem: A tree-planting programme in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa plants 1.2 million saplings each year. Assume that 65 % of saplings survive and that each surviving tree absorbs 22 kg of carbon dioxide per year once established.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of saplings that survive each year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in tonnes, absorbed each year by the surviving trees from one year's planting. (1 tonne = 1000 kg)
parts.answer: 17 160 tonnes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why planting young trees does not fully replace the value of an old natural forest that has been cut down.
parts.answer: Young trees absorb much less carbon dioxide and store less carbon than mature trees for many years; plantations often contain one species, so they support fewer species and habitats; soil and the full food web take decades to recover.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: small trees absorb/store less carbon; less biodiversity / one species; fewer habitats/niches; takes many years to develop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In parts of the Thal desert, large herds of goats graze the same land all year. Explain how this can turn grassland into bare desert.
parts.answer: Goats eat plants faster than they can regrow and pull up roots; ground becomes bare; without roots and plant cover, wind and rain erode the topsoil; soil loses organic matter and water, so new plants cannot grow.
parts.working: 1 mark each: overgrazing removes vegetation faster than regrowth; bare soil; erosion by wind/rain; soil can no longer support plants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of managing grazing so that the grassland is sustainable.
parts.answer: Reduce the number of animals; rotate grazing between areas so land can recover; fence off areas for replanting; provide alternative fodder.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Explain how each of the following increases food production:
(i) chemical fertilisers
(ii) insecticides
(iii) selective breeding.
parts.answer: (i) supply mineral ions such as nitrate for growth (making proteins), so higher yield; (ii) kill insects that eat or damage crops; (iii) produce varieties with higher yield / disease resistance / drought tolerance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two problems caused by the overuse of fertilisers and pesticides.
parts.answer: Fertiliser runoff causes eutrophication; pesticides kill non-target organisms such as bees; pesticides build up in food chains; pests become resistant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A farmer sprays a herbicide on a wheat field. How does this increase the yield of wheat?
A it kills weeds that compete with the wheat for light, water and mineral ions
B it kills insects that eat the wheat
C it adds mineral ions to the soil
D it kills fungi that cause disease in the wheat
parts.answer: A it kills weeds that compete with the wheat for light, water and mineral ions
parts.working: A herbicide is a weed-killer; removing weeds reduces competition. B describes an insecticide and D a fungicide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In some countries a large part of the grain harvest is lost while it is stored. Suggest two causes of this loss.
parts.answer: Any two: eaten by rats, mice or insect pests; damp grain becomes mouldy / decayed by fungi and bacteria; poor storage buildings let in rain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of reducing these losses.
parts.answer: Any two: dry the grain before storing it; store it in sealed, rat-proof silos or bins; keep it cool; control pests.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Drip irrigation supplies water through pipes directly to the base of each crop plant. Suggest two advantages of drip irrigation compared with flooding the whole field.
parts.answer: Any two: less water wasted by evaporation and run-off; less salt builds up in the soil; less fertiliser washed out of the soil; weeds between the rows get less water.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of drip irrigation for a small farmer.
parts.answer: The pipes are expensive to buy and install (or they can block and need maintenance).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ladybirds can be released into greenhouses to eat aphids that feed on crop plants. State one advantage of this method compared with spraying an insecticide.
parts.answer: It does not kill other useful insects / no chemicals left on food / pests do not become resistant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of this method.
parts.answer: It is slower and does not remove all the pests (or ladybirds may leave / eat other insects).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why this method works better in a greenhouse than in an open field.
parts.answer: The ladybirds cannot fly away from the crop.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A farmer grows only cotton on a very large area year after year. What is a disadvantage of this monoculture?
A The crop is easier to harvest by machine.
B Pests of cotton can spread quickly through the crop.
C More species of wild plants grow in the field.
D Soil minerals are increased each year.
parts.answer: B Pests of cotton can spread quickly through the crop.
parts.working: In a monoculture the same food plant is everywhere, so pests and diseases spread easily and build up. A is an advantage, not a disadvantage.

practice.stem: In one district of Punjab, wheat grown on rain-fed (barani) land yielded 2.1 tonnes per hectare, while wheat grown on irrigated land yielded 3.4 tonnes per hectare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield on the irrigated land. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the irrigated wheat produced a higher yield.
parts.answer: Water is a raw material for photosynthesis; water keeps cells turgid so leaves stay spread out and stomata open for carbon dioxide; water carries mineral ions up from the soil.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: photosynthesis raw material; turgor / no wilting; stomata stay open; transport of mineral ions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Prawns are farmed in ponds cut into coastal land. Describe two advantages of fish or prawn farming compared with catching wild animals.
parts.answer: Reliable supply all year; reduces pressure on wild stocks; animals grow faster with controlled feeding; easier to harvest.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three problems that intensive prawn farming can cause.
parts.answer: Uneaten food and waste pollute nearby water (eutrophication); disease spreads quickly in crowded ponds and to wild animals; antibiotics/chemicals used enter the environment; mangrove forest cleared to make ponds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained problems.

practice.stem: Urea is a nitrogen fertiliser that contains 46 % nitrogen by mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why plants need nitrate ions and why they need magnesium ions.
parts.answer: Nitrate: to make amino acids (proteins). Magnesium: to make chlorophyll.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mass of nitrogen in one 50 kg bag of urea.
parts.answer: 23 kg

parts.label: c
parts.text: A farmer wants to add 115 kg of nitrogen per hectare. Calculate how many bags of urea are needed per hectare.
parts.answer: 5 bags

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why adding twice this amount of fertiliser would not double the yield.
parts.answer: Another factor such as water, light or another mineral becomes limiting; the extra nitrate is washed out of the soil (wasted and may pollute water).
parts.working: 1 mark each: another factor limiting; extra fertiliser leached / wasted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing high-yielding varieties of crops has helped to increase world food production.
parts.answer: They were produced by selective breeding to produce more grain/fruit per plant (and to respond well to fertiliser), so more food is produced from the same area.
parts.working: 1 mark each: bred to give more yield; more food per hectare.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how agricultural machinery has increased food production.
parts.answer: Larger areas can be ploughed, sown and harvested quickly with fewer workers; crops can be harvested at the right time with less waste.
parts.working: 1 mark each: more land farmed / faster; less loss at harvest / fewer workers needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one problem of using large machinery on small farms.
parts.answer: Expensive to buy; compacts soil; fewer jobs for farm workers.

practice.stem:
Trials on wheat fields in Punjab measured grain yield with different amounts of nitrate fertiliser.
fertiliser / kg per hectare: 0, 50, 100, 150, 200
yield / tonnes per hectare: 2.1, 3.4, 4.2, 4.5, 4.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in yield, and the percentage increase, when fertiliser was increased from 0 to 100 kg per hectare.
parts.answer: 2.1 tonnes per hectare; 100 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of increasing fertiliser above 150 kg per hectare.
parts.answer: No further increase in yield (it stays at 4.5 t/ha).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why yield stops increasing at high fertiliser levels.
parts.answer: Another factor, such as water, light, another mineral or the crop's genetic potential, becomes limiting.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the data to advise the farmer how much fertiliser to use. Explain your advice.
parts.answer: About 150 kg/ha (or between 100 and 150): more gives no extra yield, wastes money and the excess may run off into rivers causing eutrophication.
parts.working: B1 amount with data reason; B1 cost / pollution reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why famine can occur in one region even when the world as a whole produces enough food for everyone.
parts.answer: Any five: unequal distribution of food between countries; poverty means people cannot buy food; drought or floods destroy local crops; war or conflict stops farming and transport; poor roads/storage so food cannot reach people or rots; rapid population increase in the region; crops grown for export or animal feed rather than local food.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point, up to 5.

practice.stem: Tunnel farming (growing crops under plastic tunnels) is widely used for vegetables in Punjab. One farmer harvested 85 tonnes of tomatoes per hectare from tunnels and 25 tonnes per hectare from open fields.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the yield was in the tunnels.
parts.answer: 3.4 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest and explain three reasons why the tunnels give a higher yield.
parts.answer: Higher temperature in winter speeds up enzymes and photosynthesis; protection from frost, wind and heavy rain; fewer pests and diseases reach the plants; humidity and water can be controlled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three reasons with explanation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some large greenhouses add extra carbon dioxide to the air. Explain why this can increase yield, and why it only works if light and temperature are also high enough.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis and is often the limiting factor; more CO₂ increases the rate of photosynthesis; if light or temperature is low, that factor limits the rate, so extra CO₂ has no effect.
parts.working: 1 mark each: CO₂ used in photosynthesis / limiting factor; faster photosynthesis so more growth; other factors may limit instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how feeding low doses of antibiotics to healthy chickens on a crowded poultry farm can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
parts.answer: Bacteria vary and some have a mutation giving resistance; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing on the resistance allele; over time most of the bacteria are resistant (natural selection).
parts.working: 1 mark each: variation/mutation; non-resistant killed; resistant survive and reproduce; resistance passed on / population becomes resistant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this is a danger to human health.
parts.answer: Resistant bacteria can pass to people through meat or contact; infections caused by them cannot be treated with that antibiotic.
parts.working: 1 mark each: bacteria transferred to humans; antibiotics no longer work for treatment.

practice.stem: A farmer compared two plots of wheat. The unsprayed plot yielded 3.2 tonnes per hectare and the plot sprayed with a pesticide yielded 4.0 tonnes per hectare. The pesticide cost Rs 9000 per hectare and the farmer sells wheat at Rs 100 per kg.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in yield, in kg per hectare, from spraying.
parts.answer: 800 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra profit per hectare after paying for the pesticide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farmer sprays the same pesticide every year. After several years it has much less effect on the pests. Explain why.
parts.answer: Some pests have a mutation giving resistance; they survive spraying and reproduce, passing on the allele; the proportion of resistant pests increases each year.
parts.working: 1 mark each: variation/resistant individuals; survive and reproduce; resistance becomes common.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how modern technology has increased food production.
parts.answer: Up to 6 of: machinery for ploughing/harvesting; chemical fertilisers supply nitrate etc.; insecticides kill pests; herbicides kill weeds; fungicides; irrigation; selective breeding of high-yield crops and livestock; greenhouses/tunnels; genetic modification; better storage/refrigeration.
parts.working: 1 mark per point described, up to 6.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one environmental problem caused by one of the methods you described.
parts.answer: e.g. fertiliser: run-off into lakes → nutrients → algal bloom → plants die from lack of light → decomposed by aerobic bacteria → oxygen used, fish die.
parts.working: Method named (1); up to 3 marks for a logical chain of explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the advantages to a farmer of monoculture (growing one crop over a large area).
parts.answer: Up to 4: easier and cheaper to use machinery; same treatment of fertiliser/pesticide everywhere; can specialise and grow the most profitable crop; large harvest sold in bulk; efficient planting and harvesting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the negative effects of monoculture on the environment.
parts.answer: Up to 6: natural habitats removed so loss of biodiversity; pests and diseases of the crop spread easily and build up; more pesticide used, killing other species; same minerals removed each year so more fertiliser needed, causing pollution; soil structure damaged / erosion; reduced food sources for wildlife; pests may become resistant.
parts.working: 1 mark per point explained, up to 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how adding chemical fertiliser can increase the yield of a crop.
parts.answer: Fertilisers supply mineral ions; nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins for growth; magnesium is used to make chlorophyll for photosynthesis; plants grow larger and produce more grain.
parts.working: 1 mark each: supplies mineral ions; nitrate for proteins; magnesium for chlorophyll; more growth / photosynthesis / yield.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using animal manure instead of chemical fertiliser on a field of maize.
parts.answer: Advantages: adds organic matter (humus) that improves soil structure and holds water; releases mineral ions slowly so less leaching; cheap and recycles farm waste. Disadvantages: amount of each mineral ion is not known; bulky and heavy to transport and spread; slower to act; may contain pathogens or weed seeds; smells; can still cause eutrophication if washed into water.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, up to 6; at least one advantage and one disadvantage needed for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A government sets a yearly catch quota and a minimum net mesh size for a sea fishery. Explain how each rule helps to keep the fishery sustainable, and suggest why these rules can be difficult to enforce.
parts.answer: Quota: limits the mass of fish removed so that it is no more than the population can replace by reproduction. Mesh size: young, small fish escape, grow and reach breeding age, so they replace the fish caught. Enforcement difficulties: many boats over a large area of sea are hard to inspect; fishers lose income, so some land catches illegally; boats from other countries; nets can be changed at sea.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for quota (limit catch; below rate of replacement); up to 2 marks for mesh (young escape; reach breeding age); up to 2 marks for enforcement problems.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why overfishing can affect other species in a marine food web.
parts.answer: Fish removed are prey for seabirds, dolphins, larger fish; these predators lose food and decline; prey of the fish (e.g. zooplankton or jellyfish) may increase; the balance of the food web changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many chickens in Pakistan are reared in large intensive sheds with thousands of birds. Give two advantages of intensive livestock production.
parts.answer: Cheaper meat and eggs; more food produced from less land; less energy lost by birds moving / keeping warm, so faster growth; easier to control feeding and disease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three disadvantages of intensive livestock production.
parts.answer: Diseases spread quickly between crowded animals; heavy use of antibiotics can lead to resistant bacteria; animal welfare concerns; waste can pollute water; high energy use for heating, lighting and feed transport.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples of ways in which crop plants have been genetically modified, and explain how each modification can help food production.
parts.answer: Insect resistance: the crop makes a protein that kills insects that eat it, so less crop is lost and less insecticide is needed. Herbicide resistance: the farmer can spray herbicide to kill weeds without harming the crop, so less competition. Extra vitamins (e.g. rice with extra vitamin A): improves the nutritional value of a staple food.
parts.working: For each of two examples: 1 mark for the modification, 1 mark for how it helps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing genetically modified crops.
parts.answer: Advantages: higher yields; less insecticide used; better nutrition; crops for difficult conditions. Disadvantages: seed is expensive and may have to be bought each year; inserted genes may spread to wild relatives by pollen (e.g. herbicide-resistant weeds); reduced genetic variation; insects that are not pests may be harmed; some people are concerned about safety of eating them.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, up to 6; at least one advantage and one disadvantage needed for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how insecticides and herbicides increase crop yields.
parts.answer: Insecticides kill insect pests that eat crops, so less damage; herbicides kill weeds; weeds compete for light, water and mineral ions; so the crop grows better and produces more.
parts.working: 1 mark each: insecticide kills pests; less crop eaten/damaged; herbicide kills weeds; less competition for light/water/ions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Insects that eat cotton plants in Pakistan have become resistant to some insecticides. Use the idea of natural selection to explain how this happened, and suggest how farmers can slow it down.
parts.answer: Variation in the insect population; mutation gives some resistance; spraying kills susceptible insects; resistant insects survive, reproduce and pass on the allele; over generations most insects are resistant. To slow it: use different insecticides in turn; spray only when needed; use biological control / resistant crop varieties.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for natural selection stages; up to 2 marks for ways to slow it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a plant breeder could use selective breeding to produce a variety of wheat that grows well in hot, dry conditions.
parts.answer: Choose parent plants with the best drought/heat tolerance; cross-pollinate them (transfer pollen, prevent self-pollination); grow the seeds; select offspring with the best tolerance; breed these together; repeat over many generations until the feature is reliable; test in field conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why selective breeding of crops is slow and why it may reduce the ability of a crop to resist new diseases.
parts.answer: Each generation needs a growing season; many generations needed; only plants with chosen features are kept so genetic variation is reduced; plants are genetically similar so a new disease can affect all of them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing crops in a greenhouse can increase yield. Refer to limiting factors in your answer.
parts.answer: Temperature kept high (heaters) so enzymes work faster; extra light (lamps) for longer; carbon dioxide added (e.g. from paraffin heaters); these remove limiting factors so the rate of photosynthesis increases; irrigation controlled; plants protected from pests, frost and wind.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, up to 6; at least one mark must explain the idea of a limiting factor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the disadvantages of greenhouse growing compared with growing in open fields.
parts.answer: Expensive to build; heating and lighting cost money and use fossil fuels (CO₂ emissions); pests and diseases can spread quickly in warm humid conditions; pollination may need to be done by hand or with bees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A country has a population of 240 million, growing by 2 % each year. Calculate the population after 10 years. Give your answer in millions to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 292.6 million

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the problems a country faces in producing enough food for a growing population. Include reasons why famine may occur.
parts.answer: Rising demand for food; less farmland as cities expand; soil erosion / desertification reduces fertile land; droughts and floods (climate change) destroy crops; water shortage for irrigation; pests and diseases; poverty means people cannot buy food; war or poor transport stops distribution; high cost of fertilisers and machinery.

practice.stem: One hectare of land produces wheat containing 20 000 MJ of energy per year. A person needs about 3650 MJ of food energy per year. When cattle eat wheat, about 10 % of the energy in the wheat ends up in the beef eaten by people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many people could be fed for one year from one hectare (i) if they eat the wheat, (ii) if the wheat is fed to cattle and they eat the beef. Give answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: (i) 5.5 people (ii) 0.5 people

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why so much energy is lost when the wheat is fed to cattle.
parts.answer: Cattle use energy for respiration (movement, keeping warm); some of the food is not digested and is lost in faeces; energy lost in urine / parts not eaten (bones, hide); so only about 10 % passes to the next trophic level.
parts.working: B1 respiration / heat loss; B1 egestion / undigested food; B1 not all parts eaten / energy in excretion.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why people still keep animals for food in areas where crops grow poorly.
parts.answer: Animals can graze on land too dry, steep or poor to grow crops, turning grass people cannot eat into food.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing a crop of chickpeas, a legume, in rotation with wheat helps to keep the soil fertile and reduces the need for nitrogen fertiliser.
parts.answer: Legumes have root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria; these convert nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds; the plant uses them to make amino acids and proteins; when the roots and leftover plant material decay, decomposers release ammonium and nitrifying bacteria make nitrate in the soil; the following wheat crop absorbs this nitrate, so less fertiliser is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each, up to 5: root nodules; nitrogen-fixing bacteria; nitrogen gas converted to nitrogen compounds; plant remains decomposed / nitrate formed in soil; next crop uses the nitrate so less fertiliser.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest the advantages of crop rotation compared with growing wheat on the same field every year.
parts.answer: Up to 5: pests and diseases of wheat do not build up because their host is absent in some years; less pesticide needed; different crops take different amounts of mineral ions / roots reach different depths, so the soil is not depleted of the same ions; less fertiliser needed and less run-off causing eutrophication; weeds are controlled more easily; soil structure is improved; the farmer has more than one crop to sell.

practice.stem: On a fish farm, tilapia fed on pellets gained 100 kg in body mass from 150 kg of feed. On a cattle farm, beef cattle gained 100 kg in body mass from 800 kg of feed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of feed needed to produce 1 kg of increase in body mass for the fish and for the cattle.
parts.answer: fish 1.5 kg; cattle 8.0 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest reasons why the cattle need much more feed to produce each kg of body mass.
parts.answer: Cattle use a lot of energy from respiration to keep their body temperature constant, while fish do not; cattle use more energy moving and supporting their body on land, while water supports the fish; much of the plant material eaten by cattle (cellulose) is not digested and is lost in faeces; energy is also lost in urine and methane.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, up to 4: energy used to keep warm / constant body temperature; energy for movement / support; undigested food lost in faeces; energy lost as heat / in urine / methane.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why fish farming is often encouraged as a more sustainable source of protein than beef farming.
parts.answer: Less feed is needed per kg of food produced, so less land is needed to grow feed; less methane, a greenhouse gas, is released; ponds can be made on land that is poor for crops; a shorter time is needed to reach harvest size.

practice.stem: On normal irrigated land a cotton crop yielded 3.0 tonnes per hectare. On nearby land where salt had built up in the soil, the yield was 1.8 tonnes per hectare.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how irrigation increases crop yields in dry regions.
parts.answer: Water is a raw material for photosynthesis; keeps cells turgid so leaves are held out to the light; stomata stay open so carbon dioxide can enter; mineral ions are dissolved and carried to the roots and through the plant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Large areas of irrigated land in Sindh have become salty. Calculate the percentage decrease in yield on salty land, and explain why salt in the soil reduces crop yield.
parts.answer: 40 % decrease. Salt lowers the water potential of soil water; less water (or none) enters root hair cells by osmosis; water may even leave the roots; plants wilt, stomata close, less photosynthesis, so yield falls.
parts.working: Calculation: M1 (3.0 − 1.8) ÷ 3.0 × 100, A1 40 %. Explanation up to 4: lower water potential in soil; less osmosis into roots / water leaves; wilting / loss of turgor; stomata close / less photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Cities in Pakistan are growing onto good farmland. Discuss how urban growth and climate change together threaten the country's future food supply.
parts.answer: Up to 6: best fertile land lost to housing and roads; population growing so demand rises while farmland shrinks; climate change brings heatwaves and droughts reducing yields; floods destroy crops; glacier melt changes river flow for irrigation; water used by cities competes with irrigation; more food imports needed; prices rise.
parts.working: 1 mark per point; full marks need both factors discussed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest four ways the country could produce more food without using more land.
parts.answer: High-yielding or drought-tolerant varieties; drip irrigation / water-saving methods; tunnel farming/greenhouses; reduce waste in storage and transport; integrated pest management; better fertiliser use.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In pea plants, the allele for tall (T) is dominant to the allele for short (t). What is the genotype of a short plant?
A TT
B Tt
C tt
D T
parts.answer: C tt
parts.working: A recessive phenotype shows only when two recessive alleles are present (homozygous recessive). Tt is tall because T is dominant, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Define the terms:
(i) allele
(ii) homozygous
(iii) phenotype
parts.answer: (i) a version (alternative form) of a gene; (ii) having two identical alleles of a gene; (iii) the observable features of an organism

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a dominant allele.
parts.answer: an allele that is expressed (shows in the phenotype) when present, even if only one copy

parts.label: a
parts.text: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white fur (b). Two black guinea pigs, both Bb, are crossed. Use a genetic diagram to show the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring.
parts.answer: parents Bb × Bb; gametes B, b and B, b; offspring BB, Bb, Bb, bb; phenotypes 3 black : 1 white
parts.working: B1 parental genotypes; B1 gametes (one allele each); B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes with ratio 3 black : 1 white

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the probability that one offspring is white.

practice.stem: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f). The dominant allele (F) gives normal mucus. A man who does not have cystic fibrosis but is a carrier has children with a woman who has cystic fibrosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the genotype of the father and of the mother.
parts.answer: Father: Ff. Mother: ff.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes of their children.
parts.answer: Parents Ff × ff; gametes F and f from father, f from mother; children Ff (no cystic fibrosis, carrier) and ff (cystic fibrosis) in a 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: parental genotypes; 1 mark: gametes; 1 mark: offspring genotypes with phenotypes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the probability that their next child will have cystic fibrosis.

practice.stem: In sheep, the allele for white wool (W) is dominant to the allele for black wool (w). A pure-breeding white ram is crossed with a black ewe to produce F1 lambs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by "pure-breeding".
parts.answer: Homozygous (both alleles the same), so the organism always passes on the same allele and breeds true.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotype and phenotype of the F1 lambs.
parts.answer: Ww; white wool.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An F1 ram is mated with several black ewes. In total 64 lambs are born. Calculate the expected number of lambs with black wool.
parts.working: M1 Ww × ww gives 1 Ww : 1 ww, so 1/2 black; A1 64 × 1/2 = 32.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two heterozygous plants are crossed. What proportion of the offspring is expected to be homozygous?
A 25 %
B 50 %
C 75 %
D 100 %
parts.working: Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, so AA + aa = 2 out of 4 = 50 %. 75 % is the proportion showing the dominant phenotype, so C is the main distractor.

practice.stem: In a plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p). Two heterozygous plants are crossed and 840 seeds are grown.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of plants with white flowers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The actual numbers were 618 purple and 222 white. Suggest why these differ from the expected numbers.
parts.answer: fertilisation is random, so ratios are only probabilities
parts.working: B1 random fusion of gametes / chance

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how a gardener could find out whether one purple-flowered plant is homozygous or heterozygous.
parts.answer: cross it with a white (homozygous recessive) plant (test cross); if all offspring purple, it is homozygous; if about half white (1 : 1), it is heterozygous
parts.working: B1 cross with white/recessive; B1 all purple → homozygous; B1 some/half white → heterozygous

practice.stem:
A family tree for an inherited condition (described in words):
Generation 1: person 1 (unaffected male) and person 2 (affected female).
Generation 2: their children are person 3 (unaffected male) and person 5 (unaffected female). Person 3 marries person 4 (unaffected female from another family).
Generation 3: persons 3 and 4 have three children: person 6 (unaffected female), person 7 (affected male) and person 8 (unaffected male).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how you can tell from the family tree that the allele for the condition is recessive.
parts.answer: persons 3 and 4 are unaffected but have an affected child (person 7); so both parents must carry a hidden (recessive) allele
parts.working: B1 unaffected parents (3 and 4) with affected child (7); B1 parents are carriers/heterozygous

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotypes of persons 3, 4 and 7, using D for the normal allele and d for the condition.
parts.answer: 3: Dd; 4: Dd; 7: dd

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the probability that the next child of persons 3 and 4 is affected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ratio 3 : 1 is seen in the offspring of a cross between two heterozygous parents.
parts.answer: each parent produces two types of gamete (A and a) in equal numbers; fertilisation is random; giving 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; AA and Aa both show the dominant feature, so 3 : 1
parts.working: B1 gametes A and a in equal proportions (meiosis); B1 random fertilisation; B1 AA and Aa same phenotype → 3 : 1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the meaning of 'genotype'.
parts.answer: the alleles (genetic make-up) an organism has, e.g. Aa

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In rabbits, black fur (B) is dominant to brown fur (b). A breeder wants to find out whether a black rabbit is BB or Bb. Which rabbit should it be crossed with?
A a black rabbit, BB
B a black rabbit, Bb
C a brown rabbit, bb
D any rabbit, because all crosses give the same result
parts.answer: C a brown rabbit, bb
parts.working: In a test cross with the homozygous recessive (bb): if any offspring are brown, the black parent must be Bb; if all are black (in a large litter), it is probably BB. Crossing with BB (A) always gives all black, so it cannot tell.

practice.stem:
A family tree for an inherited condition that affects the fingers is described in words.
Generation 1: person 1 (affected male) and person 2 (unaffected female).
Generation 2: their son, person 3, is affected. He marries person 4, an affected female from another family.
Generation 3: persons 3 and 4 have two children: person 5, an affected daughter, and person 6, an unaffected son.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the family tree shows that the condition is caused by a dominant allele.
parts.answer: Persons 3 and 4 are both affected but have an unaffected child (person 6); so both parents must carry a hidden (recessive) normal allele, and the condition allele must be dominant.
parts.working: 1 mark: two affected parents with unaffected child; 1 mark: so unaffected allele is recessive / condition is dominant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Using A for the dominant allele and a for the recessive allele, give the genotypes of persons 3, 4 and 6.
parts.answer: Person 3: Aa; person 4: Aa; person 6: aa.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Persons 3 and 4 have another child. Calculate the probability that this child will be affected.
parts.working: Aa × Aa gives 3 affected (AA, Aa, Aa) : 1 unaffected (aa); 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A family tree for an inherited condition caused by a recessive allele d (normal allele D), described in words:
Generation 1: person 1 (unaffected male) and person 2 (unaffected female).
Generation 2: their children are person 3 (affected female) and person 4 (unaffected male). Person 4 marries person 5 (affected female).
Generation 3: persons 4 and 5 have two children: person 6 (unaffected male) and person 7 (affected female).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how person 7 shows that person 4 is heterozygous.
parts.answer: person 7 is dd, so she received one d allele from each parent, including person 4; person 4 is unaffected, so he also has a D allele: Dd
parts.working: B1 person 7 (dd) received d from father/person 4; B1 person 4 unaffected so has D → Dd

parts.label: b
parts.text: Before persons 4 and 5 had any children, what was the probability that person 4 was a carrier? Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2/3: persons 1 and 2 must both be Dd (they have an affected child, person 3); their offspring are DD, Dd, Dd, dd; person 4 is unaffected, so he is one of DD, Dd, Dd, and 2 of these 3 are carriers
parts.working: M1 persons 1 and 2 both Dd, dd excluded as person 4 is unaffected; A1 2/3

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the genotype of person 6 and explain how you know.
parts.answer: Dd: he is unaffected (has D) but his mother, person 5, is dd and must have passed a d allele to him
parts.working: B1 Dd with reason (d from affected mother)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A breeder of goats in Balochistan finds that horns (h) are recessive to hornless (H). She crosses a hornless male with several horned females. Out of 24 kids, 11 have horns. Deduce the genotype of the male, with a reason.
parts.answer: Hh; the horned kids are hh, so they must have received an h allele from the male as well as from the mother
parts.working: B1 Hh; B1 horned kids need h from father

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected numbers of horned and hornless kids from this cross, out of 24.
parts.answer: Hh × hh gives 1 : 1, so 12 horned and 12 hornless

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the breeder would prefer a homozygous hornless male if she wants only hornless kids.
parts.answer: HH × hh gives all Hh, all hornless; every gamete from the male carries H
parts.working: B1 all offspring Hh; B1 all hornless/dominant allele always passed on

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt) are crossed. One offspring is chosen at random from those that are tall. What is the probability that it is heterozygous?
A 1/4
B 1/2
C 2/3
D 3/4
parts.working: Offspring are 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Among the 3 tall plants, 2 are Tt, so the probability is 2/3. 1/2 (B) is the proportion of all offspring that are Tt, not of the tall ones.

practice.stem:
In a variety of chickpea, smooth seed coat (S) is dominant to wrinkled seed coat (s). Plant K has wrinkled seeds; plants J, L and M have smooth seeds. Three crosses were made:
Cross 1: J × K → 118 smooth, 0 wrinkled
Cross 2: K × L → 52 smooth, 49 wrinkled
Cross 3: L × M → 90 smooth, 31 wrinkled

parts.label: a
parts.text: Deduce the genotypes of plants J, K, L and M. Explain your reasoning for each cross.
parts.answer: Cross 1 (J × K): all smooth from many seeds, so at least one parent is SS; if K is ss then J is SS. Cross 2 (K × L): about 1 : 1, so one parent is Ss and the other is ss; K is wrinkled = ss, so L is Ss. Cross 3 (L × M): about 3 : 1, so both are heterozygous: L Ss, M Ss. So J = SS, K = ss, L = Ss, M = Ss.
parts.working: B1 K = ss (wrinkled phenotype); B1 J = SS with reason (all smooth, no wrinkled when crossed with ss); B1 1 : 1 ratio means Ss × ss; B1 L = Ss; B1 3 : 1 ratio means Ss × Ss; B1 M = Ss.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the ratio of smooth to wrinkled seeds in cross 3, to 1 decimal place, and say whether it supports your answer.
parts.answer: 2.9 : 1; close to 3 : 1, so it supports L and M both being Ss.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which base always pairs with adenine in a DNA molecule?
A cytosine
B guanine
C thymine
D uracil
parts.answer: C thymine
parts.working: A pairs with T and C pairs with G in DNA. Uracil is not found in DNA, so D is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a gene.
parts.answer: a length of DNA that codes for a protein

parts.label: b
parts.text: Put these in order of size, smallest first: chromosome, nucleus, gene, base.
parts.answer: base, gene, chromosome, nucleus

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
parts.answer: two strands coiled into a double helix; each strand has a sequence of bases; bases pair across the strands (A with T, C with G)
parts.working: B1 two strands/double helix; B1 bases; B1 complementary pairing A–T, C–G

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a chromosome mainly made of?
A a long molecule of DNA (with proteins)
B a single gene
C a chain of amino acids only
D a molecule of glucose
parts.answer: A a long molecule of DNA (with proteins)
parts.working: Each chromosome is one very long DNA molecule (wound around proteins), carrying many genes. A single gene (B) is only a short length of a chromosome.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what is meant by:
(i) haploid nucleus
(ii) diploid nucleus
parts.answer: (i) a nucleus with one set of chromosomes (one of each pair); (ii) a nucleus with two sets of chromosomes (chromosomes in pairs).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which TWO of these human cells are haploid: sperm cell, white blood cell, zygote, egg cell, skin cell.
parts.answer: Sperm cell and egg cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each; deduct 1 mark for each extra cell listed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Mature human red blood cells contain no chromosomes. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They have no nucleus.

practice.stem: A doctor examines the chromosomes from a body cell of a person. The cell contains 22 pairs of chromosomes that are the same in males and females, and one pair of sex chromosomes, XX.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the sex of this person. Give a reason.
parts.answer: Female; she has two X chromosomes (XX).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total number of chromosomes in each body cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the number of chromosomes in each of her egg cells and which sex chromosome every egg contains.
parts.answer: 23; an X chromosome.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State where in a cell the chromosomes are found.
parts.answer: In the nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A human sperm cell contains 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human skin cell?
A 23
B 44
C 46
D 92
parts.working: Body cells are diploid (two sets), 2 × 23 = 46. 23 is the haploid number of gametes, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a sample of DNA, 22 % of the bases are adenine. Calculate the percentage of thymine, guanine and cytosine.
parts.answer: thymine 22 %; guanine and cytosine together 100 − 44 = 56 %, so guanine 28 % and cytosine 28 %

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the percentage of adenine always equals the percentage of thymine.
parts.answer: A always pairs with T across the two strands

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the sex chromosomes of a human male and a human female.
parts.answer: male XY; female XX

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use a genetic diagram to show that the chance of a baby being a boy is 50 %.
parts.answer: parents XX × XY; gametes: egg X only, sperm X or Y; offspring XX, XY in a 1 : 1 ratio (50 % boys)
parts.working: B1 parental chromosomes; B1 gametes; B1 offspring 1 : 1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement about the structure of DNA is correct?
A It is a single strand of bases.
B Its two strands are held together by pairs of bases: A with T and C with G.
C Its two strands are held together by pairs of bases: A with G and C with T.
D It contains the base uracil.
parts.answer: B Its two strands are held together by pairs of bases: A with T and C with G.
parts.working: DNA is a double helix of two strands linked by complementary base pairs A–T and C–G. C pairs the wrong bases; uracil (D) is found in RNA, not DNA.

practice.stem:
One strand of a short section of DNA has this base sequence:
A T T G C C A G T A

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the sequence of bases on the complementary strand.
parts.answer: TAACGGTCAT
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark with one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the total number of adenine bases in this double-stranded section.
parts.working: A1 3 on the first strand + 3 on the complementary strand = 6.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sequence of one strand can be used to work out the sequence of the other.
parts.answer: Bases pair in a fixed (complementary) way; A always pairs with T, and C with G.
parts.working: 1 mark: complementary base pairing; 1 mark: A–T and C–G.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which sex chromosomes can be present in a human sperm cell, and explain why half of all sperm carry each type.
parts.answer: Either one X or one Y chromosome; the male's cells are XY and meiosis separates the pair, so half the sperm receive X and half receive Y.
parts.working: 1 mark: X or Y (one only); 1 mark: XY pair separated in meiosis, giving 50 : 50.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A couple already have three daughters. State the probability that their next child will be a son. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 1/2 (50 %); each fertilisation is independent – the previous births do not affect which sperm fertilises the next egg.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1/2; 1 mark: independent events / chance is the same each time.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A hospital recorded 1000 births in one year, of which 515 were boys. Calculate the percentage of boys, and suggest why it is not exactly 50 %.
parts.answer: 51.5 %; the sex of each baby is decided by chance (random fertilisation), so a sample shows small differences from the expected 50 %.
parts.working: 1 mark: 51.5 %; 1 mark: random fertilisation / chance deviation from expected ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A goat body cell has 60 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a goat egg cell and in a goat zygote.
parts.answer: egg: 30; zygote: 60

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why it is important that gametes are haploid.
parts.answer: when two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the diploid number is restored; otherwise the chromosome number would double each generation
parts.working: B1 fertilisation restores diploid number; B1 prevents doubling each generation

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a gene and an allele, using an example.
parts.answer: a gene is a length of DNA coding for a characteristic/protein, e.g. the gene for flower colour; alleles are different versions of that gene, e.g. purple allele and white allele
parts.working: B1 gene definition; B1 allele as version of gene with example

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why identical twins have the same alleles but non-identical twins do not.
parts.answer: identical twins come from one zygote that splits (mitosis gives identical cells); non-identical twins come from two different eggs and sperm, which were made by meiosis and differ genetically
parts.working: B1 identical from one zygote/mitosis; B1 non-identical from two different gametes produced by meiosis

practice.stem: A section of double-stranded DNA from a wheat plant contains 3000 bases in total. 18 % of the bases are cytosine (C).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of each base (A, T, C and G) in the section.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of base pairs in the section.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why you do not need to measure the amount of G separately.
parts.answer: G always pairs with C, so the number of G equals the number of C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a mutation.
parts.answer: A (random) change in the base sequence of DNA / in a gene or chromosome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a change of one base in a gene can produce a new allele that gives a different phenotype.
parts.answer: The base sequence of the gene changes; this can change the sequence of amino acids in the protein made; the protein may have a different shape and work differently (or not at all), changing the feature.
parts.working: 1 mark each: changed base sequence; changed amino acid sequence; changed protein shape/function → different phenotype.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a change of one base in the gene for haemoglobin. Suggest why this changes the shape of red blood cells.
parts.answer: The haemoglobin made has one different amino acid, so it has a different shape/structure; the abnormal haemoglobin molecules stick together (at low oxygen), distorting the red blood cell into a sickle shape.
parts.working: 1 mark: different amino acid / different haemoglobin; 1 mark: abnormal haemoglobin changes cell shape.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of cell division produces gametes in humans?
A mitosis
B meiosis
C fertilisation
D binary fission
parts.answer: B meiosis
parts.working: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make haploid gametes. Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two uses of mitosis in the human body.
parts.answer: growth; repair of damaged tissue; replacement of cells (e.g. skin, blood cells)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of cells produced when one cell divides by mitosis, and how they compare with the parent cell.
parts.answer: two cells; genetically identical to the parent (same number of chromosomes)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
How many cells are produced when one cell divides by meiosis?
A 1
B 2
C 4
D 8
parts.answer: C 4
parts.working: Meiosis involves two divisions, giving four genetically different haploid cells. Mitosis (B) gives two identical cells.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether mitosis or meiosis is used in each case.
(i) growth of a root tip
(ii) formation of pollen grains in an anther
(iii) repair of a cut in the skin
(iv) formation of sperm in the testes
parts.answer: (i) mitosis (ii) meiosis (iii) mitosis (iv) meiosis

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by mitosis.
parts.answer: Nuclear division that gives rise to two genetically identical cells (with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell).
parts.working: 1 mark: nuclear division; 1 mark: genetically identical cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what must happen to the chromosomes before a cell divides by mitosis.
parts.answer: They are copied / replicated (DNA replication).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which plants use mitosis.
parts.answer: Any one: growth; repair; asexual reproduction (e.g. runners, tubers).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organ in which meiosis takes place in a human male and in a human female.
parts.answer: Male: testes. Female: ovaries.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which the cells produced by meiosis differ from the parent cell.
parts.answer: They are haploid (half the number of chromosomes); and they are genetically different (from the parent and each other).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare mitosis and meiosis. Give three differences.
parts.answer: mitosis gives 2 cells, meiosis 4; mitosis keeps the chromosome number (diploid), meiosis halves it (haploid); mitosis gives genetically identical cells, meiosis genetically different cells; mitosis for growth/repair, meiosis for gametes
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three paired differences

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where meiosis takes place in a flowering plant.
parts.answer: anthers (to make pollen) and ovules/ovary

practice.stem: A student looked at a squashed and stained onion root tip under a microscope. She counted 400 cells, of which 36 had chromosomes visible because they were dividing by mitosis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of cells that were dividing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student used cells from the tip of the root and not from higher up the root.
parts.answer: The tip is a region of growth where cells divide by mitosis; cells higher up have stopped dividing and are elongating/specialising.
parts.working: 1 mark: growth region at tip; 1 mark: cells further back no longer divide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted 400 cells and not just 20.
parts.answer: A larger sample gives a more reliable / representative value.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a stem cell.
parts.answer: An unspecialised cell that can divide by mitosis to produce cells that can become specialised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why stem cells in bone marrow must divide continuously throughout life.
parts.answer: Red blood cells (and white cells) live only a short time and are destroyed; new cells must be produced by mitosis to replace them.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood cells short-lived / constantly lost; 1 mark: replaced by mitosis of stem cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way the daughter cells of a stem cell compare genetically with the stem cell.
parts.answer: They are genetically identical (same chromosomes / same number of chromosomes).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A tumour forms when cells divide in an uncontrolled way. Name the type of cell division involved.
parts.answer: Mitosis

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a mutation in a gene that controls cell division can lead to a tumour.
parts.answer: The gene no longer stops (controls) mitosis; so cells keep dividing and form a mass of cells (tumour).
parts.working: 1 mark: loss of control of mitosis; 1 mark: repeated division forms a lump.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some cancer drugs stop chromosomes from being copied. Suggest why these drugs also cause hair loss.
parts.answer: Hair-producing cells divide by mitosis very often; the drug also stops these cells from dividing, so hair is not replaced.
parts.working: 1 mark: hair follicle cells divide rapidly; 1 mark: their division is also blocked.

practice.stem: Some cells used in medical research are grown in a flask. In good conditions each cell divides by mitosis every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Starting from one cell, calculate the number of cells after 3 hours, assuming no cells die.
parts.answer: 3 hours = 180 min = 9 divisions; 2⁹ = 512 cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why all the cells produced are genetically identical.
parts.answer: DNA (chromosomes) is copied exactly before division; each new cell gets an identical set of chromosomes
parts.working: B1 chromosomes replicated/copied exactly; B1 each daughter cell receives identical set

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation together lead to genetic variation among offspring of the same parents.
parts.answer: meiosis produces gametes with different combinations of alleles/chromosomes; each gamete is genetically different; fertilisation is random, so any sperm can fuse with any egg
parts.working: B1 meiosis gives genetically different gametes; B1 different combinations of chromosomes/alleles; B1 random fertilisation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a banana plant grown from a cutting is genetically identical to its parent.
parts.answer: it is produced by asexual reproduction, using mitosis only

practice.stem: The nucleus of a human body cell that is not dividing contains about 6.6 pg (picograms) of DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Predict the mass of DNA in the nucleus:
(i) after the DNA has been copied, just before mitosis
(ii) in each daughter cell after mitosis
(iii) in a sperm cell made by meiosis
parts.answer: (i) 13.2 pg (ii) 6.6 pg (iii) 3.3 pg
parts.working: 1 mark each: doubled = 13.2; halved back to 6.6 by mitosis; gamete has half the normal amount = 3.3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the value for the sperm cell.
parts.answer: Meiosis produces haploid cells with one set of chromosomes; so they contain half the DNA of a body cell.
parts.working: 1 mark: haploid / half the chromosomes; 1 mark: so half the DNA.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the mass of DNA in a zygote formed when this sperm fertilises an egg.
parts.answer: 6.6 pg
parts.working: 1 mark: sperm (half) + egg (half) restores the diploid amount.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Imagine that human gametes were made by mitosis instead of meiosis. Calculate the number of chromosomes in the body cells of the children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
parts.answer: children 92; grandchildren 184; great-grandchildren 368
parts.working: 1 mark each: each gamete would have 46, so each generation doubles: 92, 184, 368.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation together keep the chromosome number constant at 46 in each generation.
parts.answer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to 23 in each gamete (haploid); fertilisation joins two gametes, restoring 46 (diploid).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why each chromosome is copied before a cell divides by mitosis.
parts.answer: So that each daughter cell receives a full, identical set of chromosomes (same number and same genes as the parent).
parts.working: 1 mark: each daughter gets a complete set; 1 mark: identical to parent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to the two copies of each chromosome during mitosis.
parts.answer: The copies are separated and pulled to opposite ends (poles) of the cell; a new nucleus forms around each set.
parts.working: 1 mark: copies separate to opposite ends; 1 mark: two nuclei formed, each with one copy of every chromosome.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a cell that had copied only some of its chromosomes before division might produce daughter cells that cannot function.
parts.answer: One daughter cell would be missing some chromosomes/genes; so it could not make some essential proteins (enzymes).
parts.working: 1 mark: missing genes; 1 mark: cannot make necessary proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the molecule that carries a copy of a gene from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
parts.answer: mRNA (messenger RNA)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what determines the order of amino acids in a protein.
parts.answer: the sequence of bases in the gene (DNA)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why DNA does not leave the nucleus during protein synthesis.
parts.answer: DNA is too large to pass through the nuclear membrane / it is kept safe; a copy (mRNA) is made instead

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each of the following is found in the nucleus or in the cytoplasm of an animal cell:
(i) the gene for an enzyme
(ii) the place where the mRNA copy of the gene is made
(iii) the ribosomes where amino acids are joined
parts.answer: (i) nucleus (ii) nucleus (iii) cytoplasm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the small molecules that are joined together to make a protein.
parts.answer: Amino acids

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two examples of proteins made in the body.
parts.answer: Any two: enzymes (e.g. amylase); antibodies; haemoglobin; insulin (hormone); receptors; keratin; collagen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what decides which protein a cell makes from a particular gene.
parts.answer: The sequence (order) of bases in the gene.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the sentences using words from the list: amino acids, bases, gene, mRNA, ribosome.
A ………… is a length of DNA that codes for one protein. The order of the ………… in the DNA decides the order of ………… in the protein. A copy of the gene called ………… carries the code to a ………… .
parts.answer: gene; bases; amino acids; mRNA; ribosome

parts.label: a
