parts.text:
Where in a cell are proteins assembled from amino acids?
A nucleus
B ribosome
C cell membrane
D vacuole
parts.answer: B ribosome
parts.working: Ribosomes join amino acids in the order coded by mRNA. The nucleus holds the DNA and makes mRNA but does not assemble the protein, so A is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the information in a gene is used to make a protein.
parts.answer: the gene's base sequence is copied into mRNA in the nucleus; mRNA moves to the cytoplasm; to a ribosome; the ribosome reads the base sequence and joins amino acids in the correct order to make the protein
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of: mRNA made from gene in nucleus; mRNA moves out to cytoplasm; ribosome; base sequence read (three bases per amino acid); amino acids joined in specific order

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence of events in protein synthesis is correct?
A amino acids join at the ribosome → mRNA copy of the gene is made → mRNA moves to the nucleus
B mRNA copy of the gene is made in the nucleus → mRNA moves to a ribosome → amino acids are joined in the order set by the bases
C the gene leaves the nucleus → the ribosome copies the gene → amino acids are joined in the nucleus
D mRNA copy of the gene is made at the ribosome → mRNA moves into the nucleus → amino acids are joined
parts.answer: B mRNA copy of the gene is made in the nucleus → mRNA moves to a ribosome → amino acids are joined in the order set by the bases
parts.working: The gene stays in the nucleus and is copied into mRNA, which moves out to a ribosome in the cytoplasm, where amino acids are joined in the order coded by the mRNA bases. C wrongly has DNA leaving the nucleus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A short mRNA molecule codes for a polypeptide and has 45 bases in its coding sequence. Calculate the number of amino acids it codes for.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A protein contains 230 amino acids. Calculate the minimum number of bases in the gene that codes for it (counting one strand and ignoring the stop signal).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a sequence of three bases, rather than one base, is needed to code for each amino acid.
parts.answer: There are only 4 different bases but about 20 different amino acids; one base could code for only 4 amino acids, but three bases give 64 combinations, enough for all of them.
parts.working: 1 mark: 4 bases, 20 amino acids; 1 mark: triplets give enough combinations (4³ = 64).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mutation changes one amino acid in an enzyme. Explain how this could stop the enzyme from working.
parts.answer: The changed amino acid alters the way the chain folds, so the shape of the enzyme changes; the active site changes shape; the substrate no longer fits / is not complementary, so no enzyme–substrate complexes form.
parts.working: 1 mark each: protein shape changes; active site changes; substrate cannot fit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why some mutations in a gene have no effect on the protein.
parts.answer: The new base triplet may still code for the same amino acid / the change is in a part that does not affect the shape of the active site.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of a ribosome in protein synthesis.
parts.answer: The ribosome reads the base sequence of the mRNA (three bases at a time); and joins the amino acids together in the matching order to form a protein.
parts.working: 1 mark: uses/reads mRNA code; 1 mark: joins amino acids in the correct sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cells of the pancreas that make digestive enzymes contain very large numbers of ribosomes. Explain why.
parts.answer: Enzymes are proteins; the cells make (and secrete) large amounts of protein, so many ribosomes are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: enzymes are proteins; 1 mark: lots of protein synthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A gene contains 1 260 bases that code for a protein. Each amino acid is coded for by three bases. Calculate the number of amino acids in the protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One base in this gene is changed. Explain how this could stop the protein working.
parts.answer: the change alters the base sequence (gene mutation); so a different amino acid may be inserted; the protein folds into a different shape, e.g. an enzyme's active site changes
parts.working: B1 base sequence changed; B1 different amino acid sequence; B1 different shape/active site so protein does not function

parts.label: a
parts.text: All body cells of a person contain the same genes, but insulin is made only in certain cells of the pancreas. Explain this.
parts.answer: only some genes are expressed (switched on) in each cell type; the insulin gene is expressed only in those pancreas cells
parts.working: B1 genes switched on/off (expressed) differently; B1 insulin gene only expressed in pancreas cells

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why bacteria given a human insulin gene can make human insulin.
parts.answer: the base code is read in the same way in bacteria (universal code); the bacteria's ribosomes join amino acids in the order coded for by the gene, making the same protein
parts.working: B1 genetic code is the same/universal; B1 bacterial ribosomes make the same amino acid sequence

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the cell makes an mRNA copy of the gene rather than moving the DNA itself to the ribosomes.
parts.answer: DNA is too large to leave the nucleus / the DNA must stay in the nucleus to be protected and kept for future cell divisions; the small mRNA copy can pass out through the nuclear pores.
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA too large / must stay protected in nucleus; 1 mark: mRNA is small enough to leave the nucleus.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cells in the salivary glands make large amounts of amylase in a short time. Suggest two ways in which they can do this.
parts.answer: Many mRNA copies are made from the amylase gene; each mRNA is read by many ribosomes (cells have many ribosomes).
parts.working: 1 mark each: many mRNA copies; many ribosomes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mutation happens in the amylase gene of one skin cell. Suggest why this does not change the amylase in the person's saliva.
parts.answer: Skin cells do not use (express) the amylase gene, so no faulty amylase is made there; the mutation is only in that skin cell and the cells formed from it – the salivary gland cells still have the normal gene.
parts.working: 1 mark: gene not used/expressed in skin cells; 1 mark: mutation not present in salivary gland cells.

practice.stem:
The table gives the amino acid coded for by some mRNA base triplets. (In RNA the base uracil, U, is found in place of thymine.)
AUG: Met
UUU: Phe
GGC: Gly
AAA: Lys
GAA: Glu
UGA: stop

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use the table to write the sequence of amino acids coded for by this mRNA:
AUG UUU GGC AAA
parts.answer: Met – Phe – Gly – Lys
parts.working: 2 marks all correct in order; 1 mark with one error.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mutation changes one base in the fourth triplet. State which amino acid in the chain could be affected.
parts.answer: The fourth amino acid, Lys (lysine).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Another mutation changes the first base of the fourth triplet so that AAA becomes GAA. Use the table to give the new amino acid sequence.
parts.answer: Met – Phe – Gly – Glu

parts.label: d
parts.text: A different mutation changes the second triplet from UUU to UGA. Suggest the effect on the protein made.
parts.answer: UGA is a stop signal, so the chain stops after the first amino acid (Met); a very short protein is made that does not work.
parts.working: 1 mark: protein synthesis stops early; 1 mark: short / non-functional protein.

practice.stem: In a cell, a ribosome joins amino acids at a rate of 15 amino acids per second. A protein contains 450 amino acids.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the time, in seconds, for one ribosome to make one molecule of this protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Six ribosomes work along the same mRNA at the same time, each making its own protein molecule. Calculate the number of protein molecules made in 5 minutes.
parts.working: M1 one ribosome makes 300 ÷ 30 = 10 molecules; A1 × 6 = 60.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the minimum number of mRNA bases that code for this protein (ignore the stop signal).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by codominance.
parts.answer: both alleles in a heterozygote are expressed in the phenotype; neither is dominant
parts.working: B1 both alleles expressed; B1 in heterozygote

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the possible genotypes of a person with blood group A.
parts.answer: Iᴬ Iᴬ or Iᴬ i

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which genotype gives blood group O?
A IᴬIᴮ
B Iᴬi
C ii
D IᴮIᴮ
parts.answer: C ii
parts.working: Blood group O is the recessive phenotype, so it needs two i alleles. IᴬIᴮ (A) gives group AB because the alleles are codominant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The ABO blood group gene has three alleles: Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i. Describe the dominance relationships between these alleles.
parts.answer: Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant (both expressed together); both Iᴬ and Iᴮ are dominant to i.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person with genotype IᴬIᴮ has blood group AB.
parts.answer: Both alleles are expressed because they are codominant, so both A and B antigens are made.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the maximum number of these alleles that one person can have.
parts.answer: Two

practice.stem: In one breed of chicken, the allele for black feathers (Fᴮ) and the allele for white feathers (Fᵂ) are codominant. Chickens with both alleles have a speckled mixture of black and white feathers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A black cockerel (FᴮFᴮ) is mated with a white hen (FᵂFᵂ). State the genotype and phenotype of their chicks.
parts.answer: FᴮFᵂ; speckled (black and white feathers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the chicks are speckled and not black or white.
parts.answer: The alleles are codominant, so both are expressed: some feathers are black and some are white.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Give the blood group (phenotype) for each genotype.
(i) IᴬIᴮ
(ii) Iᴮi
(iii) ii
(iv) IᴬIᴬ
parts.answer: (i) AB (ii) B (iii) O (iv) A

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A man of blood group AB and a woman of blood group O have a child. Which blood groups are possible for the child?
A A or B only
B AB or O only
C A, B, AB or O
D O only
parts.answer: A A or B only
parts.working: Father Iᴬ Iᴮ × mother i i gives Iᴬ i (group A) or Iᴮ i (group B). AB needs both Iᴬ and Iᴮ but the mother gives only i, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A woman with blood group A (genotype Iᴬ i) and a man with blood group B (genotype Iᴮ i) have children. Use a genetic diagram to show all the possible blood groups of their children.
parts.answer: parents Iᴬ i × Iᴮ i; gametes Iᴬ, i and Iᴮ, i; offspring Iᴬ Iᴮ (AB), Iᴬ i (A), Iᴮ i (B), i i (O)
parts.working: B1 gametes; B1 offspring genotypes; B1 phenotypes; B1 all four groups identified

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first child has blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A woman of blood group A and a man of blood group B have a child of blood group O. Deduce the genotypes of the woman and the man. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: Woman Iᴬi; man Iᴮi. The child (ii) must have received an i allele from each parent; so each parent must carry i as well as their Iᴬ or Iᴮ allele.
parts.working: 1 mark: woman Iᴬi; 1 mark: man Iᴮi; 1 mark: child ii, so one i from each parent.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The couple's next child is blood group AB. State the genotype of this child and which allele came from each parent.
parts.answer: IᴬIᴮ; Iᴬ from the mother (group A) and Iᴮ from the father (group B).
parts.working: 1 mark: IᴬIᴮ; 1 mark: Iᴬ from mother and Iᴮ from father.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the possible genotypes and blood groups of the children of a man with genotype Iᴬi and a woman with genotype IᴮIᴮ.
parts.answer: Gametes: man Iᴬ or i; woman Iᴮ only. Children: IᴬIᴮ (group AB) and Iᴮi (group B) in a 1 : 1 ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: gametes; 1 mark: genotypes; 1 mark: phenotypes with ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the probability that a child of this couple has blood group AB.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why none of their children can have blood group O.
parts.answer: The woman has no i allele, so every child receives Iᴮ from her.

practice.stem:
The blood groups of 500 blood donors at a blood bank were recorded.
Group A: 125; group B: 165; group AB: 45; group O: 165

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the sample in each blood group.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Blood group is an example of discontinuous variation. Explain what this means.
parts.answer: There are a few distinct groups (categories) with no intermediates; each person fits exactly one group.
parts.working: 1 mark: distinct categories; 1 mark: no intermediates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be used to show these results.
parts.answer: Bar chart (or pie chart).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a person's ABO blood group does not change during their life, whereas their body mass can change.
parts.answer: Blood group is controlled by genes only (one gene) and is not affected by the environment; body mass is affected by the environment (diet, exercise) as well as genes.
parts.working: 1 mark: blood group genetic only / single gene; 1 mark: mass affected by environment.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Height is an example of continuous variation. State two ways in which it differs from blood group.
parts.answer: Height has a range of values with intermediates (no distinct groups); it is controlled by many genes and also affected by the environment.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a flower, the allele for red petals (Cᴿ) and the allele for white petals (Cᵂ) are codominant. Heterozygous plants have red-and-white streaked petals. Two streaked plants are crossed and 200 seeds are grown. Calculate the expected numbers of red, streaked and white plants.
parts.answer: Cᴿ Cᵂ × Cᴿ Cᵂ gives 1 : 2 : 1; red 50, streaked 100, white 50

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a gardener who wants only streaked plants cannot get them by crossing streaked plants, but can by crossing red with white.
parts.answer: streaked × streaked gives three phenotypes (homozygotes appear); red × white (Cᴿ Cᴿ × Cᵂ Cᵂ) gives all Cᴿ Cᵂ, all streaked
parts.working: B1 streaked × streaked gives red and white too; B1 red × white gives all heterozygous/streaked

practice.stem: Two babies were born in a hospital on the same night and their name tags were lost. Mr and Mrs Ahmed are both blood group O. Mrs Khan is blood group A and Mr Khan is blood group B. Baby X is blood group A and baby Y is blood group O.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain which baby belongs to the Ahmed family and which belongs to the Khan family.
parts.answer: Mr and Mrs Ahmed are both group O (ii), so all their children must be ii, group O; baby Y (group O) is theirs. Baby X (group A) cannot be the Ahmeds' child, so it is the Khans' baby; the Khans can have a group A child (Iᴬi) if Mrs Khan passes on Iᴬ and Mr Khan (Iᴮi) passes on i.
parts.working: 1 mark: Ahmeds both ii; 1 mark: can only have group O children so baby Y; 1 mark: baby X to Khans; 1 mark: Khans can produce Iᴬi if Mr Khan carries i.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the genotype that Mr Khan must have for baby X to be his child.
parts.answer: Iᴮi
parts.working: Baby X must receive i from the group B father and Iᴬ from the mother; 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why blood groups alone could not have solved the problem if both couples had been group AB.
parts.answer: AB × AB can produce children of groups A, B and AB; so both babies could belong to either couple.
parts.working: 1 mark: same possible groups for both couples; 1 mark: no way to tell them apart.

practice.stem: In cattle, the allele for red hair (Cᴿ) and the allele for white hair (Cᵂ) are codominant. Heterozygous cattle are roan. A roan bull was mated with many white cows. There were 58 calves: 31 roan and 27 white.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Draw a genetic diagram to show the expected genotypes and phenotypes of the calves, with their ratio.
parts.answer: Parents CᴿCᵂ (roan) × CᵂCᵂ (white); gametes Cᴿ and Cᵂ from the bull, Cᵂ only from the cows; calves CᴿCᵂ roan : CᵂCᵂ white = 1 : 1.
parts.working: 1 mark: parental genotypes; 1 mark: gametes; 1 mark: offspring genotypes, phenotypes and 1 : 1 ratio.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the expected number of roan calves out of 58.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The farmer says the roan bull must be pure-breeding. Use the results to explain why he is wrong.
parts.answer: Roan cattle are heterozygous (CᴿCᵂ), so they cannot be pure-breeding; the bull passed Cᵂ to the white calves and Cᴿ to the roan calves, so he produces two kinds of gamete.
parts.working: 1 mark: roan = heterozygous; 1 mark: bull gives both alleles (white and roan calves) so not homozygous.

practice.stem: A man with genotype IᴬIᴮ and a woman with genotype Iᴬi plan to have children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use a genetic diagram to find the probability that a child of this couple has blood group B.
parts.answer: Gametes: man Iᴬ or Iᴮ; woman Iᴬ or i. Children: IᴬIᴬ (A), Iᴬi (A), IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴮi (B). Probability of group B = 1/4.
parts.working: 1 mark: gametes; 1 mark: four genotypes with groups; 1 mark: 1/4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the probability that their first two children are both blood group B.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the ratio of blood groups A : AB : B expected among their children.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the food chain  algae → water flea → small fish → heron,  which organism is the secondary consumer?
A algae
B water flea
C small fish
D heron
parts.answer: C small fish
parts.working: The small fish eats the primary consumer (water flea), so it is the secondary consumer. The heron is the tertiary consumer, so D is wrong.

practice.stem:
A food web in a wheat field in Punjab:
wheat is eaten by grasshoppers, field mice and sparrows
grasshoppers are eaten by sparrows and frogs
field mice are eaten by snakes and owls
sparrows are eaten by owls
frogs are eaten by snakes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the producer in this food web.
parts.answer: wheat

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write out one food chain from the web that has four organisms.
parts.answer: e.g. wheat → grasshopper → frog → snake (or wheat → grasshopper → sparrow → owl)
parts.working: B1 correct chain with arrows pointing to the eater

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one organism that is both a primary and a secondary consumer.
parts.answer: sparrow

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the source of energy for the whole food web.
parts.answer: the Sun (light energy)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what is meant by:
(i) a producer
(ii) a consumer
parts.answer: (i) organism that makes its own organic nutrients, usually by photosynthesis; (ii) organism that gets energy by feeding on other organisms

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of decomposers in an ecosystem.
parts.answer: break down dead organisms and waste; release nutrients/minerals back into the soil (recycling)
parts.working: B1 break down dead material; B1 recycle nutrients

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In a grassland, grass is eaten by rabbits and grasshoppers. Grasshoppers are eaten by lizards and hawks. Lizards and rabbits are eaten by hawks. Which organism feeds at more than one trophic level?
A grass
B rabbit
C lizard
D hawk
parts.answer: D hawk
parts.working: Hawks eating rabbits or grasshoppers are secondary consumers (trophic level 3); hawks eating lizards are tertiary consumers (level 4). Lizards (C) only eat grasshoppers, so they feed at one level.

practice.stem: In the Thar desert, eagles eat desert snakes, desert snakes eat gerbils and gerbils eat grass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use all four organisms to write a food chain.
parts.answer: grass → gerbil → desert snake → eagle
parts.working: B1 correct order with arrows pointing towards the eater.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
From your food chain name:
(i) a herbivore
(ii) a carnivore
(iii) the producer
parts.answer: (i) gerbil (ii) desert snake or eagle (iii) grass

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the arrows in your food chain represent.
parts.answer: the transfer of energy (from one organism to the organism that eats it)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a trophic level.
parts.answer: the position of an organism in a food chain (or web)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State the trophic level of:
(i) a producer
(ii) a herbivore
parts.answer: (i) first (ii) second

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the group of organisms that feed on dead plants and animals in every food web, and give one example.
parts.answer: decomposers; e.g. fungi (mushrooms) or bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What do the arrows in a food chain show?
A the direction in which energy is transferred
B which organism is larger
C the direction in which oxygen moves
D which organism eats more food
parts.answer: A the direction in which energy is transferred
parts.working: Arrows point from the food to the feeder, showing energy transfer. They do not show size, so B is wrong.

practice.stem:
A food web in a wheat field in Punjab:
wheat is eaten by grasshoppers, field mice and sparrows
grasshoppers are eaten by sparrows and frogs
field mice are eaten by snakes and owls
sparrows are eaten by owls
frogs are eaten by snakes

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer sprays insecticide that kills most grasshoppers. Explain two possible effects on other organisms in the web.
parts.answer: frogs decrease (less food), so snakes may eat more mice, reducing mice; sparrows eat more wheat (or fewer sparrows), affecting owls; wheat may increase (less eaten by grasshoppers)
parts.working: 2 marks each for two effects with explanation (B1 effect, B1 reason): frogs fall due to less food; sparrows rely more on wheat/fall; snakes eat more mice; wheat increases

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why food webs give a more realistic picture of feeding than food chains.
parts.answer: most animals eat more than one type of food / are eaten by more than one predator

practice.stem: In the Arabian Sea off the coast of Karachi: phytoplankton are eaten by zooplankton; zooplankton are eaten by sardines and by jellyfish; sardines are eaten by tuna; jellyfish are eaten by turtles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a food web using all five organisms.
parts.answer: phytoplankton → zooplankton; zooplankton → sardine; zooplankton → jellyfish; sardine → tuna; jellyfish → turtle
parts.working: B1 producer at start; B1 all arrows from food to eater; B1 all five links correct

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the trophic level of the tuna.
parts.answer: tertiary consumer (fourth trophic level)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Plastic bags in the sea are mistaken by turtles for jellyfish. Suggest the effect on the jellyfish population if many turtles die.
parts.answer: jellyfish increase (fewer predators)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In the food chain rose bush → aphid → ladybird → sparrow, which organism is the tertiary consumer, and at which trophic level does it feed?
A ladybird, third trophic level
B sparrow, third trophic level
C sparrow, fourth trophic level
D ladybird, fourth trophic level
parts.answer: C sparrow, fourth trophic level
parts.working: The rose bush is level 1 (producer), aphid level 2 (primary consumer), ladybird level 3 (secondary consumer), sparrow level 4 (tertiary consumer). B confuses consumer number with trophic level.

practice.stem: In a lake near Hyderabad, phytoplankton are eaten by zooplankton and water snails. Zooplankton are eaten by small fish, which are eaten by herons. Water snails are eaten by ducks. Water hyacinth, a floating plant, has spread over most of the lake surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect of the water hyacinth on the phytoplankton.
parts.answer: Phytoplankton decrease; the floating hyacinth blocks light, so the phytoplankton cannot photosynthesise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this could affect the number of herons.
parts.answer: Fewer phytoplankton means less food for zooplankton/water snails, so they decrease; so fewer small fish; herons have less food so their numbers fall (or they move away).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three linked steps through the web.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the water-hyacinth leaves do not replace the phytoplankton as food for this web.
parts.answer: The animals in this web (zooplankton/small fish) do not eat water hyacinth / energy in hyacinth passes mainly to decomposers.

practice.stem: In a village pond in Sindh, small fish eat mosquito larvae and dragonfly nymphs. Dragonfly nymphs also eat mosquito larvae. All the fish are removed by netting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the number of mosquitoes might increase after the fish are removed.
parts.answer: fish eat mosquito larvae; fewer predators so more larvae survive to become adults
parts.working: B1 fish are predators of larvae; B1 more survive

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the dragonfly nymphs might first increase and then decrease.
parts.answer: at first more food (more mosquito larvae) and no competition from fish, so they increase; then the larger nymph population eats most of the larvae / food becomes scarce, so their numbers fall
parts.working: B1 more food (larvae) / less competition; B1 increase; B1 food runs out / competition rises so decrease

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why using fish to control mosquitoes may be better than spraying insecticide.
parts.answer: does not kill other (useful) insects / no chemical pollution or bioaccumulation / mosquitoes do not become resistant

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels.
parts.answer: energy is lost at each level (respiration, heat, movement, egestion, excretion, parts not eaten); only about 10 % passes on; too little energy remains to support another level
parts.working: B1 energy lost at each transfer; B1 named loss; B1 not enough energy for further level

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why eating plant food such as lentils feeds more people from the same area of land than eating meat.
parts.answer: shorter food chain; less energy lost, as energy is lost when crops are fed to animals
parts.working: B1 humans as primary consumers / shorter chain; B1 less energy lost between levels

practice.stem: In a hill forest, leopards eat wild boar and monkeys. Wild boar feed on fallen seeds, roots and young tree seedlings. Over several years leopards became rare in the area and the numbers of wild boar increased.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the numbers of wild boar increased after leopards became rare.
parts.answer: Leopards are predators of wild boar; with less predation, more boar survive and reproduce.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the number of young trees in the forest then fell.
parts.answer: More wild boar eat/dig up more seeds and seedlings; so fewer young trees grow.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use this example to explain why removing a top predator can affect organisms at every trophic level.
parts.answer: Top predator controls herbivore numbers; changes in herbivores change producer numbers, which affects all other organisms that depend on those producers (food and habitat).

practice.stem: Koalas in Australia eat only the leaves of eucalyptus trees. The red fox eats rabbits, birds, insects, fruit and food waste from towns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest which animal would be more at risk if its main food source disappeared. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: The koala; it depends on one food (eucalyptus) only, so it cannot switch; the fox has many food sources, so it can eat more of another.
parts.working: B1 koala; B1 single food; B1 fox can switch.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a food web gives a better picture of this than a single food chain.
parts.answer: A food web shows all the different things each animal eats and is eaten by.

practice.stem:
Energy in a grassland food chain (kJ per m² per year):
grass: 25 000
grasshoppers: 2 500
lizards: 200
hawks: 15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of energy transferred from the producers to the primary consumers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage transferred from the primary to the secondary consumers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways energy is lost between trophic levels.
parts.answer: respiration (heat); movement; egestion (faeces); excretion; parts not eaten (bones, roots)

practice.stem:
Dry biomass in a pond, in g per m²:
producers (algae and pondweed): 2400
herbivores (snails, water fleas): 300
carnivores (small fish): 40

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the producers' biomass that is present in the herbivores.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the same percentage for herbivores to carnivores, to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the shape of the pyramid of biomass for this pond.
parts.answer: upright pyramid – each level smaller than the one below

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the source of energy for almost all food chains.
parts.answer: the Sun (light energy)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the form in which energy is passed from a plant to an animal that eats it.
parts.answer: chemical energy (in organic compounds such as carbohydrates)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why energy is said to flow through an ecosystem, while carbon is recycled.
parts.answer: Energy enters as light and is finally lost as heat, which cannot be used again by organisms; carbon atoms are passed round and reused (by photosynthesis, respiration, decay).

practice.stem: The producers in a field fix 50 000 kJ per m² per year. Assume that 10 % of the energy at each trophic level passes to the next level.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Calculate the energy reaching:
(i) the primary consumers
(ii) the secondary consumers
(iii) the tertiary consumers
parts.answer: (i) 5000 kJ (ii) 500 kJ (iii) 50 kJ
parts.working: 1 mark each; 10 % of the level below each time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why there are very few large predators in an ecosystem.
parts.answer: Very little energy reaches the top of the food chain, so only a small number of predators can be supported.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
One large mango tree is eaten by 2000 caterpillars, which are eaten by 50 birds. Which describes the pyramids of numbers and biomass for this food chain?
A both pyramid-shaped
B pyramid of numbers has a narrow base (not pyramid-shaped), pyramid of biomass pyramid-shaped
C pyramid of numbers pyramid-shaped, pyramid of biomass has a narrow base
D neither pyramid-shaped
parts.answer: B pyramid of numbers has a narrow base (not pyramid-shaped), pyramid of biomass pyramid-shaped
parts.working: One tree supports many caterpillars, so the bottom bar of the number pyramid is narrowest, but the tree has the greatest biomass, so the biomass pyramid is pyramid-shaped. C has them the wrong way round.

practice.stem: A field of fodder crop receives 1 500 000 kJ of light energy per m² per year and fixes 15 000 kJ per m² per year in photosynthesis.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the light energy that is fixed by the crop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Goats eat all the energy fixed by the crop and convert 10 % of the energy they receive into new body tissue. Calculate the energy in the new goat tissue, in kJ per m² per year.
parts.answer: 15 000 × 0.1 = 1 500 kJ per m² per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why most of the light energy is not fixed by the crop.
parts.answer: light misses leaves / reflected; wrong wavelength; transmitted through leaves; used to evaporate water; photosynthesis limited by CO₂/temperature

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of biomass is usually a better way to show a food chain than a pyramid of numbers.
parts.answer: pyramid of numbers ignores size, e.g. one tree with many insects gives an odd shape; biomass takes the mass of organisms into account so is nearly always pyramid-shaped
parts.working: B1 numbers ignores size of organisms; B1 biomass accounts for mass/always upright

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of measuring biomass to construct a pyramid of biomass.
parts.answer: organisms must be killed and dried to find their dry mass (or biomass changes with the season / hard to sample all organisms)
parts.working: B1 any one: organisms killed/destructive; dry mass takes time; varies with season/time of year; difficult to collect all organisms (e.g. roots, soil organisms)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which energy change takes place when a plant photosynthesises?
A light energy → chemical energy
B chemical energy → light energy
C heat energy → chemical energy
D chemical energy → heat energy
parts.answer: A light energy → chemical energy
parts.working: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and it is stored as chemical energy in glucose. D happens in respiration, not photosynthesis.

practice.stem: Goats on a farm convert 5 % of the energy in the fodder they eat into meat that people eat. Each kilogram of goat meat contains about 7500 kJ of energy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy in the fodder that must be eaten by the goats to produce 1 kg of meat, in kJ.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State three ways in which energy from the fodder does not end up in the goat meat.
parts.answer: any three of: heat lost in respiration; energy used for movement; energy in faeces (undigested food); energy in urine; parts of the goat not eaten (bones, skin)

practice.stem: Of every 1000 kJ of light energy falling on a maize leaf: 200 kJ is reflected, 400 kJ passes through the leaf or is not absorbed by chlorophyll, 380 kJ is lost as heat and in evaporating water, and the rest is stored in glucose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy stored in glucose and express it as a percentage of the light falling on the leaf.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one reason why some light passes through the leaf without being used.
parts.answer: It does not hit a chloroplast / the leaf is thin / wrong wavelength is not absorbed by chlorophyll.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the efficiency of energy transfer from the Sun to producers affects every other trophic level.
parts.answer: All the energy available to consumers comes from what the producers fix.

practice.stem: In a lake, producers fix 36 000 kJ per m² per year. Transfer efficiency is 8 % from producers to primary consumers, and 10 % at each later transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy reaching the tertiary consumers, in kJ per m² per year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the transfer from producers to herbivores (8 %) is less efficient than the transfers between animals (10 %).
parts.answer: plant material contains much cellulose/lignin that herbivores cannot digest; so a larger proportion of the food is lost in faeces (egested); animal food is more digestible
parts.working: B1 cellulose/plant material hard to digest; B1 more energy lost in faeces/egestion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a pyramid of energy is always upright.
parts.answer: energy is lost at every transfer between trophic levels (e.g. as heat from respiration); so each level always has less energy than the one below
parts.working: B1 energy lost at each level; B1 so less available at each higher level

parts.label: b
parts.text: Fish farms in Thailand feed farmed fish with pellets made from wild-caught smaller fish. Use ideas about energy flow to explain why this may not be sustainable.
parts.answer: much energy is lost when small fish are fed to farmed fish; more mass of wild fish is caught than farmed fish produced; wild stocks may be overfished
parts.working: B1 energy losses mean more wild fish needed than produced; B1 overfishing of wild stocks

practice.stem:
Energy budget for a young cow over one week (kJ):
energy in grass eaten: 100 000
energy in faeces: 40 000
energy in urine: 4000
energy released in respiration: 52 000
The rest is used for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the energy used to build new body tissue (growth), in kJ, and express it as a percentage of the energy eaten.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why so much energy is lost in the faeces of a cow.
parts.answer: Grass contains a lot of cellulose; much of it is not digested/absorbed and passes out in the faeces.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why only the energy in growth is available to the next trophic level.
parts.answer: Energy lost as heat in respiration, faeces and urine is not part of the cow's body, so it cannot be eaten by a consumer.

practice.stem: On two farms, animals were given food containing 10 000 kJ of energy. Chickens converted 4 % of the energy into body mass. Tilapia fish in ponds converted 12 % of the energy into body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more energy ends up in the tilapia than in the chickens from the same feed.
parts.answer: 3 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why chickens convert less of their food energy into body mass than fish do.
parts.answer: Chickens keep a constant high body temperature, so more energy is released as heat in respiration; chickens use more energy in moving/supporting their bodies on land (fish are supported by water).

practice.stem:
Neem tree → leaf-eating insects → birds → lice living on the birds
numbers counted: 1 tree, 6000 insects, 20 birds, 600 lice

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the pyramid of numbers for this food chain.
parts.answer: Very narrow base (one tree); very wide second bar (insects); narrow third bar (birds); wider top bar (lice).
parts.working: B1 narrow producer bar with wide insect bar; B1 bird bar narrow and lice bar wider than birds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the pyramid of biomass for the same food chain is a normal (upright) pyramid.
parts.answer: The single tree has a huge mass, far more than all the insects; the mass at each level is less than at the level below (lice are tiny so their total mass is less than the birds').

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one reason why a pyramid of numbers can be misleading.
parts.answer: It does not take into account the size/mass of the organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which factor would NOT normally limit the growth of a population of rabbits?
A food supply
B predation by foxes
C disease
D a high birth rate
parts.answer: D a high birth rate
parts.working: A high birth rate increases the population; food shortage, predators and disease limit it. A (food) is a limiting factor.

practice.stem:
Students counted clover plants in ten 0.5 m × 0.5 m (0.25 m²) quadrats placed randomly in a school field 50 m × 20 m.
Counts: 3, 5, 0, 7, 4, 6, 2, 5, 8, 4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of plants per quadrat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of plants per m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of plants in the field.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State how the students made sure the quadrats were placed randomly.
parts.answer: used random number tables/generator to choose coordinates on a grid (not chosen by eye)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what is meant by:
(i) a population
(ii) a community
(iii) an ecosystem
parts.answer: (i) a group of organisms of one species living in the same area at the same time; (ii) all the populations of different species in an area; (iii) a community and its physical environment interacting together

parts.label: b
parts.text: A pond contains water lilies, frogs, dragonflies and water. Name one population in the pond.
parts.answer: e.g. all the frogs (of one species) / all the water lilies

practice.stem: Desert locusts lay eggs in moist sandy soil. After a season of unusually heavy rain in southern Sindh, the desert vegetation grew strongly and the locust population increased very rapidly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the locust population increased so quickly after heavy rain.
parts.answer: More plants grow, so more food; moist soil helps eggs hatch/survive; few predators or diseases to limit numbers at first.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two factors that eventually stop the locust population from growing.
parts.answer: any two of: food shortage, competition, predation, disease

practice.stem: A student used ten 1 m² quadrats to estimate the number of daisy plants on a school cricket ground measuring 120 m by 100 m. The counts were: 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 1, 4, 5, 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two sources of error in this method that could make the estimate of 42 000 too high or too low.
parts.answer: Quadrats not placed truly at random, so they may land in patches of daisies; daisies on the quadrat edge counted inconsistently; small or hidden plants missed; the ground is not uniform, so 10 quadrats may not represent it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of daisy plants per quadrat.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Estimate the total number of daisy plants on the ground.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the phases of the sigmoid growth curve of a population of yeast in a flask of sugar solution.
parts.answer: lag phase: slow growth as yeast adapt; exponential (log) phase: rapid growth, plenty of food, no limits; stationary phase: birth rate = death rate as food runs out / waste builds up; (death phase: numbers fall)
parts.working: B1 lag; B1 exponential with reason; B1 stationary with reason

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the yeast population eventually falls.
parts.answer: sugar used up; ethanol (toxic waste) builds up; lack of oxygen

practice.stem:
Snail counts in eight 1 m² quadrats placed randomly in a garden:
12, 15, 9, 0, 18, 11, 6, 13

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of snails per quadrat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the total population of snails in the 400 m² garden if each quadrat is 1 m².

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the result of quadrat 4 (0 snails) should not be removed.
parts.answer: it is a real result from random sampling / snails may be absent from some areas

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the estimate could be made more reliable.
parts.answer: use more quadrats / sample on several days

practice.stem:
Number of bacteria in a sample of milk kept at 30 °C:
time / hours | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14
millions of bacteria per cm³ | 1 | 1.2 | 4 | 16 | 50 | 80 | 84 | 84

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the phase of growth from 0 to 2 hours and suggest why numbers increase slowly.
parts.answer: lag phase; bacteria are adjusting to the milk / making enzymes before dividing

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase between 4 and 8 hours, in millions of bacteria per cm³ per hour.
parts.answer: 11.5 million per cm³ per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the number stops increasing after 12 hours.
parts.answer: Nutrients (lactose) are running out and waste products such as lactic acid build up (pH falls); so the death rate rises to equal the birth rate.

practice.stem:
A student placed 0.5 m × 0.5 m quadrats at random in two areas of a park and counted the dandelion plants.
open sunny area: 4, 7, 5, 6, 8, 3, 7, 8, 5, 7
shaded area under trees: 1, 0, 2, 1, 3, 0, 1, 2, 0, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean number of dandelions per quadrat in each area.
parts.answer: open: 6.0; shaded: 1.2

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each quadrat has an area of 0.25 m². Calculate the mean number of dandelions per m² in each area.
parts.answer: open: 24 per m²; shaded: 4.8 per m²

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason for the difference between the two areas.
parts.answer: Less light under the trees, so less photosynthesis/growth (also competition with tree roots for water).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why ten quadrats were used in each area rather than one.
parts.answer: To get a more reliable/representative mean, as dandelions are unevenly spread.

practice.stem:
Approximate census results for the population of Pakistan:
year | population / millions
1998 | 132.4
2017 | 207.7
2023 | 241.5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in population from 2017 to 2023. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in population per year between 2017 and 2023, in millions, to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 5.6 million per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the population has grown so quickly.
parts.answer: Death rate has fallen (better healthcare, vaccination, clean water) while birth rate stays high; more people survive to have children.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the shape of the human population curve over the last 200 years.
parts.answer: rapid (exponential) increase; death rate fell due to better medicine, vaccination, sanitation, food supply; birth rate stayed higher than death rate
parts.working: B1 rapid/exponential increase; B1 lower death rate with named reason; B1 birth rate > death rate

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two factors that could limit the future growth of a human population in a country.
parts.answer: food/water shortage; disease; family planning/contraception; space/housing; war

practice.stem:
In a greenhouse of tomato plants in Murree, aphid and ladybird numbers were counted weekly.
week | aphids | ladybirds
0 | 20 | 2
2 | 60 | 3
4 | 400 | 5
6 | 1200 | 15
8 | 500 | 40
10 | 150 | 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe and explain the change in aphid numbers from week 2 to week 6.
parts.answer: aphids increased rapidly because food (plants) was plentiful and there were few predators; exponential growth

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes in aphid and ladybird numbers after week 6.
parts.answer: ladybirds increased (more food) and ate more aphids, so aphids decreased; also limited by food
parts.working: B1 ladybird numbers rise; B1 predation reduces aphids

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the ladybird peak comes after the aphid peak.
parts.answer: ladybirds need time to reproduce after food becomes plentiful

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A population of bacteria in a flask has reached the stationary phase of its growth curve. Which statement describes this phase?
A The birth rate equals the death rate.
B The birth rate is much higher than the death rate.
C No new bacteria are being produced.
D All the bacteria have died.
parts.answer: A The birth rate equals the death rate.
parts.working: In the stationary phase, numbers stay constant because new cells are produced as fast as others die. C is wrong because reproduction still happens; it is balanced by deaths.

practice.stem:
Two species of single-celled organism, A and B, both feed on the same bacteria. Each was grown alone in a tube with a fixed supply of bacteria, then both were grown together.
day | A alone | B alone | A together | B together
0 | 10 | 10 | 10 | 10
4 | 120 | 80 | 90 | 50
8 | 400 | 220 | 300 | 40
12 | 420 | 230 | 380 | 10
16 | 420 | 230 | 390 | 0
(numbers per cm³)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the growth of each species when grown alone.
parts.answer: Both show an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve: slow start, rapid increase, then levelling off at a steady number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the results when the two species were grown together.
parts.answer: Both species compete for the same food (bacteria); species A obtains food more successfully/reproduces faster; species B does not get enough food, so its death rate exceeds its birth rate and it dies out.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why species A reached a lower number when grown with species B than when grown alone.
parts.answer: Some of the food was used by species B (competition), so less was available for A.

practice.stem: In the 1950s a virus that causes a disease of rabbits was released in Australia to control the very large rabbit population. In the first two years more than 90 % of the rabbits died. Over the following decades the rabbit population slowly increased again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rabbit population fell so sharply in the first two years.
parts.answer: The virus is a pathogen that spread quickly through the dense rabbit population; disease greatly increased the death rate (above the birth rate).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the rabbit population later began to increase again.
parts.answer: A few rabbits had natural resistance and survived; they bred and passed on the resistance; so a larger proportion of later rabbits survived the disease (natural selection).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one factor, other than disease, that could limit the size of the rabbit population.
parts.answer: food supply / predation / competition / space for burrows

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
A combustion
B decomposition
C photosynthesis
D respiration
parts.answer: C photosynthesis
parts.working: Photosynthesis takes in CO₂. Respiration releases it, so D is the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the process by which carbon dioxide is returned to the air by:
(i) animals
(ii) burning coal
parts.answer: (i) respiration; (ii) combustion

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the form in which carbon is found in plants.
parts.answer: carbohydrates / organic compounds (e.g. starch, cellulose, glucose)

parts.label: c
parts.text: State how carbon passes from plants to animals.
parts.answer: feeding (animals eat plants)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the process that:
(i) turns carbon dioxide into glucose in a leaf
(ii) releases carbon dioxide when petrol is burned in a car engine
(iii) releases carbon dioxide when fungi break down dead leaves
(iv) moves carbon from a plant into a goat
parts.answer: (i) photosynthesis (ii) combustion (iii) respiration (by decomposers) / decomposition (iv) feeding / eating (and digestion)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which carbon atoms in grass eaten by a cow can return to the atmosphere.
parts.answer: The cow respires, breathing out carbon dioxide; the cow's dung (or its dead body) is decomposed by bacteria/fungi that respire and release carbon dioxide.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the carbon compound in the air that plants take in.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name two carbon-containing compounds in a plant.
parts.answer: any two of: glucose, starch, cellulose, sucrose, protein, fats/oils

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why carbon dioxide is called a greenhouse gas.
parts.answer: It traps heat (infrared radiation) in the atmosphere.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how an increase in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere can lead to global warming.
parts.answer: More CO₂ absorbs/traps more of the heat radiated from the Earth's surface; less heat escapes to space so the mean temperature rises (enhanced greenhouse effect).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one human activity, other than burning fuels, that increases carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: deforestation (cutting down/burning forests)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle.
parts.answer: they feed on dead organisms and waste; respire, releasing CO₂ into the air
parts.working: B1 break down dead material; B1 respiration releases CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how fossil fuels were formed.
parts.answer: dead organisms did not decay fully (no oxygen/waterlogged); compressed over millions of years into coal/oil/gas
parts.working: B1 incomplete decay; B1 pressure/millions of years

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which two processes both release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere?
A respiration and combustion
B photosynthesis and respiration
C photosynthesis and decomposition
D combustion and photosynthesis
parts.answer: A respiration and combustion
parts.working: Respiration (including by decomposers) and burning both release CO₂. Photosynthesis removes CO₂, so B, C and D are wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why dead plant material builds up in a waterlogged peat bog instead of decaying.
parts.answer: Waterlogged soil has very little oxygen; decomposers cannot respire aerobically/are inactive, so decay is very slow (also acidic conditions).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how draining a peat bog for farming affects the carbon dioxide concentration in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Air (oxygen) enters the peat; decomposers become active and respire, releasing the stored carbon as carbon dioxide, so atmospheric CO₂ increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of fuel that forms if peat is buried and compressed for millions of years.
parts.answer: coal (a fossil fuel)

practice.stem: A car releases 120 g of carbon dioxide for every kilometre it travels. It is driven 15 000 km in one year.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in kg, released by the car in one year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume one tree absorbs 20 kg of carbon dioxide a year. Calculate the number of trees needed to absorb the car's yearly emissions.
parts.answer: 90 trees

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why planting trees removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
parts.answer: Trees photosynthesise, taking in CO₂; the carbon is stored in wood (cellulose) and other compounds as the tree grows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why burning coal increases the carbon dioxide in the atmosphere over a long period.
parts.answer: The carbon in coal was locked away underground for millions of years; burning it adds 'new' carbon to the atmosphere faster than photosynthesis can remove it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why burning wood from a forest that is replanted adds much less carbon dioxide to the atmosphere overall.
parts.answer: The new trees take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis as they grow; this balances the carbon released when the wood was burned.

practice.stem:
Mean CO₂ concentration at a monitoring station (parts per million):
2000: 370
2010: 390
2020: 414
Within each year the concentration is about 6 ppm higher in late spring (May) than in early autumn (September).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the CO₂ concentration rises through autumn and winter and falls through summer each year.
parts.answer: in summer more photosynthesis (more leaves, more light), removing more CO₂ than released; in winter less photosynthesis but respiration/combustion continues
parts.working: B1 photosynthesis greater in summer; B1 respiration/combustion continue in winter

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean yearly increase in CO₂ from 2000 to 2020.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two human activities that cause the long-term increase.
parts.answer: burning fossil fuels; deforestation (less photosynthesis, burning trees)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how cutting down and burning forest affects the amount of CO₂ in the atmosphere.
parts.answer: burning (combustion) releases CO₂; fewer trees so less photosynthesis removes CO₂; decomposition of remaining wood releases more CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: A company plants trees to 'offset' its emissions. Suggest one limitation of this.
parts.answer: trees take many years to grow / may be cut down or burned later / cannot absorb as much as is emitted

practice.stem:
The carbon dioxide concentration in a closed greenhouse of tomato plants in Islamabad was measured on a sunny day.
time | 00:00 | 06:00 | 12:00 | 18:00
CO₂ / ppm | 480 | 520 | 280 | 310

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of decrease in carbon dioxide concentration between 06:00 and 12:00, in ppm per hour.
parts.answer: 40 ppm per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the concentration rose between 18:00 and 06:00.
parts.answer: No light so no photosynthesis; plants (and soil organisms) still respire, releasing CO₂.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the concentration fell between 06:00 and 12:00.
parts.answer: Light intensity increases; the rate of photosynthesis becomes greater than the rate of respiration, so CO₂ is taken in faster than it is released.

practice.stem: After harvesting rice, some farmers in Punjab burn the leftover straw in their fields before sowing wheat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare what happens to the carbon in rice straw if it is burned in the field with what happens if it is ploughed into the soil.
parts.answer: Burning (combustion) releases almost all the carbon as CO₂ immediately; ploughing in lets decomposers break it down slowly by respiration; some carbon stays in the soil as humus/organic matter for longer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two other disadvantages of burning crop residues.
parts.answer: smoke/smog harms people's lungs; kills soil organisms such as earthworms and decomposers; loses minerals (e.g. nitrogen) that would return to the soil; adds soot/particles to air

practice.stem: A sealed glass bottle contains soil, small plants, woodlice and soil microorganisms. It is kept on a sunny windowsill and has not been opened for ten years, yet the plants and woodlice are still alive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how carbon is recycled inside the sealed bottle, so the plants can keep photosynthesising.
parts.answer: Plants take in CO₂ for photosynthesis and make glucose/organic compounds; woodlice eat plant material and respire, releasing CO₂; dead leaves and woodlice droppings are decomposed by bacteria/fungi, which respire and release CO₂; plants and soil organisms also respire; the released CO₂ is used again in photosynthesis.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four linked points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the garden would not survive if it were kept in a dark cupboard.
parts.answer: No light so no photosynthesis; plants would die and oxygen/food for the other organisms would run out (CO₂ would build up).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why plants need nitrate ions.
parts.answer: to make amino acids/proteins

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the structures on the roots of pea and bean plants that contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
parts.answer: root nodules

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way, other than by bacteria, that atmospheric nitrogen is fixed.
parts.answer: lightning (or the Haber process/making fertilisers)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which process changes nitrogen gas from the air into nitrogen compounds that plants can use?
A nitrogen fixation
B denitrification
C nitrification
D deamination
parts.answer: A nitrogen fixation
parts.working: Nitrogen fixation (by bacteria or lightning) turns N₂ into ammonium/nitrogen compounds. Denitrification (B) does the opposite, returning N₂ to the air.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of bacteria that:
(i) convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds
(ii) convert ammonium ions into nitrate ions
(iii) convert nitrate ions into nitrogen gas
(iv) break down proteins in dead leaves, releasing ammonium ions
parts.answer: (i) nitrogen-fixing bacteria (ii) nitrifying bacteria (iii) denitrifying bacteria (iv) decomposers (bacteria of decay)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how a goat obtains the nitrogen it needs.
parts.answer: by eating plants (proteins/amino acids in grass)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the goat uses nitrogen compounds for.
parts.answer: to make proteins (for growth and repair, enzymes)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how nitrogen leaves the goat's body while it is alive.
parts.answer: Excess amino acids are broken down (deaminated) in the liver to form urea; urea is excreted in urine.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The statements describe how nitrogen in a dead leaf becomes part of a protein in a new plant. Write the letters in the correct order, starting with D.
A Nitrifying bacteria change ammonium ions into nitrate ions.
B The plant uses the nitrogen to make amino acids and then proteins.
C Decomposers break down the protein in the dead leaf, releasing ammonium ions.
D A leaf containing protein falls to the ground.
E Root hair cells absorb nitrate ions.
parts.answer: D → C → A → E → B
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for one pair swapped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of organisms, other than bacteria, that act as decomposers.
parts.answer: fungi

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which type of bacteria converts ammonium ions into nitrate ions?
A decomposers
B denitrifying bacteria
C nitrifying bacteria
D nitrogen-fixing bacteria
parts.answer: C nitrifying bacteria
parts.working: Nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate. Denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate back into nitrogen gas, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plants are surrounded by air that is 78 % nitrogen, yet many crops are short of nitrogen. Explain why.
parts.answer: Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly; they need it as nitrate (or ammonium) ions from the soil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the ion in which plants usually absorb nitrogen and the structure that absorbs it.
parts.answer: nitrate ions; root hair cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: The concentration of nitrate inside root hair cells is often higher than in the soil water. Name the process used to absorb the nitrate and explain why the cells need oxygen to do this.
parts.answer: active transport; it needs energy from aerobic respiration (which uses oxygen)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in the protein of a chicken meal eaten by a person can end up as nitrate ions in soil.
parts.answer: Protein digested to amino acids, absorbed; excess amino acids deaminated in liver to urea; urea excreted in urine and goes to sewage/soil; decomposers convert urea to ammonium ions; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four steps in a correct order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two ways, other than by bacteria, in which nitrogen gas is converted into compounds that plants can use.
parts.answer: lightning; the Haber process (to make fertilisers)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why lightning helps to put nitrogen compounds into the soil.
parts.answer: The high energy of lightning makes nitrogen react with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides; these dissolve in rain and fall into the soil as nitrates.

practice.stem: In some Asian countries a small water fern called Azolla is grown in flooded rice fields. Azolla contains cyanobacteria that can fix nitrogen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing Azolla and then letting it die in the field increases the nitrate available to the rice.
parts.answer: The cyanobacteria fix nitrogen gas into nitrogen compounds used to make Azolla protein; when the Azolla dies, decomposers convert the protein to ammonium; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage to the farmer of using Azolla rather than buying nitrate fertiliser.
parts.answer: cheaper / adds organic matter / nitrate released slowly so less is leached

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why farmers in waterlogged rice paddies may lose nitrate from the soil.
parts.answer: waterlogged soil lacks oxygen; denitrifying bacteria (anaerobic) convert nitrate to nitrogen gas
parts.working: B1 anaerobic/no oxygen; B1 denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to nitrogen

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why ploughing to aerate soil helps to keep nitrate levels high.
parts.answer: nitrifying bacteria need oxygen to convert ammonium to nitrate; denitrifying bacteria less active in aerobic soil
parts.working: B1 nitrifying bacteria aerobic/need oxygen; B1 less denitrification

practice.stem:
Wheat was grown in plots given different amounts of nitrate fertiliser.
fertiliser / kg per hectare | 0 | 50 | 100 | 150 | 200
yield / tonnes per hectare | 2.5 | 3.8 | 4.6 | 4.9 | 4.9

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield when 100 kg per hectare was added compared with no fertiliser.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why adding more than 150 kg per hectare gave no further increase in yield.
parts.answer: Nitrate is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as water, light, other minerals or the plant's maximum growth rate limits yield.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why adding 200 kg per hectare could harm the environment.
parts.answer: Nitrate not taken up by the crop is leached by rain into rivers/lakes; causing eutrophication (algal growth, decay, oxygen loss, fish deaths).

practice.stem:
Equal samples of soil containing nitrifying bacteria were kept at different temperatures for one week and the nitrate produced was measured.
temperature / °C | 5 | 15 | 25 | 35 | 45
nitrate produced / mg per kg soil | 2 | 8 | 15 | 18 | 6

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on nitrate production.
parts.answer: Nitrate production rises from 5 °C to a peak at 35 °C, then falls sharply at 45 °C.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more nitrate was produced at 25 °C than at 5 °C.
parts.answer: 7.5 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the results in terms of the bacteria's enzymes.
parts.answer: As temperature rises, enzymes and substrate have more kinetic energy so collide more often; rate increases up to the optimum; above it the enzymes denature, so nitrification slows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why clover can grow well in soil that contains very little nitrate, while grass in the same soil grows poorly.
parts.answer: Clover has root nodules containing nitrogen-fixing bacteria; these convert nitrogen gas from soil air into ammonium/amino acids that the clover uses to make protein; grass has no nodules so depends on soil nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the bacteria in the nodules benefit from living there.
parts.answer: They get sugars/carbohydrates (energy source) from the plant and a protected place to live.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why grass growing next to clover in a lawn often grows better after the clover dies.
parts.answer: Dead clover is decomposed, releasing ammonium; nitrifying bacteria convert this to nitrate, which the grass absorbs.

practice.stem:
A new fish tank was set up with a filter containing gravel. Fish were added on day 0. The concentrations of three nitrogen compounds in the water were measured.
day | 0 | 7 | 14 | 21 | 28
ammonia / mg per dm³ | 0 | 4.0 | 1.5 | 0.2 | 0.1
nitrite / mg per dm³ | 0 | 0.5 | 3.5 | 1.0 | 0.2
nitrate / mg per dm³ | 0 | 0 | 5 | 20 | 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ammonia concentration rises first.
parts.answer: Fish excrete ammonia, and there are not yet enough nitrifying bacteria to convert it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the ammonia concentration then falls as the nitrite concentration rises.
parts.answer: Nitrifying bacteria multiply in the filter; they convert ammonia (ammonium) into nitrite.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the changes in nitrite and nitrate from day 14 to day 28.
parts.answer: A second group of nitrifying bacteria increases and converts nitrite into nitrate; so nitrite falls and nitrate rises.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the nitrate concentration can be kept low in the tank.
parts.answer: Grow water plants that absorb nitrate / change some of the water regularly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how nitrogen in the air can become part of the protein in a pea plant.
parts.answer: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules of the pea; convert nitrogen gas to ammonium/nitrogen compounds; plant receives these and makes amino acids; amino acids joined to form protein; OR free-living fixing bacteria/lightning add compounds to soil; nitrifying bacteria make nitrate; nitrate absorbed by root hairs (active transport); used to make amino acids/protein.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five correct points in a logical sequence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sheep eats the pea plant. Describe what happens to the nitrogen-containing compounds inside the sheep.
parts.answer: Proteins digested by proteases into amino acids; amino acids absorbed into blood (in small intestine/villi); used to build the sheep's own proteins (growth, enzymes); excess amino acids deaminated in liver; nitrogen part forms urea; urea removed by kidneys in urine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of decomposers in returning nitrogen to the soil.
parts.answer: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) feed on dead organisms, faeces and urine; they break down proteins and urea; releasing ammonium ions into the soil; which nitrifying bacteria then convert to nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the soil of a natural forest stays fertile for centuries without fertiliser, while a field of wheat that is harvested every year needs fertiliser.
parts.answer: In a forest, leaves, dead plants and animals fall to the ground; decomposers return their nitrogen to the soil; so the nitrogen is recycled in the same place; in a wheat field, the grain (and straw) are removed at harvest; the nitrogen in their protein is taken away and not returned; so nitrate in soil falls each year and must be replaced by fertiliser (or legumes/manure).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the roles of nitrifying, denitrifying and nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and state whether each needs aerobic or anaerobic conditions.
parts.answer: Nitrifying: convert ammonium to nitrite and then nitrate; need oxygen (aerobic). Denitrifying: convert nitrate to nitrogen gas; work in anaerobic (waterlogged) soil. Nitrogen-fixing: convert nitrogen gas to ammonium compounds; in root nodules or free in the soil (accept aerobic soil air / nodules).
parts.working: For each type: B1 role, B1 conditions (allow nitrogen-fixing condition mark for 'need nitrogen gas from soil air').

parts.label: b
parts.text: A dead fish sinks to the bottom of a river. Describe how nitrogen in its protein could become part of the protein in algae.
parts.answer: Decomposers break down the fish protein; releasing ammonium; nitrifying bacteria convert it to nitrate; algae absorb nitrate and use it to make amino acids/protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Daal (lentils) is a good source of protein. Describe what happens to this protein from when it is eaten until it becomes part of a muscle cell.
parts.answer: Protein digested by protease (pepsin in stomach, trypsin from pancreas) into amino acids; amino acids absorbed into blood capillaries in the villi of the small intestine; carried by the hepatic portal vein to the liver and then in the blood to muscles; muscle cells take up amino acids; ribosomes join amino acids to form muscle protein (assimilation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what happens to amino acids that are not needed, and how their nitrogen is eventually returned to the soil.
parts.answer: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver; nitrogen-containing part converted to urea; urea removed from blood by kidneys and excreted in urine; urine reaches soil/sewage, where decomposers convert urea to ammonium; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in protein of a dead buffalo can become part of a protein in a grass plant.
parts.answer: decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down protein in dead body; releasing ammonia/ammonium ions; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrite; then to nitrate; nitrate absorbed by root hairs (active transport); used to make amino acids, then proteins
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to five of: decomposers; ammonium/ammonia; nitrifying bacteria; nitrite → nitrate; absorption by roots/active transport; amino acids → protein in plant

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the nitrogen in cow manure spread on a field becomes available to crop plants.
parts.answer: Manure contains proteins and urea; decomposers break these down; releasing ammonium ions; nitrifying bacteria oxidise ammonium to nitrite then nitrate; nitrate is absorbed by root hairs; this needs aerobic (well-aerated) soil.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of using manure with using an artificial nitrate fertiliser.
parts.answer: Manure: cheap/available on farm, adds organic matter (humus) improving soil structure and water holding, releases nitrogen slowly so less leaching; but bulky, uneven/unknown mineral content, may smell or carry pathogens, acts slowly. Artificial: known composition, acts quickly, easy to apply; but expensive, easily leached causing eutrophication, adds no organic matter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five; max 3 for one fertiliser only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in urea in cattle urine is returned to grass plants.
parts.answer: Urea broken down by decomposers/bacteria; to ammonium ions; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate; grass roots absorb nitrate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A farmer spreads large amounts of nitrate fertiliser on fields beside a lake. Explain how this may lead to the death of fish in the lake.
parts.answer: Rain leaches nitrate into the lake; algae/water plants grow rapidly (algal bloom); algae block light so plants below die; dead plants/algae decomposed by bacteria; bacteria multiply and respire aerobically; oxygen in the water is used up; fish die from lack of oxygen (eutrophication).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six in sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three different ways in which nitrogen gas is fixed into compounds that plants can use.
parts.answer: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules of legumes; free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria in soil; lightning makes nitrogen oxides which dissolve in rain; the Haber process makes ammonia for fertilisers; fixed nitrogen becomes ammonium/nitrate in soil.
parts.working: B1 for each method (max 3) and up to 2 marks for detail of how each works.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why plants need nitrate ions and describe how a nitrate-deficient maize plant would look.
parts.answer: Nitrate is used to make amino acids; amino acids make proteins (enzymes, growth); also needed for chlorophyll; deficient plant shows stunted/weak growth; yellowing leaves (chlorosis), especially older lower leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a compost heap of vegetable peelings and animal dung needs to be turned over regularly and kept moist.
parts.answer: Turning adds oxygen; decomposers and nitrifying bacteria need oxygen for aerobic respiration; it prevents anaerobic conditions in which denitrifying bacteria would remove nitrate as nitrogen gas; moisture is needed for bacterial/fungal growth and enzyme action; too dry slows decay.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the nitrogen in the finished compost can become part of the protein in a spinach plant.
parts.answer: Compost contains protein/organic nitrogen; decomposers release ammonium; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate; nitrate absorbed by root hair cells by active transport; carried in xylem to leaves; used with glucose to make amino acids, joined into protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why nitrogen fertilisers made by the Haber process are important for feeding the world's growing human population.
parts.answer: Crops remove nitrogen from the soil when harvested; nitrate is often the limiting factor for crop growth; fertilisers replace it so yields are much higher; more food can be grown on the same land.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how farmers can reduce the amount of nitrate fertiliser lost from their fields into rivers.
parts.answer: Apply only the amount the crop needs (soil testing); apply when the crop is growing and can take it up; avoid spreading before heavy rain; split the dose into smaller applications; leave buffer strips of plants beside rivers; grow cover crops after harvest; use legumes/manure that release nitrogen slowly; avoid waterlogging/irrigate carefully.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why growing a crop of beans before a crop of wheat increases the wheat yield.
parts.answer: bean roots have nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria; these convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds/amino acids; when bean remains decay, nitrate is added to the soil, used by wheat for protein and growth
parts.working: B1 nodules with nitrogen-fixing bacteria; B1 nitrogen gas → nitrogen compounds; B1 more nitrate in soil after decay → more growth

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of crop rotation compared with using nitrate fertiliser.
parts.answer: advantage: cheaper / less nitrate runoff and eutrophication; disadvantage: slower/less nitrate added, land used for a less valuable crop

practice.stem:
Soil nitrate concentration in a maize field (mg per kg of soil). The maize was sown in April and harvested in September. The heaviest rain fell in July and August.
month | Jan | Mar | Apr | May | Jul | Sep | Nov | Dec
nitrate | 22 | 34 | 40 | 30 | 8 | 12 | 20 | 24

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in soil nitrate concentration over the year.
parts.answer: Nitrate rises from January to a peak in April (40); falls sharply to a minimum in July (8); rises again from August to December.
parts.working: 1 mark each, with at least one figure quoted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the changes you have described.
parts.answer: Rising warmth in spring increases decomposer and nitrifying bacteria activity, so nitrate builds up; from May the growing crop absorbs nitrate rapidly; heavy monsoon rain in July–August leaches nitrate / waterlogging encourages denitrification; after harvest no crop is absorbing nitrate and crop residues decay, so nitrate rises again.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest three things the farmer could do to keep more nitrate in the soil.
parts.answer: Grow a cover crop/legume after harvest; plough residues in rather than burning; avoid adding fertiliser just before heavy rain; improve drainage/avoid waterlogging; add manure/compost.

practice.stem: A rice field is flooded for most of the growing season, so its soil is waterlogged. A wheat field nearby is well drained and is ploughed regularly. Both fields started the season with the same soil nitrate concentration and no fertiliser was added to either. Over the season, the nitrate in the rice field fell much faster than in the wheat field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare how the nitrogen cycle works in the two fields. Refer to the bacteria involved and the conditions each one needs.
parts.answer: Waterlogged rice soil has very little oxygen: nitrifying bacteria, which need oxygen, are inactive, so little ammonium is changed to nitrate; denitrifying bacteria work in these anaerobic conditions and convert nitrate to nitrogen gas, which is lost to the air. Well-drained, aerated wheat soil has oxygen: nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrate, so more nitrate stays available to the crop; denitrification is slow.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five, and both fields must be covered: waterlogged soil lacks oxygen; nitrifying bacteria need oxygen and are less active; denitrifying bacteria work anaerobically and turn nitrate into nitrogen gas; nitrogen gas is lost to the air; well-drained soil is aerobic so nitrifying bacteria make nitrate; denitrification is slow in aerobic soil.

parts.label: b
