parts.text: Explain why the nitrate in the rice field fell faster than the nitrate in the wheat field.
parts.answer: Denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate into nitrogen gas in the waterlogged soil, and this gas escapes to the air; the rice plants absorb nitrate for growth; nitrate is washed out of the soil in drainage water (leaching).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two ways the rice farmer could reduce the loss of nitrate from the field.
parts.answer: Drain the field for periods so the soil has air (less denitrification); add manure or compost that releases nitrate slowly; do not spread fertiliser just before heavy rain (leaching).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible suggestions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the nitrogen cycle with the carbon cycle. Give similarities and differences.
parts.answer: Similarities: both are recycled between living things and the environment; both rely on decomposers; both are passed along food chains by feeding; both are taken in by plants first; both are affected by human activity (fertilisers / fossil fuels). Differences: carbon enters plants as CO₂ through leaves, nitrogen as nitrate through roots; plants cannot use atmospheric N₂ directly but can use atmospheric CO₂; nitrogen cycle needs special bacteria (fixing, nitrifying, denitrifying) while carbon cycle uses respiration by all organisms; carbon is released as CO₂ by respiration of all organisms, nitrogen is excreted as urea; combustion of fossil fuels is a major route for carbon but not a main route in the nitrogen cycle; nitrogen is lost from soil by leaching/denitrification.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any ten points; max 6 similarities or max 7 differences. Level answers that only describe one cycle at max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether growing beans in a plot of soil increases the growth of maize planted in the same soil afterwards.
parts.answer: Two (or more) plots/pots of the same soil; grow beans in one, leave the other bare (or grow a non-legume) as control; after the beans grow, dig the bean plants into the soil; plant the same number of maize seedlings of the same variety in each; keep other variables the same (light, water, temperature, no fertiliser); after a set time measure dry mass/height of maize; repeat with several plots and calculate means.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six, including a control and at least two controlled variables.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict the results and explain them.
parts.answer: Maize grows taller/heavier after beans; bean root nodules contain nitrogen-fixing bacteria; nitrogen added to soil when bean plants decompose (ammonium → nitrate); more nitrate allows more amino acid/protein synthesis for growth.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the first step in the development of an antibiotic-resistant population of bacteria?
A A random mutation produces a bacterium with an allele for resistance.
B The bacteria choose to become resistant when the antibiotic is used.
C The antibiotic causes all the bacteria to adapt to it.
D The resistant bacteria are killed by the antibiotic.
parts.answer: A A random mutation produces a bacterium with an allele for resistance.
parts.working: Resistance begins with a chance mutation that is present before the antibiotic is used; the antibiotic then selects for it. C is wrong: individual bacteria do not adapt in response to the drug.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the process of natural selection.
parts.answer: There is variation within a population; organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support; there is competition (a struggle for survival) for resources; individuals with features better adapted to the environment are more likely to survive; they reproduce and pass on their alleles to offspring; over many generations these alleles become more common.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: variation; overproduction; competition/struggle for survival; better adapted survive; reproduce; pass on alleles; over many generations allele frequency increases

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an antibiotic-resistant bacterium.
parts.answer: A bacterium that is not killed (or whose growth is not stopped) by an antibiotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one type of bacterium that is resistant to many antibiotics.
parts.answer: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why antibiotic resistance is a concern for hospitals.
parts.answer: Infections become difficult or impossible to treat; so patients may become seriously ill or die, and stay longer in hospital.
parts.working: B1 harder to treat; B1 longer illness/death/spread to other patients

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the process of adaptation.
parts.answer: The process, resulting from natural selection, by which populations become more suited to their environment over many generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: natural selection; population becomes more suited to its environment over many generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two causes of variation in a population that natural selection can act on.
parts.answer: Mutation; sexual reproduction (meiosis and random fertilisation).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Living organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support. State what happens as a result.
parts.answer: There is competition (a struggle for survival) for food and other resources, and many of the offspring die before they can reproduce.
parts.working: B1 competition / struggle for survival, many die.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a population of bacteria resistant to an antibiotic can develop in a hospital.
parts.answer: A random mutation gives some bacteria an allele for resistance; when the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed; resistant bacteria survive (selection pressure); they reproduce rapidly by binary fission/asexually; passing on the resistance allele; the proportion of resistant bacteria increases over generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: mutation; variation in population; antibiotic kills non-resistant; resistant survive; reproduce (rapidly); allele passed on; frequency increases. Do not credit 'bacteria adapt/become immune'.

practice.stem:
In one district of Sindh the same insecticide was sprayed to control malaria mosquitoes every year. Samples of mosquitoes were tested with a standard dose.
Year: 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021
Mosquitoes surviving / %: 4, 15, 41, 70

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the increase in the percentage of mosquitoes surviving between 2015 and 2021.
parts.answer: 66 percentage points (from 4% to 70%)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the change in the percentage of mosquitoes surviving the spraying.
parts.answer: Some mosquitoes had a mutation giving resistance; spraying killed the non-resistant mosquitoes; resistant mosquitoes survived and reproduced; they passed the resistance allele to their offspring so the proportion of resistant mosquitoes increased each generation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: variation/mutation; non-resistant killed; resistant survive and breed; allele passed on; frequency increases over generations

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to slow the spread of resistance.
parts.answer: Use different insecticides in rotation / spray less often / use other methods such as nets or removing standing water.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are patients told to complete the whole course of antibiotics even if they feel better?
A so that all the bacteria, including the less sensitive ones, are killed and cannot multiply
B so that the bacteria have time to become resistant
C so that the antibiotic can kill the viruses as well
D so that the patient's white blood cells stop making antibodies
parts.answer: A so that all the bacteria, including the less sensitive ones, are killed and cannot multiply
parts.working: Stopping early leaves the bacteria that are hardest to kill, which can multiply and pass on resistance. C is wrong because antibiotics do not kill viruses.

practice.stem: On a small island, the mean beak depth of a population of seed-eating finches was 9.2 mm. After a long drought killed most plants with small, soft seeds, the mean beak depth of the next generation was 9.7 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean beak depth. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the drought caused this change in the population.
parts.answer: During the drought, small soft seeds became scarce and mainly large hard seeds remained; birds with deeper beaks could crack them, so they were more likely to survive; they bred and passed on alleles for deep beaks to their offspring.
parts.working: B1 food changed / large hard seeds left; B1 deeper-beaked birds survived; B1 reproduced and passed on alleles

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In an industrial area, the proportion of dark-coloured moths increased over many years after tree bark was blackened by soot. What is the best explanation?
A dark moths were better camouflaged, so fewer were eaten by birds and more survived to reproduce and pass on the allele for dark colour
B pale moths turned dark because soot settled on their wings
C the moths changed colour to match the bark so that they would survive
D soot caused mutations that made all the moths dark
parts.answer: A dark moths were better camouflaged, so fewer were eaten by birds and more survived to reproduce and pass on the allele for dark colour
parts.working: Natural selection acts on existing variation: dark moths survived predation and reproduced more. C is wrong because individuals do not change their inherited colour in response to need; B describes a change that would not be inherited.

practice.stem:
A grain store used warfarin poison to kill rats. The percentage of rats trapped that were resistant to warfarin was recorded.
year: 2010, 2013, 2016, 2019
percentage resistant: 5, 18, 46, 71
After 2019 the store stopped using warfarin, and over the next few years the percentage of resistant rats fell.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean yearly increase in the percentage of resistant rats between 2010 and 2019. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 7.3 percentage points per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the population of rats became resistant to warfarin.
parts.answer: A few rats had a mutation giving resistance; warfarin killed the non-resistant rats; resistant rats survived and bred, passing on the resistance allele; over many generations the proportion of resistant rats increased.
parts.working: 1 mark each: variation / mutation present; non-resistant killed; resistant survive and reproduce; allele passed on / frequency increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Resistant rats need more vitamin K in their diet than non-resistant rats. Suggest why the percentage of resistant rats fell after warfarin was no longer used.
parts.answer: Without warfarin, resistance gives no advantage; resistant rats are less likely to survive or reproduce if vitamin K is short, so non-resistant rats increase.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no selective advantage without poison; resistant rats at a disadvantage (vitamin K) so selected against.

practice.stem:
A hospital recorded the percentage of samples (isolates) of the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus that were resistant to one antibiotic.
Year: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020
Resistant isolates / %: 5, 18, 39, 52

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in the percentage of resistant isolates per year between 1990 and 2020. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 1.57 percentage points per year

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the decade in which resistance increased most quickly.
parts.answer: 2000–2010 (21 percentage points)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using antibiotics to treat viral infections such as colds increases the problem of resistance.
parts.answer: Antibiotics do not affect viruses; but they kill non-resistant bacteria in the body, selecting for resistant bacteria which survive and multiply.
parts.working: B1 antibiotics have no effect on viruses; B1 unnecessary use increases selection of resistant bacteria

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest two other ways of reducing the development of resistant bacteria.
parts.answer: Any two of: complete the full course of antibiotics; only use antibiotics when necessary/prescribed; limit antibiotic use in farm animals; use different antibiotics/narrow-spectrum; good hygiene in hospitals to stop spread.

practice.stem:
Students counted the snails of one species with brown shells and with yellow shells in two habitats.
Woodland with dark leaf litter: brown 180, yellow 60
Grassland with pale dry grass: brown 45, yellow 105

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of brown snails in each habitat.
parts.answer: Woodland: 75%; grassland: 30%

parts.label: b
parts.text: Thrushes feed on these snails and find them by sight. Use natural selection to explain the difference between the two habitats.
parts.answer: Shell colour varies and is inherited; in woodland brown shells are camouflaged against the dark leaf litter, so yellow snails are seen and eaten more; in grassland yellow snails are camouflaged and brown ones eaten more; survivors reproduce and pass on the alleles for their shell colour, so each habitat has more of the camouflaged colour.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: variation/inherited colour; predation as selection pressure; camouflage on background (one habitat explained); survivors reproduce; alleles passed on/allele frequency changes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare natural selection with artificial (selective) breeding.
parts.answer: Similarities: both act on variation in a population; both cause alleles to become more common over many generations. Differences: in natural selection the environment determines which individuals survive and reproduce, in selective breeding humans choose; natural selection produces features that help survival (adaptation), selective breeding produces features useful to humans; selective breeding is usually faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four valid comparative points; at least one similarity and one difference for full marks

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the statement 'the bacteria became resistant because they needed to survive' is incorrect.
parts.answer: Resistance arises by random mutation, not in response to need; the antibiotic only selects bacteria that already had the resistance allele.
parts.working: B1 mutation is random/not caused by need; B1 antibiotic selects existing resistant bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text:
These statements describe natural selection.
1 individuals with the most useful features survive and reproduce
2 there is variation within a population
3 there is competition for resources such as food
4 the alleles for useful features become more common in the next generation
Which is the correct order?
A 2 → 3 → 1 → 4
B 3 → 2 → 4 → 1
C 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
D 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
parts.working: Variation exists first; competition (struggle for survival) follows from over-production; the best adapted survive and reproduce; they pass on their alleles. C puts survival before competition, which is the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Patients with tuberculosis are treated with three or four different antibiotics at the same time. Explain why this greatly reduces the chance that antibiotic-resistant bacteria will develop.
parts.answer: Resistance to each antibiotic arises by a separate rare mutation; a bacterium resistant to one antibiotic is still killed by the others; the chance of one bacterium having resistance to all of them at once is very small; so no resistant bacteria survive to reproduce and be selected.
parts.working: 1 mark each: each resistance needs a mutation / mutations rare; bacteria resistant to one are killed by another; very unlikely to be resistant to all; so resistant population cannot be selected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Some antibiotics are kept for use only against very serious infections that other antibiotics cannot treat. Suggest why hospitals limit the use of these antibiotics.
parts.answer: The less an antibiotic is used, the less bacteria are exposed to it, so there is less selection for resistant bacteria; the antibiotic therefore stays effective for when it is really needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less use means less selection for resistance; antibiotic stays effective for serious cases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature helps a desert plant in the Thar Desert to reduce water loss?
A a thick waxy cuticle
B large, thin leaves
C many stomata on the upper leaf surface
D large air spaces in the stem for floating
parts.answer: A a thick waxy cuticle
parts.working: A thick waxy cuticle reduces evaporation from the leaf surface. Large, thin leaves (B) would increase water loss.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term adaptive feature.
parts.answer: An inherited feature; that helps an organism to survive and reproduce in its environment.
parts.working: B1 inherited; B1 helps survival and reproduction

parts.label: b
parts.text: For each feature of a camel living in the Cholistan Desert, suggest how it helps the camel survive: (i) wide, padded feet; (ii) long eyelashes and nostrils that can close.
parts.answer: (i) spread the weight so the camel does not sink into soft sand; (ii) keep sand out of the eyes and nose during sandstorms.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature helps a polar bear to reduce heat loss in the Arctic?
A small ears and a thick layer of fat under the skin
B large ears with many blood vessels
C short, thin fur
D a large surface area to volume ratio
parts.answer: A small ears and a thick layer of fat under the skin
parts.working: Small ears reduce the surface area for heat loss and fat insulates the body. B and D would increase heat loss and are features of animals in hot habitats.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Snow leopards live in the high mountains of northern Pakistan. For each feature, suggest how it helps the snow leopard to survive.
(i) thick fur, even on the soles of the feet
(ii) very long, thick tail
(iii) large, wide paws
parts.answer: (i) insulation against cold / grip on snow; (ii) balance on rocky slopes or wrapped around the body for warmth; (iii) spread weight so it does not sink in snow (like snowshoes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why these features are described as adaptive features.
parts.answer: They are inherited features that help the animal survive and reproduce in its habitat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three adaptive features of a fish for living in water and give the function of each.
parts.answer: Gills for gas exchange / taking oxygen from water; streamlined body to reduce resistance when swimming; fins for balance and steering; scales for protection; lateral line to detect movement.
parts.working: 1 mark each for feature + function, any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each feature helps the lotus survive in water: (i) large air spaces in the leaf stalks and leaves; (ii) stomata on the upper surface of the floating leaves; (iii) very little xylem tissue.
parts.answer: (i) provide buoyancy so leaves float in light (and store/move oxygen to submerged parts); (ii) upper surface is in contact with air so gas exchange can take place; (iii) water supports the plant and there is plenty of water, so little transport or support tissue is needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name given to plants adapted to live in water.
parts.answer: Hydrophytes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how each of these features of xerophytes reduces water loss: (i) leaves reduced to spines; (ii) stomata sunken in pits; (iii) leaves that roll up with hairs on the inside.
parts.answer: (i) much smaller surface area for transpiration; (ii) and (iii) trap moist air near the stomata, reducing the water vapour concentration gradient so less water diffuses out.
parts.working: B1 smaller surface area; B1 humid air trapped (sunken stomata); B1 humid air trapped/reduced gradient (rolled leaves/hairs)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of the roots of xerophytes and explain how they help.
parts.answer: Very deep roots reach water deep underground; or wide shallow spreading roots absorb rain quickly before it evaporates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mangrove trees grow in salty, waterlogged mud along the coast of the Indus delta. Some of their roots grow upwards out of the mud. Suggest how these roots help the tree to survive.
parts.answer: The mud has little oxygen; the upward roots are exposed to air at low tide, so oxygen can diffuse in for the root cells' aerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each: waterlogged mud lacks oxygen; aerial roots take in oxygen from the air for respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The leaves of some mangroves have glands that excrete salt. Explain why this is an advantage.
parts.answer: Removing salt keeps the water potential of the leaf cells suitable so they do not lose water by osmosis / salt does not reach toxic concentrations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: removes excess salt; avoids water loss by osmosis / salt damage to cells.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why few other kinds of tree grow in this habitat.
parts.answer: They lack these adaptations: their roots cannot get oxygen in the waterlogged mud, or they lose water by osmosis / are damaged by the salt.
parts.working: B1 lack of adaptation linked to low oxygen or salt.

practice.stem: Leaves of two plants were tested under the same conditions. Water lost by a desert plant was 0.8 mg per cm² per hour. Water lost by a plant growing on a river bank was 6.4 mg per cm² per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times more water was lost by the river-bank plant.
parts.answer: 8 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest three leaf features of the desert plant that could explain its lower rate of water loss.
parts.answer: Thick waxy cuticle; fewer stomata / sunken stomata; small or rolled leaves / hairs trapping moist air; reduced leaf area.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the river-bank plant does not need these features.
parts.answer: Water is plentiful, so water loss can be replaced easily.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Leaves on a plant growing in deep shade under trees are larger and thinner than leaves on the same species growing in full sun. Explain how larger, thinner leaves are an advantage in shade.
parts.answer: A larger surface area absorbs more of the limited light; thin leaves let light reach all the chloroplasts / short diffusion distance for carbon dioxide; so more photosynthesis when light is limiting.
parts.working: 1 mark each: larger area absorbs more light; thin so light/CO₂ reach all cells; more photosynthesis in low light.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why leaves in full sun do not need to be as large.
parts.answer: Light is not limiting in full sun, and large thin leaves would lose more water.

practice.stem:
Students counted stomata per mm² on three plants, P, Q and R, from different habitats.
P: upper surface 380, lower surface 0
Q: upper surface 0, lower surface 450
R: upper surface 10, lower surface 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest which plant is a hydrophyte with floating leaves and which is a xerophyte. Give a reason for each.
parts.answer: P is the hydrophyte – all its stomata are on the upper surface, which is in contact with the air (the lower surface touches water). R is the xerophyte – it has very few stomata, reducing water loss by transpiration.
parts.working: B1 P; B1 reason; B1 R; B1 reason

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more stomata per mm² plant Q has in total than plant R. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: 10.0 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why plant Q has no stomata on its upper surface.
parts.answer: The upper surface is in direct sunlight and is hotter, so having no stomata there reduces water loss.

practice.stem: The fennec fox lives in hot deserts of North Africa and has very large ears. The Arctic fox lives in very cold regions and has small, rounded ears.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how ear size is an adaptive feature in each fox.
parts.answer: Large ears of the fennec fox give a large surface area; so more heat is lost to the surroundings, helping it keep cool in the hot desert; small ears of the Arctic fox reduce surface area; so less heat is lost in the cold.
parts.working: B1 large ears large surface area; B1 more heat loss/cooling in desert; B1 small ears less surface area; B1 less heat loss in cold

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one other adaptive feature of the Arctic fox and explain how it helps.
parts.answer: Thick fur traps air for insulation / white winter coat for camouflage in snow / fat layer for insulation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Define the term fitness in the context of natural selection.
parts.answer: The probability of an organism surviving and reproducing in the environment in which it is found.

practice.stem: Two mammals are modelled as cubes. The small mammal is a cube with 2 cm sides; the large mammal is a cube with 8 cm sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube.
parts.answer: 2 cm cube: 3 per cm; 8 cm cube: 0.75 per cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the ratio is for the small cube.
parts.answer: 4 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why small mammals living in cold mountain areas must eat much more food per kg of body mass than large mammals.
parts.answer: Small mammals have a larger surface area to volume ratio, so they lose heat faster for their size; they must respire more food to release energy to keep warm.
parts.working: 1 mark each: larger SA:V; lose heat faster per unit volume/mass; more respiration / food needed to replace heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some desert rodents never drink, but get water from their food and from aerobic respiration. Explain how aerobic respiration provides water.
parts.answer: Water is a product of aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
parts.working: 1 mark each: water is a product; equation or named reactants.

parts.label: b
parts.text: These rodents produce very small volumes of very concentrated urine and dry faeces. Explain how this is an advantage.
parts.answer: Less water is lost from the body in excretion and egestion, so the water gained from food and respiration is enough.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reduces water loss; water balance kept with little intake.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The rodents stay in burrows during the day and feed at night. Suggest two ways this behaviour helps them conserve water.
parts.answer: Burrows are cooler and more humid, so less water is lost by evaporation; they avoid the heat of the day so they do not need to cool by losing water.

practice.stem: In the Thar Desert at noon, the temperature of the sand surface was 58 °C and the temperature inside a lizard's burrow 40 cm below the surface was 31 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the difference between the surface and burrow temperatures at noon.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how living in a burrow during the day helps a desert lizard survive.
parts.answer: The burrow is much cooler, so the lizard avoids overheating; enzymes are not denatured; it loses less water by evaporation; it can come out at cooler times to feed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says: 'The lizards learned to dig burrows because it was hot, and then passed this habit to their young.' Explain why biologists would disagree.
parts.answer: Adaptive features are inherited; features acquired or learned during life are not passed on through genes; burrowing became common because lizards with an inherited tendency to burrow survived and reproduced more (natural selection).
parts.working: 1 mark each: acquired characteristics not inherited; natural selection of inherited variation.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which human characteristic shows discontinuous variation?
A height
B body mass
C ABO blood group
D hand span
parts.answer: C ABO blood group
parts.working: ABO blood group falls into a few distinct categories (A, B, AB, O) with no intermediates. Height (A) has a continuous range of values.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two differences between continuous and discontinuous variation.
parts.answer: Continuous variation has a range of values with intermediates, discontinuous has a few distinct categories with no intermediates; continuous is caused by both genes and the environment, discontinuous is usually caused by genes only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of each type of variation in plants.
parts.answer: Continuous: leaf length / plant height / seed mass. Discontinuous: flower colour in some species (e.g. purple or white pea flowers) / round or wrinkled pea seeds.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sort these features into continuous and discontinuous variation:
length of wheat ears; round or wrinkled pea seeds; mass of mangoes; human ABO blood group; height of maize plants
parts.answer: Continuous: length of wheat ears, mass of mangoes, height of maize plants. Discontinuous: round or wrinkled pea seeds, ABO blood group.
parts.working: 3 marks all five correct; 2 marks four; 1 mark three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define variation.
parts.answer: Differences between individuals of the same species.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identical twins have the same genes. Explain why adult identical twins can have different body masses but always have the same ABO blood group.
parts.answer: Body mass is affected by the environment (diet, exercise) as well as genes, so it can differ; blood group is controlled by genes only, so it is the same in both twins.
parts.working: 1 mark each: body mass affected by environment; blood group determined by genes only.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these two features shows continuous variation.
parts.answer: Body mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two environmental factors that could cause variation in the height of wheat plants in a field.
parts.answer: Any two: amount of water; light; mineral ions / fertiliser; temperature; soil type; pests or disease.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the height of wheat plants shows continuous variation.
parts.answer: Height can take any value in a range, because it is affected by many genes and by the environment.

practice.stem:
A student measured the lengths of 20 bean seeds from the same pod batch, in mm:
14, 16, 15, 17, 18, 15, 16, 16, 19, 13, 17, 16, 15, 18, 16, 17, 14, 16, 15, 17

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean length and the range of the seed lengths.
parts.answer: Mean 16.0 mm; range 6 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Complete a frequency table for the classes 13–14, 15–16, 17–18 and 19–20 mm.
parts.working: 2 marks all correct; 1 mark for three correct

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be drawn to show these results, and the type of variation shown.
parts.answer: Histogram (bars touching); continuous variation

practice.stem:
A study measured the mean difference in adult height between pairs of twins.
Identical twins raised together: 1.7 cm
Identical twins raised apart: 4.4 cm
Non-identical twins raised together: 4.5 cm

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identical twins have the same genes. Explain why identical twins raised apart show a larger difference in height than identical twins raised together.
parts.answer: Height is affected by the environment as well as genes; twins raised apart have different diets/living conditions, so their heights differ more.
parts.working: B1 environment affects height; B1 example such as different diet/health

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what the data for non-identical twins raised together show about the effect of genes on height.
parts.answer: Non-identical twins share the same environment but have different genes, yet differ more than identical twins raised together; so genes also affect height.
parts.working: B1 same environment but different genes; B1 larger difference shows genes have an effect

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which human characteristic shows continuous variation and is affected by the environment?
A body mass
B ABO blood group
C sex
D presence of a genetic disorder caused by a single gene
parts.answer: A body mass
parts.working: Body mass varies over a range with no distinct groups and depends on diet and exercise as well as genes. Blood group (B) is discontinuous and caused by genes alone.

practice.stem:
The masses of 50 mangoes picked from one orchard in Multan were grouped into classes.
mass / g: 150–199, 200–249, 250–299, 300–349, 350–399, 400–449
number of mangoes: 3, 9, 18, 13, 5, 2

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the modal class.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of mangoes in the modal class.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be drawn to show these data, and explain your choice.
parts.answer: Histogram, because mass is continuous data in classes with no gaps between them.
parts.working: 1 mark histogram; 1 mark continuous data / bars touching.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the shape of the distribution and state what it shows about the variation.
parts.answer: Roughly bell-shaped (normal) with most fruits in the middle classes and few at the extremes; this is continuous variation.

practice.stem: A gardener grew 100 snapdragon plants from seed. Results: red flowers 26, pink flowers 51, white flowers 23.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of plants with pink flowers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gardener says that because pink is in between red and white, flower colour in these plants shows continuous variation. Explain why he is wrong.
parts.answer: There are only three distinct colours (categories) with no range of shades between them; each plant fits clearly into one group; flower colour is controlled by genes, with little effect of the environment, so this is discontinuous variation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: distinct categories / no intermediates between groups; each plant in one group; controlled by genes only so discontinuous.

practice.stem: A student measured the heights of ten sunflower plants in a field (cm): 182, 167, 195, 174, 160, 188, 171, 179, 192, 166.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean height of the sunflowers. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the range of the heights.
parts.answer: 35 cm

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a sample of 10 plants is not enough to show the pattern of variation in the field.
parts.answer: Too few results to show the distribution; a larger sample would be more representative.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the piece of apparatus used to measure the plants and its precision.
parts.answer: A metre rule or tape measure to the nearest cm.

practice.stem:
A class survey in a school in Lahore recorded the ABO blood groups of 120 students.
A: 33; B: 41; AB: 9; O: 37

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of students with each blood group. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 number ÷ 120 × 100; A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of graph that should be used to display these results and describe one feature of it.
parts.answer: Bar chart; with gaps between the bars (categories on the x-axis).
parts.working: B1 bar chart; B1 bars separated / not touching

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why blood group is not affected by the environment.
parts.answer: It is controlled only by genes (alleles inherited from parents); it does not change with diet or lifestyle.

practice.stem: Twenty cuttings were taken from a single mint plant, so they were genetically identical. Ten were grown in full sun and ten in shade. After six weeks the mean height in the sun was 52 cm and the mean height in the shade was 34 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage by which the mean height of the plants in the sun was greater than in the shade. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what this experiment shows about the cause of variation in height.
parts.answer: The plants are genetically identical (clones), so the difference must be caused by the environment (light).
parts.working: 1 mark each: same genes / clones; difference due to environment.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The heights of the plants in the sun still varied from 46 cm to 58 cm. Suggest two reasons for this.
parts.answer: Small differences in environment such as water, soil minerals or shading by neighbours; differences in the size of the original cuttings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two (not genetic differences).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out whether leaf length in a hedge of a single plant species differs between the sunny side and the shady side of the hedge.
parts.answer: Pick leaves at random from each side (e.g. random numbers or every fifth leaf); same height on the hedge; same age of leaf (e.g. third leaf from tip); large sample (at least 30 per side); measure length from tip to base of blade with a ruler in mm; calculate mean and range for each side; draw histograms; compare.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: random sampling; control of height / leaf age; sample size ≥ 20–30; measuring method and units; mean/range calculated; histogram/comparison; repeat on another day/hedge.

practice.stem: A student grew pea plants from one packet of seeds. The dwarf plants ranged from 18 cm to 32 cm in height and the tall plants ranged from 140 cm to 190 cm. There were no plants with heights between 32 cm and 140 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the heights fall into two separate groups.
parts.answer: Tall and dwarf are controlled by a single gene with two alleles, giving discontinuous variation.
parts.working: 1 mark each: one gene / alleles; discontinuous / distinct groups.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the heights vary within each group.
parts.answer: Environmental factors such as light, water and mineral ions affect growth, giving continuous variation within each group.
parts.working: 1 mark each: environment; continuous variation within group.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the student could show that the variation within the tall group is caused mainly by the environment.
parts.answer: Grow seeds from the tall plants in identical controlled conditions (same soil, water, light) and see if the variation becomes much smaller; or grow genetically identical plants in different conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark each: controlled identical conditions / same genes; compare the spread of heights.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement describes selective breeding?
A Humans choose individuals with useful features and breed them together over many generations.
B Individuals best adapted to the environment survive and reproduce.
C A gene from another species is inserted into an organism.
D Offspring are produced by mitosis and are genetically identical.
parts.answer: A Humans choose individuals with useful features and breed them together over many generations.
parts.working: In selective breeding, humans choose the parents. B describes natural selection, where the environment does the selecting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a farmer could use selective breeding to increase the milk yield of buffaloes.
parts.answer: Choose the cows with the highest milk yield; mate them with bulls whose mothers/daughters had high milk yield; select the offspring with the highest milk yield and breed them; repeat over many generations.
parts.working: B1 select high-yield females; B1 select bull from high-yield line; B1 select best offspring to breed; B1 repeat over many generations

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that breeders select for in crop plants.
parts.answer: Any three: high yield; disease resistance; drought or heat tolerance; good taste/quality; short stems; early ripening.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that breeders select for in farm animals.
parts.answer: Any two: high milk yield; fast growth / more meat; more eggs; calm temperament; disease resistance; heat tolerance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a grower could use selective breeding to produce tomato plants with larger fruit.
parts.answer: Choose the plants with the largest fruit; cross-pollinate them; grow the seeds and select the offspring with the largest fruit; repeat for many generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: choose parents with desired feature; cross them; select best offspring; repeat over many generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the grower transfers pollen by hand and then covers the flowers with paper bags.
parts.answer: So that the grower controls which two plants are the parents; the bags stop pollen from other plants (or insects) reaching the flowers.
parts.working: 1 mark each: control of parents / chosen cross; bags prevent unwanted pollination.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by selective breeding.
parts.answer: Humans choose individuals with useful features and breed them together, and repeat this over many generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: humans choose parents with desired features; breed them / repeat over many generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two ways in which artificial selection differs from natural selection.
parts.answer: In artificial selection humans choose the parents, whereas in natural selection the environment does; artificial selection favours features useful to humans, natural selection favours features that help survival; artificial selection usually produces change much faster.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how selective breeding could produce a wheat variety that has both a high yield and resistance to a fungal disease.
parts.answer: Cross a high-yield variety with a disease-resistant variety; grow the offspring and select plants that show both high yield and resistance; breed these together; repeat over many generations until all offspring show both features.
parts.working: B1 cross the two varieties; B1 select offspring with both features; B1 breed these; B1 repeat for many generations

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why selective breeding takes many years.
parts.answer: Each generation must grow to maturity before it can be bred; desirable alleles are mixed with undesirable ones, so many generations of selection are needed.
parts.working: B1 time for each generation to mature; B1 many generations needed to fix the features

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two differences between selective breeding and genetic modification.
parts.answer: Genetic modification transfers individual genes, selective breeding mixes whole sets of genes; GM can move genes between different species, selective breeding only within one species (or very close relatives); GM is much faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one crop and one animal that have been improved by selective breeding, and state the feature selected in each.
parts.answer: e.g. wheat – higher grain yield / disease resistance; cattle – higher milk yield (or chickens – more eggs; sheep – more wool).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A breed of cattle has been selectively bred for high milk yield for many generations. Which problem is most likely to result?
A reduced genetic variation, so the breed may be more easily affected by a new disease
B the cows produce less milk each generation
C the cows become resistant to all diseases
D the calves are all genetically identical clones
parts.answer: A reduced genetic variation, so the breed may be more easily affected by a new disease
parts.working: Selecting only a few high-yielding parents reduces the variety of alleles, so the breed may lack alleles for resistance to a new disease. D is wrong: sexual reproduction still produces genetically different offspring.

practice.stem:
A farmer in Punjab compares local desi hens with a commercial breed produced by selective breeding.
desi hen: 90 eggs per year, eats 30 kg of feed per year
commercial hen: 300 eggs per year, eats 42 kg of feed per year

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of eggs produced per kg of feed by each kind of hen. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: desi hen 3.0 eggs per kg; commercial hen 7.1 eggs per kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how breeders could have produced the commercial breed from ordinary hens.
parts.answer: Choose the hens that lay the most eggs (and cockerels from high-laying families) as parents and breed them; select the best layers from the offspring and repeat over many generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: select best layers as parents and breed them; repeat selection over many generations.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Desi hens survive local diseases and summer heat better than the commercial hens. Suggest why the commercial breed may have lost these features.
parts.answer: Breeders selected only for egg production, not for disease or heat resistance; breeding from a few selected parents reduced genetic variation, so alleles for resistance may have been lost.
parts.working: 1 mark each: selected only for egg number; reduced genetic variation / alleles lost.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a breeder might cross desi hens with the commercial breed.
parts.answer: To produce hens with both a high egg yield and resistance to local diseases and heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plant breeders produced short-stemmed (semi-dwarf) wheat varieties. Suggest two advantages of short stems.
parts.answer: Less likely to fall over (lodge) in wind or rain or with heavy heads of grain; more of the plant's food goes into grain rather than stem.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why these varieties gave high yields only when farmers also used more fertiliser and irrigation.
parts.answer: They were bred to respond to high nitrate and water; without enough minerals or water, these become limiting factors so yield cannot increase.
parts.working: 1 mark each: bred to use more fertiliser/water; otherwise minerals/water limit growth.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why farmers must buy new seed of some modern varieties each year rather than saving their own.
parts.answer: Hybrid varieties do not breed true / offspring vary and lose the selected features.

practice.stem:
In a long-term experiment, maize plants were selected for high oil content in their grain.
generation: 0, 10, 20, 30
mean oil content / %: 4.7, 7.2, 9.6, 11.8

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in oil content per generation. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: 0.24 % per generation

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in oil content from generation 0 to generation 30. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the breeders achieved this change.
parts.answer: In each generation they measured oil content and used only the plants with the highest oil content as parents; repeated over many generations.

practice.stem:
A cattle farm kept records of the mean milk yield per lactation of cows over four generations of selective breeding.
Generation: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Mean milk yield / dm³: 1800, 1950, 2100, 2280, 2400

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean milk yield from generation 0 to generation 4. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in yield per generation.
parts.answer: 150 dm³ per generation

parts.label: c
parts.text: Discuss the possible disadvantages of breeding cattle selected only for high milk yield.
parts.answer: Reduced genetic variation in the herd; so the herd is more vulnerable to new diseases or environmental change; harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be expressed (inbreeding), causing health problems such as leg or udder problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: less variation; more susceptible to disease; inbreeding/harmful recessive conditions; animal welfare problems; other useful features lost

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some pedigree dog breeds have been bred from a small number of ancestors for many generations. Explain why these dogs are more likely to suffer from inherited disorders.
parts.answer: Breeding of closely related animals (inbreeding); many share the same alleles; harmful recessive alleles are more likely to be inherited from both parents; so offspring are homozygous recessive and show the disorder.
parts.working: 1 mark each: inbreeding / related parents; small gene pool; recessive alleles from both parents; homozygous recessive shows disorder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways breeders could reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Breed with unrelated dogs / outcross with another breed; test dogs for carrier alleles before breeding; keep breeding records to avoid related pairs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer has a herd of Sahiwal cows, which tolerate heat well but give a moderate milk yield. He can buy frozen semen from bulls of a high-yielding breed from a cooler country. Outline how he could use artificial insemination and selective breeding to produce cows that both tolerate heat and give a high milk yield.
parts.answer: Inseminate Sahiwal cows with semen from the high-yield breed; rear the female calves and record their milk yield and how well they tolerate heat; choose the cows that show both features as parents for the next generation; repeat selection over many generations.
parts.working: 1 mark each: cross the two breeds by AI; measure milk yield and heat tolerance of offspring; select those with both features to breed; repeat over many generations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why using artificial insemination is cheaper and safer than importing live bulls.
parts.answer: Frozen semen is small and easy to transport; one bull's semen can be used for many cows; there is no risk of the bull dying in the heat or bringing in diseases on the journey.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way genetic modification could produce a heat-tolerant, high-yielding variety of a crop faster than selective breeding.
parts.answer: Insert the gene for heat tolerance directly into the high-yielding variety, so many generations of crossing and selection are not needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mango growers in Pakistan keep varieties such as Chaunsa by grafting shoots onto rootstocks rather than growing new trees from seed. Explain why.
parts.answer: Seeds are produced by sexual reproduction, so trees grown from seed vary and may not have the parent's fruit quality; grafting is asexual, so the shoot has exactly the same genes; all the trees produce the same fruit.
parts.working: 1 mark each: seeds → sexual reproduction → variation; grafting asexual / genetically identical; keeps desired features.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A breeder wants to produce a new mango variety. Explain why she must use seeds at the start of the programme.
parts.answer: Sexual reproduction creates new combinations of alleles (variation), from which new desirable trees can be selected.
parts.working: 1 mark each: new variation / allele combinations; needed for selection.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of an orchard in which every tree is genetically identical.
parts.answer: A disease or pest could affect all the trees, since none has resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is a gene mutation?
A a random change in the base sequence of DNA
B the loss of a whole chromosome during mitosis
C the swapping of genes between plants by selective breeding
D the change in a population over many generations
parts.answer: A a random change in the base sequence of DNA
parts.working: A gene mutation is a random change in the base sequence of DNA. D describes evolution, which can result from mutation plus selection but is not itself a mutation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two factors that increase the rate of mutation.
parts.answer: Ionising radiation (e.g. X-rays, gamma rays); certain chemicals (e.g. tar in tobacco smoke).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why mutation is important for evolution.
parts.answer: It is the source of new alleles / new variation on which natural selection acts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term gene mutation.
parts.answer: A random change in the base sequence of DNA (of a gene).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether mutations happen randomly or only when an organism needs a new feature.
parts.answer: Randomly.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one inherited condition caused by a gene mutation.
parts.answer: Sickle-cell anaemia (accept cystic fibrosis or albinism).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why mutations are more likely in cells that divide often, such as cells lining the gut, than in nerve cells, which rarely divide.
parts.answer: Mutations happen mainly when DNA is copied before a cell divides; cells that divide often copy their DNA many times, so there are more chances for mistakes; nerve cells rarely copy their DNA.
parts.working: 1 mark each: DNA copied before division; errors in copying cause mutations; more divisions = more chances.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why plants grown from seeds show more genetic variation than plants grown from cuttings of one parent.
parts.answer: Seeds come from sexual reproduction: meiosis and random fertilisation give new combinations of alleles; cuttings are asexual, so they are genetically identical to the parent (apart from rare mutations).
parts.working: 1 mark each: seeds from sexual reproduction / meiosis and fertilisation mix alleles; cuttings asexual / clones.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way in which people can reduce their risk of mutations in their body cells.
parts.answer: Avoid smoking / limit X-ray exposure / use sunscreen against UV / avoid harmful chemicals.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a gene mutation can result in a protein that does not work.
parts.answer: The base sequence of the gene is changed; so the sequence of amino acids in the protein is changed; the protein folds into a different shape (e.g. an enzyme's active site changes) and cannot carry out its function.
parts.working: B1 base sequence altered; B1 different amino acid sequence; B1 different shape → loss of function

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a mutation in a cell of the testis may affect future generations, but a mutation in a skin cell will not.
parts.answer: Testis cells give rise to gametes (sperm), which pass the mutated allele to the offspring; skin cells are body cells and are not passed on.
parts.working: B1 gametes carry mutation to offspring; B1 body cell mutations not inherited

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which factor increases the rate of mutation?
A exposure to ionising radiation such as X-rays
B eating a diet rich in protein
C regular exercise
D exposure to visible light from a desk lamp
parts.answer: A exposure to ionising radiation such as X-rays
parts.working: Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays) and some chemicals damage DNA and increase the mutation rate. Visible light (D) does not carry enough energy to damage DNA in this way.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Workers in a nuclear power station wear a badge that records how much ionising radiation they receive. Explain why this exposure is checked.
parts.answer: Ionising radiation damages DNA and increases the rate of mutation; mutations can lead to cancer, so each worker's total dose must be kept below a safe limit.
parts.working: 1 mark each: radiation causes mutation / damages DNA; risk of cancer, so dose must be limited.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why pregnant workers are moved to jobs with no radiation exposure.
parts.answer: The cells of the fetus divide very often, copying their DNA each time, so mutations are more likely; a mutation in an early cell is passed to all the cells that come from it and could harm development.
parts.working: 1 mark each: rapid cell division / DNA copied often; mutation passed to many cells / harms development.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Most mutations are harmful or have no effect. Explain how a mutation could occasionally be beneficial.
parts.answer: It may produce a new allele that codes for a protein that works better or gives a new feature (e.g. resistance to a disease or poison); the organism is more likely to survive and reproduce; the allele is passed on.
parts.working: 1 mark each: new allele / changed protein; advantage to survival; passed to offspring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a mutation that has been beneficial to the organism.
parts.answer: Antibiotic resistance in bacteria; pesticide or warfarin resistance in pests.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tobacco smoke contains tar, which contains chemicals that are mutagens. Suggest how smoking can lead to lung cancer.
parts.answer: Chemicals in tar cause mutations in the DNA of lung cells; mutations in genes that control cell division; cells divide uncontrollably, forming a tumour.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mutation in lung cells; genes controlling cell division affected; uncontrolled division / tumour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the risk of lung cancer increases with the number of years a person has smoked.
parts.answer: Longer exposure to the mutagens means more mutations build up in lung cells, increasing the chance that genes controlling cell division are affected.
parts.working: B1 more exposure / mutations accumulate over time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A white (albino) crow is occasionally seen in a city park. Albinism is caused by a recessive allele that results from a mutation. Explain why albino animals are rare in the wild.
parts.answer: The mutation is rare; the albino must inherit two recessive alleles; albino animals are easily seen by predators (and may have poor eyesight), so fewer survive and reproduce.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mutations rare; need two copies / homozygous recessive; selected against (conspicuous / poor eyesight).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the allele for albinism can still be passed on in the population.
parts.answer: Heterozygous carriers have normal colour, so they are not selected against.

practice.stem:
Cultures of cells were exposed to different doses of radiation and the mutation frequency was recorded.
Dose / units: 0, 1, 2, 4
Mutations per 100 000 cells: 3, 8, 13, 23

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the relationship between radiation dose and mutation frequency.
parts.answer: Mutation frequency increases as the dose increases; it increases by 5 mutations per 100 000 cells for each extra unit of dose (directly/linearly).
parts.working: B1 positive relationship; B1 constant increase of 5 per unit / linear, with data

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use the pattern in the data to predict the mutation frequency at a dose of 3 units.
parts.answer: 18 per 100 000 cells

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some mutations occur even when the dose is zero.
parts.answer: Mutations happen randomly (spontaneously) during DNA copying, and there is always some natural background radiation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why hospital radiographers who take X-ray images stand behind a lead screen.
parts.answer: X-rays are ionising radiation that increases the rate of mutation; lead absorbs the radiation, reducing the risk of mutations that could lead to cancer.
parts.working: B1 X-rays cause mutation; B1 lead absorbs radiation / reduces cancer risk

practice.stem:
Plates of bacteria were exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light for different times. The number of colonies that grew, and the number of these that showed a new feature (mutants), were counted.
UV exposure / s: 0, 10, 20, 30
surviving colonies: 500, 320, 140, 40
mutant colonies: 0, 6, 9, 5

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mutation frequency (mutant colonies as a percentage of surviving colonies) for each exposure time. Give each answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of UV exposure time on survival and on mutation frequency.
parts.answer: As exposure time increases, fewer bacteria survive, but the percentage of survivors that are mutants increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says the 20 s exposure is 'best for producing mutants' because it produced the most mutant colonies. Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: 20 s gave the largest number of mutant colonies (9), but 30 s gave the highest mutation frequency; with only one plate per time the difference may not be reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark each: number vs frequency; need repeats / small numbers.

practice.stem: A section of a gene is 36 bases long. Each group of three bases codes for one amino acid in a protein.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of amino acids coded for by this section of DNA.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A mutation removes three bases (one complete group) from this section. Calculate the number of amino acids the section now codes for, and suggest the effect on the protein.
parts.answer: 11 amino acids; the protein is one amino acid shorter, so its shape may change and it may not work properly (e.g. an enzyme's active site may change).
parts.working: M1 (36 − 3) ÷ 3; A1 11; B1 changed shape / function of protein.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some single-base changes have no effect on the protein.
parts.answer: The new triplet may still code for the same amino acid (or the change is in a part that does not affect shape).

practice.stem: In one fish species a particular gene mutates in about 1 out of every 100 000 eggs. One female fish lays 2 million eggs in a season.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many of the eggs would be expected to carry a new mutation in this gene.
parts.answer: 20 eggs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why, despite this, most of these mutations will not appear in the adult population.
parts.answer: Most eggs and young fish die before adulthood (predation, starvation); many mutations are harmful or recessive and hidden, so they are removed or not seen.
parts.working: 1 mark each: high mortality of young; harmful mutations selected against / recessive.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why mutation is still important for the long-term survival of fish species.
parts.answer: It is the source of new alleles and variation; if the environment changes, some individuals may have alleles that let them survive, so the species can adapt by natural selection.
parts.working: 1 mark each: new alleles / variation; allows adaptation / natural selection when conditions change.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?
A renal vein
B urethra
C ureter
D renal artery
parts.answer: C ureter
parts.working: The ureter carries urine from each kidney to the bladder. The urethra carries urine from the bladder out of the body, so B is the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which substance is normally found in the glomerular filtrate but NOT in the urine of a healthy person?
A glucose
B salts
C urea
D water
parts.answer: A glucose
parts.working: All glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. Urea passes into urine, so C is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define excretion.
parts.answer: removal from the body of toxic waste products of metabolism (and substances in excess of requirements)
parts.working: B1 removal of (toxic) waste of metabolism / made by cells; B1 substances in excess

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the organ that excretes carbon dioxide and the organ that excretes urea.
parts.answer: lungs; kidneys

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the tube that carries urine out of the body from the bladder.
parts.answer: urethra

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings blood to the kidney.
parts.answer: renal artery

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three regions seen when a kidney is cut lengthwise, starting from the outside.
parts.answer: cortex, medulla, pelvis

parts.label: c
parts.text: State where the glomeruli are found.
parts.answer: cortex

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two substances that are reabsorbed into the blood from the kidney tubules.
parts.answer: glucose, water, salts (ions), amino acids

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the structure that stores urine.
parts.answer: bladder

practice.stem: A sheep kidney was cut lengthwise. It has a dark outer layer (cortex) about 5 mm thick, a paler inner region (medulla) made of cone-shaped pyramids, and a white funnel-shaped space (pelvis) at the concave side, from which the ureter leaves.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State which region of the kidney described contains:
(i) the glomeruli and Bowman's capsules
(ii) the loops of Henle and collecting ducts
parts.answer: (i) cortex; (ii) medulla

parts.label: b
parts.text: The actual length of the kidney was 60 mm. A student drew the section 150 mm long. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the glomerulus.
parts.answer: ultrafiltration of blood (forcing water and small solutes into the capsule)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the collecting duct.
parts.answer: reabsorbs water; carries urine to the pelvis

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that carries filtered blood away from the kidney.
parts.answer: renal vein

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are proteins absent from the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule?
A They are actively absorbed by the glomerulus.
B Their molecules are too large to pass through the filter.
C They are digested in the kidney.
D They are converted to urea in the glomerulus.
parts.answer: B Their molecules are too large to pass through the filter.
parts.working: Ultrafiltration lets only small molecules through the capillary wall and capsule lining. Urea is made in the liver, not the glomerulus, so D is wrong.

practice.stem:
Concentrations in g per 100 cm³:
substance | blood plasma | filtrate in Bowman's capsule | urine
water | 92 | 98 | 96
protein | 7.0 | 0.0 | 0.0
glucose | 0.10 | 0.10 | 0.00
urea | 0.03 | 0.03 | 2.00
salts | 0.72 | 0.72 | 1.50

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the table to name the substance that is not filtered. Explain why.
parts.answer: protein; molecules too large to pass through the capillary wall/basement membrane

parts.label: b
parts.text: Glucose is present in the filtrate but not in the urine. Name the process responsible and where it happens.
parts.answer: selective reabsorption; in the (proximal convoluted) tubule

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why urea becomes more concentrated in urine.
parts.answer: water is reabsorbed from the filtrate (but urea mostly is not)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how filtrate is formed in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
parts.answer: blood arrives at high pressure (afferent vessel wider than efferent); small molecules such as water, glucose, salts and urea are forced out through the capillary walls into the capsule; large proteins and blood cells stay in the blood
parts.working: B1 high pressure; B1 small molecules named pass out; B1 proteins/cells remain (ultrafiltration)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of this process.
parts.answer: ultrafiltration

practice.stem: A healthy adult produces urine at a mean rate of 1.2 cm³ per minute. The urine contains 20 g of urea per dm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of urea excreted in one day (24 hours). Give your answer in grams to 3 significant figures.
parts.working: M1 volume per day 1 728 cm³ (1.728 dm³); A1 34.6 g

parts.label: b
parts.text: On one day this person's urine gives an orange colour with Benedict's solution. Suggest an explanation.
parts.answer: glucose is present in the urine; blood glucose concentration was too high (e.g. diabetes), so not all the glucose in the filtrate could be reabsorbed
parts.working: B1 glucose in urine; B1 blood glucose too high / not all reabsorbed in the tubule (diabetes)

practice.stem:
Artificial urine samples from three patients were tested.
sample 1: Benedict's blue; biuret blue
sample 2: Benedict's orange; biuret blue
sample 3: Benedict's blue; biuret purple

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which sample is from the person likely to have diabetes. Give a reason.
parts.answer: sample 2; it gave a positive (orange) Benedict's result showing glucose in urine

parts.label: b
parts.text: Sample 3 contains protein. Suggest what this shows about the kidneys of person 3.
parts.answer: damage to the glomerulus/filter (proteins leak through)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the biuret test was carried out on the samples.
parts.answer: add biuret solution (sodium hydroxide then copper sulfate) to equal volume of urine; purple = protein

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one safety precaution when testing urine.
parts.answer: wear gloves / goggles; dispose of samples safely; wash hands

parts.label: a
parts.text: A man runs a marathon in hot weather in Dubai and drinks little water. Predict how the volume and colour of his urine will change. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: smaller volume; darker / more concentrated; much water lost as sweat, so more water reabsorbed in the tubules/collecting ducts
parts.working: B1 smaller volume; B1 darker/more concentrated; B1 more water reabsorbed due to sweating

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why urine is still produced even when the body is short of water.
parts.answer: urea (toxic waste) must still be removed in solution

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The blood in the renal vein, compared with the blood in the renal artery, has
A less urea and less oxygen.
B more urea and less oxygen.
C less urea and more oxygen.
D more glucose and more oxygen.
parts.answer: A less urea and less oxygen.
parts.working: The kidney removes urea, and kidney cells use oxygen in respiration. Oxygen does not increase as blood passes through an organ, so C is wrong.

practice.stem: In an adult, about 125 cm³ of filtrate passes from the blood into the nephrons every minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of filtrate formed per day in dm³.

parts.label: b
parts.text: On the same day the person produced 1.5 dm³ of urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtrate that was reabsorbed. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the volume of urine produced is larger on a cool, rainy day than on a hot day.
parts.answer: less water lost in sweat on a cool day; so less water is reabsorbed by the kidneys and more urine is made
parts.working: B1 less sweating; B1 less water reabsorbed / more dilute, larger volume

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the path of a urea molecule from the renal artery until it leaves the body.
parts.answer: renal artery → glomerulus → (ultrafiltration into) Bowman's capsule → tubule (proximal, loop of Henle, distal) → collecting duct → pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four correct stages in order: glomerulus; Bowman's capsule; tubule/loop of Henle; collecting duct; ureter; bladder; urethra

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the cells lining the proximal tubule have many mitochondria.
parts.answer: they reabsorb some substances (e.g. glucose, salts) by active transport; active transport needs energy from (aerobic) respiration in mitochondria
parts.working: B1 active transport/reabsorption; B1 energy/ATP from respiration

practice.stem:
Three volunteers each drank 1 dm³ of water on one day and 1 dm³ of salty soup on another. Urine volume collected in the next 2 hours (cm³):
water: 520, 480, 560
salty soup: 210, 190, 230

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean volume of urine for each drink, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference in mean urine volume.
parts.answer: salty drink raises salt concentration of blood (lowers water potential); kidneys reabsorb more water so less urine; after pure water, excess water is excreted
parts.working: B1 excess water excreted after water; B1 more water reabsorbed after salty drink

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two variables that should be controlled.
parts.answer: volume drunk; time of day; activity/temperature; body mass; food eaten before; time of last emptying of bladder

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the structure of the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule is adapted for ultrafiltration.
parts.answer: vessel leaving the glomerulus is narrower than the one entering, creating high pressure; large surface area of capillary knot; thin walls (capillary wall + capsule lining) with pores that let small molecules pass
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: narrower efferent vessel/high pressure; large surface area/many capillaries; thin walls/short distance; pores/partially permeable filter

parts.label: b
parts.text: A person's blood pressure falls very low. Suggest the effect on filtration and urine production.
parts.answer: less pressure in the glomerulus so less filtrate formed; less urine produced
parts.working: B1 less filtration; B1 less urine

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Where in the body is urea made?
A bladder
B kidney
C liver
D pancreas
parts.answer: C liver
parts.working: Urea is made in the liver by deamination of excess amino acids; the kidney only removes it, so B is wrong.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by deamination.
parts.answer: removal of the nitrogen-containing (amino) part of excess amino acids, forming urea
parts.working: B1 removal of nitrogen/amine group; B1 from excess amino acids (to form urea)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how urea travels from where it is made to the kidneys.
parts.answer: dissolved in blood plasma

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the main nitrogen-containing waste substance excreted in urine by mammals?
A ammonia
B urea
C amino acids
D protein
parts.answer: B urea
parts.working: Ammonia is converted to urea in the liver, and urea is the main nitrogenous waste in urine. Amino acids and protein are not wastes that the kidney removes in large amounts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State why ammonia must be converted to urea in the liver.
parts.answer: ammonia is very toxic; urea is much less toxic, so it can be carried in the blood and excreted safely
parts.working: B1 ammonia is toxic; B1 urea is less toxic and can be carried in blood

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what happens to the carbon-containing part of an amino acid after deamination.
parts.answer: it is converted into carbohydrate or fat (glycogen), or it is used in respiration to release energy

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the body cannot store excess amino acids in the same way that it stores excess glucose.
parts.answer: there is no storage form for amino acids (unlike glycogen for glucose), so the excess is deaminated

parts.label: b
parts.text: A wrestler eats a diet very rich in meat and eggs. Predict how the amount of urea in his urine will change, and explain why.
parts.answer: increases; more excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, forming more urea
parts.working: B1 increase; B1 more deamination of excess amino acids

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Deamination of excess amino acids removes which part of the amino acid?
A the R (side) group
B the amino (–NH₂) group
C the whole amino acid molecule
D the glucose part of the molecule
parts.answer: B the amino (–NH₂) group
parts.working: Deamination removes the amino group, which forms ammonia and then urea. The carbon-containing remainder is kept for respiration, or converted to carbohydrate or fat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the route of urea from the liver to the kidneys.
parts.answer: urea is carried in the blood plasma; it leaves the liver in the hepatic vein and travels to the heart and then to the kidneys in the renal artery; it is filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus
parts.working: 1 mark each: dissolved in plasma; hepatic vein to heart and renal artery; filtered in the glomerulus

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why deamination takes place in the liver rather than in the kidneys.
parts.answer: the liver contains the enzymes for deamination and receives amino acids from the gut in the hepatic portal vein; the kidney's job is to filter and excrete urea, not make it
parts.working: B1 liver has the enzymes and receives amino acids; B1 kidneys filter and excrete, they do not make urea

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the excretion of carbon dioxide with the excretion of urea. Give the organ for each and explain the difference in the way it is made.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide is made in respiration in cells and excreted by the lungs; urea is made in the liver from amino acids and excreted by the kidneys in urine
parts.working: 1 mark each: lungs excrete CO₂; kidneys excrete urea; urea made from excess amino acids while CO₂ comes from respiration

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare urea and urine.
parts.answer: urea is a nitrogen-containing waste substance made in the liver; urine is the liquid made by the kidneys containing water, urea and salts
parts.working: B1 urea = substance made in liver by deamination; B1 urine = solution of urea, salts in water made by kidney

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why urea must be removed from the body.
parts.answer: it is toxic (harmful) at high concentration

parts.label: c
parts.text: After deamination, the remaining part of the amino acid is not wasted. State what happens to it.
parts.answer: used in respiration to release energy, or converted to glycogen/fat for storage

practice.stem: A patient with kidney failure had a blood urea concentration of 1.2 g/dm³ before dialysis and 0.1 g/dm³ after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in urea in the blood during one dialysis session. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient's blood urea rises again between sessions.
parts.answer: the liver continues to deaminate excess amino acids, producing urea; the kidneys cannot remove it
parts.working: B1 urea still made in liver; B1 not removed by (failed) kidneys

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person eats 120 g of protein. Protein is 16 % nitrogen by mass. Calculate the mass of nitrogen in this protein.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume all this nitrogen is excreted as urea, CO(NH₂)₂. Urea has a relative formula mass of 60, and its two nitrogen atoms together have a mass of 28. Calculate the mass of urea produced.
parts.working: M1 19.2 ÷ 28 × 60 (nitrogen mass as a share of urea's formula mass); A1 = 41.1 g

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person with severe liver failure often has high levels of ammonia in the blood. Explain why.
parts.answer: the liver cannot convert ammonia to urea, so ammonia builds up in the blood; ammonia is toxic and can damage the brain; it is not excreted as it should be
parts.working: B1 liver cannot convert ammonia to urea; B1 ammonia builds up; B1 ammonia is toxic (and harms the brain)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Blood entering a kidney through the renal artery contains 6.0 mmol/dm³ of urea. Blood leaving through the renal vein contains 4.5 mmol/dm³. Calculate the percentage of urea removed from the blood.

parts.label: b
