parts.label: b
parts.text: A car moves, uses fuel and gives out waste gases, but it is not alive. State two characteristics of living organisms that a car does not show.
parts.answer: growth and reproduction
parts.working: B1 growth; B1 reproduction. Accept sensitivity (detecting and responding to stimuli) as one of the two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define excretion.
parts.answer: The removal of waste products of metabolism, toxic materials and substances in excess of requirements from the body.
parts.working: B1 removal of waste products of metabolism / toxic materials; B1 substances in excess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Define sensitivity.
parts.answer: The ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment.
parts.working: B1 detect changes / stimuli; B1 respond.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A sunflower turns its head to face the sun. Name the characteristic of living organisms shown.
parts.answer: sensitivity

parts.label: a
parts.text: The deodar tree is named Cedrus deodara. State its genus.
parts.answer: Cedrus

parts.label: b
parts.text: The cedar of Lebanon is named Cedrus libani. What does the shared first name tell you about these two trees?
parts.answer: They belong to the same genus, so they are closely related.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two rules for writing a binomial name.
parts.answer: Genus first with a capital letter; species second in lower case; printed in italics or underlined when handwritten.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the vertebrate group with each set of features.
(i) feathers, a beak and wings
(ii) moist skin with no scales; larvae with gills
(iii) fur and external ears (pinnae)
(iv) dry scaly skin; lays eggs with rubbery shells on land
(v) fins, wet scales and gills
parts.answer: (i) birds; (ii) amphibians; (iii) mammals; (iv) reptiles; (v) fish

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features that show a housefly is an insect.
parts.answer: Body in three parts (head, thorax, abdomen); three pairs of legs; one pair of antennae; wings (one or two pairs); compound eyes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature that all arthropods share.
parts.answer: Jointed legs / exoskeleton / segmented body.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Maize is a monocotyledon and mustard is a dicotyledon. State how the leaf veins of the two plants differ.
parts.answer: Maize has parallel veins; mustard has a branching network of veins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many cotyledons are found in the seed of each plant.
parts.answer: maize one; mustard two

parts.label: c
parts.text: A mustard flower has 4 petals. A lily flower has 6 petals. Which of these is a monocotyledon? Give a reason.
parts.answer: The lily – its flower parts are in multiples of three.
parts.working: B1 lily; B1 multiples of three.

practice.stem:
A student looked at four animals with a hand lens and recorded her observations.
Animal | body parts | pairs of legs | pairs of antennae | wings
1 | 3 | 3 | 1 | 2 pairs
2 | 2 | 4 | 0 | none
3 | 2 | 5 | 2 | none
4 | many similar segments | 30 | 1 | none

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the arthropod group of each animal 1 to 4.
parts.answer: 1 insect; 2 arachnid; 3 crustacean; 4 myriapod

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of legs of animal 4.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one feature, other than jointed legs, that all four animals share.
parts.answer: exoskeleton / segmented body

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three features of plant cells that are not found in animal cells.
parts.answer: cellulose cell wall; chloroplasts; large permanent vacuole containing cell sap

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how plants and animals differ in the way they obtain food.
parts.answer: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; animals feed on other organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why biologists classify living organisms into groups.
parts.answer: Makes it easier to identify and study organisms; shows evolutionary relationships; allows features of a new organism to be predicted; helps scientists communicate with one shared system.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the basis on which organisms are placed into the same group.
parts.answer: They share features (characteristics).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A cheetah's muscle cells break down glucose to release the energy it needs to chase prey. Which characteristic of living organisms is this?
A excretion
B movement
C nutrition
D respiration
parts.answer: D respiration
parts.working: Respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy. Movement is what the energy is used for, so B is the main distractor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define each of these characteristics of living organisms: (i) nutrition (ii) movement (iii) reproduction.
parts.answer: (i) taking in materials for energy, growth and development; (ii) an action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place; (iii) the processes that make more of the same kind of organism

parts.label: b
parts.text: Plants cannot walk. Give one example of movement shown by a plant.
parts.answer: leaves of a touch-me-not (Mimosa) plant fold when touched / flowers open and close / a shoot bends towards light

practice.stem: A student soaked some gram (chickpea) seeds and left them in a warm, damp place. After four days each seed had a root growing downwards, the seeds were using oxygen, and they had become larger and heavier when dried.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three characteristics of living organisms shown by the germinating seeds. For each, give the evidence from the description.
parts.answer: respiration – using oxygen; growth – larger and heavier dry mass; sensitivity / movement – root grows downwards (responds to gravity)
parts.working: 1 mark each for characteristic with evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student dried the seeds before measuring their mass to show growth.
parts.answer: Water content can change without real growth; growth is a permanent increase in dry mass.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Define the term species.
parts.answer: A group of organisms that can reproduce to produce fertile offspring.
parts.working: 1 mark: can interbreed/reproduce; 1 mark: fertile offspring.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The common myna has different local names in different languages. Explain why biologists use its scientific name, Acridotheres tristis, instead.
parts.answer: The scientific name is the same in every country and language, so everyone knows exactly which species is meant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the vertebrate group to which each animal belongs and give one feature that shows this.
(i) Indian cobra
(ii) koel (a bird of Pakistani gardens)
(iii) bullfrog
(iv) rohu (a river fish)
(v) camel
parts.answer: (i) reptile – dry scaly skin; (ii) bird – feathers / beak; (iii) amphibian – moist skin with no scales; (iv) fish – scales and fins / gills; (v) mammal – fur/hair / mammary glands / external ears
parts.working: 1 mark each for group with a correct feature.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the kingdom to which each organism belongs:
(i) yeast
(ii) the bacterium that causes cholera
(iii) a mushroom
(iv) Amoeba, a single-celled organism with a nucleus that lives in ponds
(v) a mustard plant
parts.answer: (i) fungus (ii) prokaryote (iii) fungus (iv) protoctist (v) plant

practice.stem:
The scientific names of five mammals:
Panthera tigris (tiger)
Panthera leo (lion)
Felis catus (house cat)
Canis lupus (wolf)
Canis familiaris (dog)

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many different genera are shown in the list?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the animal in the list that is most closely related to the dog. Give a reason.
parts.answer: wolf; it is in the same genus, Canis

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the second word of each name shows.
parts.answer: the species

practice.stem:
A student examined four flowering plants and recorded her observations.
plant | number of petals | leaf veins
P | 3 | parallel
Q | 5 | branching network
R | 6 | parallel
S | 4 | branching network

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each plant as a monocotyledon or a dicotyledon.
parts.answer: P monocot; Q dicot; R monocot; S dicot

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other feature, not in the table, that could be used to check whether a plant is a monocotyledon.
parts.answer: one cotyledon in the seed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Frogs and lizards both have four limbs. Give two features that distinguish a frog (an amphibian) from a lizard (a reptile).
parts.answer: frog has moist skin without scales, lizard has dry scaly skin; frog lays soft eggs (spawn) in water, lizard lays eggs with leathery shells on land; frog larvae (tadpoles) have gills
parts.working: 1 mark each for two valid differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature shared by all vertebrates.
parts.answer: a backbone (vertebral column)

practice.stem:
A student used this key to identify animals caught in a net in a pond.
1 (a) has jointed legs … go to 2
1 (b) no jointed legs … go to 4
2 (a) has 3 pairs of legs … go to 3
2 (b) has more than 3 pairs of legs … water mite
3 (a) has 3 tails at the end of the body … mayfly nymph
3 (b) has 2 tails or none … water beetle larva
4 (a) has a shell … pond snail
4 (b) no shell … flatworm

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Identify each animal:
(i) jointed legs, 3 pairs of legs, 3 tails
(ii) no jointed legs, no shell
(iii) jointed legs, 4 pairs of legs
(iv) no jointed legs, coiled shell
parts.answer: (i) mayfly nymph (ii) flatworm (iii) water mite (iv) pond snail

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how many steps of the key are needed to identify the water beetle larva.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the characteristic of living organisms shown in each example:
(i) a Venus fly-trap leaf snaps shut when an insect touches it
(ii) a yeast cell produces a bud that separates as a new cell
(iii) human kidneys remove urea from the blood
(iv) a goat eats grass
parts.answer: (i) sensitivity (movement accepted) (ii) reproduction (iii) excretion (iv) nutrition

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which features does a spider have?
A 3 body parts, 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae
B 2 body parts, 4 pairs of legs, no antennae
C 2 body parts, 5 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae
D many body segments, many pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae
parts.answer: B 2 body parts, 4 pairs of legs, no antennae
parts.working: Spiders are arachnids: two body parts, four pairs of legs and no antennae. A describes an insect; C a crustacean; D a myriapod.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An animal has moist skin without scales. It lays eggs in water and its young have gills. To which group does it belong?
A fish
B reptiles
C amphibians
D birds
parts.answer: C amphibians
parts.working: Moist scaleless skin, eggs laid in water and larvae (tadpoles) with gills are amphibian features. Fish (A) have scales and keep their gills as adults.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is characteristic of organisms in the fungus kingdom?
A cells contain chloroplasts
B cells have no nucleus
C they feed by secreting enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products
D cell walls are made of cellulose
parts.answer: C they feed by secreting enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products
parts.working: Fungi feed saprotrophically by extracellular digestion. Cellulose walls (D) and chloroplasts (A) are plant features; fungal cells do have a nucleus.

practice.stem:
Key:
1 (a) has antennae … go to 2
1 (b) has no antennae … spider
2 (a) has 3 pairs of legs … butterfly
2 (b) has more than 3 pairs of legs … go to 3
3 (a) has 2 pairs of antennae … woodlouse
3 (b) has 1 pair of antennae … centipede
Animals found in a garden in Faisalabad:
E: 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae, 2 pairs of wings
F: 4 pairs of legs, no antennae
G: 7 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae, hard grey exoskeleton
H: long body with about 20 segments, 1 pair of legs on each segment, 1 pair of antennae

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify animals E, F, G and H.
parts.answer: E butterfly; F spider; G woodlouse; H centipede

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the arthropod group to which F and G each belong.
parts.answer: F arachnid; G crustacean

practice.stem:
Key:
1 (a) fruit has wings … go to 2
1 (b) fruit has no wings … go to 3
2 (a) one wing … J
2 (b) two wings … K
3 (a) fruit is fleshy … go to 4
3 (b) fruit is dry with hooks … N
4 (a) one large seed … L
4 (b) many seeds … M

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Use the key to give the letter for each fruit.
(i) a mango: fleshy, with one large seed
(ii) a guava: fleshy, with many small seeds
(iii) a dry fruit covered in tiny hooks
(iv) a dry fruit with two wings
parts.answer: (i) L; (ii) M; (iii) N; (iv) K

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why each step of the key has exactly two statements.
parts.answer: Each step is a pair of contrasting statements, so every fruit fits only one of them and is sent along one route to a single end-point (a dichotomous key).
parts.working: B1 two contrasting/opposite statements so each organism fits only one / dichotomous.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A prawn is a crustacean and a locust is an insect. Give three ways in which a prawn differs from a locust.
parts.answer: Prawn has two pairs of antennae (locust one pair); prawn has more than four pairs of legs (locust three pairs); prawn has no wings (locust has wings); prawn body is cephalothorax and abdomen (locust head, thorax, abdomen).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three comparisons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Both animals have an exoskeleton. State one other feature they share.
parts.answer: jointed legs / segmented body

practice.stem: Bacteria are single-celled organisms. Some live in the soil of a rice field in Punjab.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the kingdom to which bacteria belong.
parts.answer: prokaryotes (prokaryote kingdom)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two structures found in a plant cell that are not found in a bacterial cell.
parts.answer: Any two: nucleus; mitochondria; chloroplasts; large permanent vacuole; cellulose cell wall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two structures that are found in a bacterial cell.
parts.answer: Any two: cell wall; cell membrane; cytoplasm; ribosomes; circular DNA; plasmids.

practice.stem: Ferns grow on the shady, damp banks of streams in the Murree hills, while flowering plants such as wild roses grow nearby.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ferns and flowering plants are both in the plant kingdom. State two features shared by all plants.
parts.answer: Cells with cellulose cell walls; chloroplasts / photosynthesis; multicellular.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features that distinguish ferns from flowering plants.
parts.answer: Ferns have no flowers; they reproduce by spores not seeds; leaves called fronds.

practice.stem: Fruit bats roost in large trees in Lahore and fly out at dusk to feed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bat flies like a bird. State three features that show it is a mammal.
parts.answer: Fur/hair; external ears (pinnae); mammary glands / feeds young on milk; (whiskers).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature a bird has that a bat does not.
parts.answer: feathers / a beak / lays hard-shelled eggs

practice.stem:
Key to some animals of Pakistan:
1 (a) breathes with gills as an adult … mahseer
1 (b) breathes with lungs … go to 2
2 (a) has feathers … peacock
2 (b) has no feathers … go to 3
3 (a) has mammary glands … go to 4
3 (b) has no mammary glands … go to 5
4 (a) lives in rivers, has flippers … Indus river dolphin
4 (b) lives on mountains, has horns … markhor
5 (a) dry skin with scales … mugger crocodile
5 (b) moist skin without scales … bullfrog

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify the animal that ends at statement 5 (b).
parts.answer: bullfrog

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of the statement that separates the Indus river dolphin from the markhor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The Indus river dolphin lives in water and has fins, like a mahseer fish. Explain why it is classified as a mammal, not a fish.
parts.answer: It feeds its young on milk from mammary glands; it breathes air with lungs, not gills; it has no scales.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three (mammary glands/milk must be one of them for full marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An animal has a long body made of many segments, a pair of jointed legs on almost every segment and one pair of antennae. To which arthropod group does it belong?
A arachnids
B crustaceans
C insects
D myriapods
parts.answer: D myriapods
parts.working: Myriapods (centipedes, millipedes) have many segments with legs on each and one pair of antennae. Crustaceans have two pairs of antennae, so B is the main distractor.

practice.stem: Plasmodium (which causes malaria), Amoeba and Chlorella (a green alga made of single cells) are all protoctists.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State one feature shared by all three organisms that shows they are not prokaryotes.
parts.answer: their cells have a nucleus (they are eukaryotic)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Chlorella has chloroplasts. Explain why it is not placed in the plant kingdom.
parts.answer: It is single-celled; plants are multicellular.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the protoctist kingdom is described as very varied.
parts.answer: It contains some organisms like animals (Amoeba, feeding on others) and some like plants (Chlorella, photosynthesising); it groups organisms that do not fit other kingdoms.
parts.working: 1 mark: some animal-like, some plant-like; 1 mark: example or idea of 'leftover' group.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Copy and complete the table using ✓ (present) or ✗ (absent).
feature | bacterial cell | animal cell
nucleus | | 
cell membrane | | 
circular DNA (loop of DNA) in cytoplasm | | 
plasmids | | 
ribosomes | | 
mitochondria | |
parts.answer: nucleus ✗ ✓; cell membrane ✓ ✓; circular DNA ✓ ✗; plasmids ✓ ✗; ribosomes ✓ ✓; mitochondria ✗ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the kingdom that contains bacteria.
parts.answer: prokaryote (prokaryotae)

practice.stem:
A student collected one leaf from each of five trees, V to Z, in a park in Lahore and recorded these descriptions.
V: simple, heart-shaped, long pointed tip, smooth edge
W: compound, 9–15 leaflets with toothed edges
X: simple, long and narrow, curved like a sickle, smooth edge
Y: compound, 3–5 large rounded leaflets with smooth edges
Z: compound, 8–16 leaflets with smooth edges
Key:
1 (a) leaf is simple … go to 2
1 (b) leaf is compound … go to 3
2 (a) leaf is heart-shaped … peepal
2 (b) leaf is long and narrow … eucalyptus
3 (a) leaflets have toothed edges … neem
3 (b) leaflets have smooth edges … go to 4
4 (a) fewer than 6 leaflets … shisham
4 (b) 6 or more leaflets … amaltas

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the key to identify trees V, W, X, Y and Z.
parts.answer: V peepal; W neem; X eucalyptus; Y shisham; Z amaltas

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the numbers of all the statements used to identify leaf Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the number of leaflets is not always a good feature to use in a key.
parts.answer: The number varies between leaves of the same tree / leaflets may have fallen off / ranges might overlap.

practice.stem: A student found two small animals on a goat in a village near Sargodha. Animal 1 had 4 pairs of legs, a body in two parts and no antennae. Animal 2 had 3 pairs of legs, a body in three parts, one pair of antennae and no wings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the arthropod group to which each animal belongs.
parts.answer: animal 1 arachnid; animal 2 insect

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature, seen in both animals, that shows they are arthropods.
parts.answer: jointed legs / exoskeleton / segmented body

parts.label: c
parts.text: Animal 2 had no wings. Explain why it is still classified as an insect.
parts.answer: It has the other insect features – three body parts, three pairs of legs and one pair of antennae; not all insects have wings.

practice.stem: Woodlice live under stones and damp leaves on land. A woodlouse has an exoskeleton, seven pairs of jointed legs and two pairs of antennae (one pair is very small).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the arthropod group to which woodlice belong. Give two reasons from the description.
parts.answer: crustaceans; two pairs of antennae; more than four pairs of legs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Most animals in this group live in water. Explain why a woodlouse is still placed in it.
parts.answer: Classification is based on body features/structure, not on habitat.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the total number of legs of a woodlouse.

practice.stem: A centipede has one pair of legs on each body segment. A millipede has two pairs of legs on most segments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A centipede has 21 leg-bearing segments. Calculate how many legs it has.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A millipede has 4 segments with one pair of legs each and 30 segments with two pairs each. Calculate how many legs it has.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the arthropod group that includes centipedes and millipedes.
parts.answer: myriapods

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says that passing faeces is an example of excretion. Explain why this is incorrect.
parts.answer: Faeces are mainly undigested food that has never been absorbed into cells; excretion is removal of toxic waste products of metabolism (e.g. urea, carbon dioxide) and excess substances.
parts.working: 1 mark: faeces not made by metabolism / never inside cells (egestion); 1 mark: definition of excretion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one substance excreted by the lungs and one excreted by the kidneys.
parts.answer: lungs: carbon dioxide; kidneys: urea (or excess water / salts)

practice.stem: The ostrich is the largest living bird. It cannot fly, but it can run at up to 70 km per hour.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the ostrich is classified as a bird even though it cannot fly.
parts.answer: It has the features of birds – feathers, a beak, wings (although small) and lays hard-shelled eggs; classification uses body features, not ability to fly.
parts.working: 1 mark: named bird features (any two); 1 mark: classification not based on flight.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature that birds share with reptiles.
parts.answer: scales (on the legs of birds) / lay eggs with shells on land / breathe with lungs / backbone

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the comparison of three kingdoms by giving one correct entry for each feature in each kingdom.
feature: cell wall made of …; how food is obtained; storage carbohydrate
kingdoms: plant, fungus, animal
parts.answer: plant: cellulose wall, photosynthesis, starch (and sucrose); fungus: cell wall (not cellulose, e.g. chitin), saprotrophic – secretes enzymes onto food and absorbs products, glycogen; animal: no cell wall, feed on other organisms (ingest), glycogen
parts.working: 1 mark per kingdom with all three entries correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says mushrooms are plants because they grow out of the soil and do not move. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Mushrooms have no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise; they feed on dead organic matter by external digestion and are made of hyphae.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which feature is typical of a monocotyledon such as wheat?
A two cotyledons in each seed
B leaves with a branching network of veins
C flower parts in multiples of three
D flower parts in multiples of five
parts.answer: C flower parts in multiples of three
parts.working: Monocots have one cotyledon, parallel leaf veins and flower parts in threes. D (multiples of four or five) and B are dicotyledon features.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure is found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells but is NOT found in a virus?
A ribosomes
B a nucleus
C a cell wall
D genetic material
parts.answer: A ribosomes
parts.working: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells both have ribosomes (as well as cytoplasm and a cell membrane); a virus has only a protein coat and genetic material. B is wrong because prokaryotic cells have no nucleus; C is wrong because animal cells have no cell wall; D is wrong because viruses do contain DNA or RNA.

practice.stem:
Leaf A: simple, smooth edge, parallel veins
Leaf B: compound (divided into leaflets), leaflets with toothed edges
Leaf C: simple, toothed edge, branching veins
Leaf D: compound, leaflets with smooth edges

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify leaves A, B, C and D. Use only features given in the descriptions.
parts.answer: 1 (a) leaf divided into leaflets (compound) … go to 2; (b) leaf not divided (simple) … go to 3. 2 (a) leaflets with toothed edges … B; (b) leaflets with smooth edges … D. 3 (a) parallel veins … A; (b) branching (net) veins … C.
parts.working: B1 first split uses a feature dividing the four into 2 + 2 (or 1 + 3); B1 each statement is a pair of contrasting statements; B1 correct observable features used throughout; B1 every leaf identified correctly with one end-point each.

practice.stem:
The base sequence of the same 300-base section of a gene was compared in four species of bird. Number of bases that differ from species W:
X: 6
Y: 27
Z: 45

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of bases that differ between species W and each of X, Y and Z.
parts.working: M1 number different ÷ 300 × 100; A1 all three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which species is most closely related to W. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: X – it has the smallest difference in base sequence, so it shared a common ancestor with W most recently.
parts.working: B1 X; B1 fewest differences / most recent common ancestor.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why scientists now use DNA base sequences as well as visible features to classify organisms.
parts.answer: Visible features can be similar in unrelated organisms (e.g. due to similar habitats); DNA sequences show evolutionary relationships more accurately.
parts.working: B1 visible features can mislead; B1 DNA reflects evolutionary relationship / common ancestry.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the structure of a virus.
parts.answer: Genetic material (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat.
parts.working: B1 genetic material / DNA or RNA; B1 protein coat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They are not made of cells (no cytoplasm, cell membrane or ribosomes); they cannot carry out the characteristics of life (respiration, nutrition, excretion, growth) on their own; they can only reproduce inside a host cell.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3: not cells; no cytoplasm/ribosomes/membrane; no respiration/nutrition/excretion; reproduce only inside living host cells.

practice.stem:
A student wrote this key for five beetles collected in a park:
1 Is it large? yes … go to 2; no … go to 3
2 Is it pretty? yes … beetle A; no … beetle B
3 Is it dark? yes … beetle C; no … go to 4
4 Is it fast? yes … beetle D; no … beetle E

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the questions in this key are not suitable, and suggest a better question for step 1.
parts.answer: 'Large' and 'pretty' are subjective / depend on the person; size varies with age; colours may change; better: 'Does it have wings?' or 'Does it have more than three pairs of legs?' (an observable, countable feature).
parts.working: B1 features are opinions / not measurable; B1 size varies with age or individual; B1 two contrasting statements needed at each step; B1 a suitable observable alternative question.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other rules for a good dichotomous key.
parts.answer: Each step has only two choices; each organism appears at only one end-point; use features that are present in all specimens / visible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Birds and reptiles both lay eggs with shells on land. Give two features that can be used to tell a bird from a reptile.
parts.answer: Birds have feathers; a beak; front limbs as wings; hard (chalky) eggshells, whereas reptiles have dry scales over the whole body and rubbery/leathery eggshells.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two contrasts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Birds have scales on their legs. Explain why this does not make them reptiles.
parts.answer: Classification uses several features; birds have feathers and a beak, which reptiles lack.

practice.stem: A scientist found a new organism growing on dead leaves in a forest in Swat. It is multicellular and made of thread-like hyphae. Its cells have nuclei and cell walls that are not made of cellulose, but no chloroplasts. It releases enzymes onto the dead leaves and absorbs the products.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the kingdom to which this organism belongs.
parts.answer: fungi (fungus kingdom)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons from the description why it is not a plant.
parts.answer: No chloroplasts / cannot photosynthesise; cell walls not made of cellulose.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason from the description why it is not an animal.
parts.answer: It has cell walls / it is made of hyphae.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe its type of nutrition.
parts.answer: It secretes enzymes onto dead leaves (extracellular digestion) and absorbs the soluble products (saprotrophic).
parts.working: B1 enzymes secreted outside onto food; B1 products absorbed.

practice.stem:
housefly: 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae, 1 pair of wings
butterfly: 3 pairs of legs, 1 pair of antennae, 2 pairs of wings
spider: 4 pairs of legs, no antennae, no wings, no tail
scorpion: 4 pairs of legs, no antennae, no wings, a long tail with a sting
crab: 5 pairs of legs, 2 pairs of antennae, no wings

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify these five arthropods. Use only the features given.
parts.answer: 1 (a) has wings … go to 2; (b) no wings … go to 3. 2 (a) one pair of wings … housefly; (b) two pairs of wings … butterfly. 3 (a) has antennae … crab; (b) no antennae … go to 4. 4 (a) has a tail with a sting … scorpion; (b) no tail … spider.
parts.working: B1 first split divides the group with a clear feature (e.g. wings); B1 pairs of contrasting statements at each step; B1 four steps for five animals; B1 only given observable features used; B1 every animal reaches one end-point correctly.

practice.stem:
These are descriptions of five vertebrates:
blue shark: scales, fins, breathes with gills
common frog: moist skin without scales, no fur or feathers, adult breathes with lungs
monitor lizard: dry scaly skin, no fur or feathers
pigeon: feathers
fruit bat: fur, wings

parts.label: a
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify these five animals. Use only features given in the descriptions.
parts.answer: e.g. 1 (a) has fins and gills … blue shark; (b) no fins or gills … 2. 2 (a) has feathers … pigeon; (b) no feathers … 3. 3 (a) has fur … fruit bat; (b) no fur … 4. 4 (a) skin dry and scaly … monitor lizard; (b) skin moist without scales … common frog.
parts.working: 1 mark: each step has two contrasting statements; 1 mark: uses only given features; 1 mark: four steps (n − 1); 1 mark: every animal correctly reached.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why 'has wings' would be a poor first question for separating the pigeon from the fruit bat.
parts.answer: Both animals have wings, so the question would not separate them.

practice.stem:
A student wrote this key to identify four small animals found under logs in a garden.
1 (a) has 6 or more legs … go to 2
1 (b) has 8 legs … spider
2 (a) has wings … beetle
2 (b) has many legs … go to 3
3 (a) one pair of legs on each segment … centipede
3 (b) two pairs of legs on each segment … millipede

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why step 1 does not work correctly.
parts.answer: An animal with 8 legs also has '6 or more legs', so both statements are true for the spider; the two statements are not mutually exclusive.
parts.working: 1 mark: both statements true for 8 legs; 1 mark: statements must be opposite / exclusive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is wrong with step 2.
parts.answer: The two statements are about different features (wings and number of legs), so an animal could fit both or neither.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Rewrite steps 1 and 2 so that the key works.
parts.answer: 1 (a) has 8 legs … spider; 1 (b) does not have 8 legs … go to 2. 2 (a) has 6 legs … beetle; 2 (b) has more than 6 legs … go to 3.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correctly rewritten step with contrasting statements on one feature.

practice.stem:
Scientists compared the amino acid sequence of the same protein in humans and five other organisms. The table shows the number of amino acids that are different from the human protein (data simplified).
organism | chimpanzee | rhesus monkey | dog | chicken | yeast
number of differences | 0 | 1 | 11 | 13 | 44

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which organism is most closely related to humans and give a reason.
parts.answer: chimpanzee; no differences in the sequence, so the most similar DNA / most recent common ancestor

parts.label: b
parts.text: The protein is 104 amino acids long. Calculate the percentage of amino acids that are the same in the chicken and human protein. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Dolphins and sharks have a similar body shape and fins, but dolphins are mammals and sharks are fish. Explain why sequence data can give a better classification than body shape.
parts.answer: Body shape can be similar because both are adapted to the same environment (swimming), not because they are related; sequences reflect inheritance / how recently they shared a common ancestor.
parts.working: 1 mark: similar features due to similar lifestyle; 1 mark: DNA/protein sequences show true relationships.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A typical bacterium is 2 µm long. A typical virus is 100 nm across. Calculate how many times longer the bacterium is than the virus. (1 µm = 1000 nm)
parts.answer: 20 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student says 'A virus is just a very small bacterium.' Give two reasons why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: A virus is not made of a cell (no cytoplasm, cell membrane, ribosomes); it has only a protein coat around genetic material; it can only reproduce inside a host cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why some biologists do not consider viruses to be living organisms.
parts.answer: They do not show the characteristics of life on their own – no respiration, nutrition, excretion or growth; they reproduce only inside other living cells.
parts.working: 1 mark: lack most characteristics; 1 mark: reproduce only in host cells.

practice.stem: A mule is the offspring of a female horse (Equus caballus) and a male donkey (Equus asinus). Mules are strong and are used to carry loads in mountain areas, but they are almost always unable to reproduce.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Use the definition of a species to explain why horses and donkeys are classified as different species.
parts.answer: A species can interbreed to produce fertile offspring; horses and donkeys produce mules, which are infertile.
parts.working: 1 mark: species definition; 1 mark: mule offspring infertile.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why horses and donkeys are able to produce offspring at all, even though they are different species.
parts.answer: They are very closely related (same genus, Equus), with similar DNA / chromosomes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a farmer who wants more mules must keep both horses and donkeys.
parts.answer: Mules cannot breed with each other, so each mule must come from a horse × donkey cross.

practice.stem: Euglena is a single-celled organism that lives in ponds. It has chloroplasts and can photosynthesise in the light, but in the dark it can take in food from the water. It has no cellulose cell wall and swims using a whip-like flagellum.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two features of Euglena that are like a plant and two that are like an animal.
parts.answer: plant-like: chloroplasts; photosynthesis. animal-like: no cell wall; moves from place to place / takes in food from surroundings

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest which kingdom Euglena belongs to and explain why.
parts.answer: protoctist; it is single-celled with a nucleus (eukaryotic) and has features of both plants and animals

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bacteria and yeast are both single-celled. Explain why they are placed in different kingdoms.
parts.answer: Yeast has a nucleus (and mitochondria) – eukaryotic – so it is a fungus; bacteria have no nucleus, DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm with plasmids – prokaryotic; kingdoms are based on cell structure, not just cell number.
parts.working: 1 mark: yeast has nucleus; 1 mark: bacteria have no nucleus / circular DNA / plasmids; 1 mark: kingdoms based on cell structure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why classification systems have changed as scientists have studied DNA.
parts.answer: DNA sequences show how closely organisms are related / their evolutionary relationships; some organisms that looked similar turned out not to be closely related, so they were moved.
parts.working: 1 mark: DNA shows relationships / common ancestry; 1 mark: some groups reorganised.

practice.stem:
A student measured four leaves from different shrubs in the school garden.
leaf | length / mm | width / mm | edge | hairs on surface
A | 86 | 20 | smooth | yes
B | 60 | 45 | toothed | no
C | 92 | 22 | smooth | no
D | 58 | 38 | toothed | yes

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the length ÷ width ratio for each leaf, to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Construct a dichotomous key to identify leaves A to D. Use features from the table.
parts.answer: e.g. 1 (a) edge smooth … go to 2; (b) edge toothed … go to 3. 2 (a) hairs present … A; (b) no hairs … C. 3 (a) hairs present … D; (b) no hairs … B.
parts.working: 1 mark: paired contrasting statements; 1 mark: three steps; 1 mark: all leaves correctly reached.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a key that uses 'leaf length more than 70 mm' might fail for other leaves from the same shrubs.
parts.answer: Leaf size varies within one plant (young/old leaves), so some leaves may fall on the wrong side of 70 mm.

practice.stem:
A student recorded features of five vertebrates.
animal | body covering | breathing organ of adult | eggs
J | scales | gills | soft, laid in water
K | moist skin | lungs (and skin) | soft, laid in water
L | dry scales | lungs | leathery shell, on land
M | feathers | lungs | hard shell, on land
N | fur | lungs | none – young born alive

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the vertebrate group of each animal J to N.
parts.answer: J fish; K amphibian; L reptile; M bird; N mammal

parts.label: b
parts.text: The duck-billed platypus has fur and feeds its young on milk, but it lays eggs. Explain which group it belongs to and why the table could mislead.
parts.answer: It is a mammal, because it has fur and mammary glands/milk; the table uses 'young born alive', which does not apply to every mammal.
parts.working: 1 mark: mammal with reason; 1 mark: egg-laying is an exception so one feature alone can mislead.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why biologists use several features, not just one, to place an animal in a group.
parts.answer: Single features can have exceptions / be shared by groups; several features give a more reliable classification.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why does bread dough rise when yeast is added and the dough is left in a warm place?
A Yeast produces ethanol, which evaporates and lifts the dough.
B Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in the dough.
C Yeast produces oxygen, which forms bubbles in the dough.
D Heat turns water in the flour into steam.
parts.answer: B Yeast respires and produces carbon dioxide, which forms bubbles in the dough.
parts.working: Yeast respires the sugars in the dough, releasing carbon dioxide gas that is trapped as bubbles. Ethanol (A) is made but it evaporates during baking and does not make the dough rise.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which enzyme is added to crushed fruit to increase the volume of juice extracted?
A amylase
B lipase
C pectinase
D protease
parts.answer: C pectinase
parts.working: Pectinase breaks down pectin in plant cell walls, so the cells release more juice and the juice is clearer. Amylase (A) digests starch, not the cell wall material that holds juice in.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three reasons why bacteria are useful in biotechnology and genetic modification.
parts.answer: Any three of: they reproduce rapidly; they can make complex molecules; there are few ethical concerns about growing them; they contain plasmids; they share the same genetic code as other organisms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why bread dough containing yeast is left in a warm place before baking.
parts.answer: Warmth gives a temperature near the optimum for yeast enzymes; so yeast respires faster and produces more carbon dioxide, making the dough rise faster.
parts.working: B1 enzymes near optimum temperature; B1 faster respiration/more CO₂

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what happens to the yeast and the ethanol when the bread is baked.
parts.answer: The yeast is killed by the high temperature; the ethanol evaporates.

practice.stem: A student boiled some glucose solution, let it cool to 35 °C, then added yeast. A layer of vegetable oil was poured on top. A delivery tube led from the flask into a test tube of limewater.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the glucose solution was boiled and then cooled before the yeast was added.
parts.answer: Boiling removes dissolved oxygen (and kills other microorganisms); cooling prevents the yeast being killed/its enzymes denatured by heat.
parts.working: B1 removes oxygen/sterilises; B1 cooled so yeast not killed

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a layer of oil was poured onto the surface of the mixture.
parts.answer: To stop oxygen from the air dissolving in the mixture, so respiration is anaerobic.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the limewater shows and the change you would see.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is produced; limewater turns milky/cloudy.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest how the student could measure the rate of respiration.
parts.answer: Count the number of bubbles entering the limewater per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of microorganism used to produce penicillin.
parts.answer: A fungus (Penicillium)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other product made on a large scale in fermenters.
parts.answer: Human insulin (by GM bacteria) / ethanol / enzymes such as pectinase or lactase / mycoprotein.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why penicillin is useful in medicine.
parts.answer: It is an antibiotic that kills (or stops the growth of) bacteria.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Sterile air is bubbled through a fermenter in which the fungus Penicillium makes penicillin. What is the main reason for adding the air?
A to supply oxygen for aerobic respiration
B to supply carbon dioxide for photosynthesis
C to cool the contents of the fermenter
D to keep the pH constant
parts.answer: A to supply oxygen for aerobic respiration
parts.working: Penicillium respires aerobically, so it needs oxygen. Fungi do not photosynthesise, so B is wrong; cooling is done by the water jacket.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzyme used to make lactose-free milk.
parts.answer: lactase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the two sugars produced when lactose is broken down.
parts.answer: glucose and galactose

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one type of organism from which this enzyme can be obtained on a large scale.
parts.answer: microorganisms such as yeasts, fungi or bacteria

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each of the following parts of a fermenter:
(i) the stirring paddles
(ii) the cold-water jacket
(iii) the filter on the air inlet
(iv) the pH probe
parts.answer: (i) mix nutrients/oxygen evenly and keep microorganisms in contact with them; (ii) remove heat released by respiration so temperature stays near optimum; (iii) remove microorganisms from incoming air to prevent contamination; (iv) measure pH so it can be kept at the optimum

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the nutrient medium contains a source of nitrogen such as ammonium salts.
parts.answer: Microorganisms need nitrogen to make proteins (for growth).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using a biological washing powder can save energy.
parts.answer: Its enzymes work at low temperatures (30–40 °C), so the water does not need to be heated as much.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the enzyme in the powder that removes greasy stains such as cooking oil.
parts.answer: lipase

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why biological washing powders are useful for delicate fabrics such as silk that would be damaged by hot water.
parts.answer: They remove stains at low temperatures, so hot water is not needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the organism or enzyme used to make each product:
(i) penicillin
(ii) ethanol for fuel from sugar
(iii) clear apple juice
(iv) lactose-free milk
parts.answer: (i) the fungus Penicillium (ii) yeast (iii) pectinase (iv) lactase

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Lactose-free milk is made by treating milk with an enzyme. Which row is correct?
A enzyme lactase; products glucose and galactose
B enzyme lactase; products glucose and fructose
C enzyme amylase; products glucose and galactose
D enzyme maltase; products glucose only
parts.answer: A enzyme lactase; products glucose and galactose
parts.working: Lactase breaks lactose (milk sugar) into glucose and galactose. Glucose and fructose (B) are the products of sucrose digestion, not lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An industrial fermenter has a jacket of cold water flowing around it. What is the main reason for this?
A to supply water as a raw material for the microorganisms
B to remove heat released by the respiring microorganisms and keep the optimum temperature
C to heat the contents so the microorganisms grow faster
D to keep the contents sterile
parts.answer: B to remove heat released by the respiring microorganisms and keep the optimum temperature
parts.working: Respiration by large numbers of microorganisms releases heat, which would denature their enzymes; the cold water jacket removes it. C is wrong because the jacket cools rather than heats.

practice.stem: In a sugar mill in Sindh, molasses from sugar cane is mixed with water and yeast in large tanks to make ethanol for use as a biofuel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the word equation for the anaerobic respiration of glucose by yeast.
parts.answer: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why air is kept out of the fermenter.
parts.answer: Ethanol is only produced in anaerobic respiration; if oxygen is present, yeast respires aerobically and produces carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol.
parts.working: B1 anaerobic respiration needed for ethanol; B1 with oxygen yeast respires aerobically (no ethanol)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of using ethanol made from sugar cane as a fuel instead of petrol.
parts.answer: It is a renewable fuel (sugar cane can be regrown) / reduces use of fossil fuels / the crop absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the enzymes in a biological washing powder that remove: (i) a blood or egg stain; (ii) a cooking oil stain.
parts.answer: (i) protease; (ii) lipase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why biological washing powders work well at 30–40 °C.
parts.answer: The enzymes are near their optimum temperature; so they digest the stains quickly into small soluble molecules that wash away (saving energy compared with a hot wash).
parts.working: B1 near optimum temperature; B1 faster digestion of stains / soluble products wash out

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a biological washing powder is less effective in a 90 °C wash.
parts.answer: At high temperature the enzymes are denatured; the active site changes shape so the stain molecules no longer fit.
parts.working: B1 denatured; B1 active site shape changed/substrate cannot bind

practice.stem: A dairy in Lahore treats milk with lactase. Before treatment the milk contains 4.8 g of lactose per 100 cm³. After treatment it contains 0.3 g of lactose per 100 cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the lactose that was broken down. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some people need to drink lactose-free milk.
parts.answer: They do not make enough lactase (lactose intolerance); undigested lactose causes stomach pain, gas or diarrhoea.
parts.working: B1 little/no lactase produced; B1 symptoms from undigested lactose

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why lactose-free milk tastes sweeter than ordinary milk.
parts.answer: Glucose and galactose taste sweeter than lactose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four conditions that are monitored and controlled inside a fermenter used to produce penicillin, and give a reason for controlling each.
parts.answer: Temperature – kept at the optimum for the fungus's enzymes; pH – kept at the optimum for enzymes; oxygen – supplied for aerobic respiration of the fungus; nutrients (glucose, ammonium/nitrogen source) – supplied for growth and energy; waste products removed – so they do not become toxic.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four conditions with reason

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the fermenter and nutrient medium are sterilised with steam before use.
parts.answer: To kill any unwanted microorganisms; which would compete with the fungus for nutrients or contaminate/spoil the product.
parts.working: B1 kill other microorganisms; B1 competition / contamination of product

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Pectinase is added to crushed mangoes to make juice. How does pectinase increase the volume of juice?
A It breaks down pectin, so cell walls break down and release more juice.
B It breaks down starch into sugars that dissolve in the juice.
C It makes the cells take in more water by osmosis.
D It breaks down protein in the cell membranes so the cells burst.
parts.answer: A It breaks down pectin, so cell walls break down and release more juice.
parts.working: Pectin holds plant cell walls together; breaking it down releases the cell contents. B describes amylase, not pectinase.

practice.stem: In one fuel plant, starch from crushed maize grains is mixed with water and the enzyme amylase. Yeast is then added and the tank is closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why amylase is added to the crushed maize before the yeast is added.
parts.answer: Yeast cannot use starch directly; amylase breaks starch down into sugars (maltose/glucose) that yeast can respire.
parts.working: 1 mark each: starch broken down to sugar; yeast uses sugar for respiration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of respiration the yeast carries out in the closed tank and state its two products.
parts.answer: anaerobic respiration; ethanol and carbon dioxide

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one disadvantage of using maize to make fuel in a country where many people are short of food.
parts.answer: Land and crops used for fuel are not used for food, so food may become scarcer / more expensive.

practice.stem:
A student cut squares of cotton cloth, each with an egg-yolk stain of the same size. Each square was placed in 100 cm³ of a biological washing powder solution at a different temperature, and the time for the stain to disappear was recorded.
temperature / °C | time to remove stain / min
20 | 18
30 | 12
40 | 7
50 | 10
60 | 25
70 | not removed after 30

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for this washing powder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times faster the stain was removed at 40 °C than at 20 °C. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 2.6 times

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the stain was not removed at 70 °C.
parts.answer: The protease is denatured; its active site changes shape so it no longer fits the protein substrate.
parts.working: 1 mark each: denatured; active site shape changed / substrate no longer fits.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: any two of: mass/concentration of powder, volume of water, size of cloth/stain, type/age of stain, amount of stirring

practice.stem:
Equal balls of dough made from flour, water, sugar and yeast were placed in measuring cylinders in water baths at different temperatures. The increase in volume of each dough after 30 minutes was recorded.
temperature / °C | increase in volume / cm³
10 | 4
20 | 10
30 | 22
40 | 30
50 | 14
60 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of rise of the dough at 40 °C, in cm³ per minute.
parts.answer: 1.0 cm³ per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of temperature on the rise of the dough.
parts.answer: Rise increases from 10 °C to a maximum at 40 °C; then falls, with no rise at 60 °C.
parts.working: 1 mark each: increase to peak at 40 °C; decrease above.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dough did not rise at 60 °C.
parts.answer: The yeast's enzymes are denatured (yeast killed), so no respiration and no carbon dioxide produced.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each temperature (at least three times) and calculate a mean.

practice.stem:
A student mixed 50 g of apple pulp with 2 cm³ of pectinase at different temperatures, then filtered for 20 minutes and measured the volume of juice. A control used boiled pectinase at 40 °C.
Temperature / °C: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
Volume of juice / cm³: 8, 14, 21, 17, 6
Control (boiled enzyme): 5 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the optimum temperature for pectinase in this experiment.
parts.answer: 40 °C (from these results)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a beaker of pulp with boiled pectinase was set up.
parts.answer: As a control; to show that the extra juice is due to the active enzyme (boiling denatures it).
parts.working: B1 control; B1 shows effect is due to active enzyme

parts.label: c
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume at 40 °C compared with the control. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why less juice was collected at 60 °C.
parts.answer: Pectinase was denatured at the high temperature; so less pectin was broken down and fewer cells released juice.
parts.working: B1 enzyme denatured; B1 less pectin broken down

parts.label: e
parts.text: Suggest how the student could find the optimum temperature more precisely.
parts.answer: Repeat with smaller temperature intervals between 30 °C and 50 °C (e.g. every 2 °C).

practice.stem:
The table shows changes in a penicillin fermenter.
Time / hours: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120
Fungal biomass / g per dm³: 1, 6, 14, 20, 21, 21, 20
Penicillin / units per cm³: 0, 0, 2, 10, 22, 31, 35

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the changes in biomass of the fungus over the 120 hours.
parts.answer: Biomass increases quickly from 1 g/dm³ to 20 g/dm³ by 60 hours; then levels off at about 21 g/dm³ and falls slightly to 20 g/dm³ by 120 hours.
parts.working: B1 rapid increase then levels off; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of penicillin production, in units per cm³ per hour, between 60 and 100 hours.
parts.answer: 0.525 units per cm³ per hour

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why most of the penicillin is produced after 60 hours.
parts.answer: Penicillin is made mainly when growth of the fungus has slowed; this happens when nutrients such as glucose start to run out.
parts.working: B1 produced after main growth phase; B1 when nutrients become limiting

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the fermentation is stopped at about 120 hours.
parts.answer: Penicillin production is slowing / nutrients are used up / the fungus is starting to die, so further time is not worth the cost.

practice.stem: A fermenter is started with 50 bacteria. In ideal conditions this species of bacterium divides once every 20 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many bacteria would be present after 4 hours, assuming every cell divides every 20 minutes.
parts.answer: 204 800 bacteria

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the number of bacteria in a real fermenter does not keep increasing at this rate.
parts.answer: Nutrients are used up; waste products (e.g. acids, toxins) build up and change pH; oxygen may become limiting/overcrowding; so the rate of division slows and some cells die.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: nutrients run out; toxic waste builds up; pH changes; oxygen/space limiting; death rate rises

practice.stem:
A student mixed 50 g of flour, 2 g of dried yeast and different masses of sugar with 30 cm³ of warm water. Each dough was pushed to the bottom of a measuring cylinder and the increase in volume was measured after 30 minutes.
Mass of sugar / g: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8
Increase in volume / cm³: 4, 12, 20, 24, 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect of sugar mass on the increase in dough volume.
parts.answer: As the mass of sugar increases the volume increase rises, from 4 cm³ with no sugar to 24 cm³ at 6 g; above 6 g it levels off (25 cm³ at 8 g).
parts.working: B1 increases then levels off; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of increase in volume, in cm³ per minute, for the dough with 4 g of sugar. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.67 cm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the dough with no sugar still increased in volume a little.
parts.answer: Yeast respired some sugars already in the flour (made from starch by amylase).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why increasing the sugar from 6 g to 8 g had little effect.
parts.answer: Sugar is no longer the limiting factor; another factor such as the amount of yeast or temperature limits the rate of respiration.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Describe how the student could keep the temperature the same for all the cylinders.
parts.answer: Stand all the cylinders in the same thermostatically controlled water bath (e.g. at 35 °C).

parts.label: f
parts.text: Suggest one improvement to make the results more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each sugar mass three times and calculate a mean.

practice.stem: A company grows genetically modified bacteria in a 10 000 dm³ fermenter. At the end of a batch the broth contains 1.2 g of insulin per dm³. Only 70% of this insulin is recovered when it is purified.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of purified insulin, in kg, obtained from one batch.
parts.answer: 8.4 kg

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the contents of the fermenter are stirred continuously.
parts.answer: Mixes nutrients so all bacteria can obtain them; spreads oxygen evenly for aerobic respiration; spreads heat evenly so there are no hot spots that denature enzymes; keeps bacteria suspended.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why probes for pH and temperature are connected to a computer.
parts.answer: So that changes are detected quickly and corrected automatically, keeping conditions at the optimum.

practice.stem: Genetically modified bacteria are grown at 30 °C in a fermenter to make a protein. During one run the cooling water stopped flowing. The temperature rose from 30 °C to 42 °C in 6 hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of temperature rise when the cooling failed, in °C per hour.
parts.answer: 2.0 °C per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the temperature of the fermenter rises when the cooling water stops.
parts.answer: The bacteria respire; respiration releases (heat) energy that is not removed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest and explain the effect of the rise to 42 °C on the production of the protein.
parts.answer: Production slows or stops; the bacteria's enzymes are moving away from their optimum / start to denature, so growth and protein synthesis decrease (cells may die).
parts.working: 1 mark each: less product; enzymes above optimum/denatured.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The pH probe shows that the pH falls during the run. Suggest why, and what is done about it.
parts.answer: Waste products (acids, carbon dioxide) from respiration build up; alkali/buffer is added automatically to keep pH at the optimum.

practice.stem:
Yeast was added to sugar-cane juice in a sealed fermentation tank. The concentration of ethanol was measured.
time / hours | 0 | 12 | 24 | 36 | 48 | 60
ethanol / % | 0 | 2 | 6 | 10 | 12 | 12

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean rate of ethanol production between 12 hours and 36 hours, in % per hour. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
parts.answer: 0.33 % per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why there is very little ethanol in the first 12 hours.
parts.answer: The yeast population is small at first / still adapting (lag phase); so little respiration takes place / yeast may use oxygen still present for aerobic respiration.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible points.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why the ethanol concentration stops rising after 48 hours.
parts.answer: Sugar is used up; ethanol reaches a concentration that is toxic and kills/inhibits the yeast.

practice.stem:
Equal masses of chopped guava were mixed with pectinase solutions of different concentrations and left at 40 °C for 15 minutes. The pulp was then filtered for 10 minutes.
pectinase concentration / % | 0 | 0.5 | 1.0 | 1.5 | 2.0
volume of juice / cm³ | 12 | 20 | 26 | 29 | 29

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in juice volume when 1.0 % pectinase was used compared with no pectinase. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why some juice was collected with 0 % pectinase.
parts.answer: Crushing/chopping breaks open some cells so some juice is released anyway.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why increasing the concentration from 1.5 % to 2.0 % did not increase the volume of juice.
parts.answer: All the pectin (substrate) has already been broken down / pectin is now the limiting factor; so extra enzyme has nothing more to act on.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State why the juice collected with pectinase also looked clearer.
parts.answer: Pectin that makes juice cloudy has been broken down.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why air is bubbled into a fermenter making penicillin but kept out of a tank making ethanol.
parts.answer: Penicillium needs oxygen for aerobic respiration to grow and make penicillin; ethanol is a product of anaerobic respiration by yeast; if oxygen were present yeast would respire aerobically; and make carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol.
parts.working: 1 mark each for four of these points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why both fermenters must be sterilised before use.
parts.answer: To kill other microorganisms that would compete for nutrients / contaminate the product.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is meant by genetic modification?
A changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes
B choosing parents with useful features and breeding them over many generations
C producing genetically identical offspring by asexual reproduction
D a random change in the base sequence of DNA
parts.answer: A changing the genetic material of an organism by removing, changing or inserting individual genes
parts.working: Genetic modification alters individual genes directly. B describes selective breeding, which works with whole organisms over many generations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three examples of genetic modification.
parts.answer: Any three of: bacteria producing human insulin; crop plants resistant to herbicides; crop plants resistant to insect pests; crops with added vitamins (e.g. rice containing β-carotene).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a plasmid.
parts.answer: A small circle (loop) of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a recombinant plasmid.
parts.answer: A plasmid that contains a gene from another organism inserted into it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of enzyme used to cut open a plasmid.
parts.answer: Restriction enzyme

practice.stem:
The steps below describe how bacteria are modified to make a human protein, but they are in the wrong order.
P – The human gene is cut out using a restriction enzyme.
Q – The modified bacteria multiply in a fermenter.
R – The gene is joined into the plasmid using DNA ligase.
S – A plasmid is cut open with the same restriction enzyme.
T – The protein is extracted and purified.
U – The recombinant plasmid is put into a bacterium.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Put steps P to U in the correct order, starting with P.
parts.answer: P, S, R, U, Q, T
parts.working: 3 marks all correct; 2 marks one step out of place; 1 mark two steps out of place

parts.label: a
parts.text:
What is the function of a restriction enzyme in genetic modification?
A to cut DNA at a specific sequence of bases
B to join two pieces of DNA together
C to make many copies of a plasmid
D to break down unwanted proteins in the bacterium
parts.answer: A to cut DNA at a specific sequence of bases
parts.working: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at particular base sequences, leaving sticky ends. Joining DNA (B) is done by DNA ligase.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the passage using words from the list. Each word may be used once.
bacterium   ligase   plasmid   restriction   sticky   gene

The human ...(1)... for insulin is cut out of a chromosome using a ...(2)... enzyme. The same enzyme cuts open a ...(3)..., a small ring of DNA, leaving ...(4)... ends. The enzyme DNA ...(5)... joins the human DNA into the ring, which is then put into a ...(6)....
parts.answer: (1) gene (2) restriction (3) plasmid (4) sticky (5) ligase (6) bacterium
parts.working: 3 marks for all six correct; 2 marks for four or five; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each example of genetic modification, state one benefit to people.
(i) bacteria that make human insulin
(ii) crop plants that are resistant to a herbicide (weedkiller)
(iii) crop plants that make their own insecticide
(iv) rice that contains extra vitamin A (β-carotene)
parts.answer: (i) large, reliable supply of human insulin for people with diabetes; (ii) farmer can spray weeds without killing the crop, so higher yield; (iii) less damage by insects / fewer insecticide sprays needed; (iv) reduces vitamin A deficiency (night blindness) in people who eat mostly rice

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two differences between genetic modification and selective breeding.
parts.answer: GM changes genes directly in a lab, selective breeding chooses parents with wanted features; GM can move genes between different species, selective breeding only within a species (that can interbreed); GM gives results faster (one generation) than selective breeding (many generations).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of a crop plant that could be produced by either method.
parts.answer: e.g. resistance to a pest or disease / higher yield

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each genetically modified organism, state the type of organism that the inserted gene came from.
(i) bacteria that make human insulin
(ii) insect-resistant cotton (Bt cotton)
parts.answer: (i) human (ii) a bacterium (Bacillus thuringiensis)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a gene from one species can work in a completely different species.
parts.answer: All organisms use the same genetic code (DNA with the same four bases coding for amino acids).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what the inserted gene in Bt cotton makes the plant produce.
parts.answer: a protein that is poisonous to insect larvae (caterpillars) that eat it

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In genetic modification, which enzyme joins a human gene into a bacterial plasmid?
A restriction enzyme
B DNA ligase
C amylase
D protease
parts.answer: B DNA ligase
parts.working: DNA ligase joins the sticky ends of the gene and plasmid together. Restriction enzymes (A) cut DNA; they do not join it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Outline how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
parts.answer: The human insulin gene is cut out of human DNA using a restriction enzyme; this leaves sticky ends; a bacterial plasmid is cut with the same restriction enzyme; the gene is inserted into the plasmid and joined with DNA ligase; forming a recombinant plasmid; the plasmid is taken up by bacteria; the bacteria multiply in a fermenter and express the gene, making insulin which is extracted and purified.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: restriction enzyme cuts out gene; sticky ends; plasmid cut with same enzyme; ligase joins; recombinant plasmid; inserted into bacteria; bacteria multiply/fermenter; gene expressed/insulin produced and purified

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the same restriction enzyme must be used to cut both the human DNA and the plasmid.
parts.answer: It produces matching (complementary) sticky ends; so the bases on the gene and plasmid pair up and can be joined.
parts.working: B1 same/complementary sticky ends; B1 bases pair so they join

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a sticky end.
parts.answer: A short single-stranded length of DNA (unpaired bases) left at the end of a cut piece of DNA.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how growing herbicide-resistant soya benefits a farmer.
parts.answer: The farmer can spray herbicide over the whole field to kill weeds without killing the crop; so less competition for light, water and ions and a higher yield.
parts.working: B1 herbicide kills weeds not crop; B1 less competition → higher yield

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one risk of growing herbicide-resistant crops.
parts.answer: The resistance gene could spread by pollen to wild relatives producing herbicide-resistant weeds (or more herbicide used, harming other plants and reducing biodiversity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'GM bacteria make human insulin because they have human DNA inside them.' Explain what else must happen for the bacterium to make insulin.
parts.answer: The inserted gene must be expressed: the bacterium copies (transcribes) the gene and uses the code to join amino acids in the right order at its ribosomes, forming the insulin protein.
parts.working: B1 gene expressed/code read; B1 amino acids joined in correct sequence at ribosomes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why bacteria, rather than human cells, are used to produce insulin on a large scale.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce very rapidly, so large numbers are produced quickly; they are easy and cheap to grow in fermenters (few ethical concerns).
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction; B1 cheap/easy to grow / no ethical concerns

parts.label: a
parts.text: A recombinant plasmid containing the human insulin gene has been made. Describe how this is used to produce large quantities of insulin.
parts.answer: Plasmids are taken up by (inserted into) bacteria; the bacteria are grown in a fermenter with nutrients at optimum conditions; they reproduce rapidly, copying the plasmid each time; the bacteria express the gene / make insulin; insulin is extracted and purified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the insulin made by the bacteria is exactly the same as human insulin.
parts.answer: It is made from the human gene / the same base sequence codes for the same sequence of amino acids.

practice.stem:
A farmer in Punjab compared two fields of maize. Field X was non-GM maize weeded by hand. Field Y was herbicide-resistant GM maize sprayed with weedkiller.
field | mean yield / tonnes per hectare
X (non-GM) | 6.2
Y (GM) | 7.4

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in yield of the GM maize compared with the non-GM maize. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why removing weeds increases the yield of maize.
parts.answer: Weeds compete with maize for light, water and mineral ions; with fewer weeds the maize photosynthesises and grows more.
parts.working: 1 mark each: competition for named resources; more growth/photosynthesis.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one reason why the farmer might not want to rely on the GM crop for many years.
parts.answer: Weeds may become resistant to the herbicide (by natural selection or by gaining the gene), so it stops working.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a brinjal (aubergine) plant can be modified to kill the fruit-and-shoot borer caterpillars that feed on it.
parts.answer: A gene for an insecticidal (toxic) protein is taken from a bacterium; it is inserted into the brinjal's DNA; the plant makes the protein in its cells, so caterpillars that eat the plant are poisoned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why growing this brinjal could be better for the environment than spraying chemical insecticides.
parts.answer: Only insects that eat the crop are affected, so useful insects such as bees and predators are not killed; fewer chemicals run off into soil and water.

parts.label: a
parts.text: One sticky end on the cut plasmid has the unpaired bases 5' to 3': AGTC. State the sequence of unpaired bases, written 5' to 3', on the sticky end of the human gene that pairs with it.
parts.answer: 5' to 3': GACT
parts.working: Pairing is A with T, G with C, T with A, C with G. The partner overhang is the reverse complement of AGTC, which is GACT written 5' to 3'. Accept GACT if the direction is given correctly; TCAG (written 3' to 5') is the same bases.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the human gene and the plasmid must have complementary sticky ends.
parts.answer: The unpaired bases on the two ends pair up (A with T, C with G); this holds the gene in place in the plasmid so ligase can join the DNA backbones.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the enzyme that seals the joins.
parts.answer: DNA ligase

practice.stem: A genetically modified rice contains about 25 µg of β-carotene in every gram of uncooked rice. The body converts β-carotene into vitamin A. In this question, assume a child's daily need for vitamin A is met by 1500 µg of β-carotene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of this rice that would supply 1500 µg of β-carotene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: 40 % of the β-carotene is lost during storage and cooking. Calculate the mass of rice that must now be eaten to supply 1500 µg.
parts.working: M1 25 × 0.6 = 15 µg per g remains; A1 1500 ÷ 15 = 100 g.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why it was thought useful to add β-carotene to rice rather than to another food.
parts.answer: Rice is the staple food eaten in large amounts every day by many people at risk of vitamin A deficiency.

practice.stem: A gene from the hepatitis B virus that codes for a protein on the virus surface has been put into yeast cells. The genetically modified yeast is grown in fermenters and the protein is purified and used as a vaccine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this vaccine cannot cause hepatitis B in the person who receives it.
parts.answer: It contains only one protein from the virus, not the whole virus / no viral genetic material; so it cannot reproduce/infect cells.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the role of the viral protein when it is injected.
parts.answer: It acts as an antigen, stimulating lymphocytes to make antibodies (and memory cells).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one advantage of making this protein in yeast rather than collecting it from the blood of infected people.
parts.answer: Large, reliable amounts can be made / no risk of passing on the virus or other blood-borne diseases.

practice.stem:
Cotton plants have been genetically modified to make a protein that is toxic to caterpillars which feed on them. Data from one cotton-growing district:
Before GM cotton: 12 insecticide sprays per season; yield 1.9 tonnes per ha
After GM cotton: 5 insecticide sprays per season; yield 2.4 tonnes per ha

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in the number of sprays and the percentage increase in yield. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: Sprays: 58.3% decrease; yield: 26.3% increase

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing insect-resistant genetically modified crops.
parts.answer: Advantages: less insecticide needed, saving money and reducing harm to farmers' health; fewer non-pest insects killed; higher yields/less crop damage, more food or income. Disadvantages: seeds may be expensive and must be bought each year; pests may evolve resistance to the toxin; genes may spread to wild relatives; reduced biodiversity if a single crop variety is grown widely; possible effects on non-target insects or on health not fully known.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side. 1 mark each for any six points across both sides: less insecticide; lower cost of spraying; safer for farmers/environment; higher yield; seed cost; pest resistance evolves; gene transfer to wild plants; reduced biodiversity; unknown long-term effects

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why rice has been genetically modified to contain β-carotene.
parts.answer: In some countries rice is the main food and people lack vitamin A; the body converts β-carotene into vitamin A, so the rice helps prevent vitamin A deficiency (which damages eyesight).
parts.working: B1 rice staple / diet lacks vitamin A; B1 β-carotene converted to vitamin A

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two concerns some people have about growing this rice.
parts.answer: Any two of: genes could transfer to wild rice varieties; farmers may depend on seed companies; effects on health not fully tested; reduced variety of crops grown; people may still lack other nutrients.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one alternative way of reducing vitamin A deficiency.
parts.answer: Encourage eating a varied diet with vegetables such as carrots and green leafy vegetables / vitamin supplements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before GM bacteria were used, insulin for people with diabetes was extracted from the pancreases of cattle and pigs. Explain the advantages of insulin produced by GM bacteria.
parts.answer: It is identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic reactions/side effects; it can be produced in large quantities; it is cheaper/supply does not depend on slaughtered animals; it avoids ethical and religious objections (e.g. pig products for Muslims, cattle products for Hindus).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a human gene can produce human insulin inside a bacterium.
parts.answer: The genetic code is the same (universal) in all organisms; the bacterium reads the same base triplets and joins the same amino acids in the same order.
parts.working: B1 genetic code universal; B1 same amino acid sequence made

practice.stem:
A trial compared genetically modified insect-resistant maize with non-GM maize.
Plants damaged by stem borer: GM field 3%; non-GM field 28%

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in plants damaged by the stem borer in the GM field compared with the non-GM field. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why 3% of the GM plants were still damaged.
