parts.answer: Some borers may be resistant to the toxin / some plants made less toxin / borers moved in from nearby non-GM plants.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Farmers are told to plant a strip of non-GM maize beside their GM maize. Explain how this slows down the evolution of resistance in the stem borer.
parts.answer: Non-resistant borers survive on the non-GM maize; they mate with any rare resistant borers from the GM field; so the resistance allele is diluted / resistant borers do not only breed with each other, and the allele does not increase quickly in frequency.
parts.working: B1 non-resistant borers survive in strip; B1 mate with resistant ones; B1 frequency of resistance allele rises more slowly

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A bacterium containing a recombinant plasmid with the human insulin gene divides into two. What happens to the plasmid?
A It is copied, so both new cells contain the insulin gene.
B It stays in one cell, so only half of the new cells contain the gene.
C It is cut up by restriction enzymes, so the gene is lost.
D It becomes part of the nucleus of each new cell.
parts.answer: A It is copied, so both new cells contain the insulin gene.
parts.working: Plasmids are copied before the bacterium divides, so every cell in the population carries the gene. D is wrong because bacteria have no nucleus.

practice.stem: Oilseed rape has been genetically modified to resist a herbicide. Wild plants closely related to oilseed rape grow at the edges of some fields and can breed with it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the herbicide-resistance gene could end up in the wild plants.
parts.answer: Pollen from the GM crop is carried (by wind or insects) to the wild plants; and fertilises them, so their offspring carry the gene.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this would be a problem for farmers.
parts.answer: The wild relatives become herbicide-resistant weeds ('superweeds'); the herbicide no longer kills them so they compete with crops.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one precaution to reduce the chance of this happening.
parts.answer: Leave a wide strip/distance between GM fields and wild plants, or grow GM crops where no close wild relatives grow.

practice.stem: Assume that a person with diabetes uses 40 units of insulin a day, and that one batch from a large fermenter of genetically modified bacteria produces 2.5 × 10⁹ units of insulin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many people one batch could supply with insulin for a whole year (365 days). Give your answer to the nearest thousand.
parts.answer: 171 000 people
parts.working: M1 40 × 365 = 14 600 units per person per year; A1 2.5 × 10⁹ ÷ 14 600 ≈ 171 000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two advantages of producing insulin in fermenters rather than extracting it from the pancreases of slaughtered animals.
parts.answer: Very large amounts can be made quickly; supply is reliable and not dependent on animals; it is identical to human insulin so fewer side-effects; acceptable to people who object to animal products (e.g. pork) for religious or ethical reasons; lower risk of passing on animal diseases.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
The restriction enzyme cuts DNA wherever it finds the base sequence GAATTC. A straight (linear) piece of human DNA has this sequence on one strand:
TTGAATTCGGCATGAATTCAAGGAATTCCT
State how many pieces of DNA will be produced when this piece is cut by the enzyme. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 4 pieces – there are 3 cutting sites, and cutting a straight piece of DNA in 3 places gives 4 pieces.
parts.working: B1 three sites; B1 four pieces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A plasmid is a ring of DNA with this sequence at only one place. State how many pieces the plasmid is cut into, and describe its shape after cutting.
parts.answer: one piece; the ring is opened into a single straight (linear) strand with sticky ends

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why scientists choose a restriction enzyme that cuts the plasmid in only one place.
parts.answer: So the plasmid is opened without losing any of its genes / it can be closed again around the inserted gene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A leaflet claims: 'GM food is dangerous because it contains genes.' Explain why this reason is not correct.
parts.answer: All food from living things (plants, animals) contains genes/DNA; DNA in food is digested in the gut like other DNA, so eating genes does not change our genes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one possible real concern about eating food from a GM crop, and how it could be checked.
parts.answer: The new protein made by the inserted gene might cause an allergy (or be harmful); it can be tested for safety/allergic reactions before the crop is approved.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one concern about GM crops that is about the environment rather than human health.
parts.answer: Genes may spread to wild plants / non-target insects may be harmed / loss of biodiversity / pests may become resistant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Farmers who grow herbicide-resistant crops can spray herbicide over the whole field during the growing season. Explain how this could reduce the number of insect-eating birds on farmland.
parts.answer: Almost all weeds are killed; so there is less food/habitat for insects that feed on the weeds; so fewer insects for birds to eat, and bird numbers fall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way a farmer could reduce this effect.
parts.answer: Leave unsprayed strips/field margins with wild plants, or use hedgerows as habitat.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which events happen when a person breathes in at rest?
A diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles contract
B diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards; external intercostal muscles contract
C diaphragm contracts and flattens; internal intercostal muscles contract
D diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards; internal intercostal muscles relax
parts.answer: A diaphragm contracts and flattens; external intercostal muscles contract
parts.working: In inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostals contract to pull the ribs up and out. B is wrong because a relaxed, domed diaphragm happens in expiration.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the movements of the diaphragm and the ribs when a person breathes in.
parts.answer: The diaphragm contracts and flattens (moves down); the ribs move upwards and outwards.
parts.working: B1 diaphragm contracts/flattens; B1 ribs up and out

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how these movements cause air to enter the lungs.
parts.answer: The volume of the thorax increases; so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure; air moves in through the trachea down the pressure gradient.
parts.working: B1 volume increases; B1 pressure decreases (below atmospheric); B1 air flows in from higher to lower pressure

parts.label: a
parts.text: List, in order, the structures that air passes through from the larynx to the alveoli.
parts.answer: Trachea → bronchus → bronchioles → alveoli
parts.working: 2 marks all in correct order; 1 mark if one error

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the function of the rings of cartilage in the trachea.
parts.answer: Keep the trachea open (stop it collapsing) when air pressure inside falls.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the cartilage rings are C-shaped and not complete circles.
parts.answer: So the oesophagus behind the trachea can expand when food is swallowed (and the trachea stays flexible).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which structure separates the thorax (chest cavity) from the abdomen?
A the diaphragm
B the sternum
C the intercostal muscles
D the trachea
parts.answer: A the diaphragm
parts.working: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of muscle and tendon that forms the floor of the thorax. The intercostal muscles (C) lie between the ribs, not between thorax and abdomen.

practice.stem:
Five students in a school in Faisalabad measured their chest circumference with a tape measure placed around the chest at the level of the nipples. Each student breathed in as far as possible and then breathed out as far as possible.
Student: A | B | C | D | E
After breathing in fully / cm: 88 | 92 | 85 | 95 | 90
After breathing out fully / cm: 83 | 86 | 81 | 88 | 85

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the chest expansion (difference between the two readings) for each student, and the mean chest expansion for the group.
parts.answer: Expansions: 5, 6, 4, 7, 5 cm; mean = 5.4 cm
parts.working: M1 subtract each pair: [5, 6, 4, 7, 5]; M1 add and divide by 5: 27 ÷ 5; A1 5.4 cm.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the chest circumference is larger after breathing in fully.
parts.answer: The external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs (and sternum) upwards and outwards, so the chest becomes wider.
parts.working: 1 mark: external intercostal muscles contract; 1 mark: ribs move up and out / volume of thorax increases.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one way to make the measurements more reliable.
parts.answer: Repeat each measurement (e.g. three times) and calculate a mean / measure at the same level (across the nipples) each time.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one: repeat and average; same position of tape each time; same person reading the tape; tape kept horizontal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how air is breathed out when a person is resting.
parts.answer: External intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax; ribs move down and in and the diaphragm domes upwards (elastic recoil of lungs), so volume decreases and pressure rises, pushing air out.
parts.working: B1 muscles relax/ribs down and in/diaphragm domes up; B1 volume decreases, pressure increases, air out

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how breathing out is different when a trumpet player blows hard into the instrument.
parts.answer: The internal intercostal muscles contract; pulling the ribs down and in more forcefully; abdominal muscles contract pushing the diaphragm further up; so volume falls more and pressure rises more, forcing air out faster.
parts.working: B1 internal intercostals contract; B1 ribs pulled down and in; B1 abdominal muscles contract/push diaphragm up; max 3

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the relationship between the actions of the internal and external intercostal muscles.
parts.answer: They are antagonistic (when one contracts the other relaxes).

practice.stem: A model of the chest is made from a glass bell jar. A Y-shaped glass tube passes through a bung in the top and two balloons are attached to the branches inside the jar. The open bottom of the jar is covered by a stretched rubber sheet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which part of the human body is represented by: the balloons; the rubber sheet; the bell jar.
parts.answer: Balloons – lungs; rubber sheet – diaphragm; bell jar – rib cage / thorax (chest wall)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe and explain what happens to the balloons when the rubber sheet is pulled down.
parts.answer: The balloons inflate; because the volume inside the jar increases; so the pressure falls and air enters the balloons through the tube from the atmosphere.
parts.working: B1 balloons inflate; B1 volume in jar increases/pressure falls; B1 air enters from outside

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one way in which the model does not show breathing accurately.
parts.answer: The bell jar is rigid so it cannot show rib movement (or the rubber sheet is pulled down, not domed and contracting; no intercostal muscles; balloons are not like alveoli).

practice.stem:
Five students counted their breaths for one minute at rest and again immediately after 2 minutes of skipping.
At rest: 14, 16, 12, 15, 13
After skipping: 27, 31, 24, 30, 26

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean breathing rate at rest and after exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 14.0 breaths per minute; after exercise: 27.6 breaths per minute

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in mean breathing rate after exercise. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the student counted breaths for one full minute rather than for 10 seconds.
parts.answer: A longer count reduces the error of starting or stopping in the middle of a breath / more accurate.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two variables that should be kept the same for each student.
parts.answer: Any two of: type of exercise; duration of exercise (2 minutes); intensity/speed; time between stopping and counting; resting before the first count; same person counting.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which statement explains why air moves into the lungs when we breathe in?
A The volume of the thorax increases so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure.
B The lungs expand by themselves and pull the ribs outwards.
C The pressure inside the thorax rises above atmospheric pressure.
D The diaphragm relaxes and domes upwards, sucking air in.
parts.answer: A The volume of the thorax increases so the pressure inside falls below atmospheric pressure.
parts.working: Muscle contraction increases thorax volume, lowering pressure, so air flows in from the higher atmospheric pressure. D describes breathing out, not in.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
During exercise a person breathes faster and more deeply. Which change in the blood is detected by the brain and causes this?
A a rise in the concentration of carbon dioxide
B a fall in the concentration of glucose
C a rise in the concentration of oxygen
D a fall in the concentration of urea
parts.answer: A a rise in the concentration of carbon dioxide
parts.working: Faster aerobic respiration in the muscles releases more carbon dioxide into the blood; the brain detects the higher carbon dioxide concentration and increases the rate and depth of breathing. Oxygen concentration does not rise during exercise (C).

practice.stem: A teacher makes a model of part of the rib cage. A vertical wooden stick represents the backbone and a second vertical stick represents the sternum. Two horizontal strips, joined to both sticks by pins that can turn, represent two ribs. Two elastic bands are attached between the ribs: the outer band runs from the upper rib near the backbone down to the lower rib near the sternum; the inner band runs from the upper rib near the sternum down to the lower rib near the backbone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which strip of elastic (the outer band or the inner band) must shorten to raise the "ribs". Give the muscle it represents.
parts.answer: The outer band (sloping down from backbone towards the front); it represents the external intercostal muscles.
parts.working: 1 mark: outer band; 1 mark: external intercostal muscles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how raising the ribs in a real person causes air to enter the lungs.
parts.answer: The ribs move up and out, so the volume of the thorax increases; the pressure inside the thorax/lungs falls below atmospheric pressure; air flows in through the trachea.
parts.working: 1 mark each: volume of thorax increases; pressure falls below atmospheric (outside) pressure; air moves in down the pressure gradient.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two ways in which this model is not like a real chest.
parts.answer: Any two: it has no diaphragm; no lungs/airways; the ribs are not curved and do not enclose a cavity; only one pair of "muscles"; elastic bands cannot actively contract.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the rate and depth of breathing increase during a football match.
parts.answer: Muscles contract more so they respire faster; producing more carbon dioxide which enters the blood; the increased carbon dioxide concentration in the blood is detected by the brain; the brain sends more nerve impulses to the intercostal muscles and diaphragm; so more oxygen is supplied for aerobic respiration and carbon dioxide is removed faster.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: more respiration in muscles; more CO₂ in blood; detected by brain; impulses to diaphragm/intercostals; more O₂ for aerobic respiration; CO₂ removed faster; (any anaerobic respiration/oxygen debt reference)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why breathing rate stays high for some minutes after the match ends.
parts.answer: Lactic acid made by anaerobic respiration must be broken down/removed; this needs extra oxygen (oxygen debt), so fast breathing continues.
parts.working: B1 lactic acid/oxygen debt; B1 extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid in liver

practice.stem:
A trace of a person's lung volume was recorded.
At rest: highest point of each breath 3.1 dm³, lowest point 2.6 dm³, 15 breaths per minute.
During exercise: highest point 4.0 dm³, lowest point 2.4 dm³, 24 breaths per minute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of air breathed in with each breath (the tidal volume) at rest and during exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 0.5 dm³; during exercise: 1.6 dm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total volume of air breathed in per minute at rest and during exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 7.5 dm³ per minute; during exercise: 38.4 dm³ per minute
parts.working: M1 tidal volume × breaths per minute; A1 both

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the advantage of the change in breathing during exercise.
parts.answer: More air reaches the alveoli per minute, so more oxygen diffuses into the blood for aerobic respiration in muscles; and more carbon dioxide is removed.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen into blood for respiration; B1 more CO₂ removed

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find out how the intensity of exercise affects the breathing rate of students. Include the method, the variables to control, how you would make the results reliable and any safety precautions.
parts.answer: Use stepping on/off a step at different rates (e.g. 10, 20, 30 steps per minute) set with a metronome for a fixed time (e.g. 3 minutes); measure resting breathing rate first and let it return to resting between trials; count breaths for 1 minute immediately after each exercise; keep same step height, same duration, same students (similar age/fitness), same time after exercise before counting; repeat for several students/three times and calculate means; safety: students with asthma or heart conditions do not take part / stop if dizzy.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: method of varying intensity; at least 3 intensities; fixed duration; resting rate measured / return to resting; breaths counted for 1 minute straight after; two controlled variables (B1 each, max 2); repeats/means; one safety point

practice.stem: Each lung is surrounded by two pleural membranes with a thin layer of pleural fluid between them. The space between the membranes is sealed and airtight. A man injured in a road accident has a wound through the right side of his chest wall that lets air into the space between the pleural membranes on that side.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the pleural fluid.
parts.answer: It lubricates the pleural membranes so the lungs can move smoothly against the chest wall (reduces friction) during breathing.
parts.working: 1 mark: reduces friction / lubrication between lung and chest wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the right lung does not fill with air when the man tries to breathe in.
parts.answer: Air enters the pleural cavity through the wound, so the pressure there is the same as atmospheric pressure; when the thorax volume increases the pressure around the lung does not fall below atmospheric; the lung is not pulled outwards and its elastic tissue makes it collapse, so no air is drawn in.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: air enters the pleural cavity; pressure around the lung equals atmospheric / does not fall; lung not pulled out with chest wall; elastic lung recoils/collapses; no pressure difference to draw air in.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the left lung still works normally.
parts.answer: The left lung is in its own separate pleural cavity, which is still sealed / airtight.
parts.working: 1 mark: separate sealed pleural cavity on the left.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is NOT a feature of an efficient gas exchange surface?
A a large surface area
B a thin surface
C a good blood supply
D a thick layer of mucus over the surface
parts.answer: D a thick layer of mucus over the surface
parts.working: A thick layer of mucus would increase the diffusion distance. The alveolar surface is moist, but only with a thin film of fluid; A, B and C are all features that speed up diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State four features of the gas exchange surface in human lungs.
parts.answer: Large surface area (many alveoli); thin walls (one cell thick); good blood supply (many capillaries); good ventilation with air; moist surface.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the function of the capillaries surrounding each alveolus.
parts.answer: To take up oxygen from and give carbon dioxide to the alveolus / carry blood close to the alveolus for gas exchange.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the inside surface of each alveolus is moist.
parts.answer: Gases dissolve in the moisture before diffusing across the wall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the blood vessel that brings deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
parts.answer: Pulmonary artery

parts.label: a
parts.text:
In which order does an oxygen molecule pass from the air in an alveolus into a red blood cell?
A alveolus wall → capillary wall → plasma → red blood cell
B capillary wall → alveolus wall → plasma → red blood cell
C plasma → alveolus wall → capillary wall → red blood cell
D alveolus wall → plasma → capillary wall → red blood cell
parts.answer: A alveolus wall → capillary wall → plasma → red blood cell
parts.working: Oxygen diffuses across the alveolus wall first, then the capillary wall, then through the plasma into the red blood cell. B reverses the two walls.

practice.stem: Both the alveoli of the human lungs and the air spaces inside a leaf of a mango tree are gas exchange surfaces.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two features that the surfaces of the air spaces in a leaf share with the alveoli of the lungs.
parts.answer: Any two: large surface area; thin; moist surface; gases reach them by diffusion.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Complete the table to show the main gas that diffuses IN to each surface on a sunny afternoon.
alveolus: ……
spongy mesophyll cell of a leaf: ……
parts.answer: Alveolus (into the blood): oxygen. Spongy mesophyll cell: carbon dioxide.
parts.working: 1 mark each. In bright light photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so the leaf takes in carbon dioxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the process that moves these gases across both surfaces.
parts.answer: Diffusion

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how oxygen moves from the air in an alveolus into a red blood cell.
parts.answer: Oxygen dissolves in the moisture lining the alveolus; diffuses through the thin alveolar wall and capillary wall; into the plasma and red blood cell where it combines with haemoglobin.
parts.working: B1 dissolves in moisture; B1 diffusion across alveolus and capillary walls; B1 into red blood cell/joins haemoglobin

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a steep concentration gradient of oxygen is maintained between the alveoli and the blood.
parts.answer: Breathing (ventilation) keeps bringing fresh air with a high oxygen concentration into the alveoli; blood flow carries oxygenated blood away; and brings deoxygenated blood with low oxygen concentration to the alveoli.
parts.working: B1 ventilation brings fresh air; B1 blood removes oxygen; B1 deoxygenated blood continually arrives

practice.stem: In a photomicrograph of lung tissue magnified 120 times, one alveolus measures 30 mm across.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the actual diameter of the alveolus in µm.
parts.answer: 250 µm
parts.working: M1 actual = image ÷ magnification = 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25 mm; A1 × 1000 = 250 µm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The wall of the alveolus is made of a single layer of flattened cells. Explain the advantage of this.
parts.answer: Short diffusion distance; so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse quickly between the air and the blood.
parts.working: B1 short distance; B1 faster diffusion

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why having millions of small alveoli is better than having a few large air sacs.
parts.answer: Many small alveoli give a much larger total surface area (for the same volume of lung); so more gas exchange can take place.
parts.working: B1 larger total surface area; B1 more diffusion/gas exchange

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row describes the movement of gases by diffusion in the alveoli?
A oxygen: alveolus air → blood; carbon dioxide: blood → alveolus air
B oxygen: blood → alveolus air; carbon dioxide: alveolus air → blood
C oxygen and carbon dioxide: both alveolus air → blood
D oxygen and carbon dioxide: both blood → alveolus air
parts.answer: A oxygen: alveolus air → blood; carbon dioxide: blood → alveolus air
parts.working: Oxygen is at a higher concentration in alveolar air and diffuses into the blood; carbon dioxide is at a higher concentration in the blood and diffuses out. B reverses both directions.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which change would reduce the rate at which oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood?
A an increase in the rate of breathing
B an increase in the speed of blood flow through the lung capillaries
C a layer of fluid collecting inside the alveoli
D an increase in the number of capillaries around each alveolus
parts.answer: C a layer of fluid collecting inside the alveoli
parts.working: Fluid in the alveoli increases the diffusion distance, so diffusion is slower. A, B and D all keep the concentration gradient steep or increase the area, so they speed diffusion up.

practice.stem: An adult human lung system contains about 300 million alveoli. Assume each alveolus has a surface area of 0.25 mm².

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the alveoli in m². (1 m² = 1 000 000 mm²)
parts.answer: 75 m²

parts.label: b
parts.text: During a race an athlete's lungs take up 4.0 dm³ of oxygen per minute. Using your answer to (a), calculate the volume of oxygen that crosses each m² of alveolar surface per minute, in cm³. Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (1 dm³ = 1000 cm³)
parts.answer: 53.3 cm³ per m² per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two features of each alveolus, other than its surface area, that help gas exchange.
parts.answer: Any two: wall one cell thick (thin); moist lining; surrounded by many capillaries (good blood supply); well ventilated.

practice.stem: The capillaries around an alveolus have a diameter of about 7 µm. Red blood cells are about 7.5 µm across, so they are squeezed as they pass through in single file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest the advantage of red blood cells being pressed against the capillary wall as they pass an alveolus.
parts.answer: The diffusion distance from the alveolus air to the haemoglobin is very short, so oxygen diffuses into the cell quickly; the cells also move slowly in single file, giving more time for loading.
parts.working: 1 mark: short diffusion distance; 1 mark: faster diffusion / more time for oxygen uptake.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A person with anaemia has fewer red blood cells than normal. Explain why this person becomes breathless when climbing stairs.
parts.answer: Less haemoglobin, so the blood carries less oxygen; muscles do not get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration during exercise; breathing rate increases (to try to take in more oxygen / remove carbon dioxide), so the person feels breathless.
parts.working: 1 mark each: less haemoglobin / less oxygen carried; not enough oxygen for respiration in muscles; faster/deeper breathing in response.

practice.stem: A student models organisms of different sizes as cubes with sides of 1 cm, 2 cm and 4 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube.
parts.answer: 1 cm cube 6 : 1; 2 cm cube 3 : 1; 4 cm cube 1.5 : 1
parts.working: M1 surface area = 6 × side²; M1 volume = side³; A1 all three ratios

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a large animal such as a buffalo needs lungs, while a single-celled organism does not.
parts.answer: As size increases, the surface area to volume ratio decreases; the body surface of a large animal is too small for its volume to absorb enough oxygen by diffusion and the distances to inner cells are too great; lungs provide a very large internal surface area.
parts.working: B1 larger size → smaller SA:V; B1 surface not enough to supply volume / diffusion distance too long; B1 lungs give large surface area

practice.stem: A climber travels from Karachi, at sea level, to a base camp at 5000 m in the Karakoram mountains.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why there is less oxygen available to the body in a visitor to a high mountain base camp than at sea level.
parts.answer: Air at high altitude has a lower pressure, so each breath contains less oxygen; the concentration gradient between the alveoli and the blood is smaller; so less oxygen diffuses into the blood.
parts.working: B1 less oxygen per breath / lower air pressure; B1 smaller concentration gradient; B1 slower diffusion into blood

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest how the visitor's breathing changes when they first arrive, and why.
parts.answer: Breathing becomes faster and deeper; to bring more air (oxygen) into the alveoli per minute.
parts.working: B1 faster/deeper; B1 more oxygen into alveoli/maintain gradient

practice.stem: Blood arriving at the lungs at rest contains 10.0 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³ of blood. Blood leaving the lungs contains 19.5 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³ of blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen taken up by each 100 cm³ of blood as it passes through the lungs.
parts.answer: 9.5 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: At rest, 5 dm³ (5000 cm³) of blood passes through the lungs each minute. Calculate the volume of oxygen taken up by the blood per minute.
parts.answer: 475 cm³ per minute

parts.label: c
parts.text: During exercise the blood flow increases to 20 dm³ per minute and blood arrives at the lungs with only 5.0 cm³ of oxygen per 100 cm³. Assuming it still leaves with 19.5 cm³ per 100 cm³, calculate the oxygen taken up per minute.
parts.answer: 2900 cm³ per minute

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why blood arriving at the lungs during exercise contains less oxygen.
parts.answer: Muscles use more oxygen in respiration, so more oxygen is removed from the blood in the tissues.

practice.stem: In a lung disease called pulmonary fibrosis, scar tissue forms in the walls of the alveoli. In a healthy person the barrier between the air in an alveolus and the blood is about 0.5 µm thick. In one patient with fibrosis it is about 3.0 µm thick.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times thicker the barrier is in the patient with fibrosis.
parts.answer: 6 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the patient has a lower concentration of oxygen in the blood leaving the lungs, especially during exercise.
parts.answer: The diffusion distance is longer, so oxygen diffuses into the blood more slowly; during exercise blood flows through the capillaries faster, so there is less time for oxygen to diffuse in; so blood leaves before it is fully loaded with oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark each: longer diffusion distance; slower rate of diffusion; less time in capillary during exercise / blood not fully oxygenated.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the patient breathes faster than a healthy person even when resting.
parts.answer: Less oxygen reaches the blood / carbon dioxide is removed more slowly; faster breathing keeps the concentration gradient steeper (more fresh air in the alveoli) to make up for the slow diffusion.
parts.working: 1 mark: low blood oxygen / high carbon dioxide detected; 1 mark: faster ventilation maintains a steeper concentration gradient.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which row gives the approximate percentages of oxygen and carbon dioxide in expired air?
A oxygen 21%; carbon dioxide 0.04%
B oxygen 16%; carbon dioxide 4%
C oxygen 4%; carbon dioxide 16%
D oxygen 21%; carbon dioxide 4%
parts.answer: B oxygen 16%; carbon dioxide 4%
parts.working: Expired air still contains about 16% oxygen and about 4% carbon dioxide. A is inspired (atmospheric) air.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three differences between inspired air and expired air.
parts.answer: Expired air contains less oxygen; more carbon dioxide; more water vapour; and is warmer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three (comparative words needed)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why expired air contains more carbon dioxide than inspired air.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide is produced by respiration in cells; it diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is breathed out.
parts.working: B1 made in respiration; B1 diffuses from blood into alveoli

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which gas makes up about the same percentage of inspired air and expired air?
A oxygen
B carbon dioxide
C nitrogen
D water vapour
parts.answer: C nitrogen
parts.working: Nitrogen (about 78–79 %) is not used or produced by the body, so its percentage hardly changes. Oxygen falls from about 21 % to 16 %, so A is wrong.

practice.stem: A student put 5 cm³ of red hydrogencarbonate indicator solution into each of two tubes, P and Q. Hydrogencarbonate indicator is red at the carbon dioxide concentration of room air, yellow at higher carbon dioxide concentrations and purple at lower ones. Tube P was left open to the room air. The student breathed out gently through a straw into tube Q for 30 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the colour of the indicator in tube Q after the student breathed out through it.
parts.answer: Yellow

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the colour change in tube Q.
parts.answer: Expired air contains more carbon dioxide than room air (about 4 % compared with 0.04 %); carbon dioxide dissolves to make the indicator more acidic, so it turns from red to yellow.
parts.working: 1 mark: more carbon dioxide in expired air; 1 mark: indicator becomes more acidic / yellow shows high carbon dioxide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the purpose of tube P.
parts.answer: It is a control, to show that the colour change is caused by the expired air and not by the indicator alone / to compare with.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State one variable that should be kept the same for both tubes.
parts.answer: Volume of indicator / time of bubbling / temperature / same concentration of indicator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the process in body cells that produces the extra carbon dioxide found in expired air.
parts.answer: Aerobic respiration

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the word equation for this process.
parts.answer: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
parts.working: 1 mark for correct reactants; 1 mark for correct products.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how carbon dioxide made in a muscle cell in the leg reaches the alveoli.
parts.answer: It diffuses out of the muscle cell into the blood in the capillaries; it is carried in the blood plasma (mainly as hydrogencarbonate ions) to the heart and then to the lungs; it diffuses from the blood into the air in the alveoli.
parts.working: 1 mark each: diffuses into blood/capillary; carried in plasma via the heart/pulmonary artery; diffuses into the alveoli.

practice.stem: A student set up two tubes, A and B, each containing 10 cm³ of limewater. They were connected so that when the student breathed in through a mouthpiece, air from the room bubbled through tube A, and when the student breathed out, expired air bubbled through tube B. Tube B turned milky after 15 seconds. Tube A was still clear after 3 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the results in tube B.
parts.answer: Expired air contains a high concentration of carbon dioxide (about 4%); carbon dioxide turns limewater milky (cloudy).
parts.working: B1 more CO₂ in expired air; B1 CO₂ turns limewater milky

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why tube A stayed clear for much longer.
parts.answer: Inspired air contains very little carbon dioxide (about 0.04%).

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one thing the student should do to make the comparison fair.
parts.answer: Use the same volume (and concentration) of limewater in each tube / breathe at the same rate and depth.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Hydrogencarbonate indicator could be used instead of limewater. State the colour it would turn in tube B.
parts.answer: Yellow

practice.stem:
A student breathed out through 5 cm³ of limewater and timed how long it took to turn milky. This was done three times at rest and three times immediately after running for 3 minutes.
At rest / s: 45, 41, 43
After running / s: 19, 23, 18

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean time for the limewater to turn milky at rest and after exercise.
parts.answer: At rest: 43.0 s; after exercise: 20.0 s

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two mean times.
parts.answer: During exercise muscles respire faster; more carbon dioxide is produced and carried to the lungs; so expired air contains more carbon dioxide (and more is breathed out per second) and the limewater goes milky sooner.
parts.working: B1 faster respiration; B1 more CO₂ in blood/expired air; B1 limewater turns milky faster

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why it is difficult to judge exactly when the limewater turns milky, and one way to improve this.
parts.answer: The change is gradual so the end point is subjective; compare against a standard tube of milky limewater / use a black card behind the tube / use a cross under the tube.
parts.working: B1 gradual/subjective end point; B1 valid improvement

parts.label: a
parts.text:
On a cold winter morning in Murree, a person's breath looks like a white mist. What is the best explanation?
A Expired air contains carbon dioxide, which is white.
B Expired air is warm and saturated with water vapour, which condenses into droplets when it cools.
C Expired air contains less oxygen, so it becomes cloudy.
D Dust particles in expired air reflect the light.
parts.answer: B Expired air is warm and saturated with water vapour, which condenses into droplets when it cools.
parts.working: Expired air is warm and saturated with water vapour from the moist alveoli; in cold air the vapour condenses into tiny droplets. Carbon dioxide is colourless, so A is wrong.

practice.stem: Inspired air contains 21 % oxygen and 0.04 % carbon dioxide. Expired air contains 16 % oxygen and 4 % carbon dioxide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the percentage of carbon dioxide is in expired air than in inspired air.
parts.answer: 100 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the oxygen in inspired air that is removed by the body. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why most of the oxygen in inspired air is breathed out again.
parts.answer: Only air in the alveoli exchanges gases and it is not completely replaced at each breath / some inspired air stays in the trachea and bronchi; diffusion only continues while there is a concentration gradient, and the blood leaving the lungs is already nearly saturated with oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two of: air in trachea/bronchi does not reach the alveoli; alveolar air not fully replaced; blood becomes saturated / gradient becomes small; limited time for diffusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why expired air is warmer than inspired air on a cool day.
parts.answer: Heat from the body (released by respiration in cells) warms the air in the airways and lungs; the air is breathed out at close to body temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark: heat from respiration / body at 37 °C; 1 mark: air warmed as it passes through the lungs and airways.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why expired air contains more water vapour than inspired air.
parts.answer: Water evaporates from the moist lining of the alveoli and airways into the air; so the air breathed out is saturated with water vapour.
parts.working: 1 mark: moist alveoli/airways; 1 mark: evaporation into the air.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why hikers walking for many hours in the dry, cold air of the northern mountains are advised to drink plenty of water even though they do not feel hot.
parts.answer: They lose a lot of water in expired air because the inspired air is very dry and they breathe faster when climbing; this water must be replaced to avoid dehydration.
parts.working: 1 mark: water lost in expired air / more breaths when climbing; 1 mark: must replace water to avoid dehydration.

practice.stem: At rest, a person breathes 8 dm³ of air per minute. Inspired air contains 21% oxygen and expired air contains 16% oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of oxygen absorbed by the body each minute and in one hour.
parts.answer: 0.4 dm³ per minute; 24 dm³ per hour
parts.working: M1 21% − 16% = 5%; M1 0.05 × 8 dm³ = 0.4 dm³; A1 24 dm³ per hour

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why expired air still contains so much oxygen.
parts.answer: Some inspired air stays in the trachea and bronchi and never reaches the alveoli; air is in the alveoli only for a short time, so not all the oxygen diffuses into the blood.
parts.working: B1 air in airways not involved in gas exchange (dead space); B1 short time in alveoli / mixing with air already in lungs

practice.stem:
Inspired air contains 0.04% carbon dioxide.
At rest: expired air 4% carbon dioxide, 16% oxygen; volume breathed 7.5 dm³ per minute
During exercise: expired air 5% carbon dioxide, 15% oxygen; volume breathed 60 dm³ per minute

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide added to the air breathed out per minute at rest and during exercise. Give your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.answer: At rest: 0.297 dm³ per minute; during exercise: 2.98 dm³ per minute
parts.working: M1 percentage difference (4 − 0.04 = 3.96%; 5 − 0.04 = 4.96%); M1 × volume per minute; A1 both

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the expired air contains a lower percentage of oxygen during exercise.
parts.answer: Muscle cells respire faster and use more oxygen; blood returning to the lungs has less oxygen, so more oxygen diffuses into the blood from the alveoli.
parts.working: B1 more oxygen used in respiration; B1 steeper gradient/more oxygen removed from alveolar air

practice.stem:
A 100.0 cm³ sample of expired air was collected in a gas syringe. It was bubbled through potassium hydroxide solution, which absorbs carbon dioxide only, and the volume was measured again. It was then bubbled through alkaline pyrogallol solution, which absorbs oxygen only, and measured again. All volumes were measured at room temperature.
Start: 100.0 cm³
After potassium hydroxide: 95.8 cm³
After alkaline pyrogallol: 79.9 cm³

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of carbon dioxide and the percentage of oxygen in the sample of expired air.
parts.answer: carbon dioxide 4.2 %; oxygen 15.9 %
parts.working: M1 decrease after potassium hydroxide = 4.2 cm³ → 4.2 %; M1 further decrease after pyrogallol = 15.9 cm³; A1 15.9 %.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The gas remaining at the end is mostly one gas. Name it.
parts.answer: Nitrogen

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sample must be at the same temperature each time its volume is read.
parts.answer: Gases expand when warmed and contract when cooled; a temperature change would alter the volume, so a change in volume would not be due only to the gas absorbed.
parts.working: 1 mark: volume of gas changes with temperature; 1 mark: so the reading would not show only the gas absorbed (invalid comparison).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Both solutions are corrosive alkalis. State one safety precaution.
parts.answer: Wear eye protection (goggles) / gloves.

practice.stem: A closed classroom has a volume of 180 m³. At the start of a one-hour lesson the air contains 0.04 % carbon dioxide. Each of the 30 students breathes out 0.25 dm³ of carbon dioxide per minute. Assume no air enters or leaves the room.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide, in m³, added to the room by the students in one hour. (1 m³ = 1000 dm³)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of carbon dioxide in the room air at the end of the lesson.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the windows should be opened between lessons.
parts.answer: To let fresh air in so that the carbon dioxide concentration falls (and oxygen is replaced), so students do not become drowsy.

practice.stem:
Samples of air were taken from deep in the lungs (alveolar air) and from the end of a normal breath out (expired air) of a resting woman.
Inspired air: oxygen 21 %, carbon dioxide 0.04 %
Expired air: oxygen 16 %, carbon dioxide 4 %
Alveolar air: oxygen 14 %, carbon dioxide 5.5 %

parts.label: a
parts.text: Suggest why the air in the alveoli contains less oxygen than expired air.
parts.answer: The alveoli are where oxygen is removed into the blood; expired air is a mixture of alveolar air and air from the trachea and bronchi (dead space), which has not exchanged gases and still has about 21 % oxygen.
parts.working: 1 mark: oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood; 1 mark: expired air mixes with air from airways that did not take part in gas exchange.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Predict how the percentage of carbon dioxide in the alveolar air would change if the person held her breath for 30 seconds. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: It would increase; carbon dioxide keeps diffusing from the blood into the alveoli but no fresh air enters to remove it.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase; 1 mark: no ventilation so carbon dioxide accumulates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why breathing must keep the concentration of carbon dioxide in the alveoli lower than in the blood arriving at the lungs.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide leaves the blood by diffusion only if its concentration in the alveoli is lower than in the blood; breathing replaces alveolar air with fresh air, keeping this gradient so carbon dioxide does not build up in the blood (where it would lower blood pH).
parts.working: 1 mark: diffusion needs a concentration gradient from blood to alveoli; 1 mark: ventilation removes carbon dioxide so it does not accumulate in the blood.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which component of tobacco smoke reduces the amount of oxygen the blood can carry?
A tar
B nicotine
C carbon monoxide
D smoke particles
parts.answer: C carbon monoxide
parts.working: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, so less oxygen is carried. Nicotine (B) is the addictive drug but does not block haemoglobin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the component of tobacco smoke that: (i) is addictive; (ii) causes cancer.
parts.answer: (i) nicotine; (ii) tar

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two diseases of the gas exchange system caused by smoking.
parts.answer: Any two of: lung cancer; chronic bronchitis; emphysema; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which disease of smokers is caused by the breakdown of the walls between alveoli?
A bronchitis
B emphysema
C lung cancer
D coronary heart disease
parts.answer: B emphysema
parts.working: In emphysema the alveolar walls break down, forming larger air spaces with a smaller total surface area. Bronchitis (A) is inflammation of the bronchi with excess mucus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: COPD is a name for two smoking-related lung conditions. Name both conditions.
parts.answer: Chronic bronchitis and emphysema.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two symptoms a person with COPD is likely to have.
parts.answer: Any two: breathlessness; persistent cough; coughing up mucus (phlegm); wheezing; frequent chest infections; tiredness.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the most effective thing a smoker with early COPD can do to stop the condition getting worse.
parts.answer: Stop smoking.

practice.stem: The label on a packet of cigarettes states that each cigarette produces 10 mg of tar and 0.8 mg of nicotine. A person smokes 15 cigarettes every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mass of tar, in grams, that the person inhales from these cigarettes in one year (365 days).

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State the harmful effect of each substance:
(i) tar
(ii) nicotine
parts.answer: (i) tar contains carcinogens / causes lung cancer (and damages cilia); (ii) nicotine is addictive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how tar in cigarette smoke can lead to lung cancer.
parts.answer: Tar contains carcinogens; these cause mutations in the DNA of cells lining the airways/lungs; the cells divide in an uncontrolled way and form a tumour.
parts.working: 1 mark each: carcinogens; mutation/damage to DNA (genes); uncontrolled cell division / tumour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways in which governments try to reduce the number of people who smoke.
parts.answer: Any two: health warnings and pictures on packets; higher taxes on cigarettes; banning smoking in public places; banning advertising; banning sale to under-18s; education campaigns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the roles of goblet cells and ciliated cells in the trachea.
parts.answer: Goblet cells secrete mucus; mucus traps dust and pathogens (bacteria); cilia beat/sweep the mucus up to the throat where it is swallowed.
parts.working: B1 goblet cells make mucus; B1 mucus traps particles/pathogens; B1 cilia move mucus up/away from lungs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why many smokers have a persistent cough and frequent chest infections.
parts.answer: Chemicals in smoke damage/paralyse the cilia; mucus is not removed and builds up in the airways; coughing is the only way to remove it; bacteria trapped in the mucus multiply, causing infections (chronic bronchitis).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: cilia damaged/stop beating; mucus accumulates (more mucus made); cough to clear mucus; bacteria breed in mucus/infection

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the alveoli in emphysema.
parts.answer: The walls of the alveoli break down; neighbouring alveoli merge into fewer, larger air spaces (and the lungs lose elasticity).
parts.working: B1 alveolar walls break down; B1 fewer larger spaces / loss of elasticity

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person with emphysema becomes breathless even when walking slowly.
parts.answer: The surface area for gas exchange is reduced; so less oxygen diffuses into the blood; muscles do not get enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, so the person breathes faster to compensate.
parts.working: B1 smaller surface area; B1 less oxygen absorbed; B1 not enough O₂ for respiration / breathe faster

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which effect on the body is caused mainly by nicotine in tobacco smoke?
A It is addictive and raises heart rate and blood pressure.
B It causes mutations that lead to lung cancer.
C It combines with haemoglobin and reduces oxygen transport.
D It breaks down the walls of the alveoli.
parts.answer: A It is addictive and raises heart rate and blood pressure.
parts.working: Nicotine is the addictive drug in tobacco; it is a stimulant that increases heart rate and blood pressure. B describes the carcinogens in tar, and C describes carbon monoxide.

practice.stem: Volunteers breathed in air containing harmless marked dust particles. After 4 hours, non-smokers had cleared 90 % of the particles from their airways, but smokers had cleared only 40 %.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the lining of the trachea and bronchi normally removes inhaled particles.
parts.answer: Goblet cells make mucus, which traps particles (and bacteria); ciliated cells have cilia that beat; the cilia sweep the mucus up to the throat, where it is swallowed.
parts.working: 1 mark each: mucus from goblet cells; traps particles; cilia beat/sweep mucus upwards to throat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times more of the particles were cleared by non-smokers than by smokers in 4 hours.
parts.answer: 2.25 times (accept 2.25)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your knowledge of the effects of tobacco smoke to explain the difference.
parts.answer: Chemicals in smoke (tar) damage or paralyse the cilia; and cause extra mucus to be made; so mucus and particles are not moved out of the airways.
parts.working: 1 mark: cilia damaged/stop beating; 1 mark: more mucus / mucus collects in airways.

practice.stem: In some cafés in large cities, customers smoke cigarettes and shisha (water pipes).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Shisha (hookah) smoke is passed through water before it is inhaled. Some people think this makes it safe. Explain why shisha smoking still harms the lungs and blood.
parts.answer: The smoke still contains tar/carcinogens and nicotine, which are not all removed by water; burning charcoal produces carbon monoxide, which combines with haemoglobin; sessions are long, so large volumes of smoke are inhaled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three of: tar/carcinogens still present; nicotine (addictive) still present; carbon monoxide from charcoal reduces oxygen transport; large volume inhaled in long sessions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why waiters working in a café where many people smoke are at risk even if they do not smoke.
parts.answer: They breathe in other people's smoke (passive / second-hand smoking); this contains the same harmful substances such as carcinogens and carbon monoxide.
parts.working: 1 mark: passive smoking; 1 mark: inhale the same harmful chemicals.

practice.stem:
A 20-year study of adults recorded deaths from lung cancer per 100 000 people per year.
Non-smokers: 10
1–14 cigarettes per day: 78
15–24 cigarettes per day: 127
25 or more cigarettes per day: 251

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for people who smoke 25 or more cigarettes a day than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 25.1 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: The more cigarettes smoked per day, the higher the death rate from lung cancer; e.g. 10 per 100 000 for non-smokers rising to 251 per 100 000 for 25 or more a day.
parts.working: B1 positive correlation; B1 data quoted with units

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how tar in cigarette smoke can lead to lung cancer.
parts.answer: Tar contains carcinogens; they cause mutations in cells lining the airways, leading to uncontrolled cell division and a tumour.
parts.working: B1 carcinogen/causes mutation; B1 uncontrolled cell division/tumour

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why some non-smokers still die of lung cancer.
parts.answer: Other causes such as breathing other people's smoke (passive smoking), air pollution, radon or inherited factors.

practice.stem:
Relative risk compares the chance of getting lung cancer with that of a person who has never smoked (relative risk = 1). A study of former heavy smokers gave these results:
Years since stopping smoking: 0 | 5 | 10 | 15
Relative risk of lung cancer: 20 | 12 | 6 | 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in relative risk between stopping (0 years) and 10 years after stopping.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the risk falls after a person stops smoking but stays above that of a person who never smoked.
parts.answer: No more carcinogens (tar) enter the lungs, so fewer new mutations happen; damaged cells may be replaced / repaired over time; but some cells already carry mutations, which can still lead to a tumour later.
parts.working: 1 mark each: no new exposure to carcinogens; damaged cells replaced/repaired; existing mutations remain so some risk stays.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A newspaper says: "These data prove that stopping smoking cures lung cancer." Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.answer: The data show risk of getting lung cancer, not cure of existing cancer; the data show a correlation / lower risk, but people who already have cancer are not cured by stopping.
parts.working: 1 mark: data are about risk/chance of developing cancer; 1 mark: stopping lowers risk, it does not treat cancer.

practice.stem:
A teacher demonstrates a smoking machine. A lit cigarette is held in a tube. A pump draws the smoke through a U-tube containing white cotton wool, then through a tube of green universal indicator solution, past a thermometer. A second U-tube with cotton wool and a second tube of indicator were set up with an unlit cigarette.
Results after 5 minutes:
Lit cigarette: cotton wool dark brown and sticky; indicator orange; temperature rose from 24 °C to 31 °C.
Unlit cigarette: cotton wool white; indicator green; temperature stayed at 24 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what the results show about tobacco smoke.
parts.answer: Smoke contains tar (brown deposit trapped by the cotton wool); smoke is acidic (indicator turned from green to orange/red); smoke is hot / burning releases heat (temperature rose by 7 °C).
parts.working: 1 mark each for three correct conclusions linked to the results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the apparatus with the unlit cigarette was set up, and state one variable that must be the same in both sets of apparatus.
parts.answer: It is a control: it shows that the changes are caused by the smoke from the burning cigarette and not by air drawn through the apparatus or the cigarette itself. Same variable: e.g. rate of pumping / volume of air drawn through, time, type of cigarette, mass of cotton wool, volume of indicator.
parts.working: 1 mark: control – changes due to burning/smoke only (comparison); 1 mark: any one valid controlled variable.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The cotton wool represents part of the human gas exchange system. Suggest which part, and suggest one way in which the model is different from that part.
parts.answer: The lungs / the mucus lining of the airways; the cotton wool cannot remove the tar (no cilia), or it cannot exchange gases / has no blood supply.
parts.working: 1 mark: lungs/airway lining; 1 mark: valid difference.

practice.stem: In emphysema, walls between alveoli break down so several small alveoli join into one large air space. Model eight healthy alveoli as spheres each of radius 0.1 mm. When their walls break down they form one sphere with the same total volume, which has a radius of 0.2 mm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the eight healthy alveoli, in mm². Give your answer to 3 significant figures. (Surface area of a sphere = 4πr²)
parts.answer: 1.01 mm²

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the surface area of the single large air space, in mm², to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why a person with emphysema is short of breath.
parts.answer: The surface area is halved (from 1.01 to 0.503 mm²) although the volume of air is the same; less oxygen can diffuse into the blood per second; so the blood carries less oxygen to the muscles and the person breathes faster/feels breathless.
parts.working: 1 mark: surface area halved / reduced; 1 mark: less diffusion of oxygen into the blood; 1 mark: less oxygen for respiration, so breathlessness.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which is the best definition of a drug?
A any substance that kills bacteria
B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
C any substance prescribed by a doctor
D any substance that is addictive
parts.answer: B any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body
parts.working: A drug is any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body; this covers medicines and misused drugs. A is too narrow because it describes only antibiotics.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For which disease would a course of antibiotics NOT be effective?
A cholera
B influenza
C tuberculosis
D typhoid
parts.answer: B influenza
parts.working: Influenza is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not affect viruses. Cholera, tuberculosis and typhoid are bacterial diseases, so the other options are treated with antibiotics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the inoculating loop is heated in a Bunsen flame until it glows red before and after use.
parts.answer: To kill any microorganisms on it, so the plate is not contaminated (and no bacteria escape afterwards).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the lid of the Petri dish is held with two short pieces of tape and not sealed all the way round.
parts.answer: Oxygen can still enter, so harmful anaerobic bacteria are not encouraged to grow; the lid cannot be opened accidentally.
parts.working: B1 allows oxygen in / prevents anaerobic conditions; B1 lid stays shut.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why plates in a school laboratory are incubated at 25 °C and not at 37 °C.
parts.answer: At 37 °C (body temperature) bacteria that cause disease in humans could grow.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the plates must not be opened after incubation.
parts.answer: Large numbers of bacteria have grown, which could include harmful ones; opening would release them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what an antibiotic is.
parts.answer: A drug (medicine) that kills bacteria or stops their growth.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A patient with a cold asks a doctor in Islamabad for antibiotics. The doctor refuses. Explain why.
parts.answer: Colds are caused by viruses; antibiotics do not affect viruses (they work on structures / processes found in bacteria), so they would not help and would increase the risk of resistance.
parts.working: B1 cold caused by virus; B1 antibiotics have no effect on viruses (or unnecessary use leads to resistance).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of organism from which penicillin was first obtained.
parts.answer: a fungus (mould), Penicillium

parts.label: a
parts.text: Antibiotics can kill bacteria inside the human body without harming human cells. Suggest why.
parts.answer: They act on structures or processes found in bacterial cells but not in human cells, such as the bacterial cell wall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two examples of medicinal drugs other than antibiotics and what each is used for.
parts.answer: e.g. painkillers (paracetamol) to relieve pain / fever; insulin to treat diabetes. Any two medicinal drugs with a correct use.
parts.working: B1 each drug with correct use.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why antibiotics should not be shared with a friend who has similar symptoms.
parts.answer: The friend's illness may be caused by a virus or a different bacterium; the dose may be wrong; incomplete courses for both encourage resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Poultry farms sometimes add small amounts of antibiotics to chicken feed to keep the birds healthy and growing quickly. Explain why this practice can be a risk to human health.
parts.answer: Constant low doses kill susceptible bacteria and select for resistant ones; resistant bacteria multiply in the chickens; they can pass to humans through meat or the environment, so human infections become harder to treat.
parts.working: B1 selection for resistance; B1 resistant bacteria increase in the animals; B1 transfer to humans / antibiotics less effective for people.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one alternative way the farmer could keep the chickens healthy.
parts.answer: Vaccinate the birds; keep sheds clean; give birds more space; use antibiotics only to treat sick birds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an antibiotic-resistant bacterium.
parts.answer: A bacterium that is not killed (and keeps growing) when exposed to the antibiotic.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why antibiotic resistance is a serious problem for the world.
parts.answer: Infections that were easy to treat may become untreatable; more people die / stay ill longer; surgery and cancer treatment become riskier; few new antibiotics are being discovered; more expensive treatments needed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why some antibiotics are kept by doctors only for patients for whom other antibiotics have failed.
parts.answer: If used rarely, bacteria are less likely to become resistant to them, so they keep working.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal has a painful tooth infection caused by bacteria. His dentist gives him paracetamol and an antibiotic. State the purpose of each drug.
parts.answer: Paracetamol: a painkiller that relieves the pain (a symptom). Antibiotic: kills the bacteria causing the infection (or stops their growth).
parts.working: B1 paracetamol relieves pain / symptoms; B1 antibiotic kills bacteria / treats the cause.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the paracetamol alone would not cure the infection.
parts.answer: It only reduces pain; it does not kill the bacteria.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The dentist tells Bilal to take the antibiotic at regular times each day. Suggest why.
parts.answer: To keep the concentration of antibiotic in the blood high enough to kill the bacteria all the time.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is an antibiotic?
A aspirin
B insulin
C penicillin
D paracetamol
parts.answer: C penicillin
parts.working: Penicillin kills or stops the growth of bacteria, so it is an antibiotic. Insulin (B) is a hormone used as a medicinal drug for diabetes, not an antibiotic; aspirin and paracetamol are painkillers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient taking an antibiotic for a chest infection develops diarrhoea. The antibiotic does not harm human cells. Suggest why the patient gets diarrhoea.
parts.answer: The antibiotic also kills the harmless/helpful bacteria that normally live in the gut; this upsets digestion / allows other microorganisms to grow, causing diarrhoea.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the patient should still finish the course.
parts.answer: to kill all of the disease-causing bacteria so none survive to multiply / become resistant

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Paper discs soaked in four different antibiotics were placed on agar covered with the same bacteria. After incubation the diameters of the clear zones were:
W: 8 mm
X: 22 mm
Y: 15 mm
Z: no clear zone
Which antibiotic would be most useful against these bacteria?
A W
B X
C Y
D Z
parts.answer: B X
parts.working: The largest clear zone shows that the most bacteria were killed or stopped from growing, so X is most effective. Z had no clear zone; the bacteria are resistant to it.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which sequence describes how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic?
A antibiotic used → bacteria learn to resist it → all bacteria pass on the learned resistance
B random mutation gives resistance → antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria → resistant bacteria reproduce
C antibiotic causes mutation for resistance → resistant bacteria die → non-resistant bacteria reproduce
D antibiotic used → bacteria form antibodies → antibodies passed to offspring
parts.answer: B random mutation gives resistance → antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria → resistant bacteria reproduce
parts.working: Resistance arises by random mutation; the antibiotic acts as a selection pressure, so resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (natural selection). A is wrong because bacteria do not 'learn' resistance; it is genetic.

practice.stem:
A student spread a harmless bacterium on a nutrient agar plate and placed five paper discs (6 mm diameter) on it. Four discs were soaked in different antibiotics and one in sterile water. After two days at 25 °C the diameters of the clear zones were measured.
penicillin 26 mm; streptomycin 18 mm; tetracycline 30 mm; erythromycin 12 mm; sterile water: no clear zone beyond the disc.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the area of the clear zone around each antibiotic disc in mm², using area = πr². Give each answer to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: penicillin 531 mm²; streptomycin 254 mm²; tetracycline 707 mm²; erythromycin 113 mm²
parts.working: M1 radius = diameter ÷ 2; A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three): π × 13², π × 9², π × 15², π × 6².

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rank the antibiotics from most to least effective against this bacterium.
parts.answer: tetracycline > penicillin > streptomycin > erythromycin

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the disc soaked in sterile water.
parts.answer: It is a control; it shows that the clear zones are caused by the antibiotics and not by the paper disc or the water.
parts.working: B1 control; B1 shows effect is due to antibiotic.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two precautions the student should take to avoid contaminating the plate or himself.
parts.answer: Flame the forceps / loop; open the lid only slightly and briefly; tape the lid (do not seal fully) and do not open after incubation; wash hands; incubate at no more than 25 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the use of an antibiotic can lead to a population of bacteria that is resistant to it.
parts.answer: A random mutation makes some bacteria resistant; the antibiotic kills the non-resistant bacteria; the resistant bacteria survive and reproduce; the resistance gene is passed on so the proportion of resistant bacteria rises (natural selection).
parts.working: B1 mutation / variation; B1 non-resistant killed; B1 resistant survive and reproduce; B1 allele / gene passed on, population becomes resistant.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why bacteria can become resistant much faster than animals become adapted to a new condition.
parts.answer: Bacteria reproduce very quickly (some divide every 20 minutes), so many generations occur in a short time; large populations mean more mutations.
parts.working: B1 rapid reproduction / short generation time; B1 large numbers so more mutations.

parts.label: a
parts.text: MRSA is a type of bacterium found in some hospitals. State what is unusual about MRSA.
parts.answer: It is resistant to many (most commonly used) antibiotics.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three ways in which doctors, hospitals and patients can reduce the development and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
parts.answer: Only prescribe antibiotics when needed (not for viral infections); patients complete the course; use a range of different antibiotics; good hygiene such as hand washing and cleaning wards; isolate infected patients.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why antibiotic resistance is a bigger danger in hospitals than in most homes.
parts.answer: Many patients are ill or have weak immune systems; antibiotics are used a lot so resistant bacteria are selected; bacteria spread easily between patients.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bacterium divides into two every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, calculate how many there would be after 3 hours if none die.

parts.label: b
parts.text: In a patient's gut there are 5 × 10⁹ bacteria of one species. One in every 10 million of them carries a mutation for resistance to an antibiotic. Calculate the number of resistant bacteria.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why even a very rare mutation for resistance can quickly become a problem when the antibiotic is used.
parts.answer: There are already hundreds of resistant bacteria; when the antibiotic kills the others, these survive and, dividing every 20 minutes, soon form a large resistant population.
parts.working: B1 some resistant cells are present in a large population; B1 they survive and multiply rapidly.

practice.stem:
A student made garlic extract at 0 %, 25 %, 50 % and 100 % concentration and soaked 6 mm paper discs in each. The discs were placed on agar plates spread with bacteria. The diameter (in mm, including the disc) of the area with no bacterial growth was measured on three plates.
0 %: 6, 6, 6
25 %: 9, 10, 8
50 %: 12, 13, 14
100 %: 16, 18, 17

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the mean diameter for each concentration to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: A2 all four correct (A1 for two or three).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the results.
parts.answer: As the concentration of garlic extract increases, the clear zone gets larger.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the 0 % result is 6 mm and not 0 mm.
parts.answer: 6 mm is the diameter of the paper disc itself; there was no clear zone around it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give two variables, other than those mentioned, that should be kept constant.
parts.answer: Volume of extract on each disc; time discs soaked; type and amount of bacteria spread; temperature and time of incubation; depth / type of agar.

practice.stem:
A patient took an antibiotic for a bacterial infection. The doctor said to take it for 7 days, but the patient felt better and stopped after day 3. The number of bacteria in samples taken from the patient (per cm³) was:
day: 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7
bacteria per cm³: 8000, 3000, 900, 200, 600, 2500

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in bacteria between day 0 and day 3. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the change in the number of bacteria after day 3.
parts.answer: The patient stopped taking the antibiotic while some bacteria were still alive; these survivors were likely the most resistant ones; they reproduced, so numbers rose again.
parts.working: B1 bacteria not all killed when course stopped; B1 survivors are more resistant; B1 they multiplied.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the doctor might do now, and why.
parts.answer: Prescribe a different antibiotic, because the surviving bacteria may now be resistant to the first one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which person's action is most likely to add to the problem of antibiotic-resistant bacteria?
A Ali finishes a full course of antibiotics for a bacterial chest infection
B Bushra takes leftover antibiotics for a few days when she has influenza
C Danish takes paracetamol for a headache
D Fatima has a vaccination against typhoid
parts.answer: B Bushra takes leftover antibiotics for a few days when she has influenza
parts.working: Influenza is caused by a virus, so the antibiotic does not help, and a short, incomplete course exposes her bacteria to the antibiotic so resistant ones survive and multiply. A completed course (A) kills the bacteria; vaccination (D) reduces the need for antibiotics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A child of mass 18 kg is prescribed an antibiotic at 25 mg per kg of body mass per day, divided into 3 equal doses. Calculate the mass of antibiotic in each dose.
parts.answer: 150 mg

parts.label: b
parts.text: The syrup contains 125 mg of antibiotic in every 5 cm³. Calculate the volume of syrup for each dose.
parts.answer: 6 cm³

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the dose is calculated from the child's body mass.
parts.answer: A larger body has more blood/tissue, so more drug is needed to reach a concentration that kills the bacteria; too much for a small child could be harmful.

practice.stem:
A student spread the same volume of a culture of harmless bacteria on agar plates containing different concentrations of an antibiotic. After 2 days she counted the colonies.
concentration / µg per cm³ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8
number of colonies | 220 | 130 | 40 | 6 | 0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in colonies at 2 µg per cm³ compared with no antibiotic. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the effect of antibiotic concentration on the number of colonies.
parts.answer: As concentration increases, the number of colonies decreases; no colonies grow at 8 µg per cm³ (largest fall between 0 and 2).
parts.working: 1 mark trend; 1 mark detail with data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Each colony grows from a single bacterium. Suggest what the six colonies at 4 µg per cm³ show.
parts.answer: A few bacteria were resistant (more resistant) to the antibiotic at that concentration and survived to multiply.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two safety precautions needed when culturing bacteria in this experiment.
parts.answer: lids taped (not sealed) and not opened; incubate at 25 °C, not 37 °C; wash hands; disinfect bench; sterilise plates before disposal

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A doctor tells a patient to finish the whole course of antibiotics even after she feels better. What is the main reason?
A Antibiotics also kill any viruses that are present.
B The bacteria that survive longest are the most resistant, and stopping early may let them multiply.
C The body needs time to make antibodies against the antibiotic.
D Unused antibiotics become poisonous after a few days.
parts.answer: B The bacteria that survive longest are the most resistant, and stopping early may let them multiply.
parts.working: Stopping early leaves the most resistant bacteria alive; they can multiply and pass on resistance. C is wrong because antibodies are made against pathogens, not against antibiotics.

practice.stem:
The same antibiotic disc test was repeated on four plates.
clear-zone diameter / mm: plate 1: 21; plate 2: 23; plate 3: 14; plate 4: 22

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the anomalous result and calculate the mean clear-zone diameter without it. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: plate 3 (14 mm) is anomalous; mean = 22.0 mm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean if the anomalous result were included, and explain why it should be left out.
parts.answer: 20.0 mm; it is far from the other values and probably due to an error, so including it would make the mean too low.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two possible causes of the anomalous result.
parts.answer: Disc not soaked for the same time / less antibiotic on it; disc not pressed flat on the agar; more bacteria spread on that plate; plate incubated at a different temperature; diameter measured wrongly.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why the zones were measured across two diameters at right angles and the values averaged.
parts.answer: The clear zones may not be perfect circles, so averaging two diameters gives a more accurate value.

practice.stem:
Samples of a gut bacterium were collected from patients in a large city. The percentage of samples that were resistant to one antibiotic was recorded.
year: 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024
resistant samples / %: 18, 23, 31, 38, 46, 52

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the trend shown by the data.
parts.answer: The percentage of resistant samples increased every time, from 18 % in 2014 to 52 % in 2024.
parts.working: B1 increases throughout; B1 data quoted with units.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the mean increase in percentage of resistant samples per year between 2014 and 2024.
parts.answer: 3.4 percentage points per year

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two reasons for this trend.
parts.answer: Antibiotics bought without prescription / overused; patients not finishing courses; antibiotics used in animal feed; resistant bacteria spread through poor sanitation / contaminated water.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Predict, with a reason, the percentage of resistant samples in 2026 if the trend continues.
parts.answer: About 59 % (52 + 2 × 3.4 ≈ 59); accept 57–60 % with reference to the same rate of increase.
parts.working: B1 value in range with reason.

parts.label: a
