parts.text: A strain of typhoid bacteria that is resistant to most antibiotics has spread in some cities. Explain why this strain is dangerous.
parts.answer: Very few antibiotics can treat infected people, so the disease lasts longer and more people may die; the strain can spread to others.
parts.working: B1 few / no effective antibiotics; B1 more severe illness / deaths / spread.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Health workers vaccinated large numbers of children against typhoid. Explain how this helps to slow the spread of antibiotic resistance.
parts.answer: Vaccinated children become immune so fewer get typhoid; fewer cases need antibiotics, so less selection pressure for resistance; fewer infected people means less spread of resistant bacteria.
parts.working: B1 fewer infections; B1 fewer antibiotics used / less selection; B1 less transmission.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Typhoid spreads through contaminated food and water. Suggest one other measure, apart from vaccination, to reduce cases.
parts.answer: Clean, treated drinking water; boiling water; proper sewage disposal; hand washing; food hygiene.

practice.stem:
Paper discs (6 mm diameter) were soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic and placed on agar covered with bacteria.
concentration / µg/cm³: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16
diameter of clear area including disc / mm: 6, 6, 9, 13, 17, 21

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the lowest concentration of the antibiotic that had any effect on the bacteria. Explain your answer.
parts.answer: 2 µg/cm³; the zone is larger than the 6 mm disc only from 2 µg/cm³ upwards.
parts.working: B1 2 µg/cm³; B1 reason (6 mm = disc only).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the pattern in the results from 2 to 16 µg/cm³.
parts.answer: Each time the concentration doubles, the zone diameter increases by about 4 mm.
parts.working: B1 increases; B1 quantified (4 mm per doubling).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Predict the zone diameter for 32 µg/cm³ if the pattern continues.
parts.answer: about 25 mm

parts.label: d
parts.text: Suggest why a doctor would want to know the lowest concentration that is effective.
parts.answer: So the dose given is high enough to kill the bacteria but not more than needed, reducing side effects and cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clear zone has a diameter of 24 mm around a disc of diameter 6 mm. Calculate the area of agar where bacteria were killed, not counting the area under the disc. Give your answer in mm² to 1 decimal place.
parts.working: M1 π × 12² for zone; M1 subtract π × 3²; A1 π × 135 = 424.1.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bacteria nearest the disc are killed while those further away are not.
parts.answer: The antibiotic diffuses out into the agar; its concentration falls with distance from the disc, so beyond a certain distance it is too dilute to kill bacteria.
parts.working: B1 diffusion from disc; B1 concentration decreases with distance.

practice.stem:
Two strains of a bacterium, A and B, were grown separately in broth. The same antibiotic was added to both at 2 hours. (Figures for this question.)
time / h | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6
strain A / millions per cm³ | 10 | 40 | 8 | 1
strain B / millions per cm³ | 10 | 40 | 160 | 640

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in strain A between 2 hours and 6 hours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many times strain B increased between 2 and 6 hours, and its doubling time.
parts.answer: 16 times; 1 hour
parts.working: B1 640 ÷ 40 = 16; B1 16 = 2⁴ in 4 hours so doubles every hour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain the difference between the two strains.
parts.answer: Strain A is sensitive: the antibiotic kills it / stops reproduction; strain B is resistant (has a mutation/gene for resistance), so it keeps reproducing.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain what would happen in a patient infected with both strains who was given this antibiotic.
parts.answer: Strain A would be killed, removing competition; strain B would survive and multiply, so the infection continues and is now all resistant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is treated with two antibiotics, P and Q, at the same time. A mutation for resistance to P occurs in 1 in 10⁷ bacteria; a mutation for resistance to Q occurs in 1 in 10⁸ bacteria. A patient has 10¹⁰ TB bacteria. Calculate the expected number of bacteria resistant to P.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The chance of a bacterium having both mutations is 1 in 10¹⁵. Calculate the expected number of bacteria resistant to both P and Q.
parts.answer: 0.00001 (10⁻⁵), i.e. almost certainly none

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answers to explain why TB is treated with two antibiotics together and not with P alone.
parts.answer: With P alone about 1000 resistant bacteria would survive and multiply; with both, bacteria resistant to P are killed by Q (and vice versa); it is extremely unlikely any bacterium is resistant to both, so all are killed and resistance does not develop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Plan an investigation to find which of three antibiotics, X, Y and Z, is most effective against a harmless bacterium. You have sterile agar plates, a culture of the bacterium, paper discs, the three antibiotic solutions, sterile water, forceps and a ruler.
parts.answer: Spread the same volume of culture evenly over each plate (sterile spreader, aseptic technique); soak discs of the same size in each antibiotic for the same time, and one disc in sterile water as a control; place discs the same distance apart with flamed forceps; tape lid, incubate upside down at 25 °C for 2 days; measure diameter of each clear zone across two diameters; repeat on 3 plates and find mean; largest clear zone = most effective; same concentration of each antibiotic.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: aseptic technique; same culture volume; same disc size/soaking time; same concentration; sterile water control disc; incubation conditions and safety (25 °C, tape, not sealed); measure clear-zone diameter; repeats and mean; conclusion criterion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which describes heroin?
A an antibiotic
B a depressant that slows the activity of the nervous system
C a stimulant that speeds up the nervous system
D a hormone that builds muscle
parts.answer: B a depressant that slows the activity of the nervous system
parts.working: Heroin is a powerful, addictive depressant drug that slows down the activity of the nervous system. C describes a stimulant, the opposite effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the addictive drug in tobacco smoke.
parts.answer: nicotine

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two effects of nicotine on the circulatory system.
parts.answer: Increases heart rate; increases blood pressure; narrows blood vessels; makes blood more likely to clot.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why many smokers find it very hard to give up smoking even when they know it is harmful.
parts.answer: Nicotine is addictive; stopping causes withdrawal symptoms such as cravings and irritability.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which component of tobacco smoke combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried by the blood?
A carbon monoxide
B nicotine
C smoke particles
D tar
parts.answer: A carbon monoxide
parts.working: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin in place of oxygen. Nicotine (B) is the addictive drug that affects the nervous system and heart rate, not oxygen carrying.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the substance in tobacco smoke that:
(i) causes addiction
(ii) is a sticky substance containing carcinogens
parts.answer: (i) nicotine (ii) tar

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two diseases of the gas exchange system caused by smoking.
parts.answer: lung cancer; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) – emphysema and chronic bronchitis

parts.label: a
parts.text: In the UK, one unit of alcohol is 10 cm³ of pure alcohol. A bottle of beer contains 330 cm³ of drink that is 5 % alcohol. Calculate the number of units in the bottle.
parts.answer: 1.65 units

parts.label: b
parts.text: A glass of wine contains 175 cm³ of drink that is 12 % alcohol. Calculate the number of units.
parts.answer: 2.1 units

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two short-term effects of drinking alcohol.
parts.answer: slower reaction time; reduced self-control; poor coordination/judgement; drowsiness (depressant)

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the meaning of withdrawal symptoms.
parts.answer: unpleasant effects felt when an addicted person stops taking a drug

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two withdrawal symptoms of heroin.
parts.answer: shaking/tremors; sweating; vomiting/nausea; cramps; anxiety; strong craving

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether heroin is a stimulant or a depressant.
parts.answer: depressant

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some weightlifters misuse anabolic steroids. State how these drugs improve performance.
parts.answer: They increase muscle growth/mass and strength; allow faster recovery so the athlete can train harder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two reasons why sports organisations ban their use.
parts.answer: gives an unfair advantage over athletes who do not use them; harmful to health; puts pressure on others to use them

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by passive smoking.
parts.answer: breathing in other people's tobacco smoke

parts.label: b
parts.text: Many governments ban smoking on public transport and in enclosed public places. Suggest two reasons for such laws.
parts.answer: to protect non-smokers (including children) from harmful smoke (CO, tar, carcinogens); to reduce disease such as lung cancer/heart disease in non-smokers; to discourage smoking

parts.label: a
parts.text: Classify each drug as a stimulant or a depressant: alcohol, caffeine, heroin, nicotine.
parts.answer: stimulants: caffeine, nicotine; depressants: alcohol, heroin
parts.working: 2 marks all four correct; 1 mark two or three correct.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the general effect of a depressant on the nervous system.
parts.answer: slows down the activity of the nervous system / brain (e.g. slower reactions)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Why are some athletes banned from competition after taking anabolic steroids?
A Steroids reduce the athlete's pain from injuries.
B Steroids increase muscle growth, giving an unfair advantage.
C Steroids are antibiotics that prevent infection.
D Steroids reduce the athlete's heart rate during a race.
parts.answer: B Steroids increase muscle growth, giving an unfair advantage.
parts.working: Anabolic steroids are hormone-like drugs that increase muscle mass and strength, which is unfair to other competitors (and has health risks). A describes painkillers, not steroids.

practice.stem:
In a road-safety study in Europe, volunteers did a computer test of reaction time after drinking different amounts of alcohol.
units of alcohol: 0, 2, 4
mean reaction time / s: 0.21, 0.27, 0.36

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage increase in reaction time after 4 units of alcohol compared with none. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car travels at 20 m/s. Calculate how much further it travels during the driver's reaction time after 4 units than after 0 units.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why alcohol increases reaction time.
parts.answer: Alcohol is a depressant; it slows the transmission of impulses in the nervous system (at synapses), so responses take longer.
parts.working: B1 depressant; B1 slows nerve impulses / synapses.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State two long-term effects of drinking large amounts of alcohol.
parts.answer: Liver damage (cirrhosis); brain damage; addiction; increased risk of heart disease / high blood pressure; social problems (loss of job, violence, family problems).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by addiction to a drug such as heroin.
parts.answer: The body becomes dependent on the drug so the person feels a strong need to keep taking it; stopping causes withdrawal symptoms.
parts.working: B1 dependence / craving; B1 withdrawal symptoms when stopped.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Heroin affects the nervous system at synapses. Suggest why a heroin user needs larger and larger doses to get the same effect.
parts.answer: The body becomes tolerant: the synapses / receptors adapt to the drug, so the same dose has less effect and more is needed.
parts.working: B1 tolerance; B1 nervous system / receptors adapt.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why injecting heroin increases the risk of HIV infection.
parts.answer: Users may share needles; blood containing the virus from an infected person is passed directly into the next person's blood.
parts.working: B1 shared needles; B1 infected blood enters bloodstream.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Give one social problem linked to heroin addiction.
parts.answer: Crime to pay for the drug; loss of job; family breakdown; homelessness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the organ that breaks down alcohol in the body.
parts.answer: liver

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why people who drink large amounts of alcohol for many years often suffer liver damage.
parts.answer: Breaking down large amounts of alcohol damages liver cells; they are replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), so the liver cannot work properly.
parts.working: B1 liver cells damaged / killed by alcohol; B1 scar tissue / cirrhosis / reduced function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest two functions of the liver that would be affected by liver damage.
parts.answer: Breakdown of toxins / drugs; deamination of amino acids to form urea; storing glycogen; making bile; making plasma proteins.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Alcohol reduces self-control. Suggest one way this can harm a person or others.
parts.answer: Risky behaviour such as violence, unprotected sex or dangerous driving.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which disease is most closely linked to heavy drinking of alcohol over many years?
A chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
B lung cancer
C liver damage (cirrhosis)
D scurvy
parts.answer: C liver damage (cirrhosis)
parts.working: The liver breaks down alcohol, and years of heavy drinking damage it. A and B are linked mainly to tobacco smoke.

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows the death rate from lung cancer per 100 000 men each year.
cigarettes per day | 0 | 1–14 | 15–24 | 25 or more
death rate | 10 | 78 | 127 | 251

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the death rate is for people smoking 25 or more cigarettes a day than for non-smokers.
parts.answer: 25.1 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the relationship shown by the data.
parts.answer: The more cigarettes smoked per day, the higher the death rate from lung cancer; e.g. 78 for 1–14 rising to 251 for 25+.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how tar in cigarette smoke can lead to lung cancer.
parts.answer: Tar contains carcinogens; these cause mutations in cells lining the airways/lungs, leading to uncontrolled cell division (a tumour).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how tobacco smoke causes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
parts.answer: Smoke damages/paralyses cilia; mucus builds up in the airways, causing coughing and infections (chronic bronchitis); walls of alveoli break down (emphysema); surface area for gas exchange is reduced, so the person becomes breathless.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two effects of nicotine on the circulatory system.
parts.answer: increases heart rate; increases blood pressure (narrows blood vessels); makes blood more likely to clot

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how smoking increases the risk of coronary heart disease.
parts.answer: Chemicals in smoke (CO, nicotine) damage the lining of arteries; fatty deposits build up in the coronary arteries, narrowing them; clots may form, blocking blood flow to heart muscle, which is starved of oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an overdose of heroin can kill.
parts.answer: Heroin is a powerful depressant; a large dose slows the brain centres controlling breathing (and heart) so much that breathing stops.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why heroin addiction can lead to financial and social problems.
parts.answer: heroin is expensive and addicts need more and more, so they spend all their money / steal; they may lose jobs; relationships with family break down

practice.stem:
In a study, men of similar age and mass trained in a gym for 10 weeks. Group A had placebo (dummy) injections; group B had anabolic steroid injections. (Figures for this question.)
group | mean gain in muscle mass / kg
A: training + placebo | 2.0
B: training + steroid | 6.1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the gain was with steroids and training than with training alone.
parts.answer: 3.05 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why group A was given a placebo injection rather than nothing.
parts.answer: So that both groups had the same treatment apart from the steroid; any difference must then be due to the steroid and not to the injection or belief in it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two harmful side effects of misusing anabolic steroids.
parts.answer: liver damage; heart disease / high blood pressure; reduced sperm production / infertility; aggressive behaviour; acne

parts.label: a
parts.text: The liver removes alcohol from the blood at about 1 unit per hour. A man at a wedding party in Manchester drinks 6 units, finishing at 11 p.m. Calculate the time at which the alcohol will have been removed.
parts.answer: 5 a.m.
parts.working: M1 6 units ÷ 1 per hour = 6 hours; A1 11 p.m. + 6 h = 5 a.m.

parts.label: b
parts.text: His friend drinks 9 units, finishing at the same time, and plans to drive at 7 a.m. Explain why this is dangerous.
parts.answer: 9 units take 9 hours, so alcohol will remain in his blood until 8 a.m.; it slows his reaction time and reduces judgement while driving.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some people chew tobacco products such as naswar instead of smoking. Explain why users of these products also become addicted.
parts.answer: They contain nicotine, which is absorbed through the lining of the mouth into the blood and reaches the brain; nicotine is addictive.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why chewing tobacco is linked to cancer of the mouth rather than the lungs.
parts.answer: The carcinogens are in contact with the cells lining the mouth for long periods; the smoke/tar does not reach the lungs because nothing is inhaled.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Anabolic steroids are similar in structure to a natural male sex hormone. Name this hormone and the organ that makes it.
parts.answer: testosterone; testes

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two harmful side effects of misusing anabolic steroids.
parts.answer: Liver damage; heart disease / high blood pressure; infertility; aggressive behaviour / mood changes; acne.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Athletes may be asked to give a urine sample at any time, not only on the day of a competition. Suggest why.
parts.answer: Steroids are often used during training to build muscle and then stopped before competitions so they are not detected; random testing catches this.
parts.working: B1 used in training / stopped before event; B1 random testing detects this.

practice.stem:
In one country the legal limit for driving is 80 mg of alcohol per 100 cm³ of blood. The table (figures for this question) shows the relative risk of a crash compared with a driver with no alcohol.
blood alcohol / mg per 100 cm³: 0, 50, 80, 100, 150
relative risk of crash: 1, 2, 4, 7, 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times greater the risk of a crash is at 150 mg per 100 cm³ than at the legal limit of 80 mg per 100 cm³.
parts.answer: 6.25 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the risk changes as blood alcohol concentration increases.
parts.answer: The risk rises as blood alcohol rises; it rises slowly at first and then very steeply above about 100 mg per 100 cm³.
parts.working: B1 risk increases; B1 increase is faster at higher concentrations (with data).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Some countries have lowered their limit to 50 mg per 100 cm³. Use the data to argue for this change.
parts.answer: At 50 mg the risk is 2 times, half the risk at 80 mg (4 times); lowering the limit could prevent many crashes.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why the risk of a crash increases.
parts.answer: Alcohol slows reaction time; it reduces judgement / self-control, so drivers take more risks.
parts.working: B1 slower reactions; B1 poor judgement / more risk-taking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A person has 750 g of haemoglobin. Each gram can carry up to 1.34 cm³ of oxygen. In a non-smoker 1 % of the haemoglobin is combined with carbon monoxide; in a heavy smoker 8 % is. Calculate the maximum volume of oxygen that can be carried by each person, and the difference to the nearest cm³.
parts.answer: non-smoker 994.95 cm³ (995); smoker 924.6 cm³ (925); difference 70 cm³

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why carbon monoxide has this effect and why the smoker becomes breathless more quickly in a game of hockey.
parts.answer: CO combines with haemoglobin (more strongly than oxygen) and is not released easily, so less haemoglobin is free to carry oxygen; less oxygen reaches the muscles; more anaerobic respiration / need to breathe faster to get enough oxygen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A café owner claims that smoking shisha (a water pipe) is harmless because 'the water filters the smoke'. One shisha session can involve inhaling about 90 000 cm³ of smoke, while one cigarette involves about 600 cm³ (figures for this question). Calculate how many cigarettes' worth of smoke volume this is.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the café owner's claim.
parts.answer: The claim is wrong: the smoke still contains nicotine (addictive) and carbon monoxide (from tobacco and the burning charcoal) and tar/carcinogens; the water does not remove most of these; a long session means a very large volume of smoke is inhaled; risks include COPD, lung cancer, heart disease; shared mouthpieces can spread infections.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four, must reach a judgement.

practice.stem:
A city began a programme in 2017 that gives people who inject heroin clean needles in exchange for used ones. (Figures for this question.)
year | 2015 | 2016 | 2017 | 2018 | 2019
new HIV infections in people who inject drugs | 480 | 500 | 420 | 300 | 210

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in new infections from 2016 to 2019.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how sharing needles spreads HIV and how the programme may have caused the change.
parts.answer: HIV is in blood; a shared needle carries infected blood directly into the next user's blood; providing sterile needles means needles are not shared, so fewer people are infected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the data alone do not prove that the programme caused the whole decrease.
parts.answer: Other factors may have changed at the same time, e.g. education campaigns, more treatment, fewer people injecting, or changes in testing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After an athlete stops taking a steroid, the concentration of its breakdown product in her urine halves every 4 days. It starts at 160 ng per cm³. A test can detect concentrations of 10 ng per cm³ or more. Calculate the number of days until the concentration falls to 10 ng per cm³.
parts.answer: 16 days
parts.working: M1 160 → 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 is four halvings; A1 4 × 4 = 16 days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why some athletes stop taking steroids several weeks before a competition yet still benefit.
parts.answer: The extra muscle built while taking steroids remains for some time after stopping; the drug can no longer be detected on competition day.

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows mean birth mass of babies.
mother's smoking | none | 1–10 a day | more than 10 a day
mean birth mass / kg | 3.40 | 3.25 | 3.15

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage decrease in mean birth mass for mothers smoking more than 10 cigarettes a day compared with non-smokers. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why smoking during pregnancy reduces the birth mass of the baby.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin in the mother's blood, so less oxygen reaches the placenta and fetus; nicotine narrows blood vessels, reducing blood flow to the placenta; less oxygen means less respiration/energy for growth of the fetus.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Alcohol also crosses the placenta. Suggest one risk to the fetus if the mother drinks alcohol.
parts.answer: damage to the developing brain/organs; low birth mass; developmental problems (fetal alcohol effects)

practice.stem:
The table (figures for this question) shows the relative risk of coronary heart disease for former smokers compared with people who have never smoked (risk = 1.0).
years since stopping | 0 | 1 | 5 | 10 | 15
relative risk | 2.0 | 1.5 | 1.3 | 1.1 | 1.0

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the risk changes after stopping smoking.
parts.answer: Risk falls quickly in the first year (2.0 to 1.5) then more slowly, reaching the non-smoker level (1.0) after 15 years.
parts.working: 1 mark fast then slow; 1 mark reaches 1.0 with figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage fall in relative risk in the first year after stopping.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why the risk falls quickly at first.
parts.answer: Carbon monoxide and nicotine leave the blood within days, so heart rate, blood pressure and oxygen supply improve and clotting decreases; damage to arteries takes longer to repair.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of drinking too much alcohol regularly on the drinker and on other people in society.
parts.answer: Drinker: depressant – slower reactions, poor coordination, reduced self-control; addiction/dependence; liver damage (cirrhosis), brain damage, weight gain; financial problems. Others: road accidents from drink-driving; violence/crime/domestic abuse; family breakdown; lost working days; cost to health services; harm to fetus if drunk in pregnancy.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six points; at least two about the individual and two about society for full marks.
